A method should work with different caller data without reading hidden shared variables. The problem is to keep the task stable while allowing its inputs to vary. Parameters give each call named local inputs; returned values carry results back. The retained Verse comparison makes the repeated pattern visible, followed by business examples and scope traces.
As a young child, you probably heard the "Old MacDonald" song.
Consider the following two verses:

| Verse 1 | Verse 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Old MacDonald had a farm | Old MacDonald had a farm |
| E-I-E-I-O | E-I-E-I-O |
| And on that farm he had a cow | And on that farm he had a duck |
| E-I-E-I-O | E-I-E-I-O |
| With a moo-moo here | With a quack-quack here |
| And a moo-moo there | And a quack-quack there |
| Here a moo, there a moo | Here a quack, there a quack |
| Everywhere a moo-moo | Everywhere a quack-quack |
| Old MacDonald had a farm | Old MacDonald had a farm |
| E-I-E-I-O | E-I-E-I-O |

As you can see, the two verses are in most part identical. We can probably
create a method named `Verse` to abstract the repetitive lines, but the method
will need two **parameters**, which are **placeholders** that allow different
values to be substituted for the animal and noise when the method is called.
The method body will use the parameters as variables to customize the print
statements.
::::{dropdown} Class-based console-project version
The top-level example above is the version to run as a standalone notebook cell. This complete project version retains the explicit `Main` structure. Save it as the only program in a separate console project; do not paste it after top-level statements in the same file.

```csharp
    internal class Program
    {
       private static void Main(string[] args)
       {
          // Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!");    // this statement is commented out

## Map Arguments to Parameters


```{index} Map Arguments to Parameters
```
Arguments are expressions at the call; parameters are named variables in the definition. Match them by position and compatible type, not by spelling.

| Call | animal in this call | noise in this call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Verse("cow", "moo")` | cow | moo |
| `Verse("duck", "quack")` | duck | quack |
| `Verse(chosenAnimal, chosenNoise)` with chosenAnimal = cow and chosenNoise = moo | cow | moo |

General syntax for a two-input helper is `static resultType Name(type1 parameter1, type2 parameter2) { ... }`; the call is `Name(expression1, expression2)`. The call does not repeat type declarations. In the simple required-parameter examples here, argument number, order, and allowed conversions must match. Swapping two strings can compile and still produce the wrong meaning, so type checking does not replace contract checking.

Each ordinary parameter receives a copy of its argument value. With integers this gives independent numerical values. Later chapters explain how a copied reference can still identify a shared object; do not generalize this into deep-copying every argument.
```{figure} ../../figures/method_parameter_copy.svg
:alt: quantity in the caller stays 4 while a separate copied parameter count changes from 4 to 5 and returns 5.

Different names and separate values in the caller and helper.
```

The first output is `Caller: 4; returned: 5`. Assigning to count does not assign to quantity. To keep the returned increase in quantity, the caller must explicitly write `quantity = Increase(quantity);`. Try that variation, then a zero input. The argument's name could also be count; equal spelling would not merge the two variables.

headings.title: Variable Scopes
body:
```{index} Variable Scopes
```

## Variable Scopes


A variable may be available for use in some parts of code, but not others.
The `scope` of a variable is the region of the program that the variable is visible,
which means it is accessible by `name` and can be used in the part of code. C# scope rules of variables can be divided into three categories as follows:

- Class Level Scope
- Method Level Scope
- Block Level Scope.

A variable declared inside a method is a `local variable`. A body local belongs to its containing block; a parameter is available in the method body. A nested-block local cannot be used outside that block. You cannot use a local variable before its declaration or read it before it has a value.
In the ordinary noncapturing examples here, each call has its own local values. Do not infer a physical memory address or allocation rule from a scope diagram.
If you called the method again, the old value is not available.

Only the *value* of the actual parameter is passed, not any
variable name, so there is *no need* to have a match between a variable name
(arguments) and the parameter name.
| Region | What can use its local name? | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parameter | The called method body | It belongs to this call. |
| Method-body local | Its containing scope after declaration | Another method cannot read it just because it uses the same spelling. |
| Nested block local | That block after declaration | Moving its use outside the block is a compile-time error. |

Scope concerns where a name can be used in source code; lifetime concerns the duration of a value/storage relationship. The later chapters have cases requiring deeper lifetime analysis. Here use separate boxes for caller and helper locals rather than claiming the compiler must allocate/release a specific memory location at each brace.
The output is `Caller x: 1; returned y: 8`. The helper's x does not overwrite the caller's x. A static local helper cannot capture the caller's local x; it receives a through its parameter. If a name is needed after a block, declare it in an appropriate enclosing scope and decide how it is initialized, rather than assuming any earlier variable remains available everywhere.

## Static Variables


You may define `static variables` (variables defined with the word `static`
inside the class, but *outside* of any method definition). These variables are
visible inside all of your methods in the class. Instead of local scope, static variables have *class scope*.
It is good programming practice generally to avoid defining static variables and
instead to put your variables inside methods and explicitly pass
them as parameters where needed. A fixed value shared by the class can be a constant. A `const` field is implicitly static; a mutable static field is not a constant. For example,
A *constant* is a name that you give a fixed data value to and you do not expect the value to change
(e.g., Pi).
This example deliberately uses class-member syntax so the fields have a class home. Limit is a fixed constant. The static calls field persists between the two Record calls, so the outputs are 1 and 2. Each call instead has its own local increment. We call through the type name, CallCounter.Record(), without constructing an object. Keep this as a contrast: routine calculations in this chapter should normally receive parameters and use locals, so their results do not depend on a hidden history of calls. Chapters 10–12 develop class design and instance state.

## Scope


1. A variable declared inside a method definition is called a *local variable*.
   This declaration may be in either the parameter
   list or in the body of the method.

2. A local variable comes into existence after the method is called, and ceases
   to exist after that method call terminates. In these noncapturing examples, a local name is visible only in its containing scope, and each call has separate local values. Scope and lifetime are different concepts; nested scopes and later captured-variable examples require more precise rules. Its *value* may be transferred outside of the method scope
   by standard means, principally:

   - If it is the expression in a return statement, its value is
     sent back to the caller.
   - It can be passed as an
     actual parameter to a further method called within its scope.

body:

## Static Storage Reference

1. There may be a declaration prefaced by the word `static` that appears
   *inside* a class and *outside* of any method definition in the class.
   Static variables are visible within each method of the class, and may
   be used by the methods.
2. A const field gives a name to a fixed compile-time value and is implicitly static. Mutable static fields instead hold shared state; do not confuse the two.

body:
(gap-return-values-out-and-ref)=
## Return Values, out, and ref

```{index} gap revision: return values, out, and ref
```
A return value is usually the clearest way to produce one result. Sometimes a method must report both success and a result, or deliberately update a caller variable. C# makes those effects explicit with `out` and `ref`. This connects the `TryParse` call in Chapter 4 to the method definitions you can now write.

General definition and call patterns (schematic):

```csharp
static bool TryRead(string text, out int value) { /* assign value on every normal return */ }
bool success = TryRead(text, out number);
static void Adjust(ref int value) { /* read or replace caller value */ }
Adjust(ref number);
```

| Parameter | Caller obligation | Method obligation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int value` | Supply a value. | Works with a local copy. | Reassignment does not replace the caller variable. |
| `out int value` | Supply a writable variable, not necessarily initialized. | Assign it before every normal return. | Produces a result in the caller variable. |
| `ref int value` | Supply an initialized writable variable. | May read and replace it. | Deliberately shares the caller variable's storage. |

Both the definition and call show the keyword. Passing an object reference by value later permits mutation of the referenced object but does not permit replacing the caller's reference variable. That is different from a `ref` parameter. Do not add `ref` merely because a value is an object.

The worked example reports failure separately from the parsed value. The method defines a stricter business contract than `int.TryParse`: quantities must be positive. Its failure result is always zero. `AddOne` then demonstrates a deliberate change to an already initialized caller variable.

See the language/API reference for this contract.[^gap-parameters]
**Guided practice.** Trace the caller variable through the four printed values: `True`, `7`, `False`, and `0`. Define `TryPercentage` with an inclusive 0-100 range and test both endpoints, a negative number, and nonnumeric text. Then explain why `ref` would be a poorer contract for that conversion. Later record parsing and linked-head replacement reuse these explicit parameter contracts.

## A Boolean Result Answers a Question

A returned result need not be a number to print. A method can answer a question, and a bool result can become the condition of an if statement. Suppose an order receives free delivery when its subtotal is at least 50. The question is whether an order qualifies, not how much its delivery costs. Keeping those contracts distinct helps explain why two related methods may have different return types.

Trace the boundary: 49.99 does not qualify, 50 qualifies, and 50.01 qualifies. The equality is part of the rule. Writing `>` instead of `>=` would still compile and would pass examples far from the threshold. The boundary cases distinguish the intended rule from that plausible defect.

The general form is `static bool QuestionName(parameterList) { return condition; }`. Here the condition already has type bool. There is no need to convert it into the strings `"true"` and `"false"`; those are text values and cannot serve as an if condition. Printing the answer inside a void method also does not give the caller a Boolean result to use.

Guided variation: qualification additionally requires a nonnegative subtotal. Explain whether that is an input precondition or a condition the method must check. Either design can be explicit, but silently switching between them makes testing and reuse confusing. State the accepted domain before writing your new tests.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Returned Values Replace Calls

headings.title: Returned Values Replace Calls
body:
```{index} Returned Values Replace Calls
```

(method-return-expressions)=

## Returned Values Replace Calls


```{index} Returned Values Replace Calls
```
You probably have used mathematical functions in algebra class, but
they all had calculated values associated with them. For instance
if you defined

> F(x)=x{sup}`2`

then it follows that F(3) is 3{sup}`2` = 9, and F(3)+F(4) is
3{sup}`2` + 4{sup}`2` = 9 + 16 = 25.

Method calls in expressions get replaced during evaluation by the value of the method.
That's why when we can directly print out (line# 12-13) the result of the method call in the
following code.

The corresponding definition and examples in C# would be the
following:


The C# syntax to notice is the **return statement**, with the word
`return` followed by an expression, value, or variable(s). Methods that return values
can be used in expressions (e.g., line# 13: F(3) + F(4)), just like in math class. When an
expression with a method call is evaluated, the method call is
effectively replaced temporarily by its returned value. Inside the
C# method, the value to be returned is given by the
expression in the `return` statement.

Since the method returns data, and all data in C# is typed,
there must be a type given for the value returned. Note that the
method header does not start with `static void`.
In place of `void` is `int`. The `void` in earlier method header
meant nothing was returned. The `int` here means that a value *is*
returned and its type is `int`.

After the method `F` finishes executing from inside

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(F(3));
```

it is as if the statement temporarily became

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(9);
```

and similarly when executing

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(F(3) + F(4));
```

the program first evaluates F(3) and effectively replaces the
call by the returned result, 9, as if the statement temporarily
became

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(9 + F(4));
```

and then the program evaluates F(4) and effectively replaces
the call by the returned result, 16, as if the statement
temporarily became

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(9 + 16);
```

resulting finally in 25 being calculated and printed.

The first result is 9; the sum is 25. A mathematical analogy describes how returned values combine, but a C# method may also print or change state. Read its contract rather than assuming all methods behave like pure mathematical functions.

```{figure} ../../figures/method_call_return.svg
:alt: A caller passes digit 4 to num in SquareTheNumber. The returned 16 becomes squaredNum in that caller.

Return to the expression that made this call.
```

| Step in `F(3) + F(4)` | Waiting expression |
| --- | --- |
| Evaluate F(3): x receives 3; return 9 | 9 + F(4) |
| Evaluate F(4): x receives 4; return 16 | 9 + 16 |
| Add the returned values | 25 |

The calls have separate parameter values. The method does not remember the previous x as input for the next call.

body:

## Returned Strings and Formatted Results


```{index} Returned Strings and Formatted Results
```
C# methods can return any type of data, not just numbers, and
there can be any number of statements executed before the return
statement. Read, follow, and run the example program, which has `string` as
`return type`:

```{dropdown} Class-based console-project version
The top-level example above is the version to run as a standalone notebook cell. This complete project version retains the explicit `Main` structure. Save it as the only program in a separate console project; do not paste it after top-level statements in the same file.

```csharp
using System;

class Return2
{
   static string LastFirst(string firstName, string lastName)
   {
      string separator = ", ";
      string result = lastName + separator + firstName;
      return result;
   }

   static void Main()
   {
      Console.WriteLine(LastFirst("Benjamin", "Franklin"));
      Console.WriteLine(LastFirst("Andrew", "Harrington"));
   }
}

// ** write your answer here **

```
```
The following original trace describes the explicit Main version just above. The top-level runnable version makes the same two calls and receives the same returned strings. First follow the completed trace; then match its steps to source lines as guided practice.
Trace the two complete calls in this worked example.

```{eval-rst}
.. list-table:: Method Execution and Returns
   :width:10 90
   :header-rows: 1

   * - #
     - Step
   * - 1
     - Start at Main
   * - 2
     - call the method, remembering where to return
   * - 3
     - pass the parameters: firstName = "Benjamin"; lastName = "Franklin"
   * - 4
     - Assign the variable separator the value ", "
   * - 5
     - Assign the variable result the value of lastName + separator + firstName which is "Franklin" + ", " + "Benjamin", which evaluates to "Franklin, Benjamin"
   * - 6
     - Return "Franklin, Benjamin"
   * - 7
     - Use the value returned from the method call so the line effectively becomes Console.WriteLine("Franklin, Benjamin");, so print it.
   * - 8
     - call the method with the new actual parameters, remembering where to return
   * - 9
     - pass the parameters: firstName = "Andrew"; lastName = "Harrington"
   * - 10
     - … calculate and return "Harrington, Andrew"
   * - 11
     - Use the value returned by the method and print "Harrington, Andrew"


```

% Lines 12: Start at Main

% Line 14: call the function, remembering where to return

% Line 5: pass the parameters: firstName = "Benjamin"; lastName = "Franklin"

% Line 7: Assign the variable separator the value ", "

% Line 8: Assign the variable result the value of lastName + separator + firstName which is "Franklin" + ", " + "Benjamin", which evaluates to "Franklin, Benjamin"

% Line 9: Return "Franklin, Benjamin"

% Line 14: Use the value returned from the function call so the line effectively becomes Console.WriteLine("Franklin, Benjamin");, so print it.

% Line 15: call the function with the new actual parameters, remembering where to return

% Line 5: pass the parameters: firstName = "Andrew"; lastName = "Harrington"

% Lines 7-9: … calculate and return "Harrington, Andrew"

% Line 15: Use the value returned by the function and print "Harrington, Andrew"

It is common to want to construct and immediately print a string,
so having `Console.Write` is definitely handy when we want it.
However, sometimes we just want to have the resulting string returned,
so that we can do something else with it. We can use
the C# library method `string.Format`, which does just what we want:
The parameters have the same form as for `Console.Write`,
but the formatted string is *returned*.


Note: The only caveat with `string.Format` is that
there is *no* special method corresponding to `Console.WriteLine`,
with an automatic terminating newline.
You can generate a newline with string.Format: Remember the
escape code `"\n"`. Put it at the end to go on to a new line.

The returned string can be saved before it is printed. `{0}`, `{1}`, and `{2}` in `string.Format` select the following argument values by position. General syntax is `string.Format(formatText, value0, value1, ...)`; interpolation is another formatting form already used in earlier chapters. Neither form prints by itself.

## Decisions, Early Returns, and Complete Return Paths


```{index} Decisions, Early Returns, and Complete Return Paths
```
Methods reuse the decisions and loops you already know. A normal path through a value-returning method must return a compatible value; writing one return somewhere is not enough. A return exits the current call immediately. A void method may use `return;` to finish early, but cannot use `return value;`.

The following valid-input contract accepts a nonnegative subtotal, gives free delivery at 50.00 or above, and charges 4.00 otherwise. The tests cover just below, at, and above the boundary.
The outputs are 4.00, 0.00, and 0.00. Without the final return, a smaller subtotal could reach the end without a result. A return followed by more work on that same path makes the later work unreachable. An accidental semicolon after `if (condition);` creates an empty decision body, so the next statement can run unconditionally. Trace the paths rather than indenting by appearance. # Strings and Their Methods

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

Business data is mostly text: customer names, email addresses, product codes, and notes. A C# `string` is an object that comes with many ready-made methods for working with that text. In this section you are the **consumer** of methods someone else wrote. To use one, you need to know only three things: its name, the parameters it expects, and what it returns. How the method does its work is the writer's concern, not yours.[^0504_strings-string-class]

You call a string method with dot notation: the string, a dot, the method name, and the arguments in parentheses, as in `email.Trim()`.

```{index} string; Length, string; indexing
```

headings.title: Length and Indexing
body:
```{index} Length and Indexing
```

## Length and Indexing

`Length` is a property, not a method, so it has no parentheses. It gives the number of UTF-16 code units; for the simple Latin-letter examples here these correspond to the visible characters. Some Unicode symbols occupy more than one code unit. Square brackets with an index give one character (a `char`). Indexes start at 0, so the last character is at `Length - 1`.
An index outside `0` to `Length - 1` stops the program with an `IndexOutOfRangeException`. Chapter 6 shows how to handle errors like this one.

```{index} string; Trim, string; ToUpper, string; ToLower
```

headings.title: Cleaning Text
body:
```{index} Cleaning Text
```

## Cleaning Text
Text typed by people or copied from other systems often has stray spaces and inconsistent capitalization. Clean it before comparing or storing it:

| Method | Parameters | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `Trim()` | none | a copy without leading and trailing whitespace |
| `ToUpper()`, `ToLower()` | none | a copy in upper or lower case |
| `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s)` | the string to check | `true` if `s` is null, empty, or only whitespace |

`IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is called on the `string` type itself rather than on one string, because it must also work when there is no string at all (`null`).

```{index} string; immutability
```

headings.title: Strings Are Immutable
body:
```{index} Strings Are Immutable
```

## Strings Are Immutable

A string never changes after it is created. Methods such as `ToUpper` do not modify the string they are called on; they return the resulting string value rather than editing the original. If you want to keep the result, assign it to a variable.
The original region remains midwest; label is MIDWEST. The common mistake `region.ToUpper();` discards the result. It is legal but does not update region. Assign back if that is the intended policy: `region = region.ToUpperInvariant();`. Invariant case conversion is useful for the simple program-owned codes here; names and natural-language text may need a different culture policy.

```

## Searching

These methods answer questions about a string without changing it. `IndexOf` returns the position of the first match, or `-1` when there is no match.

## Extracting Part of a String

`Substring(start, length)` returns `length` characters beginning at index `start`. With one argument, `Substring(start)` returns everything from `start` to the end. Combined with `IndexOf`, it can pull the parts out of a structured code such as a SKU (stock keeping unit):
```{index} string; Replace
```

## Replacing Text

`Replace(oldText, newText)` returns a copy with every occurrence replaced. For a case-insensitive search, pass `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` to `Contains` or `IndexOf`.

body:
```{index} Chaining Method Calls

## Chaining Method Calls

Because each method in this chain returns a string result, you can call the next method directly on that result. Read a chain from left to right:
```{figure} ../../figures/string_method_chain.svg
:alt: A raw SKU is trimmed, then uppercased, with intermediate returned strings and the original raw value unchanged.

A chain passes each returned value to the next operation.
```

The diagram uses ToUpperInvariant for program-owned codes; the earlier ToUpper example uses the current culture. Read left to right: raw input → trimmed result → normalized result. Keeping intermediate variables is often clearer when diagnosing a failed transformation.

| Expression for the supplied example | Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rawCode.Trim()` | elec-1042-blk | Strip surrounding whitespace only. |
| The result's `ToUpper()` | ELEC-1042-BLK | Normalize case under the current culture. |
| `code.IndexOf('-')` | 4 | Locate the first separator. |
| `code.Substring(0, 4)` | ELEC | Extract four code units before the separator. |

**Check the precondition:** IndexOf returns -1 if no separator is found. Passing that -1 as a substring length does not mean “not found”; it is an invalid range. An empty string also cannot be indexed at zero. Decide whether malformed input is rejected or given a fallback before extracting parts.
Keep chains short enough to read at a glance. If a chain grows long, store intermediate results in well-named variables.

body:
```{index} Refactor in Small Steps That Keep an Observable Contract
```

## Refactor in Small Steps That Keep an Observable Contract

An invoice caller repeats price-times-quantity arithmetic in several places. Extracting LineTotal can give that calculation one name, but a safe refactoring needs more than moving those characters into braces. First record the existing accepted inputs, numerical outputs, formatting and mutation behavior. Then choose the new method's inputs/result so that callers can express the same work without depending on its internal temporary variables.

For price 12 and quantity three, independently calculate 36 before running either version. A fixed packing charge of four makes the order total 40. Keep these two contracts distinct: LineTotal returns 36; OrderTotal returns 40. If the extracted line calculation starts adding packing as well, a caller that already adds packing can charge it twice even though both helper methods contain plausible arithmetic.

| Refactoring stage | Evidence to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Before extraction | Expected amount and current observable output |
| After extracting LineTotal | Same line amount for ordinary and zero inputs |
| After composing OrderTotal | Exactly one application of the fixed charge |
| After formatting a report | Same numerical meaning; display policy stays explicit |

A useful composition passes returned values between helpers. It does not make each helper prompt independently for the same data. If CalculateTotal reads a second quantity while the caller formats the first, the report can display one order and charge another. Keep interaction in the caller and pass the accepted values into calculation helpers.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

## Choose Tests That Can Distinguish Plausible Defects

A zero-quantity order exposes a fixed-charge rule: the line amount is zero but the order amount may still be four. That result follows from this example's contract, not a universal claim that every business must charge empty orders. If a later policy waives packing for empty orders, revise the contract and the independent expectations before revising the method.

A test with price zero and nonzero quantity checks a different route to a zero line total. A normal nonzero case checks multiplication. A changed quantity checks that a hard-coded result is not being returned. Expected values should be derived from the requirement rather than copied from the candidate implementation's output; otherwise a defective method can teach its own test what to accept.

Guided synthesis: write a report helper that calls LineTotal and returns text without printing. Keep the item description and numerical result visible in its returned sentence. Then change only the display format. Explain why calculation tests can remain unchanged even when the report's string test changes. This separation prepares the repeatable method tests and debugging workflows of Chapter 6.

## Refactor and Check a Checkout Calculation


```{index} Refactor and Check a Checkout Calculation
```
Assume a nonnegative unit price and quantity. The original program calculates one line and adds a fixed packing charge; its two orders duplicate that policy. Refactoring should preserve the numerical behavior while giving separate names to line calculation and packing. All zero-quantity orders in this example still pay the packing charge; a different policy would require a changed contract, not just a code cleanup.
Both versions print 40.00 and 14.00. OrderTotal calls LineTotal, receives its returned value, then adds packing. The console formatting stays in the caller. The first method does not prompt for a quantity or silently modify another method's locals.

Derive expected results from the requirement, not by copying the code's output. A test of 12 × 3 + 4 expects 40; a zero quantity expects 4 under this stated policy. A second ordinary case helps reveal a hard-coded answer.

| Unit price | Quantity | Expected total | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12.00 | 3 | 40.00 | 36.00 plus 4.00 packing |
| 5.00 | 2 | 14.00 | 10.00 plus packing |
| 12.00 | 0 | 4.00 | Zero line value, packing remains |
| 0.00 | 1 | 4.00 | Zero-price item under this contract |

A useful check reports expected, actual, and success, rather than merely printing a number and hoping it looks plausible. This is a testing habit; a testing framework is not required yet.
All four checks report True. Deliberately omit the packing charge and predict which checks fail before running the variation. Testing a few values supports a contract; it does not prove correctness for every possible input. Negative inputs remain outside this exercise's domain and need an explicit future policy.

**Common mistakes:** printing inside a helper intended only to calculate; returning a formatted string when the caller needs a number; using a caller variable instead of a parameter; and testing only one convenient input. headings.title: Decide What a Failure Means Before Catching It
body:
```{index} Decide What a Failure Means Before Catching It
```

## Decide What a Failure Means Before Catching It

An employee enters a delivery quantity. There are at least three different problems the application might encounter: the text is not a number, the number violates a business rule, or a separate resource needed to complete the operation is unavailable. These situations can all prevent success, but they do not call for the same response.

Validation asks whether input satisfies a stated contract. Parsing asks whether text can be interpreted as a value. Exception handling responds to an exceptional transfer of control from an operation. A catch block is not a substitute for specifying which quantities are legal, and a successful parse is not a substitute for checking the domain.

| Input or event | Classification | Appropriate next decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Text `twelve` for an integer quantity | Representation failure | Request a whole-number input |
| Integer -2 for packages | Domain failure | Explain that quantity must be nonnegative |
| End of the input stream | No further input | Stop or cancel explicitly |
| A resource operation throws a known recoverable exception | Operation failure | Report context or choose an allowed fallback |

Work through the decisions in that order. First handle a missing input value. Then try to interpret available text. Only after a value exists can the program compare it with the business bounds. If you check a default zero after a failed parse without checking the Boolean success result, you can accidentally treat failed input as a legitimate zero-quantity order.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Follow Control Through an Exception
```

headings.title: Follow Control Through an Exception
body:
```{index} Follow Control Through an Exception
```

## Follow Control Through an Exception

A try block marks the work whose failure policy you are handling. When an operation throws, normal execution of that block stops at that point; statements after the throwing operation are not completed. A matching catch handles the exception. A finally block provides cleanup when control leaves the try/catch in ordinary managed execution, including when a handled exception occurs. It does not promise that a killed process or failed machine will run your cleanup code.

Catch only a failure for which you have a meaningful policy. An empty catch that continues to print Success converts a visible failure into misleading behavior. Catching every exception and replacing it with zero may also destroy the distinction between an unavailable answer and a real zero result. File-related examples below preview Chapter 9; their resource APIs will be developed there, rather than assumed as prerequisites for validation.

Guided prediction: quantity zero is permitted, a negative quantity is rejected, and nonnumeric text asks for correction. What should the program report for `0`, `-1`, and `x`? Explain why all three should not share one generic Invalid message.

```{dropdown} Compare the outcomes
Zero is a valid value under this contract. Minus one is interpretable but outside the business domain. The letter x has no integer interpretation. Different messages identify what the user can change, while avoiding a false success result.
```
Programs fail in predictable ways: bad input, missing files, unexpected values, and invalid assumptions.
Good software does not pretend errors never happen — it handles them deliberately.
```{index} Validation vs. Exceptions
```

## Validation vs. Exceptions


- **Validation** checks expected bad input *before* doing risky work.
- **Exceptions** handle unexpected failures *at runtime*.

Validation should be your first line of defense. Exceptions are a fallback for when something still goes wrong.

headings.title: Rethrow Without Losing the Failure Origin
body:
## Rethrow Without Losing the Failure Origin

```{index} gap revision: rethrow without losing the failure origin
```
A layer may record a failure but still be unable to recover. The caller must then receive the failure, with evidence of where it began. Inside a catch block, `throw;` rethrows the current exception and preserves its original stack trace. `throw ex;` throws the caught object again from the new throw statement, resetting the visible origin there. Logging a message is not recovery.

General patterns (schematic):

```csharp
catch (Exception ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
    throw; // propagate the current failure, retaining the original trace
}
```

Use a specific catch type when you can identify the failure. The broad catch above only illustrates propagation, not a recommendation to swallow every failure. Throwing a new exception with the original as its inner exception is another contract, useful when adding meaningful context; do not silently replace the evidence.

| Action in catch | Caller receives a failure? | Diagnostic consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `throw;` | Yes. | Retains original throw information. |
| `throw ex;` | Yes. | Resets stack origin at this throw. |
| Only print a message | No, unless another failure occurs. | Caller may wrongly assume success. |

A `finally` block should complete cleanup. If cleanup throws while another exception is propagating, the new failure can mask the original. Keep cleanup reliable and avoid treating `finally` as a place to return a replacement result.

See the language/API reference for this contract.[^gap-rethrow]
**Guided practice.** Explain why the caller still executes its catch. In VS Code, inspect the exception stack and locate `Validate`. Predict what evidence changes if `throw;` becomes `throw ex;`. Keep that variation labeled as a diagnostic mistake, not a recommended repair.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^gap-rethrow]: [Microsoft: Rethrow to preserve stack details](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca2200).

headings.title: Debug One Familiar Loop from Symptom to Evidence
body:
```{index} Debug One Familiar Loop from Symptom to Evidence
```

## Debug One Familiar Loop from Symptom to Evidence
Before the retained array and CSV applications, use a calculation that needs only methods, decisions, and loops. A shop awards one credit for each of the first `days` days. With three days, the expected credits are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. This expectation comes from the problem, not from running the implementation.

The following complete cell deliberately contains a logic defect. It compiles, but the loop stops too soon. A compiler cannot infer that the business rule requires the last day.
Save this code as the Program.cs of a console project using the Appendix B workflow. Run `dotnet run` to reproduce the failure before starting a debugger. In VS Code, open the folder containing the project, set a breakpoint on `total += day`, and start the C# debugger for that project. The browser cell can demonstrate the result; the editor debugger supplies paused state.

Write the hypothesis: “the loop omits day three.” A breakpoint pauses **before** the marked statement executes. At its first stop, watch `day`, `days`, and `total`. Step Over the update, then continue to the next stop. Use the method's own frame in the Call Stack panel to inspect its local values. The call stack explains who called the method; it is not a list of all previous loop iterations.

| Observation | day | total before addition | total after addition |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| First stopped iteration | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| Second stopped iteration | 2 | 1 | 3 |
| Third iteration required by the contract | 3 | 3 | 6 |

The third row does not occur in the defective run. After the second addition, `day` becomes three and `day < days` is false. This distinguishes a missing iteration from an incorrect addition. If all three additions had occurred, investigate a later overwrite or the printed expression instead of changing the boundary blindly.

Repair only the condition to `day <= days`. Step through the same input again: a stop with day three should now appear. Keep the old input; changing both the data and the program would weaken the evidence.

headings.title: Use a Different Symptom to Challenge the Hypothesis
body:
```{index} Use a Different Symptom to Challenge the Hypothesis
```

## Use a Different Symptom to Challenge the Hypothesis
The output compares independently derived expectations with actual results. Zero checks that the loop can run no times; one exposes the original omission immediately; three preserves the original failure; four checks another ordinary case. The negative-input guard is a contract improvement, not the cause of the original wrong total. Record those as separate changes when reviewing a repair.

Guided task: suppose a variant returns 7 for three days. Fill a trace with starting total one instead of zero. Does changing `<` to `<=` alone explain or repair that symptom? Then add an intentional `total = day` in place of `total += day`. Predict the output for four days before debugging.

```{dropdown} Compare the defects
Starting at one adds an unwanted extra credit. With the corrected boundary it yields seven for three days. Assignment instead of accumulation discards earlier credits and returns four for four days. The boundary, initialization and update are separate hypotheses. A trace showing state before and after the update distinguishes them.
```

Use the existing array example after Chapter 7 to transfer this workflow to indexed input. Use the CSV exercise after Chapter 9 to investigate field selection and normalization. Their original tasks remain available; they are later applications rather than assumed knowledge for this first debugger investigation.

headings.title: Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question
body:
```{index} Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question
```

## Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question

A report says that three expense entries, 12, 8 and 5, total 20. Saying that the total is wrong identifies a symptom, but it does not yet locate the defect. First derive the expected total independently: 12 + 8 + 5 is 25. Keep the three inputs fixed. A changing input set makes it difficult to tell whether a code change repaired the problem or merely avoided it.

Suppose the program loops while index is less than the number of entries minus one. The loop body may contain correct addition and still omit the final item. This is why debugging begins with the contract and a concrete failing case rather than rewriting whichever line looks suspicious. At this point, students can use a simple three-value loop; the same workflow later applies to arrays and object state.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Test a Hypothesis Against Execution
```

headings.title: Test a Hypothesis Against Execution
body:
```{index} Test a Hypothesis Against Execution
```

## Test a Hypothesis Against Execution

State a hypothesis before stepping: perhaps the loop visits only two entries. Put a breakpoint before the loop, not after the incorrect report has already been produced. Observe index, the current input, and the accumulated total. Step over the update, then watch the loop condition. In VS Code, a breakpoint pauses execution when the running program reaches that source location; it does not itself execute or repair the line. Step Into follows a call, while Step Over completes that call without opening its internal steps.

| Observation point | Index being processed | Total after the update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First iteration | 0 | 12 |
| Second iteration | 1 | 20 |
| Expected third iteration | 2 | 25 |

If execution never reaches the third row, the evidence supports an iteration-boundary defect. If all three updates occur but the final result is still 20, investigate later reassignment or output instead. A useful observation distinguishes competing explanations. Repeatedly pressing Step without a question can produce many observations without improving understanding.

The call stack tells you how execution reached the paused method. Local variables belong to the current call; selecting another frame can show another call's values. A watch expression is a view of a value, not proof that the value satisfies a business rule. Prefer observations that do not alter program state. A debugging expression that invokes a mutating method can itself change the behavior you are trying to understand.


```{index} Keep Evidence After the Repair
```

headings.title: Keep Evidence After the Repair
body:
```{index} Keep Evidence After the Repair
```

## Keep Evidence After the Repair

After changing the boundary, rerun the exact 12/8/5 case and record expected 25 versus actual 25. Then check no entries, one entry, and a final entry whose omission would be obvious. These checks do not prove every possible input correct, but they defend against the diagnosed class of defect. Keep the failing case as a regression check rather than replacing it with a new convenient example.

Guided variation: the original failing report contains only one expense of 7 and prints zero. Predict what this says about the loop boundary. Then consider a report that prints 14 instead. The first observation suggests a skipped iteration; the second suggests duplicated processing or a different arithmetic/state problem. The workflow should follow the evidence rather than treating every wrong total as the same bug.
Debugging is a repeatable process, not guesswork.

headings.title: Introduction
body:
```{index} Introduction
```

## Introduction


The purpose of testing in software development is to establish developer’s confidence that the
code continues to have high quality and less errors, hence to ensure that the requirements of
the project are met.

Testing is a critical part of software development. In JetBrain’s The State of
Developer Ecosystem 2023 survey [1], for example, 80% of the
respondents say that “testing plays an integral role in their software development
projects.” Also, 63% of respondents say they use **Unit testing** in their projects while
47% say they use Integration testing.

It is also noteworthy that while 41% of respondents say they have less
than 1 tester/Quality Assurance Engineer per 10 developers, 32% of the respondents say
that they have 1-3 testers/QA per 10 software developers. Testing, especially unit testing,
therefore, is a common practice in real world software development.

Amazon AWS defines unit testing as:

> Unit testing is the process where you test the smallest functional unit of code.
> Software testing helps ensure code quality, and it’s an integral part of software
> development. It’s a software development best practice to write software as small,
> functional units then write a unit test for each code unit. You can first write
> unit tests as code. Then, run that test code automatically every time you make
> changes in the software code. This way, if a test fails, you can quickly isolate
> the area of the code that has the bug or error. Unit testing enforces modular
> thinking paradigms and improves test coverage and quality. Automated unit
> testing helps ensure you or your developers have more time to concentrate on coding. [2]

The notion of unit testing is straightforward in principle. When you write a program
in general, the program comprises what are properly known as units of development.
Each language has its own definition of what units are but most modern programming
languages view the **class** concept as the core unit of testing, although it can be done
at lower level such as **method** and higher level such as package. Once we have a class,
we can test it and all of the parts associated with it, especially its methods.

Unit testing is usually done by using testing frameworks. For C#, popular testing
frameworks include: MSTest, NUnit, and xUnit.
```{index} Simple Testing
```

## The Unit Testing Process


One of the fundamental principles of adopting unit testing is to follow a
TDD (Test Driven Development) approach where you will:

1. Write a failing test (to prove the point that the test works)
2. Implement the functionality to pass the test
3. Refactor the code while keeping the test green

:align: center
:width: 300px

body:
```{index} Framework Setup and Test Attributes
```

## Framework Setup and Test Attributes

Use one framework consistently in a project. The complete MSTest workflow below replaces the earlier mixed NUnit/MSTest example. `dotnet new mstest` creates the test project and its framework dependencies; `dotnet add ... reference ...` adds a reference to application code, not a test framework. MSTest discovers `[TestClass]` classes and `[TestMethod]` methods. In these introductory tests, each method is public, returns void, and takes no parameters. Assertions use `Assert.AreEqual(expected, actual)`: choose the expected value from the requirement before running the implementation.

% Testing “Rational”

% ——————–

% \*\* This section is kept here for your reference.

% With the Rational class from a previous section, we will be introducing parts of

% file :repsrc:`rational_nunit/rational_unit_tests.cs` for testing.

% .. index:: testing; assertion

% assertion testing

% Assertions

%

% A key notion of testing is the ability to make a logical assertion about something

% that generally must hold *true* if the test is to pass.

% Assertions are not a standard language feature in C#. Instead, there are a number of

% classes that provide functions for assertion handling. In the framework we are using for

% unit testing (NUnit), a class named Assert supports assertion testing.

% In our tests, we make use of an assertion method, `Assert.IsTrue()` to determine

% whether an assertion is successful. If the variable or expression passed to this

% method is *false*, the assertion fails.

% Here are some examples of assertions:

% - `Assert.IsTrue(true)`: The assertion is trivially successful,

% because the boolean value `true` is true.

% - `Assert.IsTrue(false)`: The assertion is not successful, because the boolean value

% `false` is not true!

% - `Assert.IsFalse(false)`: This assertion is successful, because

% `false` is, of course, false.

% - `Assert.IsTrue(5 > 0)`: Success

% - `Assert.IsTrue(0 > 5)`: Failure

% There are many available assertion methods. In our tests, we use `Assert.IsTrue()`,

% which works for everything we want to test. Other assertion methods do their magic

% rather similarly, because every assertion method ultimately must determine whether

% what is being tested is true or false.

% .. index:: attribute [ ]

% single: [ ]; attribute

% Attributes

% ~

% Besides assertions, a building block of testing (in C# and beyond) comes in the form

% of attributes. Attributes are an additional piece of information that can be attached

% to classes, variables, and methods in C#. There are two attributes of interest to us:

% - [TestFixture]: This indicates that a class is being used for testing purposes.

% - [Test]: This indicates that a method is one of the methods in a class being used

% for testing purposes.

% Without these annotations, classes and methods will *not* be used for testing purposes.

% This allows a class to have some methods that are used for testing while other methods

% are ignored.

% In the remainder of this section, we’re going to take a look at the strategy for testing

% the Rational class. In general, your goal is to ensure that the entire class is tested.

% It is easier said than done. In later courses (Software Engineering) you would learn about

% strategies for *coverage* testing.

% Our strategy will be as follows:

% - Test the constructor and make sure the *representation* of the rational number is

% sound. If the constructor isn’t initializing an instance properly, it is likely

% that little else in the class will work properly.

% - Then test the rest of the class. Whenever possible, group the tests in some logical

% way. In the case of the Rational class, there are three general categories (and one

% rather special one): arithmetic operations, comparisons, and conversions. In addition,

% there is the parsing test, which ensures that we can convert strings representing

% fractions into properly initialized (and reduced) rational numbers.

% Let’s get started.

% Testing the Constructor

% ~

% .. literalinclude:: ../../demos/examples/rational_nunit/rational_unit_tests.cs

% :start-after: snip-ConstructorTest-begin

% :end-before: snip-ConstructorTest-end

% :linenos:

% Testing the constructor is fairly straightforward. We essentially test three basic

% cases:

% - Test whether a basic rational number can be constructed. In the above, we test for

% 3/5, 3/-5, 6/10, and 125. Per the implementation of the Rational class (how we defined

% it), these should result in fractions with numerators of 3, -3, 3, and 12; and denominators

% of 5, 5, 5, and 1, respectively.

% - As you can observe from the code, we perform basic assertion testing to ensure that

% the numerators and denominators are what we expect. For example::

% Assert.IsTrue(r.GetNumerator() == 3)

% Tests whether the newly minted rational number, Rational(3, 5), actually has the

% expected numerator of 3.

% - If we are able to get through the entire code of the `ConstructorTest()` method,

% our constructor test is a success. Otherwise, it is a failure.

% We’ll look at how to actually run our tests in a bit but let’s continue taking a look

% at how the rest of our testing is done.

% Testing Rational Comparisons

% ~

% .. literalinclude:: ../../demos/examples/rational_nunit/rational_unit_tests.cs

% :start-after: snip-BasicComparisonTests-begin

% :end-before: snip-BasicComparisonTests-end

% :linenos:

% It is pretty well established by now that the ability to compare is of fundamental importance

% whenever we are talking about data. Everything we do, especially when it comes to searching

% (finding a value) and sorting (putting values in order) depends on comparison.

% In this test, we construct a few Rational instances (r1, r2, and r3) and perform at least

% one test for each of the essential operators (\>, \<, and =). Recall from our earlier discussion

% of the Rational class that the CompareTo method return a value `< 0`

% when one Rational is *less than* another. It returns a number

% `> 0` for *greater than*, and `== 0` for *equal to*.

% If any one of these comparisons fails, this means that we cannot rely on the ability to

% compare Rational numbers. This will likely prevent other tests from working, such as the

% arithmetic tests, which rely on the ability to test whether a *computed result* matches

% an *expected result* (e.g. 1/4 + 2/4 == 3/4).

% Testing Rational Arithmetic

% ~

% .. literalinclude:: ../../demos/examples/rational_nunit/rational_unit_tests.cs

% :start-after: snip-BasicArithmeticTest-begin

% :end-before: snip-BasicArithmeticTest-end

% :linenos:

% Testing of arithmetic is a fairly straightforward idea. For all of these tests, we

% create a couple of rational numbers (47/64 and -11/64) and then call the various methods

% to perform addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, reciprocal, and negation.

% The key to testing arithmetic successfully in the case of a Rational number is to know

% know what the result *should be*. As a concrete example, the result of adding these

% two rational numbers should be 36/64. So the testing strategy is to use the `Add()`

% method to add the two rational numbers and then test whether the result of the addition

% is equal to the *known* answer of 36/64.

% As you can observe by looking at the code, the magic occurs by checking whether the

% *computed* result matches the *constructed* result::

% Assert.IsTrue(r.CompareTo(new Rational(36, 64)) == 0);

% Because we have *separately* tested the constructor and comparison methods, we can

% assume that it is ok to rely upon comparison methods as part of this arithmetic test.

% And it is in this example where we begin to see the *art of testing*. You can write

% tests that assume that other tests of features you are using have *already passed*. In the

% event that your assumption is wrong, you’d be able to know that this is the case, because

% all of the tests you assumed to pass would not have passed.

% Again, to be clear, the arithmetic tests we have done here *assume* that we can rely on

% the constructor and the comparison operation to determine equality of two rational numbers.

% It is entirely possible that this is not true, so we’ll be able to determine this when

% examining the test output (we’d see that not only the arithmetic test fails but possibly the

% constructor and/or comparison tests as well).

% The remaining tests are fairly straightforward. We’ll more or less present them as is with

% minimal explanation as they are in many ways variations on the theme.

% Testing Rational Conversions (to other types)

%

% .. literalinclude:: ../../demos/examples/rational_nunit/rational_unit_tests.cs

% :start-after: snip-BasicConversionTests-begin

% :end-before: snip-BasicConversionTests-end

% :linenos:

% In this test, we want to make sure that Rational objects can be converted to floating point

% and decimal types (the built-in types of the C# language).

% For example, Rational(3/6) is 1/2, which is 0.5 (both in its floating-point and decimal

% representations.

% Testing the Parsing Feature

% ~

% .. literalinclude:: ../../demos/examples/rational_nunit/rational_unit_tests.cs

% :start-after: snip-ParseTest-begin

% :end-before: snip-ParseTest-end

% :linenos:

% The parsing test tests whether we can convert the string representation of a rational number

% into an actual (reduced) rational number. We test three general cases:

% - The ability to take a fraction and convert it into a rational number. This fraction may

% or may not have a “-” sign in it. For example -12/30 should be equivalent to constructing

% a Rational(-12, 30).

% - The ability to take a whole number and get a proper Rational, e.g. 123 is equal to

% Rational(123)

% - The ability to take a textual representation (1.125) and get a proper Rational(9, 8)

% representation. In this case, we are also getting an extra test to ensure the result

% is reduced.

% .. index:: Xamarin Studio; running NUnit tests

% testing; running in Xamarin Studio

% .. \_running-nunit-tests:

% Running the NUnit Tests

%

% #. In Xamarin Studio, select the rational_nunit project.

% #. In the main Xamarin Studio menu click “Run” and select “Run Unit Tests”

% A test pad should appear and show something like

% .. image:: ../../figures/NUnitTestXamarinInit.png

% :width: 350 pt

% This likely just shows the overall results in the summary line at the bottom.

% You can show details by clicking on one or more of headings at the

% top of the pad. In particular, if you click Successful Test, Failed Tests,

% and Output (and likely drag the top of the pad to make

% it large enough to see everything), you should see something like

% .. image:: ../../figures/NUnitTestXamarinDetails.png

% :width: 350 pt

% As you can see in the above displays, all of the tests in `RationalTests`

% get executed, and they all pass.

% There are no failed tests to see,

% but that part would be the most important details if any were there!

% The output just details the sequence of execution.

% Xamarin Studio remembers the headings selected, so next time you run tests,

% the same details will show.

% The testing file is using NUnit.Framework. There is a little more to this.

% If you edit the references, selecting All sources, and entering nunit

% in the search box, you see

% .. image:: ../../figures/NUnitReferencesXamarin.png

% :width: 350 pt

% Note there are more than one version of nunit.framework. On a Mac,

% the selected version worked directly, but the logical looking one, provided

% by Xamarin, did *not* work directly. Either worked if we select the context

% We waited until now to discuss unit testing, because the test classes are coded with

headings.title: Design Tests Independently of the Implementation
body:
## Design Tests Independently of the Implementation

```{index} gap revision: design tests independently of the implementation
```
A unit test checks a small behavior in isolation, such as one pricing method. An integration test checks collaborating parts, such as parsing a file and submitting its records. Passing a method test does not prove that the file path, parser, and caller work together. Start with a written contract and calculate expected results without calling the method under test.

Suppose an order of zero items costs zero, one through four items costs two dollars per item, and five or more costs nine dollars in total. A candidate that tests `quantity > 5` misses exactly five. Cases just below, at, and just above a decision boundary distinguish that defect from an arithmetic mistake.

| Case | Requirement-derived expectation | What it checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero | 0 | Empty order. |
| Four | 8 | Lower-price rule before threshold. |
| Five | 9 | Inclusive threshold. |
| Six | 9 | Upper rule after threshold. |
| Negative | Rejection | Invalid-domain contract. |

For debugging, record input, expected result, actual result, a hypothesis, and an observation that can disprove it. Put a breakpoint at the branch and watch the condition for five. After fixing the comparison, rerun the same cases as regression checks. Adding the failing result to the expected values would hide the defect rather than fix it.

See the language/API reference for this contract.[^gap-mstest]
**Guided practice.** Create a test table for a different threshold of seven before seeing code. Explain which three adjacent quantities distinguish `>` from `>=`. Translate one row into Arrange, Act, Assert in MSTest. Preserve the original failing test while repairing the method.

```

# Computing and Society

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
Optional cases extend Chapter 1.2 with software failures, boundary tests, and professional accountability. Use these after the core testing lesson.

Software now sits between people and many things that matter to them: pay, prices, credit, medical treatment, and access to services. The people affected usually never see the code and cannot check it. That gap is why computing professionals carry special responsibility for what their programs do.

```{index} software failures; case studies
```

headings.title: When Software Fails People
body:
```{index} When Software Fails People
```

## When Software Fails People

Three well-documented cases show different ways software harms people.

- **Therac-25 (1985–1987).** A radiation therapy machine delivered massive overdoses in six known accidents, killing or seriously injuring patients. Investigators found software race conditions, combined with the removal of hardware safety interlocks that earlier models had relied on and weak engineering practices.[^0605_software_responsibility-therac]
- **Knight Capital (2012).** On August 1, 2012, a trading firm deployed new code to seven of its eight order servers. On the eighth, old, unused code was reactivated. In about 45 minutes it sent millions of unintended orders, and the firm lost more than \$460 million. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission later settled charges with Knight, which paid a \$12 million penalty.[^0605_software_responsibility-knight]
- **The UK Post Office Horizon scandal (1999–2015).** Hundreds of subpostmasters, who run local post offices, were prosecuted for shortfalls that the Horizon accounting system reported. The Post Office itself brought about 700 of these prosecutions. The system had bugs, and the people accused could not see or challenge how it worked. Parliament passed the *Post Office (Horizon System) Offences Act 2024* to quash the convictions.[^0605_software_responsibility-horizon]

The lessons differ. Therac-25 shows that removing a safety check because "the software handles it" can be deadly. Knight Capital shows that deployment is part of software quality. Horizon shows the harm done when an organization trusts a system's output over the people it affects.
```{index} defect; scale of impact
```

headings.title: Small Defects at Scale
body:
```{index} Small Defects at Scale
```

## Small Defects at Scale

A defect that costs one customer a few dollars can cost customers in total a great deal, because a program repeats the same mistake every time it runs. The discount rule below is meant to give 10% off orders of \$100.00 or more, but the condition uses `>` instead of `>=`:

No single customer is likely to notice ten dollars, so the defect could run for months. This is exactly the kind of boundary error that the tests in Chapter 6 are designed to catch. Testing the values just below, at, and just above a boundary finds it:
Fixing the code is only part of the response. The company must also decide what it owes the customers who were already overcharged. That is an ethical question, not a technical one.

```{index} ethical analysis; checklist
```

headings.title: Thinking Through an Ethical Question
body:
```{index} Thinking Through an Ethical Question
```

## Thinking Through an Ethical Question

Ethical decisions in software are rarely about villains. They are usually about trade-offs under deadline pressure. A short checklist keeps the important questions from being skipped:

1. **Who is affected?** List the stakeholders: users, customers, coworkers, the organization, and people outside it.
2. **What could happen, and how bad would it be?** Consider likely and severe outcomes for each stakeholder.
3. **What do we owe them?** Consider laws, contracts, promises made to customers, and professional codes.
4. **Could we explain this decision publicly?** If a decision only works while nobody knows about it, reconsider it.

Applied to the discount defect:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Who is affected? | 9,125 customers who were overcharged; the company; the developer who must report the defect |
| What could happen? | Customers lose \$91,250 in total; if it comes out later, the company loses trust and may face legal action |
| What do we owe them? | The price the company advertised; honest disclosure; a fix that is tested |
| Could we explain it publicly? | "We found an error, fixed it, and refunded everyone" can be explained. "We fixed it quietly and kept the money" cannot. |
```{index} ACM Code of Ethics
```

headings.title: Professional Codes of Ethics
body:
```{index} Professional Codes of Ethics
```

## Professional Codes of Ethics

Professions write down what they expect of their members. The *ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct*, adopted in 2018 by the largest computing society, is the standard reference for computing.[^0605_software_responsibility-acm] A few of its principles apply directly to the work in this book:

| Principle | What it means for a programmer |
|---|---|
| 1.2 Avoid harm. | Consider who could be hurt by a feature or a failure before you ship it. |
| 1.3 Be honest and trustworthy. | Report defects and limitations, including your own. |
| 1.6 Respect privacy. | Collect and use personal data only for legitimate, stated purposes. |
| 2.1 Strive to achieve high quality in both the processes and products of professional work. | Test, review, and document, as in Chapter 6. |
| 2.5 Give comprehensive and thorough evaluations of computer systems and their impacts, including analysis of possible risks. | Say what could go wrong, not only what works. |
| 2.9 Design and implement systems that are robustly and usably secure. | Build in security from the start, as in the next section. |
```{index} ethics; summary
```

headings.title: Summary
body:
```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

Software affects people who cannot see or check it. Small defects multiply at scale, so testing boundaries is an ethical habit as well as a technical one. When a decision affects others, work through who is affected, what could happen, what is owed, and whether the decision could be explained publicly. Professional codes such as the ACM Code describe what others are entitled to expect from you.

headings.title: See the Collection Before Writing Its Loop
body:
```{index} See the Collection Before Writing Its Loop
```

## See the Collection Before Writing Its Loop
A store records quantities for four delivery slots. Four unrelated variables would require four separate names and repeated processing code. An array gives the values one name and a position-based organization. Its length is fixed when the array object is created; its elements can still change. This connects the collection idea to variables: assignment changes a value in a particular slot, while a loop chooses which slot to visit.

Use these schematic forms to distinguish three actions:

```text
elementType[] name;                         // Declare a variable for an array reference.
name = new elementType[lengthExpression];    // Create an array and store its reference.
name[indexExpression] = valueExpression;    // Replace one element of that array.
```

`[]` after the type describes the array type. Brackets after a variable name select an element. Length counts elements; an index identifies a position. For four slots, the valid indexes are zero through three. Index four is already outside the array.
The first line shows default values after allocation. The later assignment reads indexes one and three, computes `4 * 5 - 6`, and stores 14 at index two. It does not insert a fifth quantity or change the array's length.

| Index | After allocation | After four assignments | After the calculation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 0 | 7 | 7 |
| 1 | 0 | 5 | 5 |
| 2 | 0 | 9 | 14 |
| 3 | 0 | 6 | 6 |

Read the table by column to see a whole array state, or by row to follow one element. The loop's condition checks `index < quantities.Length` before each read. The semicolons in a for header separate initialization, condition and update. A comma between condition and update is not the syntax for this loop.

An initializer such as `int[] quantities = { 7, 5, 9, 6 };` creates the same four initial values more compactly. Use `foreach` when only the values matter; use an index when the task selects or changes positions. A foreach loop can stop early with `break`, but it does not directly provide the current position for an indexed update.

headings.title: Guide a Last-Element Check
body: ```{index} Guide a Last-Element Check ``` ## Guide a Last-Element Check An empty array has a real object and Length zero, but it has no last element. A variable containing null has no array object at all. First practice the empty-array distinction; Chapter 11 develops missing references further. Guided task: complete this schematic condition before reading the final element. Explain why `Length - 1` belongs in the index expression, not in the loop's upper bound when all elements are required. ```text if (values.Length /* comparison */ 0) display values[values.Length - 1]; else display "No deliveries"; ``` Predict both calls in the completed example, then change the ordinary input to a one-element array. The comparison is `>`. For an empty array, evaluating index -1 would be invalid, so the read occurs only inside the guarded branch. For one element, Length is one and its last index is zero. As a variation, change only the second slot in the four-element example and predict the entire new state before running it. The retained examples below add other loop forms, string arrays, returned arrays, defaults and library operations. ```{index} 1D Arrays ``` ```{index} array; [ ] declaration ``` An array is a **collection type** and a `data structure` that contains a number of variables that are accessed through computed indices. The variables contained in an array, also called the `elements` of the array, are all of the same type, and this type is called the `element type` of the array. [1] In C#, an array is a structure representing a **fixed length** `ordered` collection of values or objects with the **same type**. Arrays make it easier to organize and operate on large amounts of data. For example, rather than creating 100 integer variables, you can just create one array that stores all those integers and access them using array indices. [2] You have learned that a string is an immutable `sequence` of characters and how to loop through the sequence. Arrays provide more general sequences, with the same indexing notation, but with free choice of the `type` of the items in the sequence, and the ability to `change` the elements in the sequence. The collection idea connects this chapter to the next one. An array supplies an ordered group of elements, indexed access, and traversal, but its length stays fixed after creation. A `List` supports a changing number of elements; a dictionary retrieves values by key; a set represents distinct values; and stacks, queues, and priority queues select the next item by a processing rule. You do not need their syntax yet. First learn the array operations here, then compare the broader families in {doc}`Data Collections <../08_collections/0801_collections>`. The separate chapters mark a learning sequence, not a boundary between arrays and collections. ```{index} Creating Arrays ```

headings.title: Creating Arrays
body:
```{index} Creating Arrays
```

## Creating Arrays

A C# `array variable` is declared similarly to a non-array variable, with the
addition of square brackets (`[]`) after the `type` specifier to denote it as an array.
So, the general form for declaring an array variable of the element type is:

> **type**`[]` variableName;

For example, if you want to create an array called `a` with the type `int`
for elements, you declare the array variable as:

    int[] a;

In this declaration, you do *not* know how many elements will be in this array
from the preceding declaration. You must give further information to create the
corresponding `array object`. A new object can be created using the `new`
syntax. An array must get a definite length, which can be a literal integer or
any integer expression. The general syntax to create a new array is

> `new` **type**`[` *length* `]`

After the type, there are square brackets enclosing an expression for the length
of the array - this length is unchangeable after creation. For example

    int[] a;
    a = new int[4];

or, you may combine with the declaration,

    int[] a = new int[4];

to creates an array that holds 4 integers. After specifying the number of the elements
of the array, the default initial values are also assigned. For example, numerical
arrays get initialized to all 0’s (false for boolean, the character with Unicode
number zero for char, and null for objects and string) with this syntax by default, so when you loop
through the array variable:

    > foreach (int i in a)
      {
          Console.Write(i);
      }
    0000
    >

An **array initializer** consists of a sequence of variable initializers,
enclosed by “`{`” and”`}`” tokens and separated by “`,`” tokens.
An array initializer can be used in a variable declaration:

    int[] a = {0, 2, 4, 6, 8};

which is a shorthand for the equivalent `array creation expression`:

    int[] a = new int[] {0, 2, 4, 6, 8};

Note that the actual data for an array is *not* stored directly in the memory location
allocated by the declaration. The array could have any number of items, and hence
the memory requirements are not known at compile time. Like all other object
(as opposed to primitive) types, what is actually stored at the memory location declared
for `a` is a *reference* to the actual place where the data for the array is stored.
In actual compiler implementation, this reference is an address in memory. In the diagram
below, you see the object references with an arrow *pointing* to the actual location
for the object’s data after `a` is initialized:

```{figure} ../../figures/newArray1.png
:alt: new array
:width: 300px

New array.
```

The small box beside `a` is meant to indicate the memory space allocated when `a` is
declared. As you can see that space does not actually contain the array, but rather a
*reference* to the array, pointing to the actual sequence of data for the array.
Also, in the diagram you see the indices associated with each element, though they
are not actual a part of what is stored in memory.

body:

(default-fields)=

## Default Initializations

Did you notice that when the first example array of integers was created,
it was filled with zeros? It is a safety feature of C# that the internal fields
of objects always get a specific value, not random data. Here are the defaults:

| Type | Default element value |
| --- | --- |
| Primitive numeric types | 0 |
| bool | false |
| Reference types, including string | null |

```{warning}
An array with elements of reference type, like `string[]`, without a specific initializer
gets initialized to all null values. Array creation is legal, but reading a member of a null element fails.
```

This intentionally failing fragment illustrates the missing-element problem:

```csharp
string[] words = new string[10];
Console.WriteLine(words[0].Length); // Runtime error: this element is null.
```

The error is because null is not an object and has no Length property.
If you want an array of empty strings, initialize the elements with a loop:

```csharp
string[] words = new string[10];
for (int i = 0; i < words.Length; i++) {
    words[i] = "";
}
```

headings.title: LINQ Methods
body:
```{index} LINQ Methods
```

## LINQ Methods
Language-Integrated Query (LINQ) is a set of technologies integrating query capabilities into C#. The full query topic is later reading; these calls are library aggregation examples.

All C# array types derive from System.Array. Arrays provide enumeration, which permits LINQ extension calls such as Max(), Min(), Sum() and Reverse() when the appropriate namespace is imported. Reverse() produces a sequence rather than automatically changing the original array.

```csharp
using System.Linq;
int[] nums = new int[5] { 10, 15, 16, 8, 6 };
nums.Max();     // Returns 16.
nums.Min();     // Returns 6.
nums.Sum();     // Returns 55.
nums.Average(); // Returns 11.
```

The average is 55 divided by five. These fragments illustrate result values; they do not print them. The complete runnable examples earlier show how to display results.
**Check the library-method summary:** The five values 10, 15, 16, 8 and 6 have sum 55, so their average is 55 / 5 = 11. The Average result comment above is corrected to 11. Sum and Average are different aggregation contracts, even when both consume the same values. The array-processing lesson supplies complete runnable loop examples.
The array declarations and initialization forms above follow these references.[^arrays-specification][^arrays-cheatsheet]

```

## Process Positions Before Introducing a New Container

An array gives many values one shared organization. To calculate a total, the program still needs a rule for visiting those values and combining them. The accumulator pattern connects arrays to Chapter 4: initialize a running result, visit each relevant element, and update the result exactly once for that element. The array changes where input values come from; it does not change the meaning of a loop or an assignment.

Suppose daily quantities are 4, 0 and 7. Before the first iteration the total is zero because no entries have been processed. After each iteration, total should equal the sum of the processed prefix. This claim explains both the initialization and the update. It also provides a way to find a defect before the final result is printed.

| Processed positions | Next position | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 4 |
| 0 and 1 | 2 | 4 |
| 0 through 2 | End | 11 |

A for loop exposes positions and is useful when you must report an index or replace elements. A foreach loop exposes each element value directly and is useful when only those values matter. Do not assume that changing a foreach iteration variable updates an array element. Use explicit indexing when the operation is defined in terms of changing positions.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

body:
