```

## Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements

A method parameter of type int[] receives a copy of the reference value. Caller and helper can therefore refer to the same array. Replacing an element through the helper is visible through the caller's reference. Reassigning the helper's parameter to a different array changes that local parameter, not the caller's variable. This connects ordinary parameter passing from Chapter 5 with reference aliasing, without requiring pass-by-reference parameter syntax.

State whether a processing helper may mutate its input. A Total helper normally only reads values. An ApplyAdjustment helper might intentionally replace them. If a reporting task must preserve original values, computing into another array or returning a separate result is a different contract from modifying the original and restoring it afterward.

An empty array is a real collection with Length zero. A total over no quantities naturally returns zero under the sum contract. A request for the first element has no valid result on that same input. Handle the operation's domain rather than giving every array helper the same empty-case behavior. A null reference is different again: there is no array object whose Length can be read.

Guided exercise: replace the quantities with 0, 0 and 7. Predict the accumulator trace. Then predict the result for an empty array. Finally, explain whether the read-only total should change if another variable is assigned the array reference. An alias alone changes no element, but a later mutation through either alias can change what a subsequent total reads.

## Parameters to Main


The `Main` method may take an array of strings as parameter, as in this example:

```csharp
/// Demonstrate the use of command line parameters.
static void Main(string[] args)
{
   Console.WriteLine("There are {0} command line parameters.", args.Length);
   foreach(string s in args) {
      Console.WriteLine(s);
   }

}
```

By convention, the formal parameter for `Main` is called `args`,
short for arguments.

### Command Line Adder


A code block in the Main method of your project that calculates and prints
the sum of three command line parameters taken from user input:

    2 5 22

then the program prints 29.

The code could look like this:

    ////////// args array from command line.
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < args.Length; i++)

    Console.WriteLine(sum);

% See the type returned. It is an array `int[]` for the int results::

% /// Return ints taken from space separated integers in a string.

% public static int\[\] IntsFromString1(string input)

% {

% string\[\] integers = input.Split(’ ’);

% int\[\] data = new int\[integers.Length\];

% data\[i\] = int.Parse(integers\[i\]);

headings.title: References and Aliases
body:
```{index} References and Aliases
```

(alias)=

## References and Aliases


Object variables, like arrays, are references,
and this has important implications for
assignment.

With a primitive type like an `int`, an assignment copies the data:

`{image} ../../figures/intCopy.png :align: center :alt: copying an int :width: 90 pt`

In the diagram, the contents of the memory box labeled `b` is copied to the
memory box labeled `d`. The value of `d` starts off equal to the value of `b`,
but can later be changed independently.

Contrast an assignment with arrays. The value that is copied is the *reference*,
not the array data itself, so both end up pointing at the *same* actual array:

`{image} ../../figures/arrayAlias.png :align: center :alt: copying an array reference :width: 300 pt`

Hereafter, array assignments like:

    b[2] = -10;
    d[1] = 55;

would both change the *same* array. Now `b` and `d` are essentially
names for the same thing (the actual array). The technical term matches English:
The names are *aliases*.

This may seem like a pretty silly discussion. Why bother to give two different
names to the same object? Isn’t one enough? In fact it is very important
in function/method calls. An array reference can be passed as an actual value,
and it is the array *reference* that is copied to the formal parameter, so
the formal parameter name is an **alias** for the actual parameter name.

If an array passed as a parameter to a method has elements changed in the
method, then the change affects the actual parameter array.
The change *remains* in the actual parameter array *after*
the method has terminated.

```{index} array; Scale example
```

For example, consider the following function:

    // Modify a by multiplying all elements by multiplier.
    static void Scale(int[] a, int multiplier)
    {
       for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) {
          a[i] *= multiplier;  // or:  a[i] = a[i] * multiplier
       }
    }

The fragment:

    int[] nums = {2, 4, 1};
    Scale(nums, 5);

would *change* nums, so it ends up containing elements 10, 20, and 5.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```

## Advanced topic: Array of Arrays


Since you can have an array of any type, it is also possible to have an
*array of arrays* (jagged arrays). The notational difference to a
multi-dimensional array is just that each index is enclosed in
separate square brackets, with no commas.

For example, you could create a table with shape like the initial example
in {ref}`2D-arrays`, less the last two elements to show the jagged array:


This takes somewhat more memory and is longer to
access than the multidimensional arrays. For most uses, when you want to
refer to a rectangular table of data, like above,
this new version has little to offer.

There are a couple of reasons why you might want this format.

## From One Row to a Table Summary

```{index} gap revision: from one row to a table summary
```
A branch-by-day table adds a second coordinate to the one-dimensional accumulation pattern. First fix the row and traverse columns; then repeat for another row. To total one day across branches, fix the column and traverse rows. `GetLength(0)` counts rows; `GetLength(1)` counts columns. `Length` counts every element and is not a valid bound for either coordinate alone.

| Branch | Monday (column 0) | Tuesday (column 1) | Row total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| North (row 0) | 2 | 5 | 7 |
| South (row 1) | 4 | 1 | 5 |
| Column total | 6 | 6 | 12 |

For North, the accumulator moves from zero to two to seven. For Monday it moves from zero to two to six. The values are the same table; the coordinate held constant determines the question. Initialize an accumulator for each result, not once for all rows.
**Guided practice.** Change only the fixed coordinate to calculate South and Tuesday: expect five and six. Add a third branch `{ 3, 0 }` and predict Monday before running. Then wrap row accumulation in an outer loop, resetting the row total each time. This is the bridge to the existing independent branch-by-day lab, whose full report remains unchanged.

headings.title: Collection Families and Selection
body: (collections-section)= # Collection Families and Selection ```{contents} :local: :depth: 2 ``` ```{index} collections ``` ```{index} Data Collections ``` A bookstore handles many groups of values: the quantities sold during a week, the items in a customer's basket, stock quantities indexed by product code, and orders waiting for collection. Each group contains several values, but the program does different work with each one. Finding Tuesday's sales, looking up a product code, and selecting the next order are different questions. The way you organize the values should support the question you need to answer. A **collection** groups values and provides operations for working with them. Arrays are the first collection type we studied: {doc}`Chapter 7 <../07_arrays/0700_arrays>` introduced fixed-length, indexed sequences. Keeping that chapter separate gave us time to practice indexing, traversal, and multidimensional data. It did not put arrays outside the collection category. This chapter broadens our choices to other ready-made collection types in the .NET standard library. These classes are often called **built-in collections** because they come with .NET, although they are library types used by C#, rather than separate C# language features. Arrays have direct C# language syntax, such as `int[]`; collection classes such as `List` are library types. Both belong in our collection-family comparison. This section introduces the big ideas before the detailed syntax: what a collection promises, how values can be accessed, and how to choose among collection families. You will see eight useful families and small demonstrations of their behavior. The next two sections develop `List` and `Dictionary` in depth. For the other families, your goal here is to recognize the need they address and predict their basic behavior, not to memorize every method or implement a data structure. **Reading path:** First explain the access question, compare the families, and connect their operations. Work through arrays/lists, dictionaries, and shared references before the order-summary exercise. Use the linked-list, set, stack/queue, and priority-queue demonstrations to recognize their policies; their implementations and detailed APIs belong to later chapters. The operation tables are references to revisit, not a list of signatures to memorize in one sitting. ```{figure} ../../figures/collection_access_map.svg :alt: Three access questions: a position selects Tuesday in an array, a product key selects stock in a dictionary, and arrival order selects the next service request in a queue. The access question connects the task to a collection family. ``` Read each column from question to collection to operation. The diagram compares access policies, not performance. A program can need several of these policies at once.

headings.title: Collections and Operations
body:
```{index} Collections and Operations
```

## Collections and Operations


```{index} collection; element; collection operation; data structure
```
An **element** is one item stored in a collection. An array of sales quantities has numbers as its elements; a list of product codes has strings. A dictionary stores entries that associate a key with a value. The surrounding collection gives these items an organization and a set of supported actions.

Several operations recur across collection families:

| Operation | Question it answers | Bookstore example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add or insert | How does a new item enter the group? | Add a product code to the current basket. |
| Retrieve | How do you obtain a particular item? | Find the stock quantity associated with a product code. |
| Update | How does stored information change? | Replace a recorded quantity after a stock check. |
| Remove | How does an item leave the group? | Remove a canceled item from a basket. |
| Membership test | Is this item or key present? | Check whether a customer has already used a promotion. |
| Traverse | How do you visit the stored items? | Print every item on an order. |
| Inspect size | How many items are stored? | Count the orders waiting for collection. |

Not every collection offers every operation, and the method names differ. A stack deliberately limits which item you retrieve next. An array lets you replace an element but does not let you add a new position to that same array. The operations and their rules form a collection's **contract**: the behavior a programmer can rely on.

A **data structure** is an organization of stored information that supports operations. A library collection gives you an already implemented data structure through a public interface of methods and properties. You can use a list before you know how its storage grows, just as you can call `Math.Round` before implementing a rounding algorithm. Later chapters examine the implementation choices behind these operations.

Keep the question of behavior separate from the question of storage. A queue promises a first-in, first-out processing rule. That rule does not require you to know whether a particular implementation uses an array or linked nodes. Conversely, the fact that two collections both store strings does not mean that their access rules are interchangeable.

headings.title: Collection Families
body:
```{index} Collection Families
```

(collections-by-access-pattern)=

## Collection Families


```{index} collection; families; access pattern
```
An **access pattern** describes how a program usually retrieves and processes its data. Do you know an item's position? Do you know a key that identifies it? Do you only need to know whether it is present? Must items be processed in arrival order?

In the type names below, `T` stands for an element type you choose, such as `string` or `int`. `TKey`, `TValue`, and `TPriority` name the corresponding key, value, and priority types. The examples later in this section use `new` to construct a collection and dot notation to call its operations. First, read the table for the organizing idea behind each family; the next discussion explains generic type arguments before you examine the individual examples.

**Table: An introductory map of .NET collection families.** Adapted from Microsoft's collection-selection guidance, with original business examples and an added priority-queue entry.[^0801_collections-collection-guide][^0801_collections-priority-queue] These eight families are a teaching selection, not Microsoft's exhaustive classification. Sorted variants and collections for specialized settings extend this map.

| Family | Representative type | Main access rule | Business use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array | `T[]`, such as `int[]` | Retrieve by index; length is fixed. | Store one quantity for each of five business days. |
| List | `List<T>` | Retrieve by index; the sequence can grow or shrink. | Build a customer's basket as items are selected. |
| Linked list | `LinkedList<T>` | Follow linked nodes; insert or remove at a known node. | Insert a processing step beside an already located step. |
| Dictionary | `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | Retrieve a value using its unique key. | Look up stock by product code. |
| Set | `HashSet<T>` | Test membership; equal values occur only once. | Track distinct customers who used a promotion. |
| Stack | `Stack<T>` | Retrieve the most recently added item first. | Keep a history of actions to undo. |
| Queue | `Queue<T>` | Retrieve the earliest added item first. | Process service requests in arrival order. |
| Priority queue | `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | Retrieve an item with the lowest priority value first. | Process urgent requests before routine requests. |

The same business process can need several collections. A bookstore might use a dictionary for stock lookup, a list for basket contents, and a queue for orders awaiting service. Choosing one collection does not commit the whole application to that family.

Three distinctions help you read the table. **Position** identifies where an element currently sits in a sequence. **Identity** identifies which entity you mean, such as a product code. **Processing order** determines which waiting item is handled next. Confusing these ideas produces fragile programs: a product code should not silently change because an earlier item was removed from a list.

headings.title: Choosing a Collection
body:
```{index} Choosing a Collection
```

## Choosing a Collection


```{index} collection selection; duplicate; order; lookup
```
Start with the work the program must do, rather than the longest list of available methods. For a bookstore promotion, suppose the manager asks for four results: the order of product selections, the current stock for a known code, the distinct customers who participated, and the next request to process.

An ordered list preserves selections, including repeated product codes. A dictionary associates a product code with its stock quantity. A set records distinct participating customers. A queue selects the next request if the policy is arrival order; a priority queue is appropriate if a defined priority rule should determine service. These structures can collaborate in one application because they answer different questions.

Use the following questions to explain a choice:

1. **What is one element?** A product code, an integer quantity, or a request is a different unit of information. Define what an entry represents before choosing a type.
2. **How will you retrieve it?** Distinguish an index, an identifying key, a membership test, and a next-item rule.
3. **Do order and duplicates carry information?** Removing duplicates from a transaction history can lose events. Preserving every duplicate in a distinct-customer report can misstate participation.
4. **Does the size change?** Decide whether fixed positions describe the task or whether adding and removing elements is normal work.
5. **What operations must be safe?** Consider missing keys, empty collections, invalid values, and whether another part of the program shares the object.

Performance matters too, but "fast" needs an operation and a situation. A dictionary is designed for lookup by key; it does not make every kind of search or report automatically fast. A linked list can insert beside a known node without shifting a suffix, but finding that node can take traversal. Later chapters develop these costs systematically. Here, explain the behavioral fit first and avoid claims that one family is always best.

Trees and graphs extend the larger study of data structures. They model hierarchies and networks, rather than adding two more standard generic classes named `Tree<T>` and `Graph<T>` to this table. Chapters 17 and 20 teach those structures and their applications. Arrays are developed in Chapter 7; linked structures in Chapter 14; stacks and queues in Chapter 15; priority queues in Chapter 18; and hashing and sets in Chapter 19.

For this chapter's detailed coding and assignments, concentrate on lists and dictionaries. The broader family map should help you recognize alternatives and ask better questions about the data. You do not need the internal mechanics of a hash table or heap to explain why a lookup table and a waiting line have different access rules.
**Guided choice: the daily order desk**

A shop stores five daily sales totals, receives a changing sequence of basket items, looks up stock by product code, and handles requests in arrival order. For each requirement, name the identifying information (position, key, or processing order), select a family, and explain one unsuitable alternative. Then change the requirement: what if urgent requests should go first?
```{dropdown} Reasoning to compare with yours
Five fixed positions fit an array. Basket items fit a list because their number changes and repeated selections can matter. Stock lookup fits a dictionary keyed by product code. Arrival-order service fits a queue; a stack would serve the most recent request first. Urgency suggests a priority queue with an explicitly defined priority policy. These choices follow the operations, not the fact that all four groups contain business data.
```
```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[*Collections and Data Structures*](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/) and [*Selecting a Collection Class*](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/collections/selecting-a-collection-class). Microsoft Learn. Accessed October 16, 2026. The table adapts the documentation's operation-based selection approach; its eight-family grouping and bookstore examples are the author's teaching organization. The priority-queue entry is additionally supported by the API reference below.
[^0801_collections-linked-list]: The .NET [LinkedList<T> reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.linkedlist-1?view=net-10.0) describes its node-based, doubly linked organization.
[^0801_collections-priority-queue]: The .NET [PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority> reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.priorityqueue-2?view=net-10.0) specifies lowest-priority removal and does not guarantee FIFO behavior for equal priorities.
[^0801_collections-collection-interface]: `IEnumerable<T>` supplies an enumerator used by `foreach`. Enumeration order belongs to each type's contract; supporting enumeration does not imply sorted, insertion, or priority order.

This table compares selected operations rather than listing each type's complete API.

headings.title: Read an Operation as a State Change and a Result
body:
```{index} Read an Operation as a State Change and a Result
```

## Read an Operation as a State Change and a Result

The family map tells you which question a collection can answer. Now describe an operation with three parts: what must already be true, what changes, and what result the caller receives. This makes the cross-family tables below more useful than a list of names to memorize.

Consider the sequence of product codes PEN, PAD, PEN. Removing by value selects an occurrence matching a value; removing by index selects a position. Popping a stack or dequeuing a queue selects according to processing order instead. Even when each operation reduces a count by one, it need not select the same element. Compare the selection rule before comparing the method spelling.

| Intended action | Information supplied | Question to ask before calling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove a known product code from a list | Value | Which matching occurrence is removed? |
| Remove the third list position | Index 2 | Does that position exist now? |
| Take the next queued request | No identifying key | Is the queue nonempty? |
| Find stock for a product code | Key | What happens when that key is absent? |

Returning a value and mutating a collection are independent possibilities. A lookup can return a result without removing anything. A removal can both change storage and report success. A Try-style operation supplies a Boolean success signal so that an absent result can be distinguished from a legitimate default value. Read both the success flag and the output value under the documented contract.

Traversal is also an operation with a contract. Foreach provides a shared language form, but it does not make the collection families share one universal order. A sequence has positional order; a work queue has a service policy; a keyed collection has its own enumeration guarantees. If a report requires sorted product codes, request or construct that order explicitly instead of assuming that lookup storage supplies it.

Guided comparison: there are two PEN entries. Explain how Remove("PEN"), RemoveAt(2), and a queue Dequeue could affect a three-item group differently. Draw the before/after contents and identify the selected item. Then explain why the original array cannot shrink merely because an element has been set to an empty string. Replacing a value is not changing the length of the same array.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Generic Collections
body:
```{index} Generic Collections
```

## Generic Collections


```{index} generic type; type parameter; type argument; type safety
```
A collection's **family** tells you how it organizes access. Its **element type** tells you what values it stores. These are separate choices: a list of integers and a list of strings use the same sequence operations, but they store different kinds of values.

A **generic type** is defined using one or more **type parameters**, which are placeholders for types. In documentation, `List<T>` means a list whose element type is represented by `T`. When you write `List<string>`, `string` is the **type argument** you have supplied for that parameter. The library provides the reusable class; you choose its type arguments when declaring the collection.

| Library notation | Example in a program | Meaning of the type arguments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `List<T>` | `List<string>` | Each element is a string. |
| `HashSet<T>` | `HashSet<int>` | Each distinct element is an integer. |
| `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | `Dictionary<string, int>` | Keys are strings; values are integers. |
| `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | `PriorityQueue<string, int>` | Elements are strings; priorities are integers. |

Generic collections provide **type safety**: the compiler checks whether supplied values can be used as the declared types. A `List<int>` accepts integers; it will not accept the string `"twelve"`. This catches a mismatch before the program runs. It does not establish that every integer is appropriate: a negative stock quantity is still an integer, so business validation remains your responsibility.

headings.title: The Standard Library and Namespaces
body:
```{index} The Standard Library and Namespaces
```

### The Standard Library and Namespaces


```{index} namespace; standard library; System.Collections.Generic
```
A **namespace** groups related type names. Most collection classes demonstrated here belong to `System.Collections.Generic`. The `using System.Collections.Generic;` directive lets you write `List<string>` instead of the full name `System.Collections.Generic.List<string>`. It makes names available; it does not create a collection or download a package.

Creating a collection requires constructing an object, as in `new List<string>()`. The parentheses call a **constructor**, which initializes the new object. You will study constructors and your own class definitions in Chapter 10. For now, you are using classes already supplied by the library, just as earlier examples used library methods.

Some modern C# projects import common namespaces automatically. Every runnable example here includes the imports it needs so you can run it independently. The following diagram shows three collection namespaces you may encounter, rather than a complete inventory of .NET collections.

:::{figure} ../../figures/collection_namespaces.svg
:width: 700

Selected .NET collection namespaces: generic collections, older non-generic collections, and concurrent collections.
:::

Prefer the generic collection classes for new code like the examples in this chapter. Older non-generic types, such as `ArrayList` and `Hashtable`, commonly store values through `object` and do not provide the same element-type checking. Recognizing their names can help you read older programs; learning them is not a separate requirement here.

Other library collections address additional needs. Sorted dictionaries and sorted sets maintain ordering by key or element, rather than merely remembering positions. Concurrent collections support coordinated access from multiple threads. Immutable collections produce updated versions without changing the original collection. These are additional dimensions of collection design, not extra families that you must master in this lesson.

headings.title: Similar Operations, Different Methods
body:
```{index} Similar Operations, Different Methods
```

(collection-operation-syntax)=

## Similar Operations, Different Methods


```{index} collection; operation comparison; method call; property; indexer
```
The families share familiar questions: how do we put an item in, inspect it, take it out, or count the items? Their method names express different rules for answering those questions. Connect each name to the operation you already understand before learning its spelling. This is a comparison map; the worked family examples below and Sections 8.3–8.4 develop the details.[^0801_collections-collection-operations]

The general syntax for calling an instance method is:

```text
collection.MethodName(argument1, argument2, ...);
resultType result = collection.MethodName(arguments);
```

These are syntax patterns, not programs to paste unchanged. `collection` stands for an existing collection variable; the dot selects a member. Replace `MethodName` with the actual name and supply the required arguments inside parentheses. A method with no arguments still needs `()`. Use the second pattern only when the method returns a value you want to store; `resultType` must match that value's type. Some methods change the collection, some return information, and some do both.

Properties and indexers have different syntax:

```text
int size = collection.Count;
elementType item = sequence[index];
valueType value = dictionary[key];
```

`Count` is a property, so it has no parentheses. An array uses `Length` instead. Square brackets select an array/list position or a dictionary key. `elementType` and `valueType` stand for the actual stored types, such as `string` or `int`. An index and a key are different ways to identify an item, even though both use brackets.

headings.title: Put In, Inspect, and Take Out
body:
```{index} Put In, Inspect, and Take Out
```

### Put In, Inspect, and Take Out


```{index} Add; Remove; RemoveAt; Push; Pop; Peek; Enqueue; Dequeue
```
The following table shows calls on variables named for their collection family. `item`, `key`, `value`, `index`, and `priority` represent values already available to the program. These calls are alternatives for different types, not one interchangeable API.

| Family | Put an item in | Inspect or retrieve | Take an item out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array, `T[]` | Fill an existing position: `array[index] = item` | `array[index]` | No operation shrinks this same array. |
| List, `List<T>` | `list.Add(item)`; `list.Insert(index, item)` | `list[index]` | `list.Remove(item)`; `list.RemoveAt(index)` |
| Linked list, `LinkedList<T>` | `linked.AddFirst(item)`; `linked.AddLast(item)` | `linked.First.Value` or `linked.Last.Value`, when nonempty | `linked.Remove(item)`; `linked.RemoveFirst()`; `linked.RemoveLast()` |
| Dictionary, `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` | `dictionary.Add(key, value)` | `dictionary[key]`, when the key exists | `dictionary.Remove(key)` |
| Set, `HashSet<T>` | `set.Add(item)` | `set.Contains(item)` tests membership | `set.Remove(item)` |
| Stack, `Stack<T>` | `stack.Push(item)` | `stack.Peek()` inspects the top | `stack.Pop()` removes **and returns** the top |
| Queue, `Queue<T>` | `queue.Enqueue(item)` | `queue.Peek()` inspects the front | `queue.Dequeue()` removes **and returns** the front |
| Priority queue, `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>` | `priorityQueue.Enqueue(item, priority)` | `priorityQueue.Peek()` inspects the next item | `priorityQueue.Dequeue()` removes **and returns** the next item |

`Add`, `Push`, and `Enqueue` all put an item into a collection, but they express different access policies. `Remove`, `Pop`, and `Dequeue` all remove something, but they do not select it in the same way or return the same kind of result. `Peek` reads the next item without removing it. With the default priority comparer, a lower priority value is selected first; equal priorities do not guarantee arrival order.

For a list, `Remove(item)` removes the first equal item and returns a Boolean indicating success. `RemoveAt(index)` removes the item at a position and returns no value. For an integer list, this distinction matters: `Remove(2)` searches for the **value** 2, whereas `RemoveAt(2)` selects the **third position**. A set's `Add` returns `false` for a duplicate. A dictionary's `Add` rejects a duplicate key, while `dictionary[key] = value` inserts a missing key or replaces its current value. Similar names do not guarantee identical behavior.

An array's fixed length is part of its contract. Replacing a slot is an update, not insertion; setting it to zero or null does not remove the slot. Creating another array or using a resizable list is a different operation.

headings.title: Size, Membership, and Safe Access
body:
```{index} Size, Membership, and Safe Access
```

### Size, Membership, and Safe Access


```{index} Count; Length; Contains; ContainsKey; TryGetValue; TryPop; TryDequeue
```
| Family | How many items? | Is this item or key present? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Array | `array.Length` | `Array.IndexOf(array, item) >= 0` for a one-dimensional array |
| List | `list.Count` | `list.Contains(item)` |
| Linked list | `linked.Count` | `linked.Contains(item)` |
| Dictionary | `dictionary.Count` | `dictionary.ContainsKey(key)` |
| Set | `set.Count` | `set.Contains(item)` |
| Stack | `stack.Count` | `stack.Contains(item)` |
| Queue | `queue.Count` | `queue.Contains(item)` |
| Priority queue | `priorityQueue.Count` | No direct `Contains` method; searching entries is a separate task. |

A membership test answers whether an item exists, not how quickly the search runs. The family demonstrations explain the different access patterns. `foreach` visits elements across these families, but its traversal order follows each type's contract; enumerating a priority queue is not guaranteed to produce priority order.

Before indexing an array or list, check the valid range. Before reading `linked.First.Value`, check that a first node exists. Before calling `Peek`, `Pop`, or `Dequeue`, consider the empty case. These calls throw when no item is available. The library also offers Boolean-returning alternatives: `TryPeek`, `TryPop` for stacks, and `TryDequeue` for queues. Priority queues offer `TryPeek` and `TryDequeue` with both element and priority outputs. Dictionaries offer `TryGetValue` for a key that might be absent.

Their general pattern is:

```text
if (dictionary.TryGetValue(key, out valueType value))
{
    // Use value only after the lookup succeeds.
}
```

`out` allows the method to supply a value through an argument. Here the Boolean result tells the `if` whether the lookup succeeded. Section 8.4 develops this lookup pattern with runnable examples. You do not need to memorize every `Try` signature now; recognize the shared idea of checking success before using a result.

**Make the connections:** A basket needs to add and remove a chosen item; an undo history needs to remove the most recent action; a service line needs to remove the earliest arrival. Explain why these related needs lead to `Add`/`Remove`, `Push`/`Pop`, and `Enqueue`/`Dequeue`. Then identify which operations change size and which only inspect data. Use the following examples to check your predictions.

body:
```{index} Collection Examples
```

## Collection Examples


```{index} collections; examples
```
You now have the family map, the idea of a collection contract, and a way to explain a choice. The following examples make those ideas concrete. For each one, identify what is stored and predict how the collection retrieves it before running the code. The detailed list and dictionary lessons follow in Sections 8.3 and 8.4.
The next example retains the explicit type names so you can see both choices. It stores employee names in a list and associates names with training scores in a dictionary. The commented line illustrates a type mismatch; leave it commented when running the demonstration.

headings.title: Arrays and Lists
body:
```{index} Arrays and Lists
```

### Arrays and Lists


```{index} array; list; index; sequence
```
A **sequence** gives its elements positions. In the arrays and lists used here, positions are indexed from zero. Both can contain repeated values. Their order is the order of the sequence, which is not necessarily sorted order.

An array's length remains fixed after creation, but its elements can change. Fixed length does not mean read-only data. A list manages storage as elements are added or removed. Its `Count` reports the number of elements currently in the list; an array uses `Length`.

Read this example as a comparison of behavior. The weekly array still has five positions after a correction. The basket grows when a second item is added, and it retains the order of those additions.
Use an array when a fixed number of indexed positions expresses the task clearly. Use a list when the sequence changes size during normal work. A list is not automatically the best choice simply because it is more flexible: the fixed five-day structure can make the meaning of the array clear. Likewise, repeatedly replacing arrays just to add another basket item makes ordinary work harder than it needs to be.

**Check Your Understanding:** Does changing Tuesday's quantity require a list? What change to the task would make a list more useful?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
No. Replacing an existing array element does not change the array's length. A list becomes more useful if you are collecting an unknown or changing number of daily records, rather than maintaining exactly five positions.
```

headings.title: Linked Lists
body:
```{index} Linked Lists
```

### Linked Lists


```{index} linked list; node
```
A **linked list** organizes a sequence as **nodes**, each holding an element and links to neighboring nodes. .NET's `LinkedList<T>` is doubly linked: a node can refer to both its previous and its next node. You do not use `steps[1]` to retrieve its second element. You traverse the sequence or work with a node reference.[^0801_collections-linked-list]

Imagine a sequence of order-processing steps. After locating the packing step, you discover that a gift-check step belongs immediately after it. In the example below, `AddLast` returns a reference to the new node; `AddAfter` uses that reference to choose an insertion point. `var` asks C# to infer the node variable's type from the returned value.
The result is still an ordered sequence, but it has different access operations from an indexed list. Inserting beside a node you already hold avoids shifting later elements. Finding that node can still require a search, and nodes have storage overhead. A linked list is therefore not a universal replacement for `List<T>`. Chapter 14 develops these tradeoffs and their implementations.

headings.title: Dictionaries
body:
```{index} Dictionaries
```

### Dictionaries


```{index} dictionary; key; value; key-value pair
```
A **dictionary** associates a **key**, which identifies an entry, with a **value**, which is the information stored for that key. A stock lookup might use a product code as the key and an integer quantity as the value. Unlike a list index, the code expresses identity rather than position.

Keys are unique within a dictionary: one key cannot identify two separate entries. Values do not have to be unique. Two products may have the same stock quantity without being the same product. Here both codes initially map to `12`, and the program retrieves a quantity by code.
The expression `stock["NOTEBOOK"]` asks for a value associated with a key. It does not ask for the first, second, or alphabetically earliest entry. A dictionary is not an alphabetically sorted list, and you should not make a report depend on its enumeration order. You also need a policy for unknown codes; Section 8.4 teaches safe lookup and the difference between adding an entry and updating one.

headings.title: Sets
body:
```{index} Sets
```

### Sets


```{index} set; membership; uniqueness
```
A **set** stores distinct elements and emphasizes **membership**, meaning whether an element is present. Adding an equal element again does not create another copy. A set therefore answers a different question from a list: "Which customers participated?" rather than "What were all the participation events?"

If a customer uses a promotion twice, a list can record both events, while a set can record that customer's participation once. In this demonstration, `Add` returns `false` for the repeated value because no new element was added. `Contains` asks whether an element is in the set.
A set does not preserve the number of times a value appeared. If you need that number, a dictionary can associate each customer with a count. A `HashSet<T>` also does not promise sorted enumeration. Chapter 19 explains hashing, equality, and set operations; here you only need to recognize the membership and uniqueness contract.

**Check Your Understanding:** A list contains the product codes `PEN`, `PEN`, and `NOTEBOOK`. Would a set be a suitable replacement for the basket? Would it be suitable for the distinct products included in a promotion report?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
A set would lose the repeated PEN entry, so it would not preserve a basket that uses repeated entries to represent quantity. It would be suitable for a report asking only which distinct product codes appeared. The choice depends on whether duplicates carry information.
```

headings.title: Processing Order
body:
```{index} Processing Order
```

(rules-for-processing-work)=

### Processing Order


```{index} processing order; stack; queue; priority queue
```
Sometimes the important question is which item should leave the collection next. A list lets you choose a position, but that freedom puts the responsibility for enforcing the processing rule on your program. A stack or queue expresses a particular rule through its operations.

These structures do not decide an organization's policy for you. If requests should be handled in arrival order, choose a collection that expresses that policy. If urgency should take precedence, make the urgency rule explicit and choose a different structure.

headings.title: Stacks and Queues
body:
```{index} Stacks and Queues
```

### Stacks and Queues


```{index} last in first out; first in first out; push; pop; enqueue; dequeue
```
A **stack** follows **last in, first out (LIFO)**. `Push` adds an item at the top; `Pop` removes and returns the top item. Think of an undo history: the most recent action should normally be the first action undone. Storing a description of an action is only a demonstration of ordering; a real undo feature also needs a way to reverse that action.

A **queue** follows **first in, first out (FIFO)**. `Enqueue` adds an item at the back; `Dequeue` removes and returns the item at the front. This expresses an arrival-order service line.

Both collections below receive `Order A` followed by `Order B`. Predict which order each returns before running the example.
Removing an item changes the collection: each now has one item left. `Peek` lets you inspect the next item without removing it. Removing from an empty stack or queue requires a separate check or a suitable `Try...` operation; this example establishes that both are nonempty before removal. Chapter 15 develops safe operations and practical applications.

The FIFO rule is an ordering rule, not a complete definition of fairness. For example, an arrival-order queue does not by itself accommodate an urgent safety issue. You still need to decide whether arrival order expresses the policy the task actually requires.

headings.title: Priority Queues
body:
```{index} Priority Queues
```

### Priority Queues


```{index} priority queue; priority
```
A **priority queue** chooses the next item using a priority value rather than its arrival position. In .NET's default `PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority>`, the item with the **lowest priority value** is removed first. A smaller number therefore means earlier processing in this example. This is a convention you must define for the application, not an automatic interpretation of what "high priority" means.[^0801_collections-priority-queue]

Each insertion supplies two pieces of information: the element to store and its priority. A routine request arrives first, but the urgent request leaves first because its priority value is smaller.
The removed items follow the priority rule even though they arrived in another order. A priority queue does not guarantee FIFO order among items with equal priority. If arrival order must break ties, the application needs an explicit tie-breaking rule. The unique priorities in this example avoid that ambiguity. Chapter 18 develops priorities and heap implementations.

**Check Your Understanding:** Which collection fits each task: undo the latest edit, serve the earliest waiting request, or process the smallest urgency number first?

```{dropdown} Suggested Answer
Use a stack for the latest edit, a queue for arrival-order requests, and a priority queue for the smallest urgency value. All three may store the same element type; the difference is the retrieval rule.
```

headings.title: Traversal and Shared References
body:
```{index} Traversal and Shared References
```

## Traversal and Shared References


```{index} traversal; enumeration; IEnumerable; reference; alias; mutation
```
**Traversal**, also called **enumeration**, means visiting a collection's elements. `foreach` provides familiar syntax for this work, but the order and the kind of element you receive depend on the collection. Arrays and lists follow their sequence order. A dictionary enumerates key/value entries. A set supports enumeration, but its purpose is membership rather than sorted traversal. `PriorityQueue` is a special case: it exposes an `UnorderedItems` view for enumeration instead of supporting `foreach` directly on the queue. That view does not promise priority order; use successive removals when you need that order.

The enumerable collection types demonstrated here implement `IEnumerable<T>`, an interface describing how to enumerate values.[^0801_collections-collection-interface] You do not need to write an interface to use these library collections. Later chapters explain how a type can provide this capability itself. Also distinguish traversal from removal: looping through a queue with `foreach` does not serve and remove its waiting items.

Here a traversal computes a total without changing the stored quantities. The accumulator starts at zero, so an empty list would produce a total of zero.
The mutable library collection classes shown here are **reference types**. A variable refers to a collection object. Assigning that variable to another variable copies the reference, rather than making a second collection. Two names for the same object are **aliases**. Arrays have reference behavior too; this continues the idea introduced in Chapter 7.

Consider a basket shown in two parts of a program. If both variables refer to the same basket, adding an item through one variable is visible through the other. If you need a separate snapshot of a list's elements, you must explicitly create a new collection.
`basket` and `sameBasket` refer to one list containing two strings. `snapshot` is a different list containing the one string that was present when it was created. This is a copy of the elements, not a general promise to duplicate every object an element might refer to. Chapter 11 revisits that distinction with objects and composition.

Mutation means changing an existing object's state, such as adding to a list. Reassigning a variable to a different list is a different action. This distinction matters when collections are passed to methods or shared between parts of a program. An operation can affect more code than the variable name immediately in front of you suggests.

You should also check whether an operation is valid during traversal. In particular, adding or removing list elements inside a `foreach` over that same list invalidates its enumeration. Section 8.3 shows a safe removal pattern. A short loop can still be incorrect if it ignores the collection's operating rules.
**Interactive Exercise: An Order Summary**

A small order contains quantities `2`, `1`, and `3`. The starter stores them in a `List<int>`. Compute the total with `foreach` and store that total under the key `"ORD-101"` in a `Dictionary<string, int>`. Print the entry count and the saved total. Expected output is `Line items: 3` and `Saved total: 6` on separate lines.

After running your code, explain why the quantities form a list and why the saved summary uses a dictionary. Change the list to be empty and predict both results before running it again.
The list stores a sequence of quantities, including any repeated quantities. The dictionary associates an order's identity with its total. With an empty list, the entry count and calculated total are both zero. The dictionary still has one entry because the program saves that zero total under `ORD-101`; no line items is different from no saved summary.

headings.title: Summary
body:
```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

Collections combine stored values with rules for using them. Arrays and lists provide indexed sequences; linked lists organize nodes; dictionaries support key-based lookup; sets emphasize uniqueness and membership; stacks, queues, and priority queues determine what comes next. Generic type arguments specify the types of stored elements, keys, values, or priorities.

Choose the collection by explaining the task's access pattern, ordering, duplicates, and changes in size. Then check the details of its contract. The following sections put that reasoning into practice with lists and dictionaries.

Microsoft Learn. Accessed October 16, 2026. Arrays are fine if you know ahead of time how long your sequence of items is.
Then you create your array with that length, and you are all set.

If you want a variable sized container, you are likely to want a `List`.
List is a type of collection that is used when the number of elements is unknown.
As with arrays, you might want a collection of any particular type.
Unfortunately, you cannot use the simple notation of arrays to specify
the type of element in a `List`. Array syntax is
*built into* the language. Lists are handled in the *library* of types
provided by C# from .NET.
There are many situations where one general operation should work with different element types.

```{index} generics < > for generics
```

A bookstore basket starts empty and changes as a customer selects or cancels items. We need the indexed access and traversal learned with arrays, but we cannot predict the final number of items. The big idea is a **resizable ordered sequence**: `List<T>` provides indexed positions while managing changes in size.

Follow one distinction throughout this lesson: changing a value at an existing position is an update; inserting or removing an item changes the sequence and can change later positions. Use the operation comparison in {ref}`collection-operation-syntax` as a map while learning these calls.

The library operation contracts are documented in the .NET API reference.[^0802_list-list-api]

## Generics

C# collection types use *generics*: a type in angle brackets after a class name tells the compiler what element type the collection holds. The generic collection types live in the `System.Collections.Generic` namespace, which some project templates import through implicit usings. Include `using System.Collections.Generic;` when those imports are not enabled.

The generic list syntax is:

```csharp
List<T>
```

To create a list, supply a type argument for the elements it will store:
The declaration and construction patterns are:

```text
List<elementType> name = new List<elementType>();
List<elementType> name = new List<elementType> { item1, item2 };
List<elementType> copy = new List<elementType>(existingSequence);
```

These are templates. Replace `elementType` with a type such as `string` and supply actual values. Angle brackets choose the stored type. Parentheses supply constructor arguments; an empty argument list creates an empty list. The initializer's braces supply starting items. Copying into a new list differs from assigning another variable to the same list; the last example copies the elements into a new outer collection.
```{index} List; basics
```

headings.title: Lists Basics
body:
```{index} Lists Basics
```

## Lists Basics

A `List<T>` starts with an element type and then supports the everyday sequence operations you expect: add an item, count the items, read an item by index, and loop through the items. The index rules are the same as arrays: the first item is at index `0`.
A list can also be initialized with values. A `for` loop is useful when the index is part of the output or logic; a `foreach` loop is simpler when you only need each value.

`Count` is the number of stored elements. `Capacity` is the number of positions reserved internally before another growth allocation is needed; it can exceed `Count`. `Clear()` removes the elements but normally keeps that reserved capacity. Use `Count` for valid element indexes, not `Capacity`. You do not need to tune capacity for the examples in this chapter.

## Common Pitfall: Modifying a List While Iterating

`foreach` keeps an internal position in the list as it loops. Adding or removing elements through that same list while a `foreach` is still running invalidates that position, and C# detects it: the loop throws an `InvalidOperationException` rather than silently skipping or duplicating elements.

Loop over the indices backwards instead, so removing an element does not disturb the indices you still need to visit. (`List<T>` also has a `RemoveAll` method that removes every matching element in one call — it is explained once you have seen the lambda syntax it takes, in a later chapter.)

headings.title: Dictionaries
body:
# Dictionaries

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
We have explored several ways of storing a collection of the same type of data:

- arrays: built-in syntax, unchanging size of the collection
- List: generic class type, allows the size of the collection to grow

Both approaches allow reference to data elements using a
numerical index between square brackets, as in `words[i]`.
The index provides an order for the elements,
but there is no meaning to the index beyond the sequence order.

Sometimes, we want to look up data based on a more meaningful key, as in a
dictionary: given a word, you can look up the definition.

C# uses the type name [Dictionary](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-8.0), but with greater generality than in
nontechnical use. In a regular dictionary, you start with a word,
and look up the definition. The generalization is to have some piece of
data that leads you to (or *maps* to) another piece of data.
The computer science jargon is that a **key** leads you to a **value**.
In a normal dictionary, these are both likely to be strings, but in the
C# generalization, the possible types of key and value are much more extensive.
Hence the generic `Dictionary` type requires you to specify
*both a type for the key and a type for the value*.

A stock clerk knows a product code, not its position in a list. Searching for that code and coordinating a separate quantity list is unnecessary work when the program can directly associate the code with its quantity. The big idea is a **key-to-value association**. Retrieval, updating stock, and counting repeated requests all reuse that association.

Keep three questions separate: Is the key present? What value belongs to it? Does this operation insert a new entry or update an existing one? Keys identify entries; they are not sequence positions. The examples below retain the translation dictionary, then transfer the same pattern to counting.

```{figure} ../../figures/dictionary_key_value.svg
:alt: Product keys PEN and BOOK lead to stock quantities. Updating PEN from 12 to 15 changes a value without increasing the dictionary count of two.

A stable key can select a changing value.
```

Follow the arrow from key to value. The diagram does not promise enumeration order or any physical storage layout.

The library operation contracts are documented in the .NET API reference.[^0803_dictionary-dictionary-api]
```{index} Creating a Dictionary
```

## Creating a Dictionary

We can initialize an English-Spanish dictionary `e2sp` with


That is quite a mouthful! The C# `var` keyword (implicitly-typed local variable) syntax
is handy to shorten it as you do not have to repeat the type name:


The general generic type syntax therefore is:

> `Dictionary<` **keyType**`,` **valueType** `>`

For example, if you are counting the number of repetitions of words in a document, you are
likely to want a `Dictionary` mapping each word to its number of repetitions so far:


If your friends all have a personal list of phone numbers, you might look them up
with a dictionary with a string name for the key and a `List` of personal phone number
strings for the value. The type could be `Dictionary<string, List<string>>`.
This example illustrates how one generic type can be built on another.

There is no restriction on the value type. Keys need stable equality and hash behavior while stored; immutable keys such as strings make that easier to ensure. See {ref}`dictionary-efficiency`.

## Accessing Data in Dictionary

General syntax, using an existing dictionary:

```text
dictionary.Add(key, value);          // Insert a new key; reject a duplicate.
dictionary[key] = value;             // Insert or replace.
valueType found = dictionary[key];   // Key must exist.
bool exists = dictionary.ContainsKey(key);
bool removed = dictionary.Remove(key);
dictionary.Clear();
```

Brackets select a key, not an integer position. `key` and `value` must match the declared type arguments. Removal takes a key and reports success. `Clear` empties the same dictionary object; assignment to a new dictionary is a different action. The runnable examples below show both ordinary usage and the missing/duplicate-key mistakes.

Similar to an array or `List`, you can assign and reference elements of
a `Dictionary`, using square bracket notation. The difference is that the
reference is through a key, not a sequential index, as in:


or, you can use the Dictionary.Add() method:

```{index} dictionary; duplicate key
```

Unlike the indexer, `Add` does not overwrite an existing key — it throws an `ArgumentException` if the key is already present, since `Add` is meant for inserting a brand-new entry:
A dictionary does not automatically print its entries when you pass the dictionary object itself to `Console.WriteLine`. In application code, display the size with `Count`, access individual values by key, or loop through the entries.
```{index} dictionary; Keys Keys property
```

If you want to iterate through a whole `Dictionary`, you will want the syntax below,
with `foreach` and the property `Keys`:
To loop through the dictionary and access both the key and value in each entry, you may do:
In this example, we use an implicitly-typed variable `entry` to ask the compiler to infer the type.
We then use the .Key and .Value properties to refer to the data.

The documentation for `Dictionary` says
that you cannot depend on the order of processing with `foreach`, though the present
implementation remembers the order in which keys were added.

```{index} dictionary; ContainsKey
```

```

body:

```

## Properties and Methods in Dictionary

The Dictionary class provides properties and methods such as `Count`, `Keys`, `Values`, and `Add`. The `Key` and `Value` properties used during traversal belong to each entry.

It is often useful to know if a key is already in a `Dictionary`:
Note the method `ContainsKey`:

In the traversal above, `Key` and `Value` belong to each `KeyValuePair` entry, not to the dictionary itself. `Count`, `Keys`, and `Values` are dictionary properties. Read a trace of an update before trying more methods:

| Operation, starting empty | Entries afterward | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stock.Add("PEN", 12)` | PEN → 12 | 1 |
| `stock["BOOK"] = 5` | PEN → 12; BOOK → 5 | 2 |
| `stock["PEN"] = 15` | PEN → 15; BOOK → 5 | 2 |
| `stock.Remove("BOOK")` | PEN → 15 | 1 |

The row order describes program steps, not a promised dictionary enumeration order. Updating a known key does not add another copy of that key.

```{index} dictionary; KeyNotFoundException
```

Looking up a key that is not present with the indexer throws a `KeyNotFoundException`:

```{index} dictionary; TryGetValue
```

Checking `ContainsKey` and then indexing looks up the key twice. `TryGetValue` does both in one step: it returns `true` and sets an `out` variable to the value if the key is present, or returns `false` without throwing if it is not. This is the idiomatic way to look up a key you are not sure is there:

The method `Remove` takes a key as parameter. Like a `List` and other
collections, a `Dictionary` has a `Clear` method:

headings.title: Guided Practice: Update Stock Safely

Use `The pen, pen and book!` first. The ignore set excludes articles, `and`, and empty strings produced by adjacent separators. Normalization turns words into lowercase before using them as keys.

| Token | Decision | Counted entries afterward |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the | Ignore | None |
| pen | New key | pen → 1 |
| empty token | Ignore | pen → 1 |
| pen | Existing key: increment | pen → 2 |
| and | Ignore | pen → 2 |
| book | New key | pen → 2; book → 1 |
| trailing empty token | Ignore | Unchanged |

Follow one iteration per row. The important connection is the same insert/update distinction used for stock: a new word starts at 1; a repeated word updates its existing count. The ignore set answers membership; the dictionary associates each word with a number; a list of keys supplies a sortable reporting sequence.
The report prints `book: 1`, `pen: 2`, and `Distinct counted words: 2`. Dictionary traversal does not supply the report order: the copied key list is explicitly sorted. This runnable variation uses invariant lowercasing and ordinal sorting for a reproducible simple example; production word processing needs explicit language and tokenization policies. The original functions above remain available for comparison.

Notice the side effect: `ignore.Add("")` changes the caller's ignore set. Both the retained original and this runnable version do that. Before reuse, decide whether the function should be permitted to change its input collection; copying the set or skipping empty tokens locally are alternatives. Do not silently assume a method that returns a dictionary leaves all its inputs unchanged.

(dictionary-efficiency)=

## Dictionary Efficiency

You could simulate a `Dictionary` fairly easily by keeping a `List` of keys and a parallel `List` of values, in the same order. You would find the entry for a key with:

```csharp
int i = keys.IndexOf(key);
return values[i];
```

Searching through a `List` this way takes time proportional to the length of the `List` — *linear order*. Through an implementation covered in data structures courses, a `Dictionary` instead uses a *hash table*, which makes the average lookup time *constant order*: roughly the same speed whether the dictionary holds ten entries or ten million. The key's equality and hash behavior must stay stable while it is stored; the whole object need not be immutable if unrelated state changes do not affect those operations. Hash lookup is expected constant-time under suitable hashing assumptions, not an unconditional timing guarantee.

To make the data *persistent* past the end of program execution, data are stored in file system or databases (for structured data). Although a database maybe preferred in many cases, there will be times that you need to read and write files for various purposes. A file is a collection of data stored on in a storage device with a name and directory path information. A file is stored in your file system, which is part of the operating system (OS), and the OS therefore has the information about the file and how to access it. ```{index} File Stream ```

## File Stream


In .NET, file and stream I/O (input/output) refers to the transfer of data either to or from a
storage medium. The System.IO namespaces contain types that enable reading and writing,
both synchronously and asynchronously, on data streams and files, in addition to other file and stream operations.

You have already read and written streams of
characters to the `Console`. Most of the syntax that we use for files will be very similar, using
methods `ReadLine`, `WriteLine`, and `Write` in the same way you used them for the `Console`.

When you read/write a file in C# program, the data processed is seen as a **Stream**.
A stream is a sequence of bytes of data sent between the destination and the source of
the file. Streams are how data is read and written to and from files, networks, and
computer memory. For example, printing data using a printer involves sending a sequence
of bytes of data to a stream associated with a network port connected to the printer.
```{index} File handling process
```

### File handling process


For file handling operations, there are two obvious streams:

1.  The **Input Stream** that is used to read data from a file (read operation).
2.  The **Output Stream** that is used to write data into a file (write operation).

However, different task processes use different type of streams: text files, binary files,
strings, and network communications are some of the examples. The basic
stream operations therefore include the following:

1.  Creation/Opening
2.  Reading
3.  Writing
4.  Positioning
5.  Closing
```{index} The System.IO namespace
```

### The `System.IO` namespace


Files can be handled very differently by different operating systems, but
C# abstracts away the differences and provides stream interfaces between
a C# program and files through the `System.IO namespace` ({ref}`namespace <namespace>`). The System.IO namespace
contains the required classes used to handle the input and output streams and provide information
about file and directory structure.

The [System.IO namespace](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io?view=net-8.0) lists all
the classes available for use. The [File class](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.file?view=net-8.0)
is one of the classes that provides static methods for the creation, copying, deletion, moving, and
opening of a single file, and aids in the creation of FileStream objects.

Classes that are commonly used to for file handling include:
- The `FileStream` class
- Convenience class: `File` class
- Helper class: `StreamWriter`
- Helper class: `StreamReader`

```{index} Simple File Handling: File Class
```

## Simple File Handling: `File` Class


Among the file handling methods is the convenience class `File`, which provides `static methods` for the creation,
copying, deletion, moving, and opening of a single file, and aids in the creation of `FileStream` objects. For example,
the Create(), WriteAllText, ReadAllText() and File.Exists() can be used to perform basic file operations
among other methods:

**Methods in File Class**

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `AppendText()` | Appends text at the end of an existing file |
| `Copy()` | Copies a file |
| `Create()` | Creates or overwrites a file |
| `Delete()` | Deletes a file |
| `Exists()` | Tests whether the file exists |
| `ReadAllText()` | Reads the contents of a file |
| `Replace()` | Replaces the contents of a file with the contents of another file |
| `WriteAllText()` | Creates a new file and writes the contents to it. If the file already exists, it will be overwritten. |

Sine class `File` provides `static methods`, we can `call` the methods directly by using the `dot notation`
without having to create a new instance of the class. For example, with `File` class, when you want to write
some content to a file, you can simply say `File.ReadAllText(string path, string content)` to write the
string content to the path file.

You can perform tests such as the following in a small VS Code project to get familiar with the methods:

1.  Create a file using `File.Create (path)`: // path means filename + the file's directory path

        > File.Create("MyTest.txt");

2.  Check if a file exists using `File.Exists (path)`:

        > if (File.Exists("MyTest.txt"))
          {
             Console.WriteLine("MyTest.txt exists");
          }
        MyTest.txt exists

3.  Write to a file using `File.WriteAllText (path, content)`:

        > File.WriteAllText("MyTest.txt", "Hello, this is a test.");

4.  Read from a file using `File.ReadAllText(path)`:

        > File.ReadAllText("MyTest.txt");

        > Console.WriteLine(File.ReadAllText("MyTest.txt"));
        Hello, this is a test.

        >

To better organize the tests above, use VS Code and a small console project. You should
also use a variable for the filename:

## `StreamWriter`

The `FileStream` class provides a `stream` of bytes[] of data for file operations, supporting both synchronous
and asynchronous read and write operations. To use the FileStream class in C#, first of all,
you need to include the `System.IO namespace` and then you need to create an
`instance` of the FileStream class in order to use its functionalities to, for example,
create a new file or to open an existing file.

For handling files, the `StreamWriter` class is more popular in writing files
and it is very helpful in writing text data into a file. It is easy to use and provides
a complete set of constructors [^0902_file_operations-constructor] and methods to work on it. Specifically,
the `StreamWriter` class in C# is used for writing characters to stream in a particular format.

```{index} Writing Files

Observe the following program (`first_file.cs`):


Look at the code:

- The `System.IO` namespace:
  : - Namespace: Note the `using System.IO` namespace being used at the top. It gives the program
      access to the functionalities in the System.IO namespace. For your current concern,
      this means a number of classes that contains many **methods** that you use.
    - You will always need to be using `System.IO` when working with files. Here is a slightly
      different use of a dot, `.`, to indicate a *subsidiary* namespace. Under System.IO,
      there are plenty of classes (with methods defined inside) for system IO operations,
      such as:
      \- File,
      \- StreamWriter,
      \- FileStream,
      \- StreamReader,
      \- Directory,
      \- Path, etc.

- The StreamWriter Class:
  : - variable: The first line of the body of `Main` creates a `StreamWriter`
      object assigned to the variable `writer`.
    - A `StreamWriter` links C# to your computer's file system for writing, not reading.
    - Files are objects, like a Random, and you use the `new` syntax to create a new one.
    - The StreamWriter class parameter ("constructor", to be covered in later chapters)
      gives the name of the file to connect to the program, `sample.txt`, which is the
      same as the file name we saw created by the program.

    :::{warning}
    If the file already existed, the old contents are *destroyed* silently by creating a `StreamWriter`.
    :::

- writer.WriteLine():
  The writer variable is of data type (or just type) StreamWriter and
  StreamWriter has method WriteLine() just like the Console class. The difference is that
  Console.WriteLine writes to the console/terminal, whereas StreamWriter.WriteLine writes
  out a data stream to a file followed by a newline character.

  ```{index} StreamWriter; format string StreamWriter; Write
  ```

  :::{note}
  Just as you can use a {ref}`Format-Strings` with
  functions `Write` and `WriteLine` of the `Console` class,
  you can also use a format string with the corresponding methods of a
  `StreamWriter`, and embed fields by using braces in
  the format string.
  :::

- writer.Close():
  The Close() method closes the current StreamWriter object and the underlying stream.
  The Close() method is important for cleaning up. Until this line, this C# program
  controls the file, and nothing may be actually written to the operating system file
  yet: Since initiating a file operation is thousands of times slower than memory
  operations, C# *buffers* data, saving small amounts and writing a larger chunk all at once.

  :::{warning}
  The call to the `Close` method is essential for C# to make sure everything is really
  written, and to relinquish control of the file for use by other programs. It is a common bug
  to write a program where you have the code to add all the data you
  want to a file, but the program does not end up creating a file.
  Usually this means you forgot to close the file!
  :::

## Reading to End of Stream

In `first_file.cs`, we explicitly coded reading two lines. You will often
want to process each line in a file, without knowing the total number of
lines at the time when you were programming. This means that files provide us with our
second kind of a `sequence`: the sequence of lines in the file!
To process all of them will require a loop and a new test to make sure that you
have not yet come to the end of the file's stream: You can use the `EndOfStream`
property. It has the wrong sense (true at the end of the file), so we negate it,
testing for `!reader.EndOfStream` to *continue* reading.
The example program `print_file_lines.cs` below reads and prints the contents of
a file specified by the user, one line at a time:

```{index} var type; var
```

`var`

> For conciseness (and variety) we declared `reader`
> using the more compact syntax with `var`:
>
> ```
> var reader = new StreamReader(userFileName);
> ```
>
> You can use `var` in place of a declared type to shorten your code
> with a couple of restrictions:
>
> - Use an initializer, from which the type of the variable can be inferred.
> - Declare a local variable inside a method body or in a loop heading.
> - Declare only a single variable in the statement.
>
> We could have used this syntax long ago, but as the type names become longer,
> it is more useful!

You can run this program. You need an existing file to read. An obvious file is
the source file itself: {file}`print_file_lines.cs`. Or, if you have implemented/tested
the files by placing the code in your `Program.cs`, you may use the `sample.txt` file
here. In the latter case, you should see:

```
Enter name of file to print: sample.txt
This program is writing
our first file.
```

Things to note about reading from files:

```{index} StreamReader; null from ReadLine
```

- Reading from a file returns the part read, of course. Never forget the
  *side effect*: The location in the file advances past the part just read.
  The next read does *not* return the *same* thing as last time. It returns
  the *next* part of the file.
- Our `while` test conditions so far have been in a sense "backward looking":
  We have tested a variable that has *already been set*.
  The test with `EndOfStream` is *forward looking*: looking at what has not
  been processed yet. Other than making sure the file is opened, there is no
  variable that needs to be set before a `while` loop testing for `EndOfStream`.
- If you use ReadLine at the end of the file, the special value `null` (no object)
  is returned. *This* is not an error, but if you try to apply any string methods
  to the `null` value returned, *then* you get an error!

lines, it was very verbose considering the final effect of the program,
just to print the whole file.

## Run a Complete File Lifetime in an Owned Workspace
A report has two different identities: its contents and its location. Reading valid quantities from the wrong file is still a failed workflow. Start by constructing one known path, use it consistently, and make ownership of temporary files explicit. This connects Chapter 6's cleanup policy with the stream operations introduced in the preceding section.

`Path.Combine(directory, fileName)` returns a string using the platform's path rules. It does not create a directory or a file. `Directory.CreateDirectory(path)` creates the directory if needed. The general using-statement form is a syntax pattern:

```text
using (ResourceType name = acquireResource())
{
    statementsThatUse(name);
}
```

The closing brace marks disposal of the acquired resource. The related declaration form, `using ResourceType name = acquireResource();`, keeps the resource until the end of its enclosing scope. Choose the scope deliberately: a writer must be disposed before another operation relies on its completed output.

This example creates a uniquely named temporary directory owned by this run, writes two lines, closes the writer, reads those lines, closes the reader, and deletes only that owned directory. It does not overwrite a student's report or depend on a preexisting file.
Each using block releases its stream when the block ends, even if processing leaves it because of an exception. The outer finally attempts workspace cleanup after the streams have been disposed. Cleanup can itself fail in a real application; finally does not grant permissions or guarantee that a disk operation will succeed.

| Point in this program | Resource state | What is established |
| --- | --- | --- |
| After constructing reportPath | No report opened yet | A location string exists |
| Inside writer block | Writer open | Lines are being written |
| After writer block | Writer disposed | Buffered output has been finalized normally |
| Inside reader block | Reader open | The same path is being consumed |
| After reader block | Reader disposed | No stream from this example remains open |
| After finally succeeds | Owned directory removed | The example's temporary files are gone |

`Exists` being true does not prove that the report contains valid business data. Conversely, an exception while opening a missing input does not mean that a report contains zero records. Keep “no readable input” separate from “readable input containing no rows.”

## Separate a File's Location from Its Contents

A report can contain perfectly valid text and still fail to open because its path names the wrong location. A relative path is interpreted from the process's working directory, which need not be the directory containing the source file. Before changing your parsing code, establish which file the program is actually trying to open.

The resource workflow is a sequence: choose the location, acquire the resource, process data, and release the resource. Reading and writing are separate contracts. Overwriting a report, appending a new entry, and reading an existing log are not interchangeable operations just because they share a path.

| Question | Example consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Is the path relative or absolute? | Running from another working directory can select another file |
| Must the file already exist? | A missing input is different from a new output |
| May existing contents be replaced? | Opening the wrong write mode can destroy a previous report |
| Who owns the open resource? | Cleanup must occur even if processing stops early |

Use Path.Combine to assemble path components for the current platform rather than hard-coding one separator convention. This constructs a path string; it does not create directories, grant permissions, or prove that an input file exists. Likewise, checking existence before opening cannot guarantee that a later open succeeds: resource state can change between those operations.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Bound Resource Lifetime Explicitly
```

body:
