## Bound Resource Lifetime Explicitly

A StreamReader or StreamWriter owns resources that must be disposed. A using statement or declaration expresses that lifetime. The general declaration form is `using ResourceType name = acquisitionExpression;`; this is a syntax pattern. Processing statements use that acquired resource inside its permitted scope. Disposal handles resource release; it does not establish that every record was valid or that a business transaction completed successfully.

For an input import, distinguish two outcomes: the resource cannot be opened, or a particular line has invalid data. The first may prevent the whole import. The second may permit recording the line number and continuing, if that is the stated policy. Do not catch an unavailable-file exception and silently report that zero valid records were found; zero records and no readable input are different outcomes.

Guided scenario: a program writes the first two report lines and then fails on the third. What does cleanup guarantee, and what does it not guarantee? It releases owned resources during normal exception unwinding, but it does not magically restore the previous complete report. Reliable replacement may require writing a separate temporary file and a deliberate publication step. That design is an extension; recognizing partial output is already part of understanding the current contract.

## Path Strings


When a program is running, there is alway a *current directory* (or,
**present working directory**, `pwd`). Files in the present working directory can
be referred to by their simple names, e.g., *sample.txt*, so
project files can be referred to by their simple names because they are in the same
directory.

Referring to files not in the current directory is more complicated.
You should be aware from using the Windows Explorer or the macOS Finder that
files and directories are located in a hierarchy of directories in the
file system. On a Mac, the file system is unified in
one hierarchy. On Windows, each storage drive has its own hierarchy.

```{index} path separator
```

Files are generally referred to by a chain of directories before
the final name of the file desired. A *path string* (or simply **path**) is used
to represent such a sequence of names. Elements of the directory chain are separated
by operating system specific punctuation symbols: In Windows the separator is
backslash, `\`, and on a Mac it is (forward) slash, `/`. For example, on a Mac the path

```none
/Users/anh
```

starts with a /, meaning the **root** or top directory in the hierarchy, and Users is
a subdirectory, and anh is a subdirectory of Users (in this case the home directory
for the user with login anh). It is similar with Windows, except there may be a drive
in the beginning, and the separator is a \\, so

```none
C:\Windows\System32
```

is on C: drive; Windows is a subdirectory of the root directory \\, and System32 is
a subdirectory of Windows. Each drive in Windows has a separate file hierarchy
underneath it.

```{index} path; absolute
```

Paths starting from the root of a file system, with `\` or `/` are called
**absolute paths** or **full paths** because they begin with the root of the file hierarchy.
Since there is always a current directory, it makes sense to allow a path to be *relative*
to the current directory. In that case do *not* start with the slash that would
indicate the root directory. For example, if the current directory is
your user home directory, you likely have a subdirectory {file}`Downloads`, and the
{file}`Downloads` directory might contain {file}`examples.zip`. From the home directory,
this file could be referred to as {file}`Downloads\\examples.zip` in Windows or
{file}`Downloads/examples.zip` on a Mac.

Referring to files in the current directory just by their plain file name is
actually an example of using relative paths.

```{index} parent folder (..)
```

With relative paths, you sometimes want to move up the directory hierarchy: `..`
(two periods) refers to the directory one level up the chain.

For example, suppose you have a `data` directory under your `introcscs` directory,
and you place your sample.txt in the data directory. When running your project from the
project directory (Ch07File), you would refer to the sample.txt file to read as
{file}`..\\data\\sample.txt` in Windows or
{file}`../data/sample.txt` in macOS. Follow this one step at a time:
Starting from the {file}`Ch07File` project folder, where the program is running,

## Paths in C\#


The differing versions of paths for Windows and a Mac are a pain to deal with. Luckily C#
abstracts away the differences. It has a `Path` class in the `System.IO`
namespace that provides many handy functions for dealing with paths in
an operating system independent way:

For one thing, C# knows the path separator character for your operating system,
`Path.DirectorySeparatorChar`.

More useful is the function `Path.Combine`, which takes any number of string parameters
for sequential parts of a path, and creates a single string appropriate for the
current operating system. For example,
`Path.Combine("bin", "Debug")` will return `"bin\Debug"` or `"bin/debug"`
as appropriate.
`Path.Combine("..", "data", "sample.txt")` will return a string with characters
`..\data\sample.txt` or `../data/sample.txt`.

Even if you know you are going to be on Windows, file paths are a problem because
`\` is the string escape character. To enter the Windows path solve explicitly
you would need to have `"..\\data\\sample.txt"`, or the raw string prefix,
`@` can come to the rescue: `@"..\data\sample.txt"`.

Path strings are used by the {ref}`directory-class` and by the {ref}`file-class`.
You can look at the `Path` class in the C# Language Reference
for many other operations with path strings.

## Treat Each Imported Line as a Small Contract

An inventory file contains code, quantity and unit price separated by commas. Splitting a line gives pieces of text; it does not prove that there are exactly three fields, that a quantity is an integer, or that a price is nonnegative. Work from the schema toward conversion, not from a convenient Parse call toward assumptions about everything that came before it.

For a deliberately simple format without quoted separators, process a line through distinct stages. Preserve the original text and line number so that a rejected record can be explained. First count fields, then normalize only fields whose rules permit it, then parse numeric representations, and finally check the business domain. A zero quantity may be allowed even when an empty quantity field is not.

| Line | First relevant result |
| --- | --- |
| PEN,3,1.25 | Three fields; numeric and domain checks can proceed |
| PEN,three,1.25 | Quantity representation is invalid |
| PEN,-3,1.25 | Quantity is numeric but violates a nonnegative rule |
| PEN,3 | Schema is incomplete |

The order matters. Indexing the third field before checking field count can throw instead of producing a useful rejection. Normalizing every character in the entire line can alter meaningful free text. Catching every exception can hide a programming defect such as an incorrect index as though it were bad source data.

A regular expression can describe the shape of one field, such as a fixed prefix followed by digits. It does not replace business validation. A code may match a shape and still refer to an unknown product. For a small fixed delimiter format, Split and ordinary conditions may be easier to understand. The supporting regex reading develops groups, replacement and pattern-specific syntax; use a pattern only after stating what language of text it should accept.

Guided exercise: design acceptance/rejection outcomes for the four lines above, an empty line, and quantity zero. Decide whether one rejected line cancels the import or is reported while valid lines continue. Then predict the final accepted count under your chosen policy. Compare the prepared AI import candidate against that explicit policy instead of trusting a plausible explanation of its code.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
This section applies the string methods from {ref}`string-methods` (Section 5.4) to whole lines of text: splitting lines into fields, validating them, cleaning text safely, and reading structured records.

As a reminder, strings are immutable, so methods such as `Trim`, `ToUpper`, and `Replace` return new strings. Clean a line with `Trim()` and check it with `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace()` before splitting or parsing it.

This is a prepared review example, not a transcript from a named model. Predict and review it yourself first. If your course permits AI assistance, use the suggested prompt to ask for an explanation or additional checks. You can complete the entire activity with the supplied candidate and your own reasoning; no AI account is required.

A stock import uses exactly two comma-separated fields: a nonblank SKU and an integer quantity from zero through 500 inclusive. Trim the fields. This small exercise does not support quoted CSV fields or embedded commas. A missing/extra field, blank SKU, malformed number, or out-of-range quantity must be rejected.

A prepared suggestion says to split the line, read `fields[1]`, and call `int.Parse`. Explain why that can fail on a missing field or malformed quantity, and why a successfully parsed negative number still violates the contract.

**Possible AI prompt:** “Review a parser for this two-field stock schema. Use only these synthetic examples. Identify missing validation and propose test cases; do not add CSV quoting support or change the business range.” Supply a schema and a few fictional records rather than uploading a real customer or inventory export.

Complete the parser below. Set the output values only after validating all fields; initialize them to empty text and zero on rejection. Predict which three records will be accepted before running.
The accepted quantities are 12, zero, and 500. Explain why an AI suggestion that deletes every rejected line from the original file would introduce another problem: you would lose evidence needed to inspect or repair the input. Preserve the original, validate a copy, and inspect the report before writing changes. In this exercise the rejection report echoes synthetic stock lines; avoid copying that choice into logs containing personal data.

Record the schema supplied for review, one rejected suggestion or missing check, and the input/output evidence supporting your parser. ## Read a Pattern as a Description of Accepted Text

A product label consists of two uppercase ASCII letters, a hyphen and four digits. Before choosing regular-expression symbols, write accepted and rejected examples. AB-0042 fits; A-0042 has too few letters; AB-42 has too few digits; and a larger sentence containing AB-0042 is not itself one complete label. This last distinction separates finding a matching substring from validating an entire field.

For this deliberately narrow label, the pattern `\A[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}\z` uses beginning/end-of-input anchors, a range of letters repeated twice, a literal hyphen and four ASCII digits. It states shape, not whether AB is a known department. In a C# verbatim string literal the pattern can be written `@"\A[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}\z"`; ordinary C# string escaping and regex escaping are different layers. The @ belongs to the string literal form, not to the regex language.

| Pattern part | Meaning under this contract |
| --- | --- |
| \A | Beginning of the input |
| [A-Z]{2} | Exactly two letters from the stated ASCII range |
| - | The separator |
| [0-9]{4} | Exactly four ASCII digits |
| \z | End of the input |

A group such as `(?<number>[0-9]{4})` names a captured part. Extracting number as text retains leading zeros; converting it to an integer would answer a different question. Check whether a match succeeded before treating group contents as a valid field. A match object exists even when the match is unsuccessful, so object existence alone is not the success test.

Regex replacement also has a policy. Removing every nondigit character may produce a digit-only result while silently discarding an unexpected department or separator. Decide whether malformed input should be repaired, rejected or retained with a warning. A cleaning rule is not equivalent to a validation rule.

Guided exercise: test AB-0042, AB-0042 followed by a newline, lowercase ab-0042, a matching code embedded in a sentence and an empty string. Predict results under the exact anchored policy above. Then change the requirement to finding labels inside messages and explain which anchors must change. Do not broaden the policy merely because one difficult input fails. For untrusted complex patterns and long inputs, consider bounded matching behavior; the core fixed-shape examples do not teach arbitrary patterns as safe substitutes for a parser.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

## When to Use Regex vs. String Methods

| Use `string` methods | Use regex |
|---------------------|-----------|
| Exact match or replace | Pattern-based match |
| Fixed delimiter `Split(',')` | Variable whitespace or delimiters |

| Performance-critical loops | One-time validation or extraction |

Regex adds power but also complexity — prefer `Split`, `Trim`, and `Contains` when the pattern is simple and fixed.

# Privacy and Security in Code

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
Optional practice extends Chapter 1.2 after methods, decisions, iteration, and text processing. Use it when handling personal data in files or logs. The database appendix develops parameterized SQL.

Business programs handle **personal data**: names, email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, birth dates, and purchase histories. Personal data is any information that identifies a person or can be linked to one. Mishandling it harms the people it describes and exposes the organization to legal penalties. This section turns privacy and security principles into small coding habits you can use now.

```{index} privacy; law
```

headings.title: Personal Data and the Law
body:
```{index} Personal Data and the Law
```

## Personal Data and the Law

Privacy laws differ by place, but they share common ideas. Three examples:

- **GDPR** (EU Regulation 2016/679, applies from May 25, 2018) sets principles for processing personal data, including *purpose limitation* (use data only for the stated purpose), *data minimisation* (collect only what is needed), and *storage limitation* (do not keep it longer than needed).[^0905_privacy_security-gdpr]
- **CCPA** (California Consumer Privacy Act, in effect since January 1, 2020, and expanded by the CPRA from January 1, 2023) gives California residents rights to know about, delete, and opt out of the sale of their personal information.[^0905_privacy_security-ccpa]
- **FERPA** (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974) protects the privacy of student education records in the United States, including your grades in this course.[^0905_privacy_security-ferpa]

You do not need to be a lawyer to follow the habits these laws have in common: **collect less, show less, and keep less.**
```{index} masking; personal data
```

headings.title: Show Less: Masking
body:

## Show Less: Masking

Many screens and documents need only enough of a value to recognize it. A support agent confirming an account needs to see `a***@example.com`, not the full address. Masking uses the string methods from {ref}`string-methods`:
Receipts and order confirmations conventionally show only the last four digits of a card:
Masking is for display. A program that does not need a value at all should not collect or store it in the first place.


headings.title: Treat Every Input as Untrusted
body:


## Treat Every Input as Untrusted

Every value that comes from outside the program, such as keyboard input, a file, a web form, or another system, may be wrong by accident or on purpose. Check both the **type** and the **business rule** before using it. `int.TryParse` from Chapter 6 handles the type; an `if` handles the range:
Notice that the messages say *what* was wrong without crashing the program. A missing check can do more than produce a wrong answer: the OWASP Top 10, a widely used list of the most serious web application security risks, includes Broken Access Control (A01) and Injection (A05) in its 2025 edition.[^0905_privacy_security-owasp]
(injection)=

For command-building risks and parameterized SQL, see the {doc}`C# and SQLite appendix <../appendices/databases/csharp_sqlite>`.
```{index} logging; secrets
```

headings.title: Logging Without Leaking
body:
```{index} Logging Without Leaking
```

## Logging Without Leaking

Logs record what a program did so people can investigate problems later. Logs are also read by many people and kept for a long time, so they must not contain secrets such as passwords or full card numbers:

Three related principles guide secure design:

- **Confidentiality, integrity, availability.** Keep data from people who should not see it, keep it from being changed improperly, and keep the system usable for those who need it.
- **Least privilege.** Give each user and program only the access its task requires. A report that only reads orders should not be able to delete them.
- **Never store passwords.** Systems store a salted, slow *hash* of a password: a one-way value that can check a password without revealing it. Use a well-tested library for this; never write your own.

```{index} privacy; summary
```

headings.title: Summary
body:
```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

Personal data deserves care in every line of code that touches it. Collect, show, and keep only what a task needs; mask values for display; check every input for type and business rules; never build commands from input text; and keep secrets out of logs. These habits match the principles that privacy laws such as GDPR, CCPA, and FERPA share.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^0905_privacy_security-gdpr]: European Parliament and Council (2016). *Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation)*, Article 5. <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj>

[^0905_privacy_security-ccpa]: State of California, Office of the Attorney General. *California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)*. <https://oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa>

[^0905_privacy_security-ferpa]: U.S. Department of Education. *Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)*. <https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/ferpa>

[^0905_privacy_security-owasp]: OWASP Foundation (2025). *OWASP Top 10:2025*. <https://top10.owasp.org/2025/>. In the 2021 edition, Injection was ranked A03.

## Overview


To understand class and object-oriented programming (OOP), some important basic concepts learn first inlcude:

- **Class**: A class is a blueprint, prototype, or template.
- **Class Members**: In C#, a class contains members, which include **fields**, properties, **methods**, and events.
- **Class Instance**: An `object` is an `instance` of a class. Namely, an object is created based on a
  class and therefore is an instance of that class. An object can be created using the `new` keyword.

There are related terminology that you will see about class and OOP:

- **Field**: A field is a variable of any type that is declared directly in a class or struct. Fields are
  members of their containing type. A field stores a piece of data within an object. It acts like a
  variable and may have a different value for each instance of a type. [1]
- **Property**: Properties expose fields. Fields should (almost always) be kept private to a class and accessed via
  get and set properties.
- The **this** Keyword: In C#, the this keyword refers to the current instance of a class.
- **Reference Types**: A type that is defined as a class is a reference type. Other types include: interface, struct, delegate, or enum.
- **Constructor**: In C#, a constructor is called when an object is created to set default values. A constructor must have the
  **same name** as the enclosing class. Using constructor is not obligatory in C#. If no constructors are specified in a class, the compiler
  automatically creates a parameterless constructor.
```{index} Declaring Classes
```

headings.title: Declaring Classes
body:
```{index} Declaring Classes
```

## Declaring Classes


To declare a class, you need to use the `class` keyword and give a unique `identifier` (name) to the class. For example,
you want to create a customer class to include some data and methods in one unit:

```csharp
// [access modifier] - [class] - [identifier]

public class Customer
{
   // Fields, properties, methods and events go here...
}
```

Attributes to be considered when creating a class include:

- Access Modifiers: The default access for a class type is internal. Basic levels of access for a class include [2] :  
  - **public**: Access is not restricted. Anyone code can create instances of this class.
  - **protected**: Access is limited to the containing class or types derived from the containing class.
  - **internal**: Access is limited to the current assembly. [3]
  - **private**: Access is limited to the containing type.

- Class Identifier: A unique name for the class. An identifier is the name you assign to a type (class, interface, struct, delegate, or enum),
  member, variable, or namespace. An identifier begins with a letter or underscore. As a convention, use PascalCase for class names and method names.

- Class Body: The class body is surrounded by { }. The behavior and data are defined in the class body, including **fields**, properties, **methods**, and events on a class and
  are collectively referred to as **class members**.

- Base Class or Super Class: Optional. Name of the class’s superclass; preceded by a colon (:).

- Interfaces: Interface names implemented by the class; preceded by a colon (:).

## Tuples: When a Class Is Too Much

A class bundles data with the behavior that belongs to it. Sometimes a program only needs to keep two or three values together for a moment, such as a product code and its price, or the lowest and highest sales day of a week. A **tuple** groups a few values into one value without declaring a class.[^1001_class_syntax-tuple-types]


### Tuples or Classes?

| Use a tuple when | Use a class when |
|---|---|
| A method returns two or three related values | The data has behavior (methods) or rules to protect |
| The values are used briefly, inside one method or class | The type is shared across the program |
| Named fields make the meaning clear enough | It needs constructors, properties, inheritance, or interfaces |

If you find yourself passing the same tuple shape through many methods, that is a sign it should become a class. Chapter 20 uses tuples for graph edges, where a pair of locations is all an edge needs.

headings.title: A Variable Number of Arguments
body:
(gap-a-variable-number-of-arguments)=
## A Variable Number of Arguments

```{index} gap revision: a variable number of arguments
```
An invoice may contain zero, one, or several charges. Writing a separate `Sum` overload for every possible number of charges does not scale. A parameter array lets one method receive those arguments as an array. It connects familiar array traversal to a more convenient calling form.

General pattern (schematic):

```csharp
static decimal Sum(params decimal[] amounts) { /* process amounts */ }
```

`params` marks the final parameter. In this array form, callers can supply separate compatible values, an existing array, or no values. Inside the method, `amounts` is still an array with a length. The keyword does not mean that one call returns multiple answers. An empty call supplies an empty array; decide explicitly what the method should return for it.

Overloads share a method name but have different parameter lists. For example, `Sum(decimal a, decimal b)` and `Sum(decimal[] amounts)` are distinct overloads, while a changed return type alone cannot distinguish them. A parameter array often avoids a family of repetitive fixed-arity overloads. Keep the simple array form here; broader overload and polymorphism choices are developed later.

See the language/API reference for this contract.[^gap-params]
**Guided practice.** Predict `0`, `9`, and `5` before running. Write a parameter-array method that counts charges above a supplied threshold, placing the threshold before the final array parameter. Test an empty call, an exact-threshold value, and an existing array. Compare this design with the retained extra-practice overload exercise.
**Connection to the retained SumManyArgs exercise.** For question nine, define `int Sum(params int[] values)`. The final parameter collects zero or more int arguments into an array for the method body. It is a single parameter declaration with flexible call syntax, not a request to invent many overloads. You may also supply an existing int array. This array form is sufficient for the exercise; modern C# supports additional params collection forms.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^gap-params]: [Microsoft: Method parameters and modifiers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters).

### Setters


The original version of Contact makes a Contact object be
*immutable*: Once it is created with the constructor, there is no way
to change its internal state. The only assignments to the private
instance variables are the ones in the constructor. In real life
people can change their email address. We might like to allow that
with our Contact objects. Users can read the data in a Contact with the
*getter* methods. Now we need *setter* methods. The naming conventions
are similar: start with “Set”. In this case we must supply the new data,
so setter methods need a parameter:

```csharp
      public void SetPhone(string newPhone)
      {
         phone = newPhone;
      }
```

In `SetPhone`, like in our original constructor, we illustrate using a
*new* name for the parameter that sets the instance variable. For
comparison we use the alternate identifier matching approach in the
other setter:

```csharp
      public void SetEmail(string email)
      {
         this.email = email;
      }
```

Now we can alter the contents of a Contact:

    Contact c1 = new Contact("Marie Ortiz", "773-508-7890", "mortiz2@luc.edu");
    c1.SetEmail ("maria.ortiz@gmail.com");
    c1.SetPhone("555-555-5555");
    c1.Print();

headings.title: Statistics Exercise

## Statistics Exercise

```{index} Statistics Exercise
```

Modify the project [averager](https://github.com/mstbit/introcs-csharp-examples/tree/master/averager) so the `Averager` class is
converted to `Statistics`. Besides having methods to calculate the count
of data items and average, also calculate the standard deviation with
a method `StandardDeviation`.
It turns out that the only other instance variable needed is
the sum of the squares of the data items, call it `sumOfSqr`.
Before calculating the standard deviation, suppose we
assign the current average to a local variable `avg`.
Then the handiest form of expression for the standard deviation is

```
Math.Sqrt(sumOfSqr/dataCount - avg*avg)
```

Modify the demonstration program to show the standard deviation, too.

This is the **population** standard deviation: variance is the mean of the squared values minus the square of the mean. For values 2 and 4, `sumOfSqr = 20`, `dataCount = 2`, and `avg = 3`, so variance is `20/2 - 9 = 1` and standard deviation is 1. The older expression divided the subtraction by the count and was incorrect. Return `double.NaN` when empty.

For small classroom values, clamp a tiny negative variance caused by rounding with `Math.Max(0, variance)`. For large nearly equal values this formula can lose substantial precision; a running variance algorithm is a later numerical-method improvement, not something a clamp repairs. State whether you intend population or sample statistics; this exercise uses population statistics.

body:

(unneeded-constructor-code-exercise)=

## Unneeded Constructor Code Exercise

```{index} Unneeded Constructor Code Exercise
```

Recall that objects are always initialized. Each instance variable
has a default value assigned before a constructor is even run.
The default value for numeric instance variables is 0, so the
call to `Clear` in the constructor could be left out, leaving the
body of the constructor empty! Try commenting that line out
and test that the behavior of demo program is the same.

Emphasizing the fact that you are thinking about the
initial values of instance variables is not a bad idea. Hence
a common practice is to
explicitly assign even the default values in the constructor, as
we did initially with the call to `Clear` inside the constructor.

If no constructor definition is explicitly provided at all,
the compiler implicitly creates one with no parameters and an empty body.
This means that the entire constructor in `Averager` could be omitted.
Comment the whole constructor out and check.

There is a defensive programming
reason to provide even the do-nothing constructor explicitly:
If you use the implicit constructor and then decide to add a constructor
with parameters, the implicit constructor is no longer defined by the compiler,
so any remaining call to it in your code becomes an error.

we could avoid repeated division by saving the average as an

(and still keep `dataCount`). We can manage to
keep the same public interface to the methods. With these

body:
```{index} Beyond Getters and Setters
```

## Beyond Getters and Setters

```{index} Beyond Getters and Setters
```

```{index} Averager; incremental average; running sum
```

Thus far we have had very simple classes with instance variables and
getter and setter methods, and maybe a ToString method.
These classes were designed to introduce the basic syntax for
classes with instances. The classes have just been containers for data
that we can read back, and change if there are setter methods - pretty
boring and limited. Many objects have more extensive behaviors, so we will
take a small step and imagine a somewhat more complicated `Averager` class:

- A new `Averager` starts with no data acknowledged.
- Be able to enter data values one at a time (method `AddDatum`).
  We will use `double` values.
- At any point be able to return the average of the numbers entered so far
  (method `GetAverage`).
  The average is the sum of all the values divided by number of values.
  With `double` values we assume a `double` average.
  This does not make sense if there
  are no values so far, but with double type we can use the value
  `NaN` (Not a Number) in this case.
- Be able to return the number of data elements entered so far
  (method `GetDataCount`)
- Be able to clear the `Averager`, going back to no data elements
  considered yet, like in a new `Averager` (method `Clear`)
- It is good to have a `ToString` method. We choose to have
  it label the number of data items and the average of the items.

The object starts from a fixed
state (no data) so we do not need any constructor parameters.

We can imagine a demonstration class `AveragerDemo` with a `Main` method
containing

```csharp
using System;
namespace IntroCS
{
   class AveragerDemo
   {
      public static void Main()
      {  // body chunk
         Averager a = new Averager();
         Console.WriteLine("New Averager: " + a);
         foreach (double x in new[] {5.1, -7.3, 11.0, 3.7}) {
            Console.WriteLine ("Next datum " + x);
            a.AddDatum (x);
            Console.WriteLine("average {0:G15} with {1} data values",
                              a.GetAverage(), a.GetDataCount());
         }
         a.Clear();
         Console.WriteLine("After clearing:");
         Console.WriteLine("average {0:G15} with {1} data values",
                           a.GetAverage(), a.GetDataCount());
      }                            // end chunk
   }
}


```

It should print

```none
New Averager: items: 0; average: NaN
Next datum 5.1
average 5.1 with 1 data values
Next datum -7.3
average -1.1 with 2 data values
Next datum 11
average 2.93333333333333 with 3 data values
Next datum 3.7
average 3.125 with 4 data values
After clearing:
average NaN with 0 data values
```

Now that we have a clear idea of the proposed outward behavior, we
can consider how to implement the `Averager` class.

We could store a list of all the data values entered in any instance,
requiring a large amount of memory for a long list. However, this
functionality was built into early calculators, with very limited memory.
How can we do it without remembering the whole list?
Consider a concrete example:

If I have entered numbers 2.1, 4.5 and 5.4, and want the average, it is

> {math}`(2.1+4.5+5.4)/3=12.0/3=4.0`

If I want to include a further number 5.0, the average becomes

> {math}`(2.1+4.5+5.4+5.0)/4=17.0/4=4.25`

Note the relationship to the previous average expression:

> {math}`=((2.1+4.5+5.4)+5.0)/4=(12.0+5.0)/(3+1)`

In the numerator we have added the latest value to the previous sum,
and in the denominator the count of data items is increased by one.
All we need to remember to
go on to include the next item is the sum of values so far and the
number of values so far. We can just have instance variables
`sum` and `dataCount`.

You might think how to create this class....

The full `Averager` code follows:

Several things to note:

- We show that a constructor, like an instance method, can include a call
  to a further instance method. Though we illustrate this idea, the
  constructor code is
  actually unneeded. See the {ref}`unneeded-constructor-code-exercise` in the class-instance lesson.
- We have methods that are not ToString or mere getters or setters of instance
  variables. The logic of the class requires more.
- The `GetAverage`
  method does return data obtained by reading instance variable, but it does
  a calculation using the instance variables first. See
  {ref}`alternate-internal-state-exercise`.

The code for both classes is in project [averager](https://github.com/mstbit/introcs-csharp-examples/tree/master/averager).

The output keeps 15 significant digits to match the original demonstration. Explicitly choosing display precision separates the stored double value from its presentation. Clear returns count and sum to zero; `0.0 / 0` yields NaN, which models the undefined average of an empty population in this contract. Compare this policy with CashRegister's intentionally different zero-average policy before reusing either model.


## Missing Is Different from Empty

A reference can identify an object or contain null. An empty order object still exists and can answer Count; a missing order reference cannot receive an instance call. A nullable annotation describes intended use for the compiler's analysis. It is not a runtime constructor check, and adding a null-forgiving exclamation mark does not create an object.

When a relationship is required, reject an absent value at the boundary that establishes the relationship. When it is optional, give absence a deliberate meaning and test that path. Returning a default zero for an absent invoice may confuse missing data with an invoice whose real total is zero. The supporting nullability reading retains the operators and all original variants; use them to implement a policy that has already been stated.

Guided check: distinguish an order with no lines, no order object, and an order whose total is zero after discounts. Which operations are valid on each? A useful object contract keeps these cases distinguishable rather than treating every unusual state as null.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Objects, References, and State
body:
```{index} Objects, References, and State
```

## Objects, References, and State

A manager sees two screens showing the same product. If one screen changes its price, should the other screen change too? The answer depends on whether the screens refer to one shared object or to independent objects. Before combining classes, make that sharing visible.

Chapter 10 taught you to create a valid object. This section asks what happens when you assign that object to another variable, pass it to a method, or store it in a collection. Use a drawing with variables as boxes and objects as separate records. Draw a reference as an arrow, not as another copy of the record.

headings.title: Assignment Copies a Reference
body:
```{index} Assignment Copies a Reference
```

## Assignment Copies a Reference


```{index} Assignment Copies a Reference
```
A class is a reference type. Assignment copies a reference to an object; it does not call the constructor or copy every field. Two variables that refer to the same object are **aliases**. An alias gives another route to the same state.

Predict both printed prices before running the cell. There is one `StockItem` object and two local variables. The setter checks the new price before replacing the field, so all aliases observe the same valid state.
The two prices are 12.00. `ReferenceEquals` asks whether two references identify the same object. It does not compare business identifiers or prices. Reassigning `otherScreen` to a new object would change that variable's arrow; it would not redirect `original`.

Passing a reference-type argument to an ordinary parameter copies the reference too. A method can use that reference to change the shared object. Reassigning the parameter itself changes only the method's local copy. This behavior is ordinary pass-by-value: the copied value happens to be a reference. You do not need a `ref` parameter to call a method that changes an object's state.

headings.title: Identity and Business Equality
body:
```{index} Identity and Business Equality
```

## Identity and Business Equality


```{index} Identity and Business Equality
```
**Object identity** means being the same runtime object. **Business equality** means matching according to a stated domain rule. Two independently created product objects may represent the same stock-keeping unit (SKU), even though they have different identities.

For this chapter, SKU comparisons are case-sensitive. The constructor trims surrounding spaces but does not change letter case. Decide that policy before writing comparisons. A title and a price are not reliable identifiers: names can repeat and prices can change across catalog versions.
The first answer is false and the second is true. This does not mean `==` automatically compares the fields of every class. Here it compares the two `string` SKU values, which have value-based equality. For your own ordinary classes, do not assume that field-by-field equality appears automatically.

Name a method such as `HasSameSku` when that is the rule you need. An application may need several comparisons: identical object, same catalog product, or equal receipt contents. One vague idea of “equal” cannot safely replace all three. Overriding equality and defining operators are optional extensions, not prerequisites for this chapter.

headings.title: Mutable and Immutable Objects
body:
```{index} Mutable and Immutable Objects
```

## Mutable and Immutable Objects


```{index} Mutable and Immutable Objects
```
An object is **mutable** when its observable state can change after construction. An **immutable** object keeps its observable state fixed. The `Product` below has read-only properties and no method that changes its fields. Its property values are strings and a decimal, so sharing it cannot later change the catalog values through a setter.

Read-only access to a reference is not enough to make a whole object immutable. A read-only property could still return a mutable list or another mutable object. You must inspect what callers can reach through the public members.
Changing the catalog means creating another `Product`; the existing quote still refers to the original version. This is one simple policy for preserving quoted prices. A larger sales system might instead store an explicit sale-time price on each order line. Either approach needs a stated rule for which price belongs to an existing order.

Use mutability when changes are part of the object's job, such as adding lines to an order. Prefer fixed value objects when sharing should be harmless, such as a product description used by several order lines. Immutability is a design choice, not a requirement that every class avoid setters.

headings.title: Copies Need a Depth Policy
body:
```{index} Copies Need a Depth Policy
```

## Copies Need a Depth Policy


```{index} Copies Need a Depth Policy
```
Creating a new outer object does not automatically duplicate everything it references. A **shallow copy** copies the immediate values and references. A **deep copy** also copies selected referenced objects. Deep copying is a policy about a graph of objects; it is not a universal command to duplicate everything.

Consider two orders that both refer to one immutable `Product`. Independent order collections with a shared product can be correct. If the product were mutable, a price edit could affect both orders. Draw the reachable objects and identify which changes the design permits before deciding that a copy is “independent.”

The next section uses fixed products and order lines, together with an order that owns its changing collection. That makes the sharing policy small enough to explain and test.

```{index} Choose Copy and Equality Semantics Together
```

## Choose Copy and Equality Semantics Together

An order line refers to a product, but a point on a warehouse plan may simply consist of two coordinates. Before choosing class, struct or record, ask what one value means, whether it can change, and what callers should expect when it is assigned or compared. The forms below solve related modeling problems, but none is an automatic replacement for every ordinary class.

Assigning a struct variable copies its value. That copy contains the values of its fields; if one of those fields is itself a reference, both copies can still refer to a shared object. Value-type copying is not a promise that every reachable object has been recursively duplicated. A record class is a reference type with compiler-supported value-oriented equality and copying syntax; assigning its variable still copies a reference. A record struct combines record features with value-type copying.

| Choice | Assignment behavior | Design question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary class instance | Another reference to the same object | Is identity and a controlled lifecycle important? |
| Struct value | Copy of its fields | Is this a small coherent value with a meaningful default? |
| Record class instance | Another reference on assignment | Does value-oriented equality fit a reference-based data model? |
| Record struct value | Copy of its fields | Do both value copying and record conveniences fit? |

For positional records, the parameter list declares the data used by generated members. A with expression creates a copied result with selected changes; it is not a deep-cloning operator. If a copied record contains a mutable list, later changes to that list may be visible through both record objects. Keep this distinction beside the syntax so that a concise expression does not suggest stronger isolation than it provides.

Default struct values deserve a separate check. The runtime can produce the zero-initialized value even when your preferred constructor would enforce a stronger business rule. If all-zero fields make no sense for the model, consider how every public operation handles that state rather than assuming clients can never obtain it. Readonly limits mutation through the struct's own fields; it does not freeze a separately referenced mutable collection.

Guided prediction: two variables hold equal coordinate values, then one is assigned a changed coordinate. Which variable changes? Now repeat with two references to one mutable class instance. Explain the observation using assignment semantics, not the spelling of the variable names. Finally, consider a record containing an array and identify which part of a with copy remains shared.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Structs: Define a Value Type
body:
```{index} Structs: Define a Value Type
```

(struct-value-types)=

## Structs: Define a Value Type


```{index} Structs: Define a Value Type
```
A delivery charge belongs to one quote. Copying that charge should give another value, rather than another reference to shared editable state. A **struct** lets you define a value type with named properties, constructors, and methods. Assignment and ordinary parameter passing copy its value, just as they do for `int` and `decimal`.[^1101_objects_references-structs]

Here `DeliveryCharge` groups an amount and a zone. `readonly` prevents its instance state from being changed after construction; the get-only properties expose its values. The explicit constructor uses the same syntax you learned for classes. Predict which amount changes when `revised` is assigned a new value.
The two variables contain independent values. A mutable struct would also copy its fields on assignment, but mutable value types can make updates confusing, especially inside collections. Prefer a small, fixed value when introducing structs.

`default(DeliveryCharge)` supplies zero for both numeric properties without running this two-argument constructor. A struct design must account for its default value; constructor validation alone cannot exclude it. A non-nullable struct cannot contain `null`; `DeliveryCharge?` can, as the nullability reading explains.

Value copying is not a promise about stack versus heap storage. A struct can be a field inside a class or an element of an array. Also, if a struct contains a reference such as a `List<string>`, copying the struct copies that reference and can still share the list. Choose a type by its meaning and copying policy, not by assuming structs are always faster.

headings.title: Records: Data and Equality
body:
```{index} Records: Data and Equality
```

(record-data-types)=

## Records: Data and Equality


```{index} Records: Data and Equality
```
An invoice address is often compared by its contents. Two separately constructed addresses with the same city and postal code should compare equal even though they are different objects. A **record** asks the compiler to generate data-oriented members, including value-based equality and a readable `ToString`.[^1101_objects_references-records]

`record Address(string City, string Zip);` is short for a **record class** declaration. The parenthesized parameters generate a constructor and public properties with the same names. In this positional record class, those properties use `init`: they can be supplied during initialization but cannot be reassigned afterward. The following program uses ordinary construction, assignment, and equality before introducing copying with `with`.
Assignment to `alias` still copies a reference: a record class remains a reference type. The generated `==` instead compares the record's data, so `first` and `imported` compare equal. The `with` expression creates a copy and initializes the listed changes; it leaves `first` unchanged. No mutation of the old address is needed.

Generated record equality is not automatically the business rule you need. Two product snapshots with the same SKU but different prices need not be equal as records. Decide whether the operation asks for matching SKU, matching all recorded data, or the identical object. An ordinary class does not automatically gain record-style `==` by having similar properties.

Records are not automatically deeply immutable. You can declare mutable properties, and even an init-only property can refer to a mutable list. Generated equality uses each member's equality behavior: distinct lists containing the same elements are not automatically compared element by element. The later copy-depth discussion applies to `with` too.

(record-struct-choice)=

## Record Structs and Choosing a Type


```{index} Record Structs and Choosing a Type
```
A **record struct** combines value-type copying with generated record members. Unlike a positional record class, a plain positional `record struct` generates settable properties. Use `readonly record struct` for a fixed value with init-only positional properties. Here each measurement is a small amount, not a shared entity.[^1101_objects_references-records]
These declarations define one item's type. A collection such as `List<Address>` or `List<PackageSize>` holds multiple items; neither declaration replaces the collection.

| Declaration | Assignment | Equality to keep in mind | Typical role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary `class` | Copies a reference | Default `==` compares identity unless customized | An order with a lifecycle and shared state |
| `struct` | Copies its value | `Equals` compares fields by default; `==` is not automatically supplied | A small value with explicit members |
| `record` / `record class` | Copies a reference | Generated value-based equality | An address or snapshot compared by data |
| `record struct` | Copies its value | Generated value-based equality and `==` | A small data value with convenient record syntax |

For the class examples in this chapter, continue using ordinary classes. Choose a struct when independent value copying fits the domain; choose record syntax when its generated data comparison fits the intended rule. These choices do not remove validation responsibilities. In particular, positional records do not automatically check business constraints such as positive dimensions.

Before continuing, predict whether `Address b = a;` creates a new object and whether `PackageSize b = a;` can share mutable numeric properties. Then change one value in each runnable example and explain the output using copying and equality separately.

headings.title: Establish Required and Optional Relationships at Their Boundary
body:
```{index} Establish Required and Optional Relationships at Their Boundary
```

## Establish Required and Optional Relationships at Their Boundary

An order line requires a product to calculate its amount. An order may optionally have a delivery note. Both are relationships, but absence has different meanings. Reject a missing required product when the line is created; allow an absent optional note only when callers know how that state is represented and displayed.

A nullable reference annotation such as `string?` communicates that absence is permitted for that reference. A nullable value type such as `int?` can distinguish an unknown quantity from a known zero. They are related ways of representing missing information, but nullable reference annotations do not wrap a runtime object or validate the constructor. Runtime guards remain necessary when a public contract rejects null.

| State | Meaning | Suitable check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product reference absent | Required relationship cannot be established | Reject at construction |
| Optional note absent | No note was supplied | Follow the documented no-note path |
| Note is empty text | An existing string contains no characters | Apply a separate text rule if needed |
| Quantity is zero | A known numeric value | Apply the business rule for zero |

Conditional access can skip a member access when a reference is absent; null coalescing can select a fallback value. Neither operator determines whether that fallback is a sensible business result. Returning zero for an unknown quantity may make arithmetic convenient while hiding incomplete data. State the policy first, then choose syntax to express it. The supporting nullability lesson retains the full operator and pattern variations.

Guided contract design: a customer can place an order without a note but never without an order line's product. List constructor outcomes and the expected total calculation for both relationships. Then check that a rejected construction or mutation leaves any already valid order state unchanged.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
A program that uses classes can still put all meaningful work in `Main`. Object-oriented design becomes useful when related objects take responsibility for their own behavior. An order-processing program gives you three distinct concepts: a product, a line requesting some quantity of that product, and an order containing lines.

Start from a use case: an employee adds two notebooks and three pens, then requests the order total. Name the responsibilities before writing fields. A class is justified by a coherent job, not simply by finding a noun in a problem statement.
```{figure} ../../figures/object_references.svg
:alt: Two variables alias one customer; an order owns private lines that refer to products.

References can be shared. Composition assigns responsibility for storing and protecting collaborators; it does not automatically clone every referenced object.
```

headings.title: Has-a Relationships
body:
```{index} Has-a Relationships
```

## Has-a Relationships


```{index} Has-a Relationships
```
**Composition** builds a larger object from smaller objects. An order has lines; a line refers to a product. In contrast, an order is not a product. Inheritance would make the wrong promise in that relationship.

The term **aggregation** is sometimes used for a looser relationship in which an object refers to independently managed objects. In this design the order creates its lines, while several lines can share a product created by client code. State the actual ownership and sharing rules rather than relying on the terminology alone.

| Type | Responsibility | Information it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product | Describe one catalog version. | SKU, name, unit price. |
| OrderLine | Describe one requested quantity and calculate its amount. | Product reference and quantity. |
| Order | Maintain its lines and calculate the complete amount. | A private collection of order lines. |
| Console client | Accept input and display a result. | The public operations of the model. |

For the core example, repeated products create separate lines. There is no automatic merging or stock reservation. Those would be additional business rules with their own tests.

headings.title: Let Each Object Calculate Its Own Result
body:
```{index} Let Each Object Calculate Its Own Result
```

(instance-methods)=

## Let Each Object Calculate Its Own Result


```{index} Let Each Object Calculate Its Own Result
```
`Product` protects its construction rules. `OrderLine` rejects a null product and nonpositive quantity before storing either value. Its `LineTotal` is calculated from the two values, so there is no second total field to become stale.

The example contains every class it needs. The program appears before the type declarations because these are ordinary top-level C# statements. Trace the property accesses from the client through the line to the product.
The line's constructor receives a reference to the product. It does not duplicate that product. Sharing is safe here because `Product` has no public state-changing operation. `OrderLine` is also fixed after construction. An order can therefore expose line objects without giving clients a way to rewrite their quantities.

If your design requires editable quantities, decide whether the order replaces a line or the line offers a validated operation. Do not add a setter merely because a property exists. The public surface should follow the use cases.

headings.title: Keep Collection Ownership Inside the Order
body:
```{index} Keep Collection Ownership Inside the Order
```

## Keep Collection Ownership Inside the Order


```{index} Keep Collection Ownership Inside the Order
```
A private field is not protected if a public method hands the same mutable list to callers. A caller could clear the list, add a null, or bypass validation. The order should provide operations that preserve its rules instead.

`Add` creates and validates the line before inserting it. If construction fails, the existing list is unchanged. `Total` loops over current lines, starting at zero, so an empty order has a well-defined total. The private `readonly` field cannot be reassigned after initialization; its list can still change through `Add`. Readonly field binding is different from an immutable collection.
The output is two lines and a total of 18.00. `Main` coordinates the use case without calculating line amounts itself. Ask where each rule belongs: a negative unit price belongs to the product boundary; a positive quantity belongs to the line boundary; whether duplicate products merge belongs to the order's contract.

Avoid storing both `Total` and all the ingredients used to calculate it unless you also design how every update keeps them synchronized. Recalculation is a clear starting point for a small order. Later performance chapters give you tools to judge whether caching is justified.

headings.title: Return Useful Results Without Exposing Storage
body:
```{index} Return Useful Results Without Exposing Storage
```

## Return Useful Results Without Exposing Storage


```{index} Return Useful Results Without Exposing Storage
```
`GetLines` returns a new array. Replacing an element in that array does not replace a line in the order's private list. The array is a shallow snapshot: its entries still refer to the same line objects. Because those lines and their products are immutable in this design, callers cannot use those references to change an existing line's amount.

A shallow copy would not provide the same protection with mutable line objects. Explain both the outer collection and its reachable elements when describing a snapshot.
The snapshot still has one entry, the order now has two, and the order total is 18.00. The snapshot replacement did not edit the order. This is a promise about the public API, not about preventing all possible code changes by the programmer who owns the source.

For a durable project, put `Product`, `OrderLine`, and `Order` in separate `.cs` files and keep the console entry point short. File organization should make responsibilities easy to locate; it does not change object relationships at runtime.

headings.title: Test Through the Surface a Client Is Allowed to Use
body:
```{index} Test Through the Surface a Client Is Allowed to Use
```

## Test Through the Surface a Client Is Allowed to Use

A collaboration test should establish observable behavior, not reach into another class's private list to force the result. Create two independent orders, add a line to one, and check both totals. If adding to the first changes the second, shared storage has crossed an ownership boundary even if the added line itself has the right amount.

Arrange a state in which a rejected update would be visible. Record the original count and total, attempt the invalid change, and assert that both remain unchanged. Checking only that an exception was thrown can miss a method that mutates state and then throws. A failure policy includes what happened to state, not merely which message appeared.

| Case | Observation to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Two orders share one immutable product | Independent line lists and totals |
| Invalid quantity is rejected | Prior count and total remain intact |
| A snapshot is obtained | The documented outer-copy/sharing policy holds |
| Optional information is absent | The explicit no-information behavior occurs |

Guided challenge: a developer returns the internal line list to make a report easy. Show how a client could change the order without calling its validation methods. Then compare returning a copied outer sequence whose immutable product/line objects remain shared. Explain which mutation path is blocked and why this is not necessarily a deep copy of every reachable object.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
A printed total is useful evidence, but one successful order does not establish the contract of an order system. Test the boundaries between the collaborating objects: valid product values, valid line quantities, list ownership, and the effect of rejected operations.

Use the testing workflow from Chapter 6. State an expected result before running the program, arrange the objects, act through public methods, and compare the observed state with that expectation. Small console assertions make the examples self-contained; a durable test project can express the same checks with the course's unit-testing framework.

headings.title: Contracts Describe Observable Behavior
body:
```{index} Contracts Describe Observable Behavior
```

## Contracts Describe Observable Behavior


```{index} Contracts Describe Observable Behavior
```
A **precondition** describes an input or state required for an operation. A **postcondition** describes what is true after a successful operation. An **invariant** is a condition the model preserves at its public boundaries.

For this order model, products have nonblank identifiers and nonnegative prices; lines have products and positive quantities; the order total is the sum of its lines. An invalid add must leave the existing order unchanged. The total of an empty order is zero. These rules are precise enough to check without inspecting private fields.

Create a boundary table before writing assertions:

| Case | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Empty order | Zero lines and zero total. |
| Valid quantity one | One line with one unit's amount. |
| Quantity zero | Reject; preserve previous lines and total. |
| Repeated SKU | Separate lines; sum quantities for the SKU. |
| Changed snapshot array | Existing order unchanged. |

A contract also identifies what is outside scope. This model does not reserve warehouse stock, calculate tax, or connect to a database. Do not infer those guarantees from a passing total check.

headings.title: Arrange, Act, Assert
body:
```{index} Arrange, Act, Assert
```

## Arrange, Act, Assert


```{index} Arrange, Act, Assert
```
The helper below throws if an expectation fails. A normal printed result means the checks completed; an exception points to a failed claim. The test data uses small decimal prices whose expected totals you can calculate independently.

Predict the empty and nonempty totals, then run the complete cell. You can temporarily change the expected value to see how the assertion reports a failure.
This is a unit-oriented check of the model, even though several small objects participate. A test framework can provide named tests and richer reports, but the important reasoning is the same. Keep expected values independent: calling `Total` to compute its own expected result would not challenge the implementation.

A passing check is evidence for the exercised cases, not a proof for all inputs. Include cases that would reveal likely defects, such as using only the last line's amount or increasing the line count before validation finishes.

headings.title: Rejected Changes Must Preserve State
body:
```{index} Rejected Changes Must Preserve State
```

## Rejected Changes Must Preserve State


```{index} Rejected Changes Must Preserve State
```
Failure behavior is part of the contract. Save the line count and total before an invalid add. Catch only the exception type you expect, then check both that rejection occurred and that observable state is unchanged.

Do not catch every exception and print “passed.” A null-reference bug or a failed assertion should not be mistaken for the intended quantity rejection.
The validation lives in `OrderLine` and completes before the order stores the new line. This ordering makes failure atomic at the model level: the invalid operation changes nothing. Database transactions in the optional appendix solve a related problem across persistent changes, but no database is needed to understand this object-level promise.

Also test two orders sharing one product. Adding a line to the first order must not add it to the second. Shared immutable catalog data is allowed; a shared order list would violate the intended independence.

headings.title: Refactor Without Changing the Contract
body:
```{index} Refactor Without Changing the Contract
```

## Refactor Without Changing the Contract


```{index} Refactor Without Changing the Contract
```
**Refactoring** changes internal organization while preserving intended observable behavior. Suppose a console program keeps product names, prices, and quantities in parallel lists. Each insertion must update all three lists in the same order, so a missing update can silently pair the wrong price with a product.

First capture a few expected orders as checks. Introduce `Product` and `OrderLine`, move line calculations into the line class, and move the line collection into `Order`. Keep the public task the same: add requested products and obtain the correct total. Run the checks after each small change.

Do not combine a refactor with an unexplained change in business policy. Merging duplicate lines, rounding tax, or changing case-sensitive SKU matching changes behavior. Make that a separate requirement with new expectations.

A useful review asks who owns each rule. The model should not read from `Console` just to calculate a total. The console client should not reach into the list to repair invalid quantities. Separating those jobs lets tests use fixed inputs without simulating keyboard interaction.

# Nullability and Missing Data

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
This supporting reading extends Chapter 6's basic missing-input checks after you have studied object references and composition. Nullable annotations describe whether data may be missing; they do not validate an object at runtime. Apply these ideas to required constructor data, optional relationships, and tests of missing-data behavior.

Read the value-type and reference-type sections with References, Identity, and Copying; revisit conditional member access with Composition. The operator table is a reference, and the pattern-matching and LINQ practice are extension material. This page does not add a fourth required class meeting.
```{index} Nullable Value Types
```

headings.title: Give Missing Data Its Own Meaning
body:
```{index} Give Missing Data Its Own Meaning
```

## Give Missing Data Its Own Meaning
An unrecorded score, a recorded zero and an empty label are different states. Replacing every missing value with zero may make a screen easy to print while making its calculation wrong. Connect nullability to Chapter 11's object contracts: choose what may be absent, what absence means, and where a required value is enforced.

For a value type, the schematic declaration `ValueType? name = null;` creates a nullable value that can hold either an ordinary value or no value. `int?` is shorthand for Nullable<int>. Read `HasValue` before an explicit `.Value` access; accessing Value when HasValue is false throws. `GetValueOrDefault()` supplies the type's default, which may erase the distinction your business rule needs.

For a reference type, `string?` annotates a reference that may be null. Under nullable analysis, `string` expresses an intended non-null contract to the compiler. These annotations guide warnings; they do not install runtime validation. Required constructor input still needs a guard, and the null-forgiving `!` operator only suppresses a warning.
The output preserves absence separately from zero. Empty is a real string object with Length zero; absent has no object whose Length can be read. `absent?.Length` produces a nullable length, and `?? -1` supplies a display fallback only when that result is missing.

| Expression or policy | Missing reference | Empty string | Nonempty string |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `text?.Length` | null | 0 | Actual length |
| `text?.Length ?? -1` | -1 | 0 | Actual length |
| `text ?? "Unknown"` | Unknown | Empty string retained | Original text |

Read `?.` as conditional access, not a request to manufacture a default object. In `order?.ShippingAddress?.City ?? "Unknown"`, a missing order or address stops that access chain, then the final fallback provides a display value. An empty City is retained because empty is not null. If blank cities are also unacceptable, validate that separately.

headings.title: Guide a Required-Value Guard and an Optional Label
body:
```{index} Guide a Required-Value Guard and an Optional Label
```

## Guide a Required-Value Guard and an Optional Label
Suppose a customer must have a name but may omit a delivery note. The required name belongs in a constructor or boundary guard. The note can remain null in the model; its display fallback belongs where the display is produced. Do not use `note!` to make a missing note behave like a real string: it has no such runtime effect.

Guided prediction: what should the following print for null, empty and “Leave at desk”? The empty note has been supplied explicitly; this policy preserves it. Then change the policy to treat whitespace-only notes as absent and explain which condition must be added.
Use `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(note)` if the revised domain treats null, empty and whitespace-only strings alike. That is a business normalization decision, not the definition of null. As a second variation, replace a required-name `!` with an explicit argument guard and explain the difference between an early, informative rejection and a later NullReferenceException. The operator table below remains a quick reference. Pattern matching and LINQ exercises are optional extensions; neither is required to apply these missing-data contracts.

```csharp
int? y = null;   // OK
```

## The Null Operators


| Operator | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `x ?? y` | Null-coalescing | Return `x` if not null, else `y` |
| `x ??= y` | Null-coalescing assignment | Assign `y` to `x` only if `x` is null |
| `x?.Member` | Null-conditional | Access `Member` only if `x` is not null |
| `x?[i]` | Null-conditional index | Index only if `x` is not null |

## Practice


1. Write `int SafeParse(string? input)` that returns the parsed integer, or `0` if `input` is null or not a valid number. Use `int.TryParse`.
2. Given `List<string?> names`, use LINQ and `??` to produce a `List<string>` where every null is replaced with `"Anonymous"`.

   ```csharp
   if (user != null && user.Address != null)
       Console.WriteLine(user.Address.City);
   ```

## Substitution Is a Client's Behavioral Expectation

A derived discount policy may add fields and implementation details, but a caller using the base policy contract should still receive a result satisfying that contract. Inheritance is therefore more than reusing a convenient constructor. Ask whether the derived object can be used wherever the base behavior is promised without forcing the caller to know which subtype it received.

For a contract that accepts nonnegative subtotals and returns a discount between zero and the subtotal, a derived implementation that rejects every subtotal below 100 has strengthened the accepted-input requirement. A caller that was valid for the base contract can now fail. A derived implementation returning more than the subtotal has weakened the promised result. Both problems remain even when the code compiles.

Construction also follows a responsibility order. Base initialization establishes base state; derived initialization establishes additional state. Do not duplicate base validation in every client or assume that a base reference removes the derived object's fields. Reference type controls what the caller can name directly; the object still has its complete runtime identity.

Guided comparison: an Order has a collection of lines. Is it a subtype of a line? No: composition represents that has-a relationship. A special discount policy can plausibly be a policy if it preserves the policy contract. Draw the client call and state the promise being relied on before choosing inheritance merely to avoid a few repeated assignments.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
Chapter 11 composed an order from products and lines. Each object had a clear job without inheriting from a custom base class. Inheritance becomes useful when one type promises to behave as a more general type and client code can depend on that relationship.

Use discounts to examine that promise. A checkout needs a policy that accepts a nonnegative subtotal and returns an amount between zero and that subtotal. Several implementations can satisfy the same behavioral expectation. This section first uses a base class; the final section compares that design with an interface.
The supporting [OOP examples and variations](1204_oop_examples.ipynb) retains the original programming-paradigm discussion, separation of concerns, and Vehicle/Car illustration alongside these business models.

## Is-a Is a Behavioral Promise


```{index} Is-a Is a Behavioral Promise
```
A **base class** defines members that a **derived class** inherits. A derived object can be used through a base-type reference. The practical question is whether the derived type preserves the expectations of clients written for the base type.

An order has products and lines, so it uses composition. A percentage discount can be one kind of discount policy, so a small hierarchy may fit. Do not choose inheritance only to avoid copying a few lines of code. Reusing implementation without preserving behavior can create misleading types.

| Relationship | Suitable starting design |
| --- | --- |
| An order contains lines. | Composition. |
| A line refers to a product. | Composition and explicit sharing. |
| Several discount kinds support the same operation. | A base class or interface. |
| Two classes happen to print similar text. | A helper method may be enough. |

A class can inherit directly from one class. That does not mean a program must put all related business concepts in one hierarchy. Keep the relationship shallow enough to explain with concrete requirements.

`base.Apply` explicitly requests the base implementation. Here it performs the input validation before the derived method calculates a different valid result.
The results are 100.00 and 90.00. The percentage constructor validates its rate before storing it. The inherited input contract still matters: a negative subtotal is rejected by both implementations. Private state and validated operations keep the hierarchy's rules understandable.

Constructors are not inherited as ordinary methods. Each constructor must establish the valid state of its own type. When a base constructor requires arguments, use an initializer such as `: base(name)` to supply them before the derived constructor body runs.

## Substitution Preserves the Contract


```{index} Substitution Preserves the Contract
```
A **substitution** is using a derived object where a base type is expected. A client that accepts `DiscountPolicy` should continue to receive a valid result for a valid input. A derived class that returns a negative amount or rejects inputs the base accepts breaks that expectation even if its code compiles.

Write down the behavior you need before designing the hierarchy:

- Accept every nonnegative decimal subtotal in the exercise's domain.
- Reject a negative subtotal.
- Return an amount from zero through the original subtotal.
- Avoid changing the caller's order or printing from the calculation.

These are behavioral obligations. The compiler checks type compatibility and method signatures; it does not prove business invariants. Boundary checks help expose violations. Chapter 21 later develops more formal contract reasoning.

## Distinguish Choosing a Member from Dispatching Its Implementation

A variable's compile-time type determines which members a call can name and participates in overload resolution. A virtual call can then dispatch to an override selected from the runtime object. These are different decisions. Overloading adds a signature choice; overriding changes implementation of an inherited virtual contract. Hiding a nonvirtual member with new is another behavior and should not be described as runtime overriding.

| Situation | What determines the important choice? |
| --- | --- |
| Overloaded method candidates | Compile-time argument/type rules |
| Override of a virtual member | Runtime object for the chosen virtual call |
| Hidden nonvirtual member | The member selected through the reference's static type |

Trace a base-typed reference holding a derived policy object. For a virtual Calculate call, follow the override implemented by that object. Now change only the variable declaration to the derived type: the stored object has not changed, although more members may become available to the caller. A cast is not a request to construct a new object or change the object into another subtype.

An abstract class can leave some behavior unimplemented while supplying common state or concrete operations. It cannot be directly instantiated as a completed object. A concrete derived type must provide the required behavior before clients can use an instance. The requirement belongs to the type contract, not to a convention that an unimplemented method should return zero.

Guided trace: use two derived policies through a sequence of base references. Predict which implementation each virtual call reaches and check that every result satisfies the shared domain/result conditions. Then compare the preserved hiding/override variants in the supporting reading; use them to explain why matching method names alone do not prove identical dispatch.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
A client should not need a separate calculation branch for every discount class. Runtime polymorphism lets one call use the implementation associated with the actual object. The declared type of a variable describes the operations available to the client; the runtime object determines which override runs.

Keep the object diagram from the previous section. A variable declared `DiscountPolicy` can refer to a percentage or fixed policy. Changing the variable's declared type does not replace the object or strip away its derived behavior.

## Virtual Calls Select an Override



A base method marked `virtual` allows a derived class to override it. The derived method uses `override` with the matching signature. In the loop below, every variable has the same declared base type, but each object's override provides its calculation.

Before running, identify the three actual object types and calculate their results independently. There is no cast or type-name comparison in the client loop.
The output is 100.00, 90.00, and 95.00. If a fourth policy preserves the same contract, this loop does not need another branch. That is the useful extension point: clients depend on the behavior available through the general type.

A nonvirtual method is not overridden by merely declaring another method with the same name. C# also supports member hiding, but hiding follows different selection rules and is outside this core sequence. Use explicit `override` when the intended behavior is runtime replacement of a virtual member.

body:
