## Overriding Is Different from Overloading


```{index} Overriding Is Different from Overloading
```
**Overriding** supplies a derived implementation for an inherited virtual or abstract member. **Overloading** gives methods the same name with different parameter lists. Overload selection uses the call's available type and argument information; it does not provide the same extension mechanism as a virtual call.

Keep the distinction concrete: `Apply(decimal subtotal)` overridden in two policy classes is one polymorphic operation. `Print(string)` and `Print(int)` are two overloads selected by the argument type. Changing only a return type is not enough to define a distinct overload.

An overridden `ToString` is another familiar virtual operation. It should return a useful text representation rather than perform printing as a side effect. Formatting an object and changing its business state are separate responsibilities.

An **abstract class** cannot be directly instantiated. It can contain shared implementation and abstract members that concrete derived classes must implement. Use it when a general type has useful common behavior but has no sensible complete instance by itself.

The following payment example gives every payment a validated amount. The abstract operation produces a description that each concrete kind supplies. The array demonstrates the same runtime-dispatch idea as the policy loop.
`protected` permits a derived type to call the base constructor while preventing client code from constructing the abstract base directly. The abstract class can own state and concrete methods. The derived `Describe` implementations use `override`, just as with virtual methods.

body:

## Depend on the Capability the Client Needs

A checkout coordinator needs a way to request payment. It need not know every field or helper method of a particular payment provider. An interface names the small capability the client relies on. An implementing class can have a different internal representation and still satisfy that capability, provided its behavior and failure policy meet the contract.

Supplying the collaborator through a constructor makes the dependency visible. The coordinator can reject a missing required collaborator at construction rather than failing unexpectedly during a later transaction. This is an application of composition and null contracts, not a requirement to use an elaborate dependency-injection framework.

A test double can record a requested amount and return a prepared response. That permits a test of the coordinator's interaction without contacting a real payment service. Check more than whether any call occurred: the amount, number of calls, result interpretation and state on rejection can all matter. A recording double observes collaboration; it does not by itself prove that the real external service works.

Guided design: a report formatter needs only a way to produce a line of text. Compare making every formatter inherit a large invoice-processing base class with supplying a small formatting capability. State which parts are actually shared and which are accidental similarities. An interface does not imply that all implementations share state, a base implementation or the same operational cost.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
A checkout needs a discount calculation, not necessarily a family of classes sharing fields. An interface gives that requirement a name. A class can implement the capability while keeping its own representation and constructor design.

Connect the idea to Chapter 11: `Checkout` has a discount component. Composition describes the relationship; an interface describes the operations that the component promises. These techniques work together rather than competing for a single “best” programming style.

## A Small Capability Contract


```{index} A Small Capability Contract
```
The `IDiscountPolicy` interface declares one operation. Implementations provide a public method with the required signature. They do not use `override` merely to implement this interface. The `I` naming prefix is a convention that makes interface types recognizable.

The exercise contract additionally requires nonnegative input, rejection of negative subtotals, and a result between zero and the subtotal. Those business rules need explanation and checks; the interface declaration alone cannot express all of them.
An interface is not simply an abstract class with a different name. It describes a capability without requiring a shared instance-field representation or constructor. A class may implement several interfaces but inherits directly from at most one class. This chapter uses only method signatures; modern C# supports additional interface features that are unnecessary here.

Keep contracts small enough that implementations can satisfy them coherently. A single interface requiring discounts, database persistence, console menus, and stock reservations would combine unrelated responsibilities.

This is **constructor injection**: supplying a dependency explicitly instead of hard-coding its creation inside the client. It does not require a framework or a dependency-injection container.

Because checkout only calls the interface, a new policy does not require editing its calculation method. The model still needs validation at the right boundary; injection is not a substitute for a behavioral contract.
The two checkout objects share the same client implementation and use different components. They do not inherit from separate “ordinary checkout” and “member checkout” classes. If discount selection changes at a business boundary, constructor creation can choose a different component without multiplying checkout subtypes.

A field declared `readonly` prevents the checkout from reassigning that collaborator after construction. It does not guarantee that the supplied implementation has no mutable fields. State any side-effect expectations and test the implementations you accept.


A **test double** is a deliberately simple substitute used to observe a collaboration. Here a recording policy counts calls and returns the input unchanged. It satisfies the result contract and makes delegation visible without relying on a particular percentage formula.

Check that checkout passes the actual subtotal and invokes the collaborator exactly once. These observations would reveal a client that ignores its dependency, calls it twice, or supplies the wrong amount.
A call-count check is useful here because delegation is the behavior under test. Do not assert every private helper call in an application: that would make harmless refactoring difficult. Prefer checks of observable results, with targeted collaboration checks where they clarify the contract.

## Choose Composition, an Interface, or a Base Class


```{index} Choose Composition, an Interface, or a Base Class
```
Start with the smallest design that supports the requirements. A concrete collaborator is enough when there is one implementation. Introduce an interface when clients need interchangeable capabilities or a clear testing boundary. Use a base class when the types share a meaningful substitution relationship and common behavior or state.

| Need | Design to consider |
| --- | --- |
| Order owns several lines. | Composition with a concrete line type. |
| Checkout supports several discount calculations. | Composition through a small interface. |
| Several payment kinds share validated amount state. | An abstract base class with overrides. |
| One calculation repeated in one class. | A private helper method. |

Do not create an interface for every class automatically. An interface adds another contract to maintain. Likewise, do not build a deep hierarchy to anticipate features that do not exist yet. Use an explicit use case and a short test to justify an extension point.

In Chapter 13, interfaces become contracts for abstract data types, and generics let one implementation support multiple element types. The connection is behavioral: clients rely on an operation's promise while representation details remain hidden. For persistence after this chapter, use the optional database appendix.

headings.title: Programming Paradigms and Separation of Concerns
body:
```{index} Programming Paradigms and Separation of Concerns
```

## Programming Paradigms and Separation of Concerns

```{index} Programming Paradigms and Separation of Concerns
```

Languages such as Java, C++, C#, and Python are general-purpose high-level programming languages and they support multiple
programming **paradigms**; which means you can use C# to develop computer programs using
different styles such as:

- procedural programming: (focused on procedures and functions),
- object-oriented programming (based on objects and classes), and
- functional programming (emphasizing mathematical functions and immutability).

Object-oriented programming (OOP) is one of the popular programming paradigms.
**Separation of concerns** is an important design goal that classes and objects can support. Separation of concerns is a design principle to separate a computer program
into different sections with each section addresses a separate concern. For OOP design,
the concerns are separated into objects. Architectural patterns such as model-view-controller (MVC) can separate stored state and business behavior from presentation and interaction. These design goals also apply outside OOP.

The most popular model of OOP is a class-based model. In OOP, a class is a
**template** for creating objects, and an **object** entity is
an instance of a class. Each object follows the member definitions of its class. Creating an instance is **instantiation**; inheritance instead relates a derived class to a base class. In .NET, some classes
(e.g., Console) are supplied by the standard libraries and users can also define classes (e.g., UI).

While procedural programming is about writing procedures or methods that perform
operations on the data, object-oriented programming (OOP) provides a clear structure
for the code to reduce **complexity** and to make the programs **reusable**.

The four basic principles of object-oriented programming are: [^1204_oop_examples-oop-microsoft]

- **Abstraction**: Modeling the relevant attributes and interactions of entities as classes
  to define an abstract representation of a system.
- **Encapsulation**: Hiding the internal state and functionality of an object and only
  allowing access through a public set of functions.
- **Inheritance**: Ability to create new abstractions based on existing abstractions; which
  enables code **reusability**.
- **Polymorphism**: Ability to implement inherited properties or methods in different
  ways across multiple abstractions.

**Data abstraction** describes operations and their meaning while hiding representation choices. Abstract classes and interfaces can express contracts, but abstraction is a broader design idea and does not require either keyword.

To further explain the four pillars of OOP [^1204_oop_examples-oop-techtarget]:
The **encapsulation** principle states that all important information is contained inside
an object and only select information is exposed. The implementation and state of
each object are privately held inside a defined class. Client code uses the accessible members rather than directly changing private fields. Encapsulation can protect state invariants and reduce accidental changes; it is not a security boundary against arbitrary hostile code.

The **abstraction** principle states that objects only reveal internal mechanisms that
are relevant for the use of other objects, hiding any unnecessary implementation code.
An implementation can change while its public contract remains stable. This can let clients keep using the same operations after internal changes.

The **inheritance** principle states that classes can reuse code and properties from
other classes. Relationships and subclasses between objects can be assigned,
enabling developers to reuse common logic, while still maintaining a unique hierarchy.
Inheritance can reuse common behavior, but it does not automatically improve accuracy or design. The derived type still needs to preserve the base contract.

The **polymorphism** principle states that objects are designed to share behaviors,
and they can take on more than one form. The program determines which meaning or
usage is necessary for each execution of that object from a parent class, reducing
the need to duplicate code. A child class is then created, which extends the
functionality of the parent class. Polymorphism enables different types of objects
to pass through the same interface.

## Abstract Classes and Interfaces Compared

```{index} Abstract Classes and Interfaces Compared
```

The original comparison table is retained in corrected form. Both abstract classes and interfaces can express abstractions. An abstract class can supply instance state, constructors for derived classes, and shared implementations. An interface can describe a capability implemented by otherwise unrelated types. Neither can be instantiated directly as a complete concrete object.

| Feature | Abstract class | Interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type relationship | A class derives directly from at most one class. | A class can implement multiple interfaces; an interface can inherit other interfaces. |
| Instance state | Can store instance fields. | Does not supply per-object instance fields. |
| Construction | Can initialize shared state through a constructor invoked by a derived class. | Does not provide instance constructors for implementing objects. |
| Operations | Can combine concrete, abstract, and virtual members. | Can declare contracts; modern C# also permits default implementations and other advanced members. |
| Access | Can expose public/protected members and hide private implementation. | Ordinary signatures used in this course are public contracts; modern interfaces have additional access and member rules. |
| Reuse | Can share state and behavior within a meaningful subtype family. | Can share a capability across unrelated implementations. |
| Evolution | Adding an abstract requirement can break derived implementations; adding suitable concrete behavior may not. | Adding a required member can break implementers; default implementations can sometimes provide a migration path. |

The current chapter deliberately uses ordinary interface signatures. The table does not turn advanced interface features into prerequisites, but it avoids the old claim that every interface contains only method signatures.[^1204_oop_examples-interfaces]

The earlier abstract Animal example also combined an abstract Sound with a concrete Sleep method. Here is that small variation, separate from the current payment example.

### Additional Abstract and Interface Variations

```{index} Additional Abstract and Interface Variations
```

The original abstraction lesson also illustrated a Circle area, a Rectangle with both area and perimeter, a failed attempt to construct an abstract class, and an animal interface. Retain those small cases as well as the current payment/capability examples.

Use different type names in this one-cell comparison so the two contracts do not conflict: AreaShape requires area only; MeasuredShape requires area and perimeter. Circle stores its radius and returns pi times radius squared. MeasuredRectangle stores width and height and implements both required operations. An interface supplies a contract for a capability, rather than an instance-field representation or a constructor.

**Intentional compile-time error:** `MeasuredShape shape = new MeasuredShape();` attempts to instantiate an abstract class and produces CS0144. Construct a concrete MeasuredRectangle instead. A concrete derived class must implement every inherited abstract operation.

The interface variation calls sound and running behavior through IAnimal. Public implementations do not use override simply because they satisfy an interface. Compare this with the abstract Animal/Sleep example above and with the current IDiscountPolicy contract.

headings.title: ADT Contracts
body:
# ADT Contracts

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

An **abstract data type** starts with behavior. Before deciding whether data should be stored in an array, linked nodes, or a hash table, we decide what operations the type promises to support.
```{index} Describe the Observable History First
```

headings.title: Describe the Observable History First
body:
```{index} Describe the Observable History First
```

## Describe the Observable History First

An undo history is not defined by an array or a linked node. It is defined by what a client can observe after a sequence of operations. If the client records A, records B, and then undoes once, it expects B to be removed before A. An implementation can store those entries in different ways while preserving that behavior. This separates the abstract data type, the behavioral contract, from the data structure used to realize it.

Write the history on paper before writing a class. For each operation, record the result, the resulting abstract contents, and the empty/failure policy. If the contract says an unsuccessful TryPop leaves state unchanged, returning false after already decrementing Count violates the contract even if later tests happen to restore the count.

| Operation | Result | Abstract history, oldest to newest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Empty | [] |
| Push A | Recorded | [A] |
| Push B | Recorded | [A, B] |
| TryPop | Success, B | [A] |
| TryPop | Success, A | [] |
| TryPop | Failure | [] |

The empty failure is part of the behavior, not an implementation detail to settle later. A different ADT might throw on an empty Pop. Both can be coherent contracts, but a client written for one cannot assume the other. Also specify whether null entries, duplicates, or a fixed capacity are allowed. These policies determine which tests should succeed and what failure must preserve.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
```

headings.title: Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
body:
```{index} Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge
```

## Separate Client Knowledge from Implementation Knowledge

A C# interface can express operation names and types, for example a success-returning method with an out result. It cannot by itself express every ordering rule or state invariant. Two classes can compile against the same interface and still behave differently. Tests and explanations connect the syntax to the promised history.

The client should not need to know the backing array's capacity or the head node's field name. If a capacity change affects returned values or exposes unused slots, representation details have leaked through the abstraction. Conversely, the implementer must know enough about storage to maintain its invariants. Abstraction assigns different responsibilities to the two roles; it does not mean that implementation details are unimportant.

Guided exercise: keep the interface unchanged but change removal to return A before B. Identify the first row at which this behavior differs from the specified history. Then explain why a test that checks only Count would miss the defect. Extend the history with a failed removal followed by a new push; this checks whether failure left the structure reusable.

```{dropdown} Contract checkpoint
The first successful removal must return B. A queue-like implementation could keep the right counts while returning the wrong element. Checking returned values, order, state after failure, and later reuse tests more of the contract than checking size alone.
```
```{index} abstract data type
```
```{index} contract; data structure
```

headings.title: What an ADT Specifies
body:
```{index} What an ADT Specifies
```

## What an ADT Specifies

An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does **not** require one particular internal representation.

For a stack, the contract might say:

| Operation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Push(item)` | Add an item to the top. |
| `Pop()` | Remove and return the top item. |
| `Peek()` | Return the top item without removing it. |
| `Count` | Report how many items are stored. |

This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.
```{index} interface; ADT
```

headings.title: Interfaces as Contracts
body:
```{index} Interfaces as Contracts
```

## Interfaces as Contracts

In C#, an `interface` is a natural way to write an ADT contract. It names the operations but leaves the storage strategy to a class.
```{index} client code
```

headings.title: Client Code Depends on Behavior
body:
```{index} Client Code Depends on Behavior
```

## Client Code Depends on Behavior

**Client code** is code that uses a type. If client code only needs stack behavior, it should not care whether the stack is backed by a `List<T>`, an array, or linked nodes.

That means this is a better variable type for many methods:

```csharp
static void UndoLastAction(IStack<string> actions)
```

than this:

```csharp
static void UndoLastAction(ListStack<string> actions)
```

The first version accepts any stack implementation that satisfies the contract.
```{index} invariant
```

headings.title: Contracts Include Rules
body:
```{index} Contracts Include Rules
```

## Contracts Include Rules

A contract includes more than method names. It also includes rules:

- `Pop` removes the same item that `Peek` would return.
- `Count` increases after `Push` and decreases after `Pop`.
- `Pop` and `Peek` on an empty stack are errors.

A rule that must remain true for the object to be valid is called an **invariant**. Data-structure code often exists to preserve invariants while operations run quickly.

body:
```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

An ADT names behavior. An interface can express that behavior in C#. Implementations provide storage and algorithms behind the contract. This separation lets programs change representation without changing every caller.

headings.title: Representations and Costs
body:
# Representations and Costs

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

Once an ADT contract is clear, the next question is representation: how should the data be stored so the required operations are correct and efficient?
```{index} One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work
```

headings.title: One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work
body:
```{index} One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work
```

## One Behavior Can Have Different Physical Work

Use the undo contract from the preceding lesson. An array representation might keep active entries in positions zero through Count minus one. A linked representation might keep the newest entry at the head. The same Push/Pop history can be correct in both, yet their storage and work differ. To compare them fairly, hold the abstract behavior fixed and change only the representation.

For the array, Count and capacity answer different questions. Count describes active entries; capacity describes available slots in the allocated backing storage. A push with unused capacity writes one entry and increases Count. A push into full storage may allocate a larger array, copy active entries, and then append. Calling both pushes constant work ignores the copying performed by the growth case.

For a linked representation, a push can create one node whose next reference identifies the old head. Updating the head then makes the new node first. A pop can advance head to its next node. This avoids an array-wide growth copy, but node allocation and extra references are still real costs. Neither representation is universally better merely because one operation has a simple asymptotic label.

| Representation question | Array-backed history | Linked history |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How are active values located? | Used prefix of slots | Nodes reachable from head |
| What marks empty? | Count equals zero | No head node, with matching Count |
| What may make a push expensive? | Growth and copying | Allocation and runtime costs |
| What must stay hidden? | Unused capacity | Internal node links |

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Define What You Count
```

headings.title: Define What You Count
body:
```{index} Define What You Count
```

## Define What You Count

If the input size is the number n of active entries, counting element copies explains an array growth. Counting only calls to Push hides the difference among calls. Big-O summarizes a bound as n grows; it does not supply the cost model for you. State whether the analysis counts comparisons, copies, reference updates, or another operation.

An amortized append claim concerns a whole sequence of operations, including occasional expensive growth. It is not a claim that every individual append is cheap, and it is not an average over randomly selected inputs. Likewise, constant auxiliary storage describes additional working memory under a model; it does not mean the data structure itself occupies no memory.

Guided comparison: an array with Count three and capacity four receives two pushes. Explain why the first can use a free slot and the second may require growth. Draw the abstract history after both calls, then draw the different physical storage states. Keeping those drawings separate prevents a copied backing array from being mistaken for a changed ADT result.
```{index} representation; data structure
```
```{index} representation independence
```

headings.title: One Contract, Multiple Representations
body:
```{index} One Contract, Multiple Representations
```

## One Contract, Multiple Representations

The same stack ADT can be represented in more than one way:

| Representation | Main idea |
| --- | --- |
| Array-backed stack | Store items in contiguous slots and track the top index. |
| List-backed stack | Delegate storage growth to `List<T>`. |
| Linked-node stack | Store each item in a node that references the next node. |

If all three preserve the same contract, client code can use them through the same interface. This is **representation independence**.
```{index} array-backed stack
```

headings.title: Array-Backed Stack
body:
```{index} Array-Backed Stack
```

## Array-Backed Stack

An array-backed stack stores items from left to right. The next available index is also the current count.

```text
items: [A] [B] [C] [ ] [ ]
count: 3
top:   C
```

Pushing writes into `items[count]`, then increments `count`. Popping decrements `count`, reads the value, and clears the slot.
```{index} linked nodes
```
```{index} reference; linked structure
```

headings.title: Linked Nodes and References
body:
```{index} Linked Nodes and References
```

## Linked Nodes and References

A linked representation stores each item in a small object called a node. Each node holds a value and a reference to the next node.

```text
top -> [C | next] -> [B | next] -> [A | null]
```

The variable `top` does not contain the whole stack. It contains a reference to the first node. Following references reveals the rest of the structure.

headings.title: Counting Work and Big-O
body:
```{index} Counting Work and Big-O
```

## Counting Work and Big-O


```{index} Big O; input size; auxiliary space
```
Let `n` be the number of records. Count a representative operation before comparing implementations. **Big-O** describes an upper bound on how work grows with input size, ignoring fixed factors for sufficiently large inputs. It is not an elapsed time or automatically a worst-case claim.

| Bound | Example | Effect of doubling input |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | Reading one array slot | Bounded work independent of size. |
| O(log n) | Repeatedly halving a search interval | About one extra halving. |
| O(n) | Scanning all records | About twice the work. |
| O(n log n) | A typical comparison sort | Slightly more than twice the work. |
| O(n²) | Comparing every pair | About four times the work. |

These are useful upper bounds; a linear scan is also O(n²), but O(n) is more informative. A **tight bound**, written Θ, describes the actual growth order under the stated model. Later chapters use Θ when both upper and lower growth bounds are known.
This example counts exactly `n` additions. Array access and fixed-width arithmetic are treated as constant-cost operations. A comparison of long strings can depend on string length.

Specify the case: a search may stop at the first record or inspect all `n`. **Amortized cost** averages over a sequence of operations: geometric array growth permits O(1) amortized append even though a resizing append takes O(n). This does not make every append constant-time. **Auxiliary space** counts extra storage beyond the input; a running total takes O(1), while an additional copy takes O(n). Chapter 21 develops formal bounds and richer cost models.

Before running, predict the addition counts for sizes zero, one, four, and eight. Then explain why reading only `expenses[0]` has a different growth bound and needs a nonempty-input precondition.
```{index} operation cost
```
```{index} Big O; collection operations
```

headings.title: Operation Costs
body:
```{index} Operation Costs
```

## Operation Costs

A data structure is not just correct or incorrect. It also has costs.

| Operation | Array/List-backed stack | Linked-node stack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Push` | Usually O(1); occasional resize costs O(n) | O(1) |
| `Pop` | O(1) | O(1) |
| `Peek` | O(1) | O(1) |
| Random access by index | O(1), if exposed | O(n) |
| Extra memory per item | low | one extra reference per node |

The best representation depends on the workload. If a program mostly pushes and pops at one end, either representation can work. If it needs fast index access, linked nodes are the wrong fit.

body:

2. Explain why resizing an array-backed stack is occasional O(n), even though most pushes are O(1).
3. Choose a representation for an undo history and justify it using operation costs.

headings.title: Summary
body:
```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

A representation is the hidden storage strategy behind an ADT contract. Arrays, lists, and linked nodes make different tradeoffs in speed, memory use, and flexibility. Data-structure design is the art of matching those tradeoffs to the operations a program performs most often.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```

# Generics for Reusable ADTs

You have been using generics since Chapter 8: `List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`. In an ADT, generics let one contract and one implementation work with many element types while preserving compile-time type checking.
For the caller obligations of the ref swap exercise, review {ref}`Chapter 5 parameter passing <gap-return-values-out-and-ref>`.
```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

```{index} generic type
```

headings.title: Why Generics Exist
Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types
body:
```{index} Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types
```

## Reuse an Algorithm Without Erasing Its Types

An undo history of product codes and a history of numeric adjustments can follow the same push/pop rules. Writing two unrelated implementations repeats the same invariant and creates two places to repair a defect. A generic type makes the element type a parameter while leaving the behavioral algorithm shared.

Read `History<T>` as a type definition with an element-type placeholder. Read `History<string>` as one constructed type whose element operations must accept strings. The placeholder is not a variable containing an element and is not a request to decide the type afresh on every assignment. A History<int> and a History<string> are different constructed types even though their operation names are the same.

The general class pattern is `class Container<T> { /* members that use T */ }`. A generic method has its own type parameter list, as in `static T Identity<T>(T value)`. These are declaration patterns, not complete programs. In concrete use the compiler checks compatible argument/result types. That lets a bad element insertion be rejected before a client discovers an incompatible value during a later cast.


```{index} State Which Operations the Generic Code Needs
```

headings.title: State Which Operations the Generic Code Needs
body:
```{index} State Which Operations the Generic Code Needs
```

## State Which Operations the Generic Code Needs

An unconstrained T supports being stored, passed and returned. It does not promise a Price property or a meaningful greater-than operation. If the algorithm needs ordering, supply an ordering policy or an appropriate constraint. If it needs key identity, supply an equality/hash policy with its consistency requirements. Ordering and equality are related concepts but different contracts.

| Algorithm purpose | Information needed beyond storage |
| --- | --- |
| Return the most recently stored item | No ordering comparison |
| Sort values for a report | A consistent ordering policy |
| Find a key in a hash table | Equality and compatible hashing |
| Call an element-specific capability | An explicit capability constraint |

A comparer can say that two invoices have equal totals even when they are distinct invoices. A key-equality policy might instead use invoice ID. Choosing a generic collection does not choose those business meanings automatically. Avoid solving a missing requirement by converting every value to text and comparing that text; it can change numeric order and lose distinctions.

Guided design: create a generic history interface for values that never need to be compared. Would requiring all element types to implement an ordering interface help? It would unnecessarily reject useful element types. Add constraints because an operation needs them, not because generics seem advanced. The short lambda/query forms later in this lesson are a bridge for reading policy arguments; the fundamental generic contract does not depend on mastering LINQ.

headings.title: Ordering and Equality Are Different Contracts
body:
```{index} Ordering and Equality Are Different Contracts
```

## Ordering and Equality Are Different Contracts


```{index} Ordering and Equality Are Different Contracts
```
An ordering comparer answers before, tied, or after with a negative value, zero, or a positive value. An equality comparer answers whether two values identify the same key. A price tie does not make two products the same product. Supply the same ordering policy to sorting and binary search; supply matching Equals and GetHashCode policies to hash collections. Equal keys must have equal hash codes, but unequal keys can collide. Never change a stored key in a way that changes its equality or hash value.
The named AmountComparer implements IComparer<Invoice>. Comparing Amount uses decimal.CompareTo, which avoids arithmetic subtraction and conversion. A comparer must be consistent and transitive. Array.Sort does not promise arrival order for tied values. A stable sorting algorithm preserves that order; Chapter 16 makes the distinction visible.

headings.title: Reading Short Expressions and Queries
body:
```{index} Reading Short Expressions and Queries
```

## Reading Short Expressions and Queries


```{index} Reading Short Expressions and Queries
```
Later collection examples sometimes use compact C# forms. The expression x => x > 0 is a lambda: a function receiving x and returning the comparison result. A library method can call that function for each value. Where filters values, Select transforms them, OrderBy orders them, and ToArray materializes a separate array. These LINQ extension methods require using System.Linq. Prefer an explicit loop when it makes the algorithm or mutation clearer. Query pipelines can defer work until enumeration; ToArray executes the pipeline now.
An expression-bodied member such as public int Count => items.Count; is shorthand for a getter returning that expression. A target-typed new() uses the declared variable type, so List<int> values = new(); constructs a List<int>. Neither abbreviation changes the data-structure contract. Named classes and explicit constructors remain useful while learning a new model.

headings.title: Iterators
body:
# Iterators

Every type in this chapter has been an ADT you interact with through explicit operations: `Push`, `Pop`, `Get`, `Set`. `foreach` is different — it is a loop that lets a *type* decide what "give me the next element" means, without the caller ever touching an index or a key. This section covers how that contract works, and how to implement it for your own types.

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

```{index} IEnumerable; IEnumerator
```

headings.title: Why foreach Works
Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One
body:
```{index} Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One
```

## Separate Producing a Sequence from Storing One

A collection knows where its elements are stored. A client often needs only to visit those elements in the promised order. Enumeration provides a boundary between those responsibilities. Foreach asks for an enumeration protocol rather than directly reading private array slots or node links.

For a simple countable sequence 2, 4, 6, imagine an enumerator positioned before the first value. A successful MoveNext advances to the next value and permits reading Current. After the final value, MoveNext reports false. The client does not invent an extra zero value merely because iteration has ended. This success/result separation resembles the Try operations from earlier collection lessons.

| Request | Outcome | Current value to consume |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First MoveNext | true | 2 |
| Second MoveNext | true | 4 |
| Third MoveNext | true | 6 |
| Fourth MoveNext | false | No next element |

An IEnumerable<T> describes something that can provide enumeration. An IEnumerator<T> represents progress through one enumeration. They are not interchangeable names for a collection. Multiple enumeration requests can have separate progress states, and a producer may compute elements instead of keeping all of them in a list.


```{index} A Yield Point Suspends Rather than Finishes the Sequence
```

headings.title: A Yield Point Suspends Rather than Finishes the Sequence
body:
```{index} A Yield Point Suspends Rather than Finishes the Sequence
```

## A Yield Point Suspends Rather than Finishes the Sequence

The pattern `IEnumerable<T> Produce(...) { ... yield return value; ... }` defines an iterator. Yielding supplies one element and suspends that enumeration's progress until the consumer requests another. An ordinary return from a value-returning method finishes that call; yield return participates in a sequence of resumptions. Explain this distinction before treating yield as abbreviated list construction.

Laziness changes when work and failures occur. Obtaining an enumerable need not run every statement that will produce its values. If the consumer stops after two elements, later elements may never be computed. An expensive calculation inside an iterator is not paid simply because an enumerable variable has been declared, but repeated enumerations may repeat that work. Do not promise caching unless the implementation explicitly provides it.

The producer also needs a mutation policy. An enumeration over shared mutable storage can be affected by changes made after the enumerable is obtained. Library collections may detect invalid mutation during enumeration; custom types must state their own behavior. Returning IEnumerable<T> does not automatically create a snapshot or make private storage immutable.

Guided prediction: an iterator announces each produced number and yields 2, 4, 6. A caller breaks after consuming 4. Which production announcements should appear? Then run a second enumeration and ask whether it starts with a fresh progress state. Use the existing runnable iterator examples to check your prediction and distinguish fresh enumeration from continuing one enumerator.
```{index} yield return
```

headings.title: Writing an Iterator with yield return
body:
```{index} Writing an Iterator with yield return
```

## Writing an Iterator with yield return

Implementing `IEnumerator<T>` by hand — tracking a position field, writing `MoveNext()` and `Current` yourself — is tedious for something as simple as "count from one number to another." The `yield return` statement lets the compiler generate that machinery for you. A method that contains `yield return` becomes an iterator: each call to `yield return` produces one element and pauses; the method resumes from that point the next time an element is requested.

Nothing about `EvenNumbers` mentions `IEnumerator`, `MoveNext`, or `Current` — the compiler builds a hidden class that implements all of it. The method's return type is `IEnumerable<int>`, and the body describes *what to produce*, not *how to track position*.

```{index} IEnumerable; custom implementation
```

headings.title: Making Your Own Type foreach-able
body:
```{index} Making Your Own Type foreach-able
```

## Making Your Own Type foreach-able

A standalone iterator *method* is useful, but sometimes the thing you want to iterate is a type you have already defined — an ADT you built, not a built-in collection. To make `foreach` work directly on an instance of your type, implement `IEnumerable<T>` and put a `yield return` inside `GetEnumerator()`:

`IEnumerable<T>` requires the generic `GetEnumerator()`. The second, non-generic `IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` line is boilerplate C# requires because `IEnumerable<T>` itself extends the older, non-generic `IEnumerable` — it just forwards to the generic version above it. Once both are present, `NumberRange` works with `foreach`, LINQ, and any other API that accepts `IEnumerable<T>`, exactly like `List<T>` does.

```{index} iterator; lazy evaluation
```

headings.title: Iterators Are Lazy
body:
```{index} Iterators Are Lazy
```

## Iterators Are Lazy

An iterator method does not run its body when you call it — it runs one step at a time, only as far as the caller actually asks for elements. Calling `EvenNumbers(1, 1000000)` returns instantly; the loop body only executes as `foreach` requests each next value. This matters for two reasons: an iterator can describe an infinite or unbounded sequence without ever running forever, and a `foreach` that stops early (with `break`) never computes the elements it never asked for.

body:
# Dynamic Arrays

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

A dynamic array gives the programmer the feel of a growable sequence while storing values in ordinary contiguous array storage behind the scenes.
```{index} contiguous storage
```

headings.title: Contiguous Storage
body:
```{index} Contiguous Storage
```

## Contiguous Storage

An array stores elements in numbered positions. If the array has five slots, valid indexes are `0` through `4`.

```text
index:  0   1   2   3   4
value: [10][20][30][  ][  ]
```

The array has a fixed **capacity**: the number of slots available. A dynamic array also tracks **count**: the number of slots currently being used.
```{index} capacity
```
```{index} resizing; dynamic array
```

headings.title: Resizing by Copying
body:
```{index} Resizing by Copying
```

## Resizing by Copying

When the array fills up, the dynamic array cannot stretch the existing array. It allocates a larger array, copies the existing values, then continues adding into the new storage.

A common strategy is to double the capacity each time resizing is needed. This makes individual resize steps expensive, but keeps most `Add` operations cheap.
```{index} indexed access
```

headings.title: Worked Example: A Small Dynamic Array
body:
```{index} Worked Example: A Small Dynamic Array
```

## Worked Example: A Small Dynamic Array

This class stores integers in an internal array. `Add` appends to the next free slot. The indexer reads an existing value by index.
```{index} amortized cost
```

headings.title: Cost of Append and Indexing
body:
```{index} Cost of Append and Indexing
```

## Cost of Append and Indexing

Dynamic arrays have two different stories:

- Reading `items[index]` is O(1) because the index points directly to the slot.
- Most appends are O(1), but an append that triggers resizing is O(n) because it copies existing values.

Over many appends, doubling capacity gives **amortized O(1)** append cost. Amortized means the occasional expensive resize is spread across many cheap operations.
```{index} sequence; invariant; Count; Capacity
```

headings.title: A Sequence Contract and Its Invariants
body:
```{index} A Sequence Contract and Its Invariants
```

## A Sequence Contract and Its Invariants

A service desk keeps work orders in processing order. The values might be strings such as `WO-10` and `WO-30`, but the representation should work for other types too. Chapter 13 separated an ADT's behavior from its implementation. Here the behavior is an ordered sequence: append a work order, read its position, insert an urgent order, and remove a completed order.

For an array-backed implementation, three facts must remain true after every public operation:

1. `0 <= Count <= Capacity`.
2. The live sequence occupies indexes `0` through `Count - 1` without gaps.
3. Values outside that range are storage, not members of the sequence.

A zero in an integer array is not a reliable empty marker: zero might be a real value. `Count` determines membership. With `Count = 3` and `Capacity = 5`, reading index `4` must fail even though the underlying array physically has that slot. An insertion at index `3` is valid because it appends; a read at index `3` is invalid.

**Check your understanding (basic):** An array has capacity eight and count three. List the legal read indexes and the legal insertion indexes. Explain why these sets differ.
```{index} dynamic array; resize trace; alias
```

headings.title: Trace Growth Before Writing Code
body:
```{index} Trace Growth Before Writing Code
```

## Trace Growth Before Writing Code

Start with capacity two. Appending `WO-10` and `WO-30` uses both slots. Before a third append, allocate four slots, copy the two live references, and replace the private storage reference. The logical sequence has not changed yet. Only then write the new value and increase `Count`.

```text
Before growth: items -> [WO-10][WO-30]                 Count = 2
New storage:   larger -> [WO-10][WO-30][unused][unused]
After growth:  items -> [WO-10][WO-30][unused][unused]   Count = 2
After append:  items -> [WO-10][WO-30][WO-40][unused]    Count = 3
```

For reference-type elements, copying the array copies references, not the referenced objects. The work order objects would retain their identity. Our string labels let you concentrate on the sequence rather than object mutation.

| Append number | Count after append | Capacity | Existing entries copied |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| 3 | 3 | 4 | 2 |
| 4 | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| 5 | 5 | 8 | 4 |
| 6 | 6 | 8 | 0 |
| 7 | 7 | 8 | 0 |
| 8 | 8 | 8 | 0 |
| 9 | 9 | 16 | 8 |

**Predict (basic):** Before reading on, give the capacity and copy count for append 10. Does it resize again?
```{index} dynamic array; insertion; removal; shifting
```

headings.title: Middle Updates: Preserve the Unread Values
body:
```{index} Middle Updates: Preserve the Unread Values
```

## Middle Updates: Preserve the Unread Values

Suppose the live values are `[10, 20, 40, 50]`, and you must insert `30` at index two. First ensure space for a fifth value. Then shift from the right end toward the insertion point:

| Step | Live values and destination slot | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | `[10, 20, 40, 50, unused]` | Index two must become available. |
| Copy index 3 to 4 | `[10, 20, 40, 50, 50]` | Save the last value first. |
| Copy index 2 to 3 | `[10, 20, 40, 40, 50]` | The old index three is already safe. |
| Write 30 at index 2 | `[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]` | Increase count after storing the new value. |

Shifting left to right would overwrite values you have not copied yet. The temporary duplicates in the trace are expected; the sequence invariant applies at the operation boundary.

Removal moves in the opposite direction. To remove index one from `[10, 20, 30, 40]`, save `20`, copy `30` left, then copy `40` left. Reduce count to three and clear the formerly live final slot. Clearing prevents a removed reference from being retained unnecessarily; it does not reduce capacity.

Insertion at index `i` moves `n - i` existing entries. Removal moves `n - i - 1`. Appending and removing the last item move no entries, although an append may still resize.

**Trace (applied):** Insert at index zero and then remove the last item. Record each assignment. Explain why reversing the insertion loop corrupts the original sequence.
```{index} generics; dynamic array; bounds checking
```

headings.title: Complete Generic Implementation
body:
```{index} Complete Generic Implementation
```

## Complete Generic Implementation

The following implementation gives the work-order sequence a reusable element type `T`. `EnsureRoom` handles physical storage; `Insert` handles logical order. Keeping these responsibilities separate means growth cannot accidentally change count.

`default!` clears the unused slot. The exclamation mark suppresses a nullable-analysis warning for that storage assignment; it does not check anything at runtime. Clients cannot read the cleared slot because the indexer checks `Count`.

Run this cell independently. Expect count three, capacity four, the labels in order, and then removal of `WO-10`. This is an instructional implementation: it omits shrinking, iterators, concurrency, and protection against enormous capacity overflow.

Read the implementation in operation order. `Insert` validates before mutation, grows before shifting, moves right to left, writes the new value, and increments count once. `RemoveAt` validates before mutation, saves the result, compacts left to right, decreases count once, and clears the unused slot.

**Modify (applied):** Add `Contains(T value)` using `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`. Test repeated values and a missing value. Explain why supporting generics does not make searching constant-time.

```{index} amortized analysis; worst case; dynamic array
```

headings.title: Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost
body:
```{index} Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost
```

## Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost

For nine appends, the trace copies `2 + 4 + 8 = 14` existing entries and writes nine new entries. Counting these array writes gives 23 writes across nine operations. Some individual appends are costly, but the total grows in proportion to the number of appends.

For a longer sequence, copy sizes form `2 + 4 + 8 + ...`. Each term is twice the previous one, so the sum stays below twice the final number of inserted items. Adding one write per appended item still gives a total proportional to `n`. Dividing total work by `n` gives a constant amortized cost. This is a bound over an operation sequence, not an assumption about random inputs.

Growing by one slot each time would copy `2 + 3 + 4 + ... + (n - 1)` entries. That total grows quadratically. Avoiding spare capacity would therefore make repeated appends progressively expensive.

The tradeoff is spare storage. Doubling leaves unused slots after growth, and a resize temporarily keeps both old and new arrays alive. Amortized O(1) also does not guarantee a short pause for every append. A system with a strict response deadline may reserve capacity ahead of time.

**Explain (challenge):** Compare doubling with adding one slot using ten appends starting at capacity two. Count copies, not elapsed milliseconds. State both the worst-case cost of one append and the amortized cost of the whole sequence.


# Linked Nodes

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

A linked list stores a sequence as separate node objects connected by references. The representation makes insertion and deletion local, but finding a position requires traversal.
Replacing a caller head reference uses ref; review {ref}`Chapter 5 parameter passing <gap-return-values-out-and-ref>`.
```{index} node
```
```{index} linked list
```

headings.title: Nodes and References
body:
```{index} Nodes and References
```

## Nodes and References

Each node stores a value and a reference to the next node.

```text
head -> [10 | next] -> [20 | next] -> [30 | null]
```

The list variable stores a reference to the first node, often called the **head**. The last node points to `null`.
```{index} traversal; linked list
```

headings.title: Traversal
body:
```{index} Traversal
```

## Traversal

A linked list cannot jump directly to index `7`. To find an item, code follows references one node at a time. This is called **traversal**.
```{index} insertion; linked list
```

headings.title: Insertion After a Node
body:
```{index} Insertion After a Node
```

## Insertion After a Node

If you already have a reference to a node, inserting after it is local. Create a new node, point it to the old next node, then point the current node to the new node.

```text
before: [A] -> [C]
after:  [A] -> [B] -> [C]
```
```{index} deletion; linked list
```

headings.title: Deletion After a Node
body:
```{index} Deletion After a Node
```

## Deletion After a Node

Deleting after a known node is also local. Skip over the next node by changing one reference.

```text
before: [A] -> [B] -> [C]
after:  [A] --------> [C]
```
```{index} Costs and Tradeoffs
```

headings.title: Costs and Tradeoffs
body:
```{index} Costs and Tradeoffs
```

## Costs and Tradeoffs

Linked lists make some updates cheap only after the position is known.

| Operation | Singly linked list cost |
| --- | --- |
| Read first item | O(1) |
| Traverse all items | O(n) |
| Find by value | O(n) |
| Insert after known node | O(1) |
| Delete after known node | O(1) |
| Read by index | O(n) |

The phrase "known node" matters. If the program must search for the node first, that search is part of the total cost.
```{index} alias; linked list; reference
```

headings.title: References Are Paths, Not Copies
body:
```{index} References Are Paths, Not Copies
```

## References Are Paths, Not Copies

Work orders may also be represented by separate node objects. A node's `Next` is a reference to another node, not an embedded copy of the remaining list. Assigning `current = head` copies a reference: both variables initially identify the same object. Changing `current` to `current.Next` moves a cursor without moving `head`.

```text
head ----> [WO-10 | next] ---> [WO-30 | null]
current --^
```

If you traverse by repeatedly assigning to `head`, you lose your entry point to the sequence. A separate cursor preserves the list. Also distinguish changing a reference from changing an object: setting `current = current.Next` moves the cursor; setting `current.Next = ...` changes a link in the sequence.

**Trace (basic):** Draw both arrows before and after one cursor advance. Which variable still reaches the first work order?
```{index} linked list; insertion invariant; cycle
```

headings.title: Insertion Order and Lost Links
body:
```{index} Insertion Order and Lost Links
```

## Insertion Order and Lost Links

You know the node for `WO-10` and want to insert `WO-20` before `WO-30`. Preserve the old successor before overwriting its only incoming list link.

| Step | References | What remains reachable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create B | `A.Next = C`, `B.Next = null` | A still reaches C. |
| Save successor | `B.Next = A.Next` | B now reaches C too. |
| Connect B | `A.Next = B` | A reaches B, then C. |

The correct two assignments are `inserted.Next = node.Next; node.Next = inserted;`. Reversing them makes `inserted.Next` refer to `inserted` itself. The result is a cycle, and the original successor is disconnected from this chain. A traversal waiting for `null` would never finish.

For an empty list there is no predecessor. Inserting at the front sets `newNode.Next = head` before replacing `head`. The same steps work when the old head is null. A list wrapper is useful because it owns the head reference and can update it safely.

**Debug (applied):** Explain the reversed-assignment bug using named nodes A, B, and C. Do not run an unbounded traversal of the broken chain.
```{index} linked list; removal; head; tail
```

headings.title: Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants
body:
```{index} Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants
```

## Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants

To remove B after A, preserve B's successor by setting `A.Next = B.Next`. Removing the first node instead requires `head = head.Next`, because there is no preceding node to update. Unlinking does not destroy the object immediately: other references might still reach it, and .NET manages reclamation of unreachable objects.

A wrapper with a tail reference must maintain these rules:

- An empty list has count zero and both head and tail null.
- A nonempty list has a reachable head and tail, and `tail.Next` is null.
- Following `Next` from head visits exactly `Count` nodes and reaches tail last.

Removing the only node must clear both endpoints. Removing the last node of a longer chain must move tail to the predecessor. A tail reference makes append constant-time but does not make removal of the last node constant-time: a singly linked list still has to find that predecessor.

**Predict (applied):** A one-node list is emptied and then appended to. What goes wrong if removal leaves tail pointing to the old node?
```{index} linked list; generic implementation; tail reference
```

headings.title: A Complete Singly Linked Sequence
body:
```{index} A Complete Singly Linked Sequence
```

## A Complete Singly Linked Sequence

This wrapper presents the same `Add`, `Insert`, indexer, and `RemoveAt` operations as the dynamic array. Nodes are private so client code cannot accidentally create cycles or change count without updating the wrapper.

`NodeAt` validates the index, then follows links. `head!` and `Next!` express facts established by the list invariants after validation; they do not create runtime null checks. If those invariants are broken, the suppression cannot repair them.

Run the cell independently. It inserts the middle order, removes the head, empties the list, and appends again. The last line should be `count=1, first=WO-40`.

Notice that the interface hides implementation choices. `Insert(1, value)` first locates the predecessor and then rewires links. Although the rewiring is O(1), this index-based operation is O(n) in the worst case. The earlier `InsertAfter` example had a different assumption: its caller already held a node reference.

The demonstration prints by repeated indexing only because the list is tiny. For a long linked list, that pattern repeats traversal: indexes zero through `n - 1` require roughly `0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1)` link advances. A cursor or iterator should visit the sequence once instead.

**Extend (challenge):** Add an iterator using chapter 14's `yield return`. Compare a single traversal with repeated indexer reads. Explain what should happen if clients modify the list during iteration; production collections define such behavior explicitly.

```{index} doubly linked list; predecessor; memory overhead
```

headings.title: Doubly Linked Lists: A Different Tradeoff
body:
```{index} Doubly Linked Lists: A Different Tradeoff
```

## Doubly Linked Lists: A Different Tradeoff

A doubly linked node stores both `Next` and `Previous`. A known node can therefore find its predecessor without a search, and a stored tail can support constant-time removal at the end. The price is another reference per node and more links to maintain.

```text
null <- [A] <-> [B] <-> [C] -> null
```

Removing B connects `A.Next` to C and `C.Previous` to A. Removing an endpoint also changes the wrapper's head or tail. This representation still does not provide direct indexing: to find a numeric position, follow links from an endpoint.

**Compare (applied):** For frequent removal of a known item, explain what information singly and doubly linked lists require. Include the cost of locating the item if it is supplied only by value.
```{index} practice
```

# Representation Tradeoffs and Verification

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

This lab compares array-backed and linked-node representations by counting visits and explaining tradeoffs. The goal is not to prove that one representation is always better. The goal is to connect a workload to a representation choice.
```{index} Array Search and Indexing
```

headings.title: Array Search and Indexing
body:
```{index} Array Search and Indexing
```

## Array Search and Indexing

Arrays are strong at indexing. Searching by value still requires checking elements until the value is found or the array ends.
```{index} Linked Traversal
```

headings.title: Linked Traversal
body:
```{index} Linked Traversal
```

## Linked Traversal

A linked representation visits nodes by following references. There is no direct index jump.
```{index} Middle Insertion Costs
```

headings.title: Middle Insertion Costs
body:
```{index} Middle Insertion Costs
```

## Middle Insertion Costs

In an array, inserting into the middle requires shifting later elements. In a linked list, insertion after a known node changes references locally, but finding that node may still require traversal.
```{index} Decision Guide
```

headings.title: Decision Guide
body:
```{index} Decision Guide
```

## Decision Guide

| Workload | Better starting representation | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frequent indexing | Dynamic array | O(1) direct access by index |
| Frequent append | Dynamic array | Amortized O(1) append |
| Frequent insertion after known nodes | Linked list | O(1) reference update |
| Frequent search by value | Neither is ideal alone | Both may scan O(n) |
| Low per-item memory overhead | Dynamic array | No per-node reference field |

Use this table as a starting point, then adjust based on real operation counts and program constraints.
```{index} Lab Tasks
```

body:


headings.title: Separate Location Cost from Update Cost
body:
```{index} Separate Location Cost from Update Cost
```

## Separate Location Cost from Update Cost

A service desk stores `n` work orders. Two requests that sound similar can require different work: “insert at position 400” supplies an index; “insert after this node” supplies a location handle. Compare the same request and the same assumptions before claiming a speed advantage.

| Request | Dynamic array | Singly linked list with head and tail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read index i | O(1) | O(i + 1), O(n) worst case |
| Append | O(1) amortized, O(n) on resize | O(1) with stored tail |
| Insert at front | O(n) shifts | O(1) |
| Insert by index in middle | O(n) shifts, possibly growth | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove by index in middle | O(n) shifts | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove last | O(1), without shrinking | O(n) find predecessor |
| Search unsorted values | O(n) | O(n) |
| Visit every item once | O(n) | O(n) with cursor |

The linked wrapper in this chapter exposes indices rather than public node handles. Its middle insertion therefore includes traversal. A different API could expose validated handles, but it must specify ownership and what happens when a handle refers to a removed node.

**Reason (applied):** A developer claims `Insert(400, value)` is constant-time because it changes two links. Identify the omitted work. Would adding a tail field fix it?
```{index} operation count; workload model
```

headings.title: Count a Concrete Workload
body:
```{index} Count a Concrete Workload
```

## Count a Concrete Workload

Use eight initial orders and spare array capacity. Compare a front insertion, a last-position read, and a front removal.

| Operation | Array work | Linked work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert at front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |
| Read last position after insertion | One indexed read | Eight link advances from head |
| Remove front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |

If readers request the last position 100 times between these updates, the array uses 100 indexed reads while the linked sequence uses 800 link advances. If the workload instead performs many front updates and few index reads, the preference may reverse. Include the whole operation mix.

Counts of different primitives are not interchangeable seconds. Copying a reference, following a link, allocating a node, and checking a bound have different costs. Counts explain how work grows; benchmarks answer a narrower question about a specific implementation and machine.

**Transfer (challenge):** Compare 100 last-index reads plus one front insertion for 1,000 orders. State your assumptions about spare capacity and any stored tail. Then change the request to “read the tail value.” Explain why changing the API changes the comparison.
```{index} boundary tests; invariants; sequence contract
```

headings.title: Test the Contract Before Comparing Speed
body:
```{index} Test the Contract Before Comparing Speed
```

## Test the Contract Before Comparing Speed

Both implementations should produce the same logical result for the same legal operation sequence. Test correctness first. A fast implementation that loses an order is not an alternative representation of the same ADT.

| Test | Operations | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty start | Construct | Count zero; read index zero throws. |
| Single element | Add A; remove index zero | Returns A; count zero. |
| Reuse after emptying | Previous test; add B | Read index zero returns B. |
| Middle insertion | Add A, C; insert B at one | A, B, C in that order. |
| Middle removal | Previous test; remove one | Returns B; leaves A, C. |
| Duplicate values | Add A twice; remove zero | One A remains. |
| Invalid insertion | Insert at count plus one | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |
| Invalid removal | Remove at count | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |

Do not test only printed output from the happy path. Check count after each operation, and verify remaining values after removal. A useful additional check compares a generated operation sequence against C# `List<T>` as a reference implementation. It does not make timing comparisons fair; it checks observable behavior.

**Design (applied):** Write the smallest operation sequence that reveals a stale-tail bug. State the expected result before running it.
```{index} memory locality; reference type; allocation
```

headings.title: Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation
body:
```{index} Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation
```

## Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation

For `int` elements, the backing array places the integer values together. For reference-type elements, the reference slots are contiguous but their target objects need not be. Sequential array access often benefits from memory locality. A linked traversal follows separately allocated node objects, which may be scattered in memory.

Linked lists also pay for a node object and link field per item. Dynamic arrays pay for spare capacity and occasional replacement arrays. Neither representation has universally smaller memory usage: the element type, spare capacity, object layout, and workload matter.

Begin with a dynamic array such as `List<T>` for ordinary indexed application sequences. Justify a linked structure when its operations and API offer a concrete benefit, such as repeated front removal or insertion at already known positions. Do not replace every `List<T>` just because some linked updates have constant cost.

**Decision memo (challenge):** Recommend a representation for a dispatch application. Give two frequent operations, one worst-case risk, a memory tradeoff, and a measurement that could change your recommendation.
```{index} summary
```

headings.title: Summary
body:
```{index} Summary
```

## Summary

Arrays and linked lists both represent sequences, but they optimize different operations. A strong data-structure choice starts with the workload: what the program does most often, what must be fast, and what tradeoffs are acceptable.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```
[^1403_comparison_lab-1]: Later chapters revisit these same tradeoffs in stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, and graphs.

headings.title: Stacks
body:
# Stacks

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
```{index} stack; LIFO
```

headings.title: Stack Behavior
body:
```{index} Stack Behavior
```

## Stack Behavior

A **stack** is an abstract data type where the most recently added item is the next item removed. This access rule is called **last in, first out**, or **LIFO**.

The core operations are small:

- `Push(value)` adds a value to the top.
- `Pop()` removes and returns the top value.
- `Peek()` returns the top value without removing it.
- `Count` reports how many values are currently stored.

The point of a stack is not that it stores data in a new magical way. The point is that it restricts access so the program can only work with the top item.
The last action pushed was `Save report`, so it is the first action popped. The stack keeps the order of pending undo actions aligned with how users expect undo to work.
```{index} stack; underflow
```

headings.title: Empty Stacks and Safe Access
body:
```{index} Empty Stacks and Safe Access
```

## Empty Stacks and Safe Access

Calling `Pop` or `Peek` on an empty stack is an **underflow** error. In C#, `Stack<T>` throws an exception if the stack is empty. Production code should usually check `Count` before removing an item, or use `TryPop` and `TryPeek` when available.
The loop checks `Count` before each `Pop`, so it never tries to remove a value after the stack has become empty.
```{index} stack; delimiter matching
```

headings.title: Matching Delimiters
body:
```{index} Matching Delimiters
```

## Matching Delimiters

Stacks are useful for nested structures because the most recent opening item must be closed first. Parentheses, brackets, braces, HTML tags, and method calls all have this nested shape.
The stack stores exactly the unmatched opening delimiters, with the most recent one on top. A mismatched type or a closing delimiter with no opening returns false immediately. Success also requires an empty stack at the end. This checks delimiter characters only; it does not parse C# strings or comments.

**Trace:** For `([)]`, show the stack after each character until rejection. Why would merely counting openings and closings accept some invalid expressions? Each character is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(d) auxiliary space for maximum nesting depth d.
```{index} stack; implementation
```

headings.title: Stack Implementation Choices
body:
```{index} Stack Implementation Choices
```

## Stack Implementation Choices

A stack can be implemented with an array, a dynamic array, or linked nodes. The public behavior stays the same, but the representation affects growth, memory use, and constant factors.

An array-backed stack usually stores the top item at `items[count - 1]`. Pushing appends at the end; popping reads that end slot and decrements `count`.
This tiny implementation is bounded: it cannot grow past four values. A production dynamic-array stack would resize when full, much like the dynamic arrays in the previous chapter.
```{index} trace the stack invariant
```

headings.title: Trace the Stack Invariant
body:
```{index} Trace the Stack Invariant
```

## Trace the Stack Invariant

A report editor saves versions in order. With count three, the live array slots are `0..2`, and the top is index two. `Peek` must preserve count; `Pop` removes only that top value.

| Operation | Bottom to top | Count | Returned value |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Push Draft | Draft | 1 | None |
| Push Reviewed | Draft, Reviewed | 2 | None |
| Peek | Draft, Reviewed | 2 | Reviewed |
| Pop | Draft | 1 | Reviewed |
| Pop | Empty | 0 | Draft |

An invariant is a rule preserved after every completed operation. Here `0 <= Count <= Capacity`, the live values occupy consecutive slots, and `items[Count - 1]` is the top when count is positive. An empty pop must reject the request before decrementing count. Zero or null can be valid data; count determines emptiness.

**Predict:** Push A, push B, pop, push C, then peek. Give the returned values and final count. Which slots are live?
```{index} a complete generic array stack
```

headings.title: A Complete Generic Array Stack
body:

## A Complete Generic Array Stack

Chapter 14's dynamic array becomes a stack by exposing only the final live slot. This implementation doubles capacity when full and clears popped slots so unused storage does not retain object references. `default!` suppresses a nullable warning for unused storage; it is not a runtime check.

`TryPop` returns false on empty input and places a default value in its output parameter. Always check the Boolean: a default value could also have been successfully popped. Expect Approved, Reviewed, Draft, followed by `empty=True`.

**Extend:** Add `TryPeek` with the same success rule. Test empty, singleton, duplicate, and zero-valued stacks without changing count.

For local VS Code practice, download {download}`the complete implementations and verification program <../../demos/15_stacks_queues/ServiceDeskStructures.cs>` and use it as `Program.cs` in a console project. The program compares stack/queue behavior with standard library collections and checks boundary cases.
```{index} correctness and cost of stack operations
```

headings.title: Correctness and Cost of Stack Operations
body:
```{index} Correctness and Cost of Stack Operations
```

## Correctness and Cost of Stack Operations

`Push` preserves the invariant by growing without changing count, writing to the first unused slot, and increasing count once. `Pop` first obtains the current top, then reduces count and clears precisely the slot that left the live range. It never shifts other values.

Pop and peek take O(1) time. Push takes O(1) on most calls, O(n) when growth copies n live values, and O(1) amortized across repeated pushes using the chapter 15 doubling argument. A linked stack can push and pop at the head in O(1) link operations, but allocates a node per push. Array locality and spare capacity are different memory tradeoffs.

**Check:** For five pushes starting at capacity two, count the existing entries copied. Explain why removing every item from this array stack needs only n pops, while repeatedly removing index zero from an array sequence moves `n(n - 1)/2` entries.
