headings.title: Separate Logical Order from the Positions That Store It
body:
```{index} Separate Logical Order from the Positions That Store It
```

## Separate Logical Order from the Positions That Store It

In a ring queue, removing the front does not require shifting every later value. A front index and Count identify the logical sequence within fixed circular storage. With capacity four, front at three and Count two, the live positions are three and zero. The next insertion belongs at (front + Count) modulo capacity, which is position one. Raw left-to-right array printing would not show service order.

| Logical position | Physical position when front is 3 and capacity is 4 |
| --- | --- |
| First | 3 |
| Second | 0 |
| Next insertion | 1 |

Count distinguishes full from empty when the wrapped insertion position coincides with front. Element values cannot safely act as empty markers because zero or null may be legitimate stored values under the contract. A bounded queue rejects overflow before writing; a growing queue allocates new storage and copies logical order to consecutive positions before resetting front.

A deque permits both ends, so it needs additional endpoint/update reasoning. It does not supply arbitrary middle indexing or priority selection merely because it is more flexible than a queue. Guided trace: enqueue three entries, remove two, then enqueue enough to wrap. Write logical order after every step and compare it with physical slots. Repeat the exercise after a growth copy; the representation changes while service order must remain the same.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} queue; FIFO
```

headings.title: Queue Behavior
body:
```{index} Queue Behavior
```

## Queue Behavior

A **queue** is an abstract data type where the earliest added item is the next item removed. This access rule is called **first in, first out**, or **FIFO**.

The core operations are:

- `Enqueue(value)` adds a value to the back.
- `Dequeue()` removes and returns the front value.
- `Peek()` returns the front value without removing it.
- `Count` reports how many values are waiting.
The first customer enqueued is the first customer served. Unlike a list, a queue communicates that callers should not pick arbitrary positions from the middle.
```{index} queue; worklist
```

headings.title: Worklists and Scheduling
body:
```{index} Worklists and Scheduling
```

## Worklists and Scheduling

Queues often represent work that should be processed in arrival order: help-desk tickets, print jobs, messages, or search states. This pattern is called a **worklist** because the collection stores work that remains to be done.
A queue makes the scheduling policy explicit: new work joins the back, and existing work leaves from the front.
```{index} ring buffer; queue implementation
```

headings.title: Ring Buffers
body:
```{index} Ring Buffers
```

## Ring Buffers

An array-backed queue cannot simply remove index `0` by shifting every element left. That would make each dequeue expensive. A **ring buffer** solves this by letting the front and back indexes wrap around the array.

For a bounded queue, the important state is:

- `front`: the index of the next item to remove
- `back`: the index where the next item will be added
- `count`: the number of stored items
The modulo operation wraps an index back to zero after it reaches the end of the array. This avoids shifting values after every dequeue.
```{index} deque
```

headings.title: Deques
body:
```{index} Deques
```

## Deques

A **deque**, pronounced like "deck", is a double-ended queue. It allows adding and removing at both the front and the back. That makes it more flexible than a stack or queue, but still more controlled than arbitrary list indexing.

C# does not provide a dedicated `Deque<T>` in the base class library. For small examples, `LinkedList<T>` can demonstrate double-ended operations.
A deque is useful when both ends have meaning, such as browser history, task stealing, or algorithms that need to expand from the front while sometimes adding urgent items to the front.
```{index} trace wraparound and distinguish full from empty
```

headings.title: Trace Wraparound and Distinguish Full from Empty
body:
```{index} Trace Wraparound and Distinguish Full from Empty
```

## Trace Wraparound and Distinguish Full from Empty

A ring buffer stores logical order across the end of physical storage. Start with capacity four, `front = back = count = 0`. Back is the next insertion slot, not the last occupied slot.

| Operation | Slots 0, 1, 2, 3 | Front | Back | Count | Logical order |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Enqueue A, B, C | A, B, C, unused | 0 | 3 | 3 | A, B, C |
| Dequeue | unused, B, C, unused | 1 | 3 | 2 | B, C |
| Enqueue D | unused, B, C, D | 1 | 0 | 3 | B, C, D |
| Enqueue E | E, B, C, D | 1 | 1 | 4 | B, C, D, E |
| Dequeue B | E, unused, C, D | 2 | 1 | 3 | C, D, E |

`front == back` occurs when the buffer is empty and when it is full. Count distinguishes those states. For logical position i, the physical slot is `(front + i) % Capacity`. The invariants are positive capacity, a front index inside the array, and `0 <= Count <= Capacity`. The next insertion slot is `(front + Count) % Capacity`.

**Trace:** Continue until empty, then enqueue F. Give every front, back, and count. Explain why physical slot zero does not always hold the oldest item.
```{index} a complete bounded generic queue
```

headings.title: A Complete Bounded Generic Queue
body:
```{index} A Complete Bounded Generic Queue
```

## A Complete Bounded Generic Queue

This implementation derives back from front and count, so it does not maintain a redundant third state variable. Enqueue checks for full storage before writing; dequeue checks emptiness before advancing front. Both clear or fill one slot and update count once.

Capacity is fixed. A full enqueue throws and preserves the waiting tickets. That overflow policy is part of the contract; silently overwriting the oldest ticket would implement different behavior. Capacity one is legal and exposes full/empty mistakes quickly.

**Test:** Fill a capacity-one queue, reject a second enqueue, remove the original item, reject an empty dequeue, and reuse it. Verify returned values and count after each request.
```{index} linked queue endpoints and growth choices
```

headings.title: Linked Queue Endpoints and Growth Choices
body:
```{index} Linked Queue Endpoints and Growth Choices
```

## Linked Queue Endpoints and Growth Choices

A singly linked queue uses a head for removal and a tail for insertion. Empty means count zero and both endpoints null. A nonempty chain reaches tail last, and `tail.Next` is null. Removing the only node must clear tail as well as head; otherwise a later enqueue may attach to a detached node.

Unlike removing the last item of a singly linked list, queue dequeue removes the head and needs no predecessor search. Each enqueue/dequeue performs a fixed number of link changes. The program still pays for allocation and memory management.

**Trace:** Draw both endpoints for enqueue A, dequeue A, and enqueue B. Identify the stale-tail bug if dequeue omits the empty case.
```{index} growing a ring and choosing a deque representation
```

headings.title: Growing a Ring and Choosing a Deque Representation
body:
```{index} Growing a Ring and Choosing a Deque Representation
```

## Growing a Ring and Choosing a Deque Representation

A growable ring allocates a larger array when full. Copy logical item i from `(front + i) % oldCapacity` into new slot i, then set front to zero. Count stays unchanged; the next insertion slot becomes count. For the full layout `[E, B, C, D]` with front one, growth must produce `[B, C, D, E, unused, ...]`, not `[E, B, C, D, ...]`.

The bounded ring above has O(1) worst-case operation work and no growth. A doubling ring has O(n) worst-case enqueue during resizing and O(1) amortized enqueue. `Queue<T>` provides a growable application collection; bounded buffers need an explicit reject, wait, or overwrite policy.

A deque can use a doubly linked list or a ring with both-end operations. In a ring, adding at the front moves front to `(front - 1 + Capacity) % Capacity`; removing the back uses `(front + Count - 1) % Capacity`. Validate full/empty states first. C# remainder can be negative, which is why the front formula adds capacity.

**Transfer:** Trace add-back A, add-front B, remove-back, remove-front at capacity three. Compare a ring's locality and spare slots with a doubly linked deque's node/link overhead.

headings.title: Choosing the Access Rule
body:
```{index} Choosing the Access Rule
```

## Choosing the Access Rule

Stacks, queues, and deques are easiest to choose when you name the rule for the next item:

| Situation | Next item should be | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| Undo the most recent edit | Most recently saved | Stack |
| Serve customers fairly | Earliest waiting | Queue |
| Process both urgent and normal work | Either front or back | Deque |

The access rule is more important than the English noun. A "list of tasks" might be a stack, a queue, or a deque depending on how tasks should be removed.
This example uses two structures because there are two policies: urgent tasks use most-recent-first, and normal tasks use first-come-first-served.
```{index} backtracking; stack
```

headings.title: Backtracking with a Stack
body:
```{index} Backtracking with a Stack
```

## Backtracking with a Stack

Backtracking means trying a path, then returning to an earlier choice if that path does not work. A stack records the path because the most recent choice is the first one to undo.
`Stack<T>` enumeration visits the top first, so the displayed path starts with the current location and moves backward through recent choices.
```{index} breadth-first order; queue
```

headings.title: Breadth-First Processing with a Queue
body:
```{index} Breadth-First Processing with a Queue
```

## Breadth-First Processing with a Queue

Queues are central to breadth-first processing. When each item can discover more items, newly discovered items go to the back so earlier layers finish first.
This is the same queue pattern used later for breadth-first graph traversal. The queue preserves discovery order across layers.
```{index} stack; operation cost; queue; operation cost
```

headings.title: Comparing Costs
body:
```{index} Comparing Costs
```

## Comparing Costs

For the restricted operations, these structures are usually designed to make the main access rule fast:

| Structure | Operation | Typical cost |
|---|---|---:|
| Growable array stack | Push / pop | O(1) amortized push; O(n) growth; O(1) pop |
| Bounded ring queue | Enqueue / dequeue | O(1); full enqueue rejects |
| Growable array queue | Enqueue / dequeue | O(1) amortized enqueue; O(n) growth; O(1) dequeue |
| Deque | Add/remove either end | O(1) with the right representation |
| List used as queue | Remove index 0 | O(n) |

The tempting implementation is not always the right one. Removing from the front of a plain array or list usually shifts many values.
`RemoveAt(0)` is simple to read, but it moves the remaining elements left. `Queue<T>` communicates the intended operation and avoids relying on a slow pattern.
```{index} undo and redo require two histories
```

headings.title: Undo and Redo Require Two Histories
body:
```{index} Undo and Redo Require Two Histories
```

## Undo and Redo Require Two Histories

A realistic undo operation restores a prior state, rather than just printing an action name. Save the previous report state on undo before an edit. Undo saves the current state on redo and restores the latest undo state. Redo reverses that transfer.

| Request | Current state | Undo, bottom to top | Redo, bottom to top |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Draft | Empty | Empty |
| Edit Reviewed | Reviewed | Draft | Empty |
| Edit Approved | Approved | Draft, Reviewed | Empty |
| Undo | Reviewed | Draft | Approved |
| Redo | Approved | Draft, Reviewed | Empty |
| Undo; edit Revised | Revised | Draft, Reviewed | Empty |

A new edit after undo clears redo because it creates a new branch of history. This small editor stores complete immutable string snapshots. Large editors may store inverse commands or smaller changes to limit memory use.

**Predict:** Undo twice after the final edit. What states return? What should an extra undo do when its history is empty?
```{index} worklist order, duplicate discovery, and fairness
```

headings.title: Worklist Order, Duplicate Discovery, and Fairness
body:
```{index} Worklist Order, Duplicate Discovery, and Fairness
```

## Worklist Order, Duplicate Discovery, and Fairness

For the page-link example, after processing home the queue is `[products, support]`. Products adds pricing behind support; support then adds faq and contact. The processing order is home, products, support, pricing, faq, contact. Newly discovered pages join the back, so earlier layers finish first.

Mark a page discovered when it is enqueued. If both products and support link to pricing, only the first discovery enqueues it. Marking only when dequeuing can put duplicate pending entries into the queue. A visited set also prevents a link back to home from causing endless processing. The graph chapters develop the full traversal argument; here the important fact is the worklist policy.

Always serving urgent tickets before normal tickets may starve normal work if urgent arrivals never stop. A deque that adds urgency at the front changes service order; it does not guarantee fairness. A policy such as at most two urgent tickets before one waiting normal ticket makes a different promise.

**Design:** Trace that two-to-one policy for urgent U1, U2, U3 and normal N1, N2. Specify ordering within each group and behavior when either group is empty. What additional policy would you need if tickets have different processing times?

**Transfer:** A service desk needs a queue for waiting tickets and a stack for recently completed tickets that may be restored. Explain why these are two contracts. headings.title: Specify the Answer Before Counting Comparisons
body:
```{index} Specify the Answer Before Counting Comparisons
```

## Specify the Answer Before Counting Comparisons

A roster contains codes A, C, C, F. Searching for C could mean finding any occurrence, the first position, every matching position, or simply whether it exists. Those are different result contracts. A faster implementation of a weaker task is not automatically a better solution to the original task.

A first-match linear search examines positions in arrival order. Before examining position i, the invariant is that no earlier position matches. On C, it visits A and then the first C, returning position one. On a missing Z, it reaches the end, and the empty unexamined suffix establishes that no position matched. Empty input reaches that conclusion without reading any element.

| Target | Positions visited by first-match scan | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0 | 0 |
| C | 0, 1 | 1 |
| Z | 0, 1, 2, 3 | Missing |

Binary search answers a question using an ordered region. Each comparison rules out part of the search interval only because the ordering policy is consistent with the ordering used to prepare the data. A visually sorted report using one policy cannot safely be searched using another. Also do not return the position in a sorted snapshot as though it were the original arrival position.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Trace a Shrinking Candidate Region
```

headings.title: Trace a Shrinking Candidate Region
body: ```{index} Trace a Shrinking Candidate Region ``` ## Trace a Shrinking Candidate Region For a half-open interval [lo, hi), every candidate is at least lo and strictly before hi. Empty means lo equals hi. A midpoint comparison removes a region that cannot contain the desired result under the contract. The important progress argument is that every continuing iteration strictly shrinks the candidate region. Merely changing lo or hi is not enough if an update can leave the same interval. A common off-by-one mistake mixes an inclusive upper bound with a loop intended for half-open intervals. Trace an empty array, one element, and a missing target outside each end before celebrating a successful middle match. For duplicates, an ordinary any-match binary search need not return the first occurrence; Chapter 23 develops lower and upper bounds for that stronger query. Guided workload decision: a report is prepared once and searched one thousand times. List the preparation work as well as the query work. Now suppose a new record arrives after every query. Explain which assumption changed and why the original recommendation may need revision. The following preserved workload material develops that comparison without equating one quick benchmark with a universal threshold. ```{index} Searching Ordered and Unordered Data ``` An inventory application must distinguish finding an item from ordering the entire catalog. A search contract states which answer you need: the first match, any match, all matches, or a missing result. Representation affects the cost of producing that answer. Chapter 13 introduced comparison, equality, and operation counts; Chapter 14 introduced array and linked storage. Apply those ideas to a service desk looking for a ticket ID. Every example below owns its array and includes the complete search implementation. Empty input and missing targets are ordinary cases to test, not unusual afterthoughts.

headings.title: First-Match Linear Search
body:
```{index} First-Match Linear Search
```

## First-Match Linear Search


```{index} First-Match Linear Search
```
Linear search visits values in order and returns immediately when equality succeeds. It accepts unsorted data. Return the first matching index or -1; preserve the input and do not treat index zero as a missing result.

The processed prefix contains no match. When the loop reaches the end, every position has been checked, so -1 is justified. A match at index k needs k+1 equality checks. A missing target needs n checks; an empty array needs zero. This is O(n) worst-case work under the fixed-cost comparison model.
The results are 0, -1, and -1. An equality comparer makes the matching rule explicit. For symbolic IDs you might choose case-sensitive or case-insensitive string equality, but use the same policy consistently. Matching a customer's name is not necessarily the same as identifying the customer's record.

For linked nodes, linear traversal is also natural: follow each Next reference once. Repeatedly requesting an item by numeric index can rescan the list from its head and accidentally turn a linear task into quadratic work.

headings.title: Binary Search Requires the Right Order
body:
```{index} Binary Search Requires the Right Order
```

## Binary Search Requires the Right Order


```{index} Binary Search Requires the Right Order
```
(binarysearching)=

Binary search repeatedly discards half of a sorted, random-access sequence. The data must be sorted under the same ordering comparer used by the search. Sorting by price and then searching by product ID does not meet that precondition.

The interval [low, high) contains all remaining candidates. Start low at zero and high at Length. Compare the middle value: equality returns its index; a smaller middle excludes the left portion and the middle; a larger middle excludes the middle and the right portion. The interval shrinks on every unsuccessful comparison.

The safe midpoint expression low + (high - low) / 2 avoids adding two large indexes. High is a boundary, not always a valid element index. The method never indexes an empty interval.
There are at most floor(log2 n)+1 comparisons for a nonempty array, and O(1) auxiliary storage in this iterative version. The method returns any matching index: duplicate values do not imply the first matching index or the first arrival.

Trace a missing target 20 in [8,17,42,42,60]. The interval narrows until its boundaries meet between 17 and 42. Missing searches and singleton ranges are essential tests because an incorrect boundary update can skip candidates or fail to make progress.

headings.title: Library Results Have Their Own Contract
body:

## Library Results Have Their Own Contract


```{index} Library Results Have Their Own Contract
```
Array.IndexOf uses -1 for a missing value. Array.BinarySearch returns a negative encoded insertion position instead; test result >= 0 before using it as an index. The bitwise complement ~result decodes the position where a missing value could be inserted while preserving order.

Do not mix a teaching method's sentinel with a library method's contract. Read the API promise and check boundaries before using a returned index. The required learning is the sign test; insertion-position encoding is an applied extension.

```{index} Choose a Search for the Workload
```
One scan may be cheaper than sorting solely to answer one query. Repeated searches on static data can justify a sorted snapshot: sorting once has its own preparation cost, followed by logarithmic searches. Updates may invalidate that snapshot. A dictionary supports exact-key access but does not replace an ordered range query.

State the input size, required answer, update pattern, equality policy, and representation before choosing an algorithm. A stopwatch observation can support a particular measurement; it cannot establish a general growth bound. The next sections make sorting work visible and connect preparation to a complete reporting workload.

headings.title: Maintain a Sorted Prefix While Preserving Every Record
body:
```{index} Maintain a Sorted Prefix While Preserving Every Record
```

## Maintain a Sorted Prefix While Preserving Every Record

Sorting has at least two obligations: output order must satisfy the chosen comparison policy, and output must contain exactly the input occurrences. Producing 1, 2, 3 from input 3, 1, 2 looks right, but so would returning a fixed 1, 2, 3 regardless of input. Tests need to challenge preservation as well as ordering.

Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix. The next item is saved outside the moving region. Larger prefix items shift one position right until the saved item fits. Assigning the saved item back closes the hole. This explains why writing over the next item before saving it can lose data even though the remaining positions appear ordered.

| Input prefix and next item | Work | Resulting prefix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [4], next 2 | Save 2, shift 4, insert 2 | [2, 4] |
| [2, 4], next 3 | Save 3, shift 4, insert 3 | [2, 3, 4] |

Before each outer iteration, the processed prefix is sorted and is a permutation of the corresponding original prefix. The inner shifts preserve all saved occurrences while opening the correct position. When the prefix includes the full array, both obligations hold. This is a reasoning structure, not simply a description of what a successful example happened to print.

Equal keys reveal another contract. If the inner loop moves only items strictly greater than the saved key, equal-key items retain their previous relative order. This is stability. Moving equal items as well can change that order. Use labeled records, such as two invoices with the same total but different IDs, to see the distinction; identical integer values cannot show which occurrence moved.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Preparation, Mutation, and the Report Caller
```

headings.title: Preparation, Mutation, and the Report Caller
body: ```{index} Preparation, Mutation, and the Report Caller ``` ## Preparation, Mutation, and the Report Caller Sorting an array in place changes the order seen through its aliases. If arrival order is a business record, sort an independently ordered outer copy. That preserves original positions but still shares references to mutable objects. State whether the report needs only an order snapshot or a deeper data snapshot. Guided check: sort quantities 4, 2, 3 and record both comparisons and shifts. Then use already sorted 2, 3, 4. Explain why the amount of work differs even though both inputs have length three. Finally, test all equal values and reverse order, checking that each result preserves occurrence counts. A sorting algorithm's name is not a substitute for these contracts. ```{index} Basic Sorting with Insertion Sort ``` A payroll report may need employees in name order or invoices in amount order. A sorting algorithm must preserve every occurrence while arranging elements according to a comparison rule. Calling a library sort is useful, but implementing one small sort lets you see the work behind that operation. Insertion sort is the core teaching algorithm in this chapter. It keeps a sorted prefix and inserts one new value into that prefix. Advanced sorting implementations and detailed comparisons remain in Part VI.

headings.title: Insert into a Sorted Prefix
body:
```{index} Insert into a Sorted Prefix
```

## Insert into a Sorted Prefix


```{index} Insert into a Sorted Prefix
```
At the start of iteration i, positions zero through i-1 are sorted and contain the same occurrences as before. Save values[i] before shifting anything. Move larger prefix values one position to the right, then store the saved value in the gap.

For [30,10,20], insert 10 into [30] to obtain [10,30,20]. Then save 20, shift 30, and place 20 between 10 and 30. The array is never extended or shortened. The saved current value prevents shifts from overwriting the item being inserted.

| Pass | Sorted prefix afterward | Remaining values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | 30 | 10, 20 |
| Insert 10 | 10, 30 | 20 |
| Insert 20 | 10, 20, 30 | None |

Use a strict greater-than comparison when shifting. Equal keys stay in their original relative order, which makes this implementation stable.

## Sorting Objects Uses an Ordering Policy


```{index} Sorting Objects Uses an Ordering Policy
```
The comparer returns a negative value, zero, or a positive value. These mean before, tied, or after; callers should test the sign rather than assume the magnitude is exactly one. Define ordering separately from object identity and business equality.

The invoice comparer orders by amount only. Two invoices with the same amount are tied even though they have different identifiers. Stable sorting retains their arrival order. If the business requires amount then ID, include that second key in the comparer rather than relying on an accidental order.

```{index} Count Work for Different Inputs
```
On already sorted data, each new item needs one failed shift comparison, for n-1 comparisons when n is positive. On distinct reverse-sorted data, item i crosses the entire prefix: 1+2+...+(n-1) = n(n-1)/2 comparisons. Therefore the implementation has linear best-case and quadratic worst-case comparison work.

The array is sorted in place with constant auxiliary element storage. Shifting still performs writes, so comparisons are not the only possible cost model. Use the counter to test a specific comparison claim; do not confuse the counter with wall-clock time.


A sorted result alone is insufficient: a broken implementation could discard a value and still look ordered. Check length and occurrence preservation as well as ordering. Use a separately sorted copy as a small reference, and include duplicates, negative values, empty input, a singleton, and already sorted data.

In application code, normally use the library operation unless a requirement justifies a custom algorithm. Array.Sort mutates its array and does not promise stable ties. headings.title: Tree Vocabulary
body:
```{index} Tree Vocabulary
```

## Tree Vocabulary


```{index} tree; root; leaf; subtree
```
A **tree** is a collection of nodes connected by parent-child relationships. The **root** is the starting node. A **leaf** has no children. A **subtree** is a node together with everything below it.

Many real systems have this shape: folders contain folders, supervisors manage teams, expressions contain subexpressions, and web pages link to lower-level navigation sections.
This first representation uses `Left` and `Right` references, so it is a **binary tree**. The values could represent labels, numbers, records, or any other data.
A tree models a hierarchy with one route from the root to each node. In a nonempty tree, every node except the root has exactly one parent. There are no cycles, and all nodes belong to the same connected structure. A structure with shared children or a link back to an ancestor needs graph algorithms instead of these tree algorithms.

A company's departments form a general tree: a manager can have more than two direct reports. `Left` and `Right` deliberately restrict the example to two children. The names indicate positions, not a numerical ordering rule. A binary tree can contain unsorted labels or numbers.

For the course catalog example, draw each reference as an edge:

```text
        Courses
       /       \
Programming   Databases
   /    \
 C#    Python
```

`Courses` has depth zero, `Programming` has depth one, and `C#` has depth two. There are five nodes and four edges. Every non-root node contributes its one incoming edge, so a nonempty tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges. An empty tree has no root and zero edges.

Before running the next example, identify all leaves. A node with only one child is an internal node, not a leaf. Two labels can be equal and still belong to different nodes; a node is an object, while its label is stored data.
A recursive method needs two promises. First, it must know when to stop. Second, every recursive call must move closer to that stopping point.

Recursion is not magic; it is ordinary method calls plus the call stack. The hard part is choosing a smaller version of the problem that has the same shape as the original problem.

headings.title: Base Case and Recursive Case
body:
```{index} Base Case and Recursive Case
```

## Base Case and Recursive Case

```{index} Base Case and Recursive Case
```
A **base case** returns an answer directly. A **recursive case** calls the same method on a smaller input and uses that result to build the current answer.

The contract accepts integers 0 through 100; zero returns zero and negative input is rejected. The cap keeps this linear-depth teaching demo small, rather than promising an unlimited safe recursion depth. For n>0, the nonnegative integer measure n decreases strictly. Assume the smaller call returns the correct sum of 1 through n−1; adding n gives the required sum through n. This is an induction argument: direct base case, smaller correct result, correct combination.

headings.title: Tracing the Call Stack
body:
```{index} Tracing the Call Stack
```

## Tracing the Call Stack

```{index} Tracing the Call Stack
```
The call stack stores each active method call until that call returns. A trace can make the order of calls and returns visible.

Each frame retains its own n and resumes after the smaller call returns. For 4!, calls enter with 4,3,2,1; returns deliver 1,2,6,24. The suspended multiplication is work done during unwinding. Zero factorial is one. A long holds 20! but not 21!, so the public contract rejects larger inputs; checked arithmetic makes accidental overflow visible. A mathematically terminating recursion can still exhaust the runtime stack.

headings.title: Recursive Structure
body:
```{index} Recursive Structure
```

## Recursive Structure


```{index} tree; recursive structure
```
Trees are recursive because each child is the root of a smaller tree. That means many tree algorithms follow the same pattern:

1. Stop if the current node is `null`.
2. Do some work at the current node.
3. Recur into one or more child subtrees.

This is not recursion for its own sake. It mirrors the structure of the data.
`Count` treats the current node as one item plus the size of each child subtree. `CountLeaves` changes the base case: a node with no children contributes one leaf.
The recursion needs two guarantees. First, a null reference represents an empty subtree and contributes zero. Second, each recursive call receives a smaller subtree. In a finite tree with no cycles, repeated calls eventually reach null. A cycle would break this termination argument.

For the subtree rooted at 3, `Count(3)` waits for `Count(1)` and `Count(6)`. Both return one, so the call returns `1 + 1 + 1 = 3`. The call at 8 combines that result with the one node rooted at 10 and returns five. Each return summarizes a subtree; it does not count the same node again.

| Call | Left result | Right result | Returned count |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Count(1) | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Count(6) | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Count(3) | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| Count(10) | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Count(8) | 3 | 1 | 5 |

`CountLeaves` has a different meaning: an internal node contributes no leaf of its own, while a node with two null children contributes one. That distinction explains why adding one unconditionally would count nodes instead of leaves.

headings.title: Complete a Recursive Summary Before Designing a New Query
body:
```{index} Complete a Recursive Summary Before Designing a New Query
```

## Complete a Recursive Summary Before Designing a New Query
A tree call returns a summary of its subtree. Counting nodes and counting leaves have different meanings even though both visit the same structure. Before inventing another query, decide what null contributes, what a leaf contributes, and how an internal node combines its children.

Use root 8 with left child 3 and right child 10; node 3 has only a left child 1. For a leaf count, null contributes zero and a real leaf contributes one. An internal node contributes the sum of its child leaf counts, without adding one for itself.

| Subtree root | Is it a leaf? | Left leaf count | Right leaf count | Return |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | Yes | Not needed | Not needed | 1 |
| 3 | No | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 10 | Yes | Not needed | Not needed | 1 |
| 8 | No | 1 | 1 | 2 |

Guided task: complete the leaf condition and the returned combination in this schematic method before reading the runnable checkpoint.

```text
if (node is null) return 0;
if (node.Left is null /* combine with */ node.Right is null) return 1;
return CountLeaves(node.Left) /* combine */ CountLeaves(node.Right);
```

Both child references must be null for a leaf. A node with just one child remains internal. Adding one at every internal node would turn this calculation into a node count.
The missing operators are `&&` and `+`. The empty and singleton cases distinguish two different base meanings. As a variation, give node 10 one child 12: it stops being a leaf but still contributes one leaf through 12, so the total remains two. Give it two children instead and the total becomes three. Derive those returns before running them.

For independent work, design a query that counts nodes with exactly one child. State its contribution for null, a leaf, a one-child node and a two-child node before writing the recursion. Reuse the same return-table method to test the proposed rule. These are content-section reasoning steps; the chapter lab then applies tree operations to its service-desk model.

headings.title: A Visit and a Returned Result Are Different Events
body:
```{index} A Visit and a Returned Result Are Different Events
```

## A Visit and a Returned Result Are Different Events

A traversal chooses when to visit a node relative to its children. A recursive aggregation also returns results from children to their caller. These events can happen at different times. Printing a node before recursing gives preorder; computing its subtree size cannot finish until the child sizes are known.

Use a small tree with root B, left child A and right child C. Preorder visits B, A, C; inorder visits A, B, C; postorder visits A, C, B. These names describe timing, not three different storage layouts. The same nodes and edges support all three orders.

| Moment during Count(B) | Known information | What must wait? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enter B | B exists | Its subtree count |
| Left call returns | Left count is 1 | Right count |
| Right call returns | Right count is 1 | Nothing needed for the sum |
| Return from B | 1 + 1 + 1 is 3 | Caller may now use 3 |

An empty subtree returns zero directly. That is not an arbitrary special case appended to the algorithm; it makes the recurrence Count(node) = 1 + Count(left) + Count(right) valid for a leaf. A missing return, or adding one for an empty subtree, changes the contract across every ancestor that uses the result.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Count Active Calls Separately from Visited Nodes
```

headings.title: Count Active Calls Separately from Visited Nodes
body:
```{index} Count Active Calls Separately from Visited Nodes
```

## Count Active Calls Separately from Visited Nodes

A traversal visits n nodes, but it does not keep all n calls active simultaneously in every shape. On a balanced tree, the active recursive path follows the tree's height. On a chain, the height can grow with n, so the same recursion can need linear active stack depth. Total calls and maximum simultaneous calls answer different cost questions.

A queue-based level-order traversal has a different live frontier. It can hold nodes across a wide level. Choosing recursion or a queue is therefore a question about visit policy and storage as well as syntax. Neither approach makes a cyclic shared graph into a proper tree; the ownership and acyclicity assumptions from the structural lesson matter.

Guided trace: add D as C's right child. Predict all three visit orders and every returned Count value. Draw arrows for calls going down and results coming back. Then turn the four nodes into a right-only chain and explain which values remain the same and which storage claim changes. The number of nodes is still four; the maximum active depth is different.

headings.title: Traversal Orders
body:
```{index} Traversal Orders
```

## Traversal Orders


```{index} preorder traversal; inorder traversal; postorder traversal
```
A **traversal** visits every node in a tree. For binary trees, the common depth-first traversal orders differ only in when the current node is processed:

- **Preorder**: node, left, right
- **Inorder**: left, node, right
- **Postorder**: left, right, node
The tree shape is the same in all three traversals. Only the timing of `Console.Write` changes.
Trace the same five-node tree with the root at 8. In preorder, you process 8 before entering the call for 3. In inorder, the call at 8 stays suspended until the entire left subtree returns. In postorder, both subtrees finish before 8 is processed.

| Order | Sequence | Use in a hierarchy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preorder | 8, 3, 1, 6, 10 | Print a department heading before its teams. |
| Inorder | 1, 3, 6, 8, 10 | List keys in order when the tree is a BST. |
| Postorder | 1, 6, 3, 10, 8 | Total child budgets before computing a department total. |

Inorder traversal is sorted here because this particular tree obeys the binary search tree rule. Inorder traversal of an arbitrary binary tree is not necessarily sorted.

Every traversal visits each node exactly once. If processing a node costs constant time, total work is Θ(n). Recursive calls retain their local state while waiting for descendants, so the largest number of active calls is proportional to height: O(h + 1) extra space for a nonempty tree. Returning a list of all values also uses Θ(n) space for that result. The output list and the call stack are different costs.

**Predict:** move 6 from the right child of 3 to the left child of 10. Which traversal sequences change? The node count stays the same, but the order depends on the references, not only the stored values.

headings.title: Height and Shape
body:
```{index} Height and Shape
```

## Height and Shape


```{index} tree height; tree depth
```
A node's **depth** is its distance from the root. A tree's **height** is the longest downward path from the root to a leaf. Height matters because many tree operations follow one path from the root toward a leaf.
This version defines an empty tree as height `-1`, so a single-node tree has height `0`. Some texts define height differently; always check the convention being used.
Height counts edges in this chapter. Null has height -1, a leaf has height zero, and every internal node adds one to the larger child height. For the six-node example, the call at 6 returns one, the call at 3 returns two, and the root returns three. Depth belongs to a specific node; height summarizes a subtree.

Height computation visits both children, so it costs Θ(n), even when the tree is short. A search may follow only one path; computing the height of an uncached tree examines every node. In a chain of n nodes, height is n - 1 and recursion can require n active calls. Large adversarial chains can exhaust the call stack. Production trees often control height or use iterative algorithms.

**Check the boundaries:** an empty tree has zero nodes, zero leaves, and height -1. A singleton has one node, one leaf, and height zero. A chain with several nodes still has only one leaf. These cases distinguish correct base cases from methods that merely work on a symmetric example.

headings.title: The BST Invariant
body:
```{index} The BST Invariant
```

## The BST Invariant


```{index} binary search tree; BST invariant
```
A **binary search tree** is a binary tree with an ordering rule, often called an **invariant**:

- every value in a node's left subtree is less than the node's value;
- every value in a node's right subtree is greater than the node's value.

This rule must be true at every node, not only at the root.
The valid range narrows as the recursion moves down the tree. A right child must be greater than its parent and also remain within any limits inherited from ancestors.
A BST stores a set of unique keys in these examples. A duplicate insertion leaves the tree unchanged. If a business application needs multiple records with the same key, decide whether to store a list of records at each key or use a different comparison key. Sending equal values arbitrarily left or right would conflict with the strict invariant used here.

The rule applies to entire subtrees. In the changed example, 9 is greater than its parent 3, but it is still in the left subtree of 8, where every key must be less than 8. Checking only each node against its immediate children would miss this error.

The validator passes an **exclusive lower bound** and an **exclusive upper bound** down the recursion. For the right child of 3 inside the left subtree of 8, the permitted range is `3 < key < 8`. Both ancestor constraints survive. Bounds use `long` because every `int` value, including `int.MinValue` and `int.MaxValue`, must fit strictly inside the initial range. Using those `int` limits as exclusive sentinels would wrongly reject valid boundary keys.

This validator assumes the references already form a tree. It checks ordering, not cycles or shared-node ownership. Validation visits all nodes in a valid tree, so its worst-case work is Θ(n).

headings.title: Search
body:
```{index} Search
```

## Search


```{index} binary search tree; search
```
BST search uses comparison to discard one subtree at each step. If the target is smaller than the current node, search left. If it is larger, search right. If it is equal, the value has been found.
This `Contains` method is iterative: it walks one path from the root down. A recursive version would follow the same comparisons.
For the tree built above, search for 7 follows `8 → 3 → 6 → 7`. Search for 2 follows `8 → 3 → 1 → null`. The failed search stops when it reaches an empty position; it does not inspect 6, 10, or 14.

At each step, the invariant proves that a discarded subtree cannot contain the target. If 7 is smaller than 8, every key in 8's right subtree is too large. The same argument applies again at the next node. A search examines at most h + 1 nodes in a nonempty tree of height h, giving O(h + 1) time and O(1) extra space for this iterative method.

That bound describes the actual shape. It becomes O(log n) when height is logarithmic, and O(n) for a chain. The basic BST implementation does not promise logarithmic height.

headings.title: Insertion
body:
```{index} Insertion
```

## Insertion


```{index} binary search tree; insertion
```
Insertion searches for the place where the value belongs. When the search reaches an empty child reference, the new node is attached there.

This implementation ignores duplicate values. Another design could store a count at each key. Placing equal keys on one side would require changing the invariant and validator together.
For a BST, inorder traversal visits values in sorted order. That makes it a useful check when testing insertion.
Recursive insertion returns the root of the updated subtree. The assignments `node.Left = Insert(...)` and `node.Right = Insert(...)` reconnect that result to its parent. The public method similarly assigns the returned root to `root`; otherwise the first insertion into an empty tree would be lost.

Trace adding 4 to a tree containing `8, 3, 10, 1, 6`. Comparisons choose 8's left child, then 3's right child, then 6's left child. The null call creates node 4. Returning from that call assigns it to `6.Left`; the calls at 3 and 8 return their existing nodes. Only one new reference changes. Keys already in the tree keep their relative order.

| Position | Comparison | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | 4 < 8 | Continue left. |
| 3 | 4 > 3 | Continue right. |
| 6 | 4 < 6 | Continue left. |
| null | Empty subtree | Return a new node containing 4. |

Adding 6 again follows the path to the existing 6 and returns it unchanged. Successful and duplicate insertions both cost O(h + 1); recursive insertion uses O(h + 1) call-stack space. A stored Count should increase only when a new node is created.

Sorted inorder output checks the ordering rule, but also compare the output with the intended set. A broken insertion that drops an entire subtree can still produce sorted output. Correctness requires both ordering and preservation of the expected keys.

headings.title: Shape and Performance
body:
```{index} Shape and Performance
```

## Shape and Performance


```{index} binary search tree; height; balanced tree
```
A BST is efficient when its height stays small. If inserted values arrive in sorted order, the tree can become a chain. Then search behaves like scanning a linked list.
Balanced tree structures, such as AVL trees and red-black trees, add rules that keep height under control. This chapter focuses on the basic BST first so the ordering idea is clear.
A perfect binary tree of height h contains `1 + 2 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h + 1) - 1` nodes. Each extra level can roughly double the number of stored keys, so a tree with well-distributed branches can have logarithmic height. A chain adds only one node per level. Inserting n distinct sorted keys into this basic implementation performs roughly `0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1)` comparisons, giving Θ(n²) total construction work.

| Operation | Basic BST cost | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Search, add, remove, find minimum | O(h + 1) | Follow one or a constant number of root-to-descendant paths. |
| Inorder traversal, uncached height, full validation | Θ(n) in the worst case | Examine every node. |
| Read stored Count | O(1) | Read a maintained field. |

Random-looking input is not a guarantee of balanced height. AVL and red-black trees enforce additional rules after updates; this chapter leaves their rotations for later study. Choose a balanced library structure when a service needs a logarithmic worst-case guarantee. For the simple teaching tree, the input order is part of the performance story.

headings.title: Removal and Subtree Replacement
body:
```{index} Removal and Subtree Replacement
```

## Removal and Subtree Replacement

```{index} binary search tree; removal; inorder successor
```

Removing from a BST has more cases than search or insertion:

| Case | Basic idea |
|---|---|
| Leaf node | Remove the parent's reference to it. |
| One child | Replace the node with its child. |
| Two children | Replace the node's value with its inorder successor or predecessor, then remove that moved value. |

The two-child case is why removal is often taught after search and insertion. It is not conceptually impossible, but it has more structural bookkeeping.
Finding the minimum and maximum helps explain removal: an inorder successor is the smallest value in the right subtree.

Use `TicketTree` below as an ordered set of active service-ticket IDs. `Add` and `Remove` report whether membership changed; `Count` changes once per successful operation. `TryMinimum` distinguishes an empty tree from a valid key zero. The public API keeps nodes private so callers cannot silently break the invariant.

Deletion returns the updated subtree root, just as insertion does. A leaf returns null. A node with one child returns that child. These cases also handle deleting the root because the public method stores the return value in `root`.

For two children, find the smallest key in the right subtree, the **inorder successor**. Copy that key into the current node, then delete the original successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child; it may have a right child, which must be reattached. Replacing the key without removing its original node would leave a duplicate. Removing the successor by discarding its entire subtree would lose records.

This class stores IDs only. For nodes containing an ID and a record, transfer the matching record as well as the ID, or move the entire node. Keeping an old record with a new key would corrupt the application even if the key ordering remained valid.

The original ticket tree and the final tree after closing 1, 10, and 8 show how the references change:

```text
        8                       11
       / \                     /  \
      3   12                  3    12
     / \  / \                  \     \
    1  6 10 14                  6    14
          \
          11
```

Read the demonstration as three different reference updates:

| Remove | Case at that moment | Reference update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Leaf under 3 | Set `3.Left` to null. |
| 10 | One child, 11 | Set `12.Left` to node 11. |
| 8 | Root with two children | Replace root ID with 11, then set `12.Left` to null. |
| 99 | Missing key | Return false; preserve keys and Count. |

For root 8, the successor is 11 after the earlier removal of 10. It is the smallest key greater than 8. Every old left key remains less than 11, and every remaining right key is greater than 11. Deleting the old successor location restores uniqueness.

The outer removal sets `removed = true`. The internal successor deletion uses a separate flag, and only the public method decrements Count. One requested deletion removes one logical key even though the implementation also visits the successor location. The sum of these paths is O(h + 1), not a full traversal.

**Predict:** rebuild the original demonstration tree and remove 8 first. Its successor is 10, which has right child 11. After replacement, `12.Left` must refer to 11. Then test removal from an empty tree, a singleton, and a root with only one child. These cases reveal missed root assignments and lost child links.

body:

## An Ordered Service Desk

```{index} binary search tree; ordered set; service desk
```

A service desk assigns unique integer IDs to active tickets. Staff need to locate an ID, list active IDs in order, find the smallest active ID, and remove closed tickets. The BST is an index over IDs; it does not imply that the smallest ID is the most urgent ticket. A queue preserves arrival order, while this tree preserves key order.

The `TicketTree` class from the previous section supplies the basic operations. Each example below includes its own class and setup so you can run it independently. Download {download}`the complete source and verification program <../../demos/17_trees/TicketTree.cs>` for use in a console project.

Before adding more operations, write down the contract: no duplicate IDs; keys strictly increase in inorder traversal; Count equals the number of reachable nodes; unsuccessful updates preserve membership. Empty minimum lookup reports false rather than inventing an ID.

headings.title: Range Queries and Pruning
body:
```{index} Range Queries and Pruning
```

## Range Queries and Pruning

```{index} binary search tree; range query; pruning
```

Suppose staff want all active IDs from 25 through 60, inclusive. One method gets every ID and filters the resulting list. A BST can also skip subtrees that cannot contain a match. **Pruning** means using a proved constraint to avoid visiting part of a structure.

At key 20, the entire left subtree is below the lower bound 25. At key 60, the entire right subtree is above the upper bound 60. For keys within the interval, process left, node, and right to keep the result ordered. Bounds are inclusive for the query even though the BST's ordering invariant is strict.

The standalone example exposes nodes only to make the recursion visible. The same method could be private inside `TicketTree`, with a public `Range(lower, upper)` wrapper.

The result is `30, 40, 50, 60`. The method visits five of the seven nodes; it skips 10 and 70. The number of matching keys alone does not determine cost: searching for an empty interval can still walk a long path. In a tree of height h returning k keys, this traversal takes O(h + k + 1) time; a chain or a query covering the whole tree can require Θ(n). Its recursion uses O(h + 1) space, plus the returned values.

Pruning is safe because of the BST invariant. Applying this method to an arbitrary binary tree could silently omit valid matches. Test a range with no matches, one exact key, all keys, and reversed bounds. The method defines reversed bounds as an empty query.

headings.title: Level Order with a Queue
body:
```{index} Level Order with a Queue
```

## Level Order with a Queue

```{index} tree; level order traversal; queue
```

Depth-first traversals finish descendants before moving to another branch. **Level order** visits nodes by depth: root first, then its children, then their children. Use the Chapter 15 queue as a worklist of nodes discovered but not yet processed.

When you remove a node from the queue, append its existing children from left to right. The queue keeps earlier levels ahead of later ones. In a proper tree, each non-root node has exactly one parent, so it is enqueued once. Graphs with shared descendants or cycles need an additional visited set, a topic for Chapter 20.

The pending IDs evolve as `40`, then `20, 60`, then `60, 10, 30`, then `10, 30, 50, 70`. Dequeue processes the front, and child discovery appends at the back. The visit order is `40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70`, which differs from preorder and inorder.

Each node is enqueued and dequeued once, giving Θ(n) work. Queue space depends on the tree's width and can reach O(n), even when height is small. A recursive depth-first traversal uses space proportional to height instead. For an empty tree, initialize no pending node and produce no output.

headings.title: Priority Describes Removal, Not a Fully Sorted Array
body:
```{index} Priority Describes Removal, Not a Fully Sorted Array
```

## Priority Describes Removal, Not a Fully Sorted Array

A service desk chooses the lowest numbered priority next. That is a removal contract. It does not require that every stored element be maintained in complete sorted order, nor does it say that equal priorities must leave in arrival order. State the priority direction and tie policy before interpreting a printed storage array.

A min-heap requires each parent's priority to be no greater than its children's. The root is therefore a minimum, but siblings need not be ordered. In the array [1, 4, 2, 7, 6, 3], the values 4 and 2 can appear in that order without violating the heap. Reading the array from left to right is not the same as repeatedly removing the minimum.

| Operation needed | Heap property helps with it? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inspect the minimum | Yes | It is at the root |
| Remove the minimum and restore the property | Yes | Only a repair path is needed |
| Print everything in sorted order without changing storage | Not directly | Heap order is weaker than total order |
| Find an arbitrary ID | Not directly | Priority ancestry does not locate arbitrary keys |

The complete-tree shape lets an array encode parent/child positions without one node object per edge. With zero-based positions, a non-root index i has parent (i-1)/2 using integer division; its potential children are 2i+1 and 2i+2. A child position must still be checked against Count. Capacity is not the number of live heap entries.

Guided drawing: place the six array values above into the implicit tree. Check each parent-child relation. Then compare positions one and two: their values are out of sorted-array order but are allowed as siblings. This single counterexample explains why ordinary binary search cannot be applied to heap storage.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Priority Queue Behavior
body:
```{index} Priority Queue Behavior
```

## Priority Queue Behavior


```{index} priority queue
```
A **priority queue** removes the item with the next priority, not necessarily the item that arrived first. In C#'s `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>`, lower priority values come out first by default.
The outage has priority `0`, so it is processed before lower-urgency work. Priority queues are useful for schedulers, event simulations, pathfinding, triage, and any workflow where "next" means most important rather than oldest.
A priority queue defines how you select the next element. It does not promise that enumeration is sorted or that arbitrary keys are easy to locate. The numerical priority has an application meaning: here zero is most urgent. Dequeue from an empty queue is an error; `TryDequeue` reports false instead.

Equal priorities need a policy. The .NET library does not guarantee arrival order for ties. If the service desk requires first-arrived service among equally urgent tickets, use the pair `(urgency, arrivalNumber)` as the priority. Tuple comparison considers urgency first and arrival second. Each arrival number is unique within the queue, so the resulting order is deterministic.
The order is T-101, T-100, T-102. A later urgent ticket can move ahead, while equal-urgency tickets retain their arrival order. The queue alone does not prevent starvation if urgent work arrives indefinitely. Fairness requires an additional scheduling policy.

The manual implementation in this section is a **binary** heap. The current .NET `PriorityQueue` uses four children per parent internally. Its API behavior is the same priority-queue idea, but the binary index formulas below describe the teaching implementation, not the library's internal layout. [Microsoft's PriorityQueue documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.priorityqueue-2) describes both tie behavior and the library representation.

headings.title: Heap Representation
body:
```{index} Heap Representation
```

## Heap Representation


```{index} heap; min-heap; complete tree
```
A **heap** is a common priority-queue representation. A binary heap has two key rules:

- **Shape rule**: the tree is complete, filled level by level from left to right.
- **Order rule**: in a min-heap, each parent priority is less than or equal to its child priorities.

Because the shape is complete, a heap can be stored compactly in an array. For an item at index `i`, the children are at `2 * i + 1` and `2 * i + 2`.
The array is not fully sorted. It only guarantees that each parent is no larger than its children. That weaker rule is enough to keep the minimum at the root.
For a non-root index i, its parent is `(i - 1) / 2`, using integer division. Valid child indexes must be less than Count. Count describes occupied positions; the backing array may have extra capacity that is not part of the heap.

```text
          1 (0)
        /       \
     3 (1)     2 (2)
    /    \     /    \
 7 (3) 5 (4) 6 (5) 4 (6)
```

The values obey parent-child order, but siblings and separate subtrees can be out of numerical order. For example, 3 precedes 2 in the array. Repeatedly removing the root produces a sorted sequence; reading the raw array does not. The complete shape guarantees height Θ(log n) for a nonempty binary heap.
A priority queue is an access rule. The next section implements it with a binary heap, while application code may use the library PriorityQueue. Enumeration is not a sorted report; repeated removal is the operation whose priority order is specified.

headings.title: Repair Only the Part an Operation Can Disturb
body:
```{index} Repair Only the Part an Operation Can Disturb
```

## Repair Only the Part an Operation Can Disturb

Enqueue adds a new entry at the next open leaf position so the complete shape is preserved. All old parent-child relations are unchanged. Only the new entry's path toward the root can violate min-heap order. Bubble-up compares with the parent and swaps while the child is smaller. Moving upward strictly decreases its index, so repair terminates.

Start with [2, 5, 4] and enqueue 1. Appending produces [2, 5, 4, 1]. Comparing 1 with parent 5 gives [2, 1, 4, 5]. Comparing that 1 with root 2 gives [1, 2, 4, 5]. Do not sort the whole array; that would enforce a stronger and more expensive condition than the operation needs.

Dequeue first saves the root result. Move the last live entry to the root and reduce Count. The only possible ordering defects now lie downward from that replacement. Choose the smaller existing child before swapping; exchanging with an arbitrary child can leave a smaller sibling above a larger parent relation.

| Heap after removing 1 | Inspection | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [5, 2, 4] | Children 2 and 4 | Choose 2 |
| [2, 5, 4] | 5 has no child | Stop |

A singleton removal needs no child access after Count becomes zero. An empty removal must follow the stated failure policy without first reading position zero. Also clear unused reference slots when the implementation owns a backing array and should release references to removed objects. Reducing Count hides a slot from the abstract sequence, but it does not itself erase a stored reference.

The height of a complete heap is logarithmic in its live size, which bounds the number of repair levels. Array growth can add copying to an enqueue, so qualify an operation's cost rather than ignoring representation maintenance. Bulk building by bottom-up repair is a related algorithm with a different aggregate argument; it is not proved merely by multiplying one operation's bound.

Guided exercise: repeat enqueue with a value 6 that already belongs below its parent. Predict how many swaps occur and distinguish swaps from comparisons. Then remove down to empty and enqueue again. Those cases test both the invariant and whether endpoint handling leaves the structure reusable.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Enqueue and Bubble Up
body:
```{index} Enqueue and Bubble Up
```

## Enqueue and Bubble Up


```{index} heap; bubble up
```
To insert into a heap, place the new item at the end to preserve the complete-tree shape, then **bubble up** while it violates the heap order rule.
The new value `0` starts at the end. It swaps with larger parents until the min-heap property is restored.
Trace the appended zero from index seven to the root:

| Stage | Index path | Array |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Append | 7 | 1, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6, 4, 0 |
| Swap with 7 | 7 → 3 | 1, 3, 2, 0, 5, 6, 4, 7 |
| Swap with 3 | 3 → 1 | 1, 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 4, 7 |
| Swap with 1 | 1 → 0 | 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 4, 7 |

Before insertion, every old parent-child relation satisfies the order rule. Appending adds only one possible violation between the new item and its parent. Each swap repairs that relation and moves the possible violation upward. Stop at the root or when the parent is no larger. This explains why repairing one path is sufficient.

headings.title: Dequeue and Sink Down
body:
```{index} Dequeue and Sink Down
```

## Dequeue and Sink Down


```{index} heap; sink down
```
To remove the minimum item, remove the root, move the last item to the root, then **sink down** until the heap order rule is restored.
Both bubble-up and sink-down follow one root-to-leaf path, so their work grows with heap height, not with every item in the heap.
In the removal example, replacing root 1 with the last value 4 gives `4, 3, 2, 7, 5, 6`. Compare both children before choosing the swap: 2 is smaller than 3, so swap indexes zero and two. The result is `2, 3, 4, 7, 5, 6`. The next child is 6; 4 is already no larger, so stop.

Choosing a larger child can leave the root larger than the other child. Sink-down must choose the smaller existing child and handle a last parent with only a left child. Removing the last array position preserves the complete shape. For a singleton, removal leaves no root to repair.

The complete generic heap below hides the backing list and accepts an optional comparer. The element type must support the default ordering, or you must supply a comparer. `Peek` and `Dequeue` throw on empty; `TryDequeue` distinguishes empty from a stored default value. Equal values are legal, but this heap does not impose stable arrival order on equal comparisons.
`List<T>` grows its storage when necessary. Bubble-up uses O(log n) comparisons, but a single enqueue that copies a full backing array can take O(n) time. Across a long sequence, storage growth contributes amortized O(1) per append; enqueue therefore has amortized O(log(n + 1)) time. Dequeue repairs at most one downward path and takes O(log(n + 1)); it does not shrink this backing list. Peek and Count take O(1). The iterative repair uses O(1) extra space, while the stored items use O(n) space.

`IsValid` scans all parent-child relations, so it takes Θ(n) time. It is a diagnostic method, not part of every production operation. `Snapshot` also takes Θ(n) time and space to copy the occupied values. Checking the minimum alone would miss a violation inside a subtree. Test empty and singleton states, duplicate priorities, an odd final child, ascending/descending input, draining, and reuse.

A heap can also be built from an existing array by sinking internal nodes from right to left. Most nodes are near leaves and require little repair; summing that work gives O(n) bottom-up construction. Repeated insertion has an O(n log n) worst-case bound. This chapter implements repeated enqueue first; bottom-up construction is an extension.

headings.title: Keep the Boundary of the Best K Items
body:
```{index} Keep the Boundary of the Best K Items
```

## Keep the Boundary of the Best K Items

A sales report needs the largest three amounts from a stream. Sorting every amount is one possible solution, but the requested result is smaller than the full sorted input. A min-heap of the currently retained best three exposes the weakest retained amount at its root. That is exactly the boundary a new candidate must beat.

For amounts 7, 2, 9, 4, 10, retain 7, 2 and 9 first. Their minimum is 2. Candidate 4 replaces 2; candidate 10 replaces the new minimum 4. The retained values are 7, 9 and 10. Their heap storage need not be printed in sorted report order; sorting only the final retained values is a separate reporting step.

| Candidate | Decision | Retained values as a set of amounts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7, 2, 9 | Fill three places | 2, 7, 9 |
| 4 | Replace the smallest retained amount | 4, 7, 9 |
| 10 | Replace the smallest retained amount | 7, 9, 10 |

After each processed prefix, the heap contains the best min(k, processed count) entries under the chosen comparison policy. If a new candidate is no better than the root and the heap is full, at least k retained entries are already as good, so discarding it preserves the invariant. If it is better, replacing the weakest retained entry restores the best-k claim. This argument explains the algorithm rather than just observing a successful result.

Decide whether k zero is a valid request, what to do when fewer than k entries exist, and how tied amounts affect which record IDs are retained. Keeping amounts alone loses record identity. A report requiring deterministic tie order needs a secondary policy, not an assumption about library heap stability.

Priority also differs from fairness. A permanently urgent stream can delay ordinary requests indefinitely even when each minimum-priority removal is correct. Aging, reserved service opportunities or another explicit scheduling policy may be needed. That is a requirement choice layered on the structure, not a defect fixed by reversing the heap comparison.

Guided variation: select the smallest three amounts instead. Explain why a max-heap exposes the weakest retained boundary for that goal. Then retain complete invoice records with equal amounts and state what additional information your comparison must use if arrival order breaks ties.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
A priority queue is useful when the next item is chosen by urgency or score rather than arrival position. Use a clearly stated tie rule for service work and a clearly stated retained-set rule for top-k reporting.

The following applications use the library queue so you can focus on the workload. The heap implementation in the previous section explains the repair work behind this behavior. A dictionary-based cancellation index is introduced only after hash collections in the next chapter.

headings.title: Top-K with a Min-Heap
body:
```{index} Top-K with a Min-Heap
```

## Top-K with a Min-Heap

```{index} top-k; min-heap; streaming
```

Keep the k largest observed transaction amounts without sorting the entire input. Maintain at most k retained values in a min-heap. The root is the smallest retained value, so it is the candidate to discard when a larger value arrives.

**Invariant:** after each input, the heap contains the largest `min(k, valuesSeen)` values of that prefix, including repeated values. If fewer than k values are stored, add the next value. Once full, a value no larger than the root cannot improve the retained multiset; a larger one replaces that root.

For k = 3, retained values after the first three inputs are 72, 84, 91. Processing 99 drops 72; 67 changes nothing; 88 drops 84; 95 drops 88; the second 95 drops 91. The final result is `99, 95, 95`. Repeated equal amounts remain separate observations.

For n inputs and positive k, maintenance has an O(n log(k + 1)) upper bound and O(k) storage, or fewer entries when n < k. Producing the final ordered result costs O(k log(k + 1)) in the worst case. k = 0 returns immediately; negative k is rejected. If record identity or tie order matters, include an explicit secondary priority and define which tied records to retain.
