headings.title: A Collision Is Not Evidence That Keys Are Equal
body:
```{index} A Collision Is Not Evidence That Keys Are Equal
```

## A Collision Is Not Evidence That Keys Are Equal

A hash function maps keys to a finite bucket range, so different keys can map to the same bucket. The hash narrows the search; equality identifies the actual key. In a table of five buckets using a simple remainder demonstration, integer keys 2, 7 and 12 all map to bucket two. Keeping only one value at that position would lose entries unless the ADT intentionally replaces an equal key.

A chained bucket can examine the entries for actual equality. An open-addressed representation follows a probe sequence instead. Removing an entry in open addressing must preserve the ability to find later entries whose probe passed through its slot. Turning a deleted slot directly into never-used can stop a search too soon; the distinction between deleted and never occupied matters.

Guided trace: insert the three colliding keys, remove seven, then find twelve. Explain why a search must still reach twelve. Now grow the bucket range and recompute placement; copying each entry to its old numeric slot is not sufficient because the mapping depends on the table size. Hash distribution, equality consistency, load and deletion policy work together.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Dictionary Contracts and Key Equality
body:
```{index} Dictionary Contracts and Key Equality
```

## Dictionary Contracts and Key Equality

```{index} dictionary; key equality; hashing
```

A dictionary associates one value with each distinct key. Looking up a customer ID asks for that ID's record; it does not ask for the first record in order. C# `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` uses hashing for key-based access. `Add` rejects an existing key, indexer assignment inserts or replaces, and `TryGetValue` reports whether a key exists without treating a missing key as a successful default value.

This dictionary treats `T-100` and `t-100` as equal, so assignment changes the owner rather than adding another key. Choose the equality policy when creating the collection and apply it consistently. For symbolic ticket IDs, ordinal comparison avoids culture-dependent language rules. This example deliberately ignores case; other applications may need case-sensitive identifiers.

Hashing and equality must agree: equal keys must have equal hash codes. Different keys may have the same hash code, so a lookup must still compare actual keys. A custom comparer supplies both operations. Do not modify fields that determine a stored key's equality or hash code; its new bucket may no longer match the location used during insertion. Strings are immutable, which avoids that particular mutation hazard. [Microsoft's GetHashCode contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode) explains this agreement.

headings.title: Hash Codes and Bucket Mapping
body:
```{index} Hash Codes and Bucket Mapping
```

## Hash Codes and Bucket Mapping

```{index} hash function; bucket; negative hash code
```

Separate two steps: compute an integer hash code, then map that code into one of m buckets. Hash codes can be negative. C# remainder can also be negative, and `Math.Abs(int.MinValue)` cannot fit in an `int`. Reinterpret the code as an unsigned integer before remainder to obtain a valid index without that overflow.

`unchecked((uint)hash)` keeps the original bits and interprets them as a nonnegative number; it does not claim that the code is a unique identifier. BucketCount must be positive. The result lies from zero through m - 1. Equal hash codes always map to the same bucket for a fixed m, but many different codes also map there.

String hash codes may vary across processes or platforms. Use them for temporary placement, not as permanent customer IDs or persisted checksums. The teaching map below uses integer IDs themselves as simple hash codes so its collision trace is reproducible. This is an illustration, not a general recommendation for distributing arbitrary business keys.

headings.title: Separate Chaining and Complete Operations
body:
```{index} Separate Chaining and Complete Operations
```

## Separate Chaining and Complete Operations

```{index} separate chaining; collision; hash-table update
```

A collision occurs when different keys choose the same bucket. **Separate chaining** stores a collection of entries at each bucket. A lookup computes the bucket and compares keys within that chain. An update must search the chain before appending; otherwise it can create duplicate keys. Removal must preserve the other colliding entries.

With four buckets, IDs 101, 105, and 109 all choose bucket one. To find 109, inspect 101, then 105, then 109. To report that 113 is absent, inspect the entire chain. A successful lookup may stop early; an unsuccessful one must establish that no matching key exists.

The complete `TicketMap` stores integer ticket IDs and string owners. `Put` returns true for a new key and false for replacement. `Remove` reports whether membership changed. `TryGetValue` returns false on absence; ignore its output value in that case.

Each stored entry belongs to the bucket computed from its ID and the current bucket count. Count equals the total number of entries, and each ID occurs once. The internal entries are immutable; replacement installs a new entry with the same ID. An update returns before increasing Count or testing growth because it adds no key.

After removal, another colliding ID remains reachable in the same chain. Our chains are lists, so removal may shift later entries within that chain. The cost depends on chain length rather than the total number of buckets. This map keeps capacity after deletions and has no iterator API; production libraries provide more policies and interfaces.

headings.title: Load Factor and Rehashing
body:
```{index} Load Factor and Rehashing
```

## Load Factor and Rehashing

```{index} load factor; resizing; rehashing
```

Define load factor α = n / m, where n is the number of entries and m is the number of buckets. Before adding 113, the map has three entries in four buckets, so α = 0.75. A fourth new key would exceed the teaching threshold, so the map doubles to eight buckets before inserting it.

Changing the bucket count changes placement. Copying old bucket lists to the same array indexes is insufficient. Recompute every entry's bucket under the new capacity, a process called **rehashing**.

| ID | Bucket with m = 4 | Bucket with m = 8 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 101 | 1 | 5 |
| 105 | 1 | 1 |
| 109 | 1 | 5 |
| 113 | 1 | 1 |

Growth splits this collision group into two chains. It does not guarantee that all collisions disappear. A poor hash function can keep many keys in one chain even at low load factor.

Under well-distributed hashes and constant-time hashing/equality, chaining operations have expected O(1 + α) work. A pathological chain can require O(n) work. This resize visits all entries and initializes a larger bucket array, giving O(n + m) work for that operation. Geometric growth contributes amortized constant work per new key when load is kept bounded; one growth-triggering insertion can still be linear.

The threshold 0.75 belongs to this teaching map, not to a universal hash-table rule. Separate chaining permits α greater than one. Open addressing needs unused slots and becomes much more expensive as occupancy approaches one. Key hashing itself is an additional cost, such as scanning characters in a long string.

headings.title: Open Addressing and Deleted Slots
body:
```{index} Open Addressing and Deleted Slots
```

## Open Addressing and Deleted Slots

```{index} open addressing; linear probing; tombstone
```

**Open addressing** stores entries directly in the table. **Linear probing** tries the chosen slot, then subsequent slots with wraparound until it finds the key or a place to insert. A lookup may stop at a slot that has never been occupied, because insertion would have stopped there too. It cannot stop merely because a previous entry was removed.

For capacity seven, IDs 10, 17, and 24 all start at slot three. Linear probing stores them at three, four, and five. Clearing slot three after deleting 10 would make a naive search for 17 stop early. A **tombstone** marks a deleted slot through which lookup must continue.

Limit a search to at most m probes so a full table cannot cause an endless loop. Insertion can reuse a tombstone, but it must still search far enough to rule out an existing equal key. Otherwise it can add a duplicate before reaching the old copy. Over time, many tombstones lengthen searches; rebuilding the table can remove them.

This example demonstrates a deletion rule, not a complete open-addressed dictionary. The chapter's complete implementation uses chaining. Both strategies must combine placement with actual key equality; neither treats a collision as a duplicate by itself.

The complete teaching map uses separate chaining. The probing/tombstone example is an optional comparison, not another full map implementation you must build. The next section applies dictionary and set contracts to business reconciliation.

headings.title: A Set Answers Membership; a Count Answers Multiplicity
body:
```{index} A Set Answers Membership; a Count Answers Multiplicity
```

## A Set Answers Membership; a Count Answers Multiplicity

Two departments submit product IDs for reconciliation. A set represents which IDs occur, regardless of how many times they were entered. A dictionary of counts represents how often each ID occurs. Choosing between them changes the information retained, not merely the syntax of the container.

Let the warehouse IDs be {A, B, C} and the sales IDs be {B, C, D}. Intersection gives IDs recognized by both: {B, C}. Warehouse minus sales gives {A}; sales minus warehouse gives {D}. The direction of difference matters. A union gives all recognized IDs {A, B, C, D}; it does not establish that either department's quantities agree.

| Question | Operation | Result for this example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which IDs are shared? | Intersection | B, C |
| Which warehouse IDs are absent from sales? | Warehouse minus sales | A |
| Which sales IDs are absent from warehouse? | Sales minus warehouse | D |
| Which IDs appear anywhere? | Union | A, B, C, D |

Now suppose sales submits B twice. A set still contains one B. That is correct for unique membership and wrong for a task that must detect repeated submissions. A frequency dictionary can increment B's count to two. State whether duplicates are errors, repeated events, or information to discard before building either representation.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Choose Equality Before Comparing the Groups
```

headings.title: Choose Equality Before Comparing the Groups
body:
```{index} Choose Equality Before Comparing the Groups
```

## Choose Equality Before Comparing the Groups

If product IDs are case-insensitive under the business contract, B and b must use compatible equality in both collections. Normalizing only one side can produce false missing-ID reports. For hashed keys, equal keys must have equal hash codes under the selected policy. A good hash distribution improves performance but cannot repair inconsistent equality.

Do not mutate fields that determine a key's hash/equality while that key is stored. The entry may remain physically present in a bucket chosen by its old meaning while a new lookup examines another location. Immutable key data or remove/change/reinsert workflows make that boundary explicit.

Set-operation APIs also have mutation contracts. Some operations modify the receiving set; query-based forms may produce a sequence instead. If the original warehouse membership must remain available, work on a copy or choose a nonmutating approach deliberately. Assigning another variable to the same set object does not create independent storage.

Guided exercise: add B twice and lowercase a once to the sales input. Produce two answers: a unique-ID reconciliation under a stated case policy and a repeated-ID report. Explain which information a set has discarded and why the frequency report cannot be reconstructed from that set alone.
Keyed access and membership answer different questions. A dictionary maps an ID to a record. A set records whether an ID belongs to a group. Business reconciliation often needs set operations as well as individual lookups.

Use the same equality rule for all collections that participate in one calculation. The examples use ordinal case-insensitive equality for submitted symbolic IDs and preserve original sets when a report needs several answers.

headings.title: Sets and Frequency Counts
body:
```{index} Sets and Frequency Counts
```

## Sets and Frequency Counts

```{index} HashSet; set; frequency count
```

A set stores keys without associated record values. Use `HashSet<T>.Add` to detect a first occurrence, or a dictionary to count occurrences. Give both the same comparer when they must agree about what counts as equal.

The set has two distinct statuses, and the counts are open three and closed two. The example prints keys in an explicit order; a hash collection's enumeration order is not a sorting contract. Sort keys separately when a report requires an order. Neither a set nor a dictionary supplies the priority-selection operation of a heap.

headings.title: Union, Intersection, and Difference
body:
```{index} Union, Intersection, and Difference
```

## Union, Intersection, and Difference


```{index} Union, Intersection, and Difference
```
Let registered contain everyone registered for a workshop and attended contain everyone who checked in. Their intersection contains registered attendees. Registered minus attended identifies no-shows. Attended minus registered identifies walk-ins. Their union contains everyone appearing in either source.

HashSet operations such as IntersectWith and ExceptWith mutate the receiving set. Construct a copy first when you need to retain both source sets. Enumeration is not a sorted-report contract: copy to a list and sort explicitly for predictable output.

headings.title: Lookup and Missing Values
body:

## Lookup and Missing Values


```{index} Lookup and Missing Values
```
TryGetValue separates an absent key from a stored default value. Do not use a balance of zero, an empty owner name, or a null-like sentinel as an implicit membership test unless the contract explicitly excludes those values.

Choose Add when duplicate keys are errors; use indexer assignment when replacement is intended. If imports may repeat customer IDs, state whether a repeated row updates, accumulates, or rejects. Hashing provides access; it does not choose the business policy.

headings.title: Keys Must Keep Their Meaning
body:
```{index} Keys Must Keep Their Meaning
```

## Keys Must Keep Their Meaning


```{index} Keys Must Keep Their Meaning
```
Do not change fields that determine a key's equality or hash while that key is stored. The key can become inconsistent with its original bucket. Immutable string IDs avoid that mutation hazard. A custom business object may instead need a comparer based on an immutable ID, as introduced in Chapter 13.

A hash collection does not provide sorted order, range queries, or next-priority removal. For those requirements choose another structure, or maintain multiple indexes with a clear consistency policy. The next section coordinates dictionary membership with the priority queue from Chapter 18.

headings.title: Coordinate Indexes with One Consistency Story
body:
```{index} Coordinate Indexes with One Consistency Story
```

## Coordinate Indexes with One Consistency Story

A dispatch system wants quick lookup by ticket ID and repeated service by priority. One collection may not efficiently supply both operations under the required policies. A dictionary can locate the current ticket by ID while a priority queue selects service candidates. Using two indexes introduces an obligation: their views must not cause cancelled or superseded work to be served.

One design permits stale queue entries and checks them when removed. The dictionary holds authoritative current state. A queue candidate is served only if its ID still exists and its version matches the current ticket. Cancellation removes or marks the authoritative record; old queue entries can be skipped later. Versioning matters when the same ID can be updated: mere presence is not proof that the old priority entry still describes the current work.

| Event | Authoritative lookup | Old queue entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Register ticket | Present with current version | Eligible when selected |
| Cancel ticket | Absent or explicitly cancelled | Skip |
| Change priority/version | Updated current version | Skip if its version is stale |

The alternative is to remove/update queue entries eagerly, which needs suitable index support and its own maintenance rules. Compare complete workflows rather than declaring either approach universally faster. Lazy cleanup simplifies some updates but can retain stale storage and make later removals perform extra work.

Guided trace: register ticket A, cancel A, register a new version of A, then remove an old queue candidate. Explain why matching only the ID can serve the wrong version. Extend the trace with a failed lookup and check that it changes neither index. The existing cancellation example is an entry point to this consistency reasoning, not a guarantee that every multi-index update is automatically transactional.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
A service application may need exact lookup, uniqueness checks, ordered reports, and priority dispatch at the same time. Name each operation before choosing a representation. Multiple indexes are useful only if updates preserve a clear agreement between them.

headings.title: Match the Structure to the Workload
body:
```{index} Match the Structure to the Workload
```

## Match the Structure to the Workload

```{index} workload; data-structure choice
```

The same service desk has several access needs. Use a priority queue for the next urgent ticket, a dictionary for its owner, and a set for uniqueness or closed-ticket membership. A tree supports ordered keys and range queries. Each structure preserves a different relationship; the application must keep shared IDs consistent.

| Need | Structure | Cost under stated assumptions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Select next urgency | Heap priority queue | O(log n) repair; backing-array growth can make one enqueue O(n). |
| Find owner by ID | Hash dictionary | Expected O(1) with well-distributed hashing and bounded load; worst-case O(n). |
| Reject duplicate ID | Hash set or dictionary | Expected O(1) under the same assumptions. |
| Ordered interval report | Balanced search tree | O(log n + k) for k results; the Chapter 16 unbalanced tree depends on actual height. |
| Process by arrival | FIFO queue | Constant-time endpoints in the linked representation. |

These bounds assume fixed-cost comparison and hashing. They describe operations, not measured milliseconds. A tiny list can still be a practical choice when there are few records and little repeated lookup.

Download {download}`the complete heap and chained-map source with verification <../../demos/19_hash_collections/HeapHashStructures.cs>` to use in a console project.

headings.title: Count Work Before Timing
body:
```{index} Count Work Before Timing
```

## Count Work Before Timing

```{index} hashing; operation count; performance measurement
```

One stopwatch measurement includes runtime warm-up, scheduling noise, and timer granularity. It cannot establish a complexity bound. First compare the amount of relevant work. In the controlled example below, the list must inspect every key for an absent lookup, while an explicitly constructed chain table inspects only the selected bucket.

The small hash function deliberately maps nonnegative integer IDs by remainder. This is a reproducible placement experiment, not instrumentation of .NET Dictionary.

The absent lookup uses 1000 comparisons in the list and 10 in the selected chain. With a constant hash function, all keys would occupy one chain and the lookup would again require 1000 comparisons. Collision distribution explains the difference.

A benchmark should separate construction from the operation being studied, repeat lookups over representative hit/miss keys, warm up the runtime, report variation, and include realistic key-hashing costs. Those measurements complement the analysis; they do not turn expected constant-time hashing into a worst-case guarantee. Chapter 19 develops analysis and measurement further.

headings.title: Dispatch from Two Consistent Indexes
body:
```{index} Dispatch from Two Consistent Indexes
```

## Dispatch from Two Consistent Indexes

```{index} priority queue; dictionary; consistency
```

The service desk keeps active records in a dictionary and pending IDs in a priority queue. A simple cancellation policy removes the active record while leaving its old queue entry in place. On dequeue, skip IDs no longer active. This is **lazy deletion**: defer physical cleanup until an obsolete entry reaches the front.

This example allows each ID to be registered once during the batch. If an ID can be reused or reprioritized, an old entry may still refer to an active ID. Use a generation/version field and verify it on dequeue, or implement an indexed heap with explicit updates. Presence alone would then be insufficient.

The cancelled urgent ticket is skipped, then T-100 and T-102 are served in their arrival order. Immediately after cancellation, the dictionary has two entries but the queue still has three. Equal Counts are not the invariant. Every active record has one live pending entry, while pending may also contain inactive IDs.

Skipping one stale entry costs one heap removal. Across a batch, each enqueued entry is removed at most once, but a single request for the next active ticket may skip many cancelled entries. Cancellation also leaves queue storage occupied until cleanup. Analyze both the whole workload and an individual call; do not promise that lazy deletion makes every dispatch O(log n).

headings.title: Explain the Selection
body:
```{index} Explain the Selection
```

## Explain the Selection


```{index} Explain the Selection
```
A dynamic array supports fast indexed access and sequential reports. Linked storage makes known-node updates convenient but does not make locating a node free. Stacks and queues restrict access order. Balanced ordered collections support ordered lookup; a heap supports priority selection; a hash collection supports equality-based access.

For cancellation, the dictionary identifies active records while pending heap entries can become stale. Lazy deletion skips stale entries when removing them. This simple example forbids ID reuse during the batch; reuse or reprioritization needs a version policy. Treat that policy as an extension after ordinary dictionary and set operations, not as a prerequisite for understanding hashing.

headings.title: Graph Vocabulary and Models
body: # Graph Vocabulary and Models

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

headings.title: Vertices and Edges
body:
```{index} Vertices and Edges
```

## Vertices and Edges

```{index} graph; vertex; edge; isolated vertex
```

A graph consists of a set of **vertices** and a set of **edges** connecting them. A vertex models an item; an edge models a relationship. A facilities team might model rooms as vertices and direct passageways as edges. A dependency model might instead use tasks as vertices and prerequisite relationships as edges.

Keep the vertex set separate from the edge set. A room with no modeled passageways is still a vertex. Such an **isolated vertex** has degree zero. If you create vertices only while reading edges, you can silently lose isolated rooms, devices, or customers.

The following office-route model has six vertices and four undirected edges. Labels are symbolic identifiers, not measured physical locations. The diagram expresses the relationships, while the arrays store them.

```text
Lobby -- Hall -- Lab       Remote
          |
        Office -- Storage
```

The drawing is not a floor plan: line lengths do not represent distance, and a crossing in a drawing would not create a new vertex unless the model explicitly added one.

headings.title: Directed and Undirected Relationships
body:
```{index} Directed and Undirected Relationships
```

## Directed and Undirected Relationships

```{index} directed graph; undirected graph; arc; indegree; outdegree
```

An **undirected edge** represents a two-way relationship. One logical edge between Hall and Lab connects them in both directions. A **directed edge**, also called an arc, has a source and destination; Hall → Lab does not imply Lab → Hall.

Direction depends on the question. A prerequisite arrow from Programming I to Programming II means the first must precede the second. An import arrow might instead mean that the source file depends on the destination file. State the convention before interpreting incoming and outgoing edges.

For directed graphs, **outdegree** counts outgoing edges and **indegree** counts incoming edges. A workflow approval step can have several incoming prerequisites and one outgoing next step.

Approve has indegree two and outdegree one. Every directed edge contributes once to the total indegree and once to the total outdegree, so each total equals E, the number of directed edges. In an undirected graph, each ordinary edge contributes one to each endpoint's degree, giving degree sum 2E. These equalities are useful representation checks; they do not prove every edge is the intended one.

headings.title: Weights and Model Assumptions
body:
```{index} Weights and Model Assumptions
```

## Weights and Model Assumptions

```{index} weighted graph; unweighted graph; edge weight
```

A **weighted graph** assigns a value to each edge, such as transfer time, cost, capacity, or distance. Define units and the meaning of combination. Walking times can be added along a route. Capacities generally do not add in the same way, so an algorithm that sums weights may answer the wrong business question for that model.

The route examples use nonnegative integer minutes. Zero can represent a rounded transfer time between adjacent work areas. Absence is a different state: no direct route exists. A directed weighted model could give different costs in opposite directions; an undirected one stores one shared cost.

This is the cost of one specified route, not a claim that the route is fastest. Negative weights may make sense in some other domains, but this chapter's walking-time contract rejects them. Later algorithms must state their own weight assumptions; a storage representation alone does not make an optimization method valid.

headings.title: Neighbors, Degree, and Connectivity
body:
```{index} Neighbors, Degree, and Connectivity
```

## Neighbors, Degree, and Connectivity

```{index} neighbor; degree; connected graph; connected component
```

Two vertices are **adjacent** when an edge directly connects them. A vertex's neighbors are its adjacent vertices. In the simple undirected model, degree equals the number of distinct neighbors.

```text
Lobby:   Hall
Hall:    Lobby, Lab, Office
Lab:     Hall
Office:  Hall, Storage
Storage: Office
Remote:  (none)
```

Hall has degree three; Remote has degree zero. The sum of these degrees is eight, consistent with four undirected edges. A **connected graph** has a route between every pair of vertices. A **connected component** is a maximal connected group of vertices. Here five rooms form one component and Remote forms another. An isolated vertex is a component of one vertex.

Direct adjacency differs from connectivity. Lobby and Storage have no direct edge, but the model includes the route Lobby, Hall, Office, Storage. A `HasEdge` lookup cannot by itself decide whether some longer route exists. Full reachability algorithms are deferred to Chapter 26.

headings.title: Walks, Paths, and Cycles
body:
```{index} Walks, Paths, and Cycles
```

## Walks, Paths, and Cycles

```{index} walk; path; cycle; path length
```

A **walk** is a sequence in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge in the required direction. A walk may repeat vertices and edges. A **path** in this chapter is a walk without repeated vertices. A **cycle** is a closed walk with no repeated edges or vertices except its start/end. In a simple undirected graph, it uses at least three edges.

`Lobby, Hall, Office, Storage` is a path of three edges. `Lobby, Hall, Lobby` is a walk, but not a path. `Lobby, Storage` is invalid because it requests a missing direct edge. The sequence's number of edges is one less than its number of listed vertices; its weighted cost is the sum of those edges' weights.

A one-vertex path has zero edges and zero cost if that vertex exists. An empty sequence will be defined as invalid in the route checker later in this chapter. An unknown label is also invalid. These conventions prevent an absent room from being mistaken for a valid isolated room.

**Predict:** add the edge Lab–Office to the diagram. Which degrees change? A cycle Hall, Lab, Office, Hall now exists. Do all vertices become connected? Remote is still isolated. An edge update can change local degree and larger connectivity properties at the same time.

headings.title: Simple-Graph Contracts
body:
```{index} Simple-Graph Contracts
```

## Simple-Graph Contracts

```{index} simple graph; multigraph; self-loop; graph contract
```

A **simple graph** has no self-loops and at most one edge between a given pair of vertices. A **self-loop** joins a vertex to itself. A **multigraph** may store several distinct edges between the same endpoints, such as separate transport services. Choose the model that matches the domain before selecting storage.

For an undirected simple graph, `(Hall, Lab)` and `(Lab, Hall)` refer to the same logical edge. A raw set of ordered tuples treats them as different tuples unless you normalize their order. Adjacency storage can instead represent the one edge as two reciprocal entries and count it once.

The complete route graph in the next section adopts an explicit contract: vertex labels use ordinal, case-sensitive equality; vertices are added explicitly; both endpoints must exist; self-loops and negative minutes are rejected; repeated edge assignment replaces its weight; removing a vertex removes every incident edge. An isolate stays present until explicitly removed.

Before implementing, identify what the graph omits. A room-level model might ignore doors, stairs, access permissions, or opening hours. Its routes can support decisions only within those assumptions.

headings.title: Adjacency Representations
body: # Adjacency Representations

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

headings.title: Adjacency Matrices
body:
```{index} Adjacency Matrices
```

## Adjacency Matrices

```{index} adjacency matrix; vertex index; symmetry
```

An adjacency matrix reserves one cell for each ordered pair of vertices. A row describes outgoing connections from its vertex; a column describes incoming connections to its vertex. Map symbolic labels to dense integer indexes before accessing the array.

For the six-room undirected graph, a Boolean matrix has 36 cells, although only eight are true. Four logical edges appear twice, once in each direction. Its diagonal is false because the model rejects self-loops. An isolated vertex still has a row and column, both empty.

The Hall row is `1 0 1 1 0 0`; the Remote row is all zeros. In an undirected matrix, `[i, j]` equals `[j, i]`. A directed matrix need not be symmetric. Do not infer a reverse arc merely because an undirected example wrote both cells.

Once indexes are known, direct edge lookup reads one cell in O(1) time. Enumerating a vertex's neighbors scans its entire row, Θ(V) time. Adding or removing vertices in a tightly sized matrix can require a new array and remapping many indexes. Keeping spare capacity or inactive indexes changes that tradeoff and needs its own policy.

headings.title: Weights and Absence
body:
```{index} Weights and Absence
```

## Weights and Absence

```{index} weighted adjacency matrix; nullable weight; zero-weight edge
```

A nullable weight matrix separates a missing edge (`null`) from an existing edge with weight zero. Initializing every cell to zero and treating zero as absence would erase valid zero-minute routes. The diagonal remains null under this simple-graph contract; a zero-cost path from a vertex to itself does not imply a stored self-loop.

headings.title: Adjacency Collections
body:
```{index} Adjacency Collections
```

## Adjacency Collections

```{index} adjacency list; neighbor map; sparse graph
```

An adjacency list stores each vertex's actual neighbors. The term includes several concrete choices: a list, a set, or a dictionary of neighbor-to-weight pairs. These choices have different lookup and update costs.

A list supports neighbor iteration but must scan to find a particular neighbor, and it can contain duplicates unless insertion checks for them. A hash set supports expected constant-time membership for unweighted edges. A neighbor dictionary supports expected constant-time lookup and weight replacement while keeping one entry per neighbor. All retain explicit entries for isolated vertices.

In this undirected model, each logical edge has two stored adjacency entries. The space bound is Θ(V + E), since doubling E changes only the constant factor. A directed outgoing adjacency representation stores one entry per arc. Forgetting the reverse entry in an undirected update creates an asymmetric representation of a supposedly symmetric relationship.

Sorting the keys above is a reporting choice, not a hash-table guarantee. The underlying neighbor dictionary does not promise numerical or alphabetical traversal order. Later graph algorithms may produce different valid visit orders when neighbor enumeration order differs.

headings.title: Density and Workload Costs
body:
```{index} Density and Workload Costs
```

## Density and Workload Costs

```{index} graph density; dense graph; representation cost
```

For a simple undirected graph with V vertices, the maximum number of edges is `V(V - 1) / 2`: choose an unordered pair of distinct endpoints. The directed maximum without loops is `V(V - 1)` because each pair has two possible directions. Density is actual edges divided by the relevant maximum. For fewer than two vertices, this chapter reports density zero to avoid division by zero.

| Operation | Matrix with known indexes | List per vertex | Hash neighbor map |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Storage | Θ(V²) | Θ(V + E) | Θ(V + E) |
| Direct edge lookup | O(1) | O(deg(u)) | Expected O(1) |
| Iterate neighbors of u | Θ(V) | Θ(deg(u)) | Θ(deg(u)) |
| Set edge weight | O(1) | O(deg(u)) to find it | Expected amortized O(1) |
| Add an isolated vertex | May require Θ(V²) copying | Amortized O(1) in a growable indexed collection | Expected amortized O(1) |

Hash bounds assume well-distributed hashing and fixed-cost label operations; growth can make an individual insertion expensive. Label-to-index lookup is additional work for the matrix. The table's update costs describe directed entries; an undirected edge updates two entries with the same asymptotic bound.

This graph has 60 of 1225 possible edges, about 4.90% density. A matrix reserves 2500 pair cells; adjacency collections store 120 neighbor entries plus 50 vertex entries. These are counts of storage locations, not equal-size bytes. Dictionary objects, hashing, and arrays have different overheads, so small graphs may favor a matrix even when sparse.

Choose by operations as well as density. Frequent pair checks with a fixed dense vertex set favor a matrix; scanning neighbors in a large sparse graph favors adjacency collections. No fixed density cutoff is a universal decision rule.

body:


## A Protected Route Graph

```{index} graph API; undirected invariant; defensive copy
```

Encapsulation should protect graph rules, not merely hide a field's name. `RouteGraph` uses private neighbor dictionaries and returns copied arrays for vertices and neighbors. A caller can edit its copy without changing the stored graph. Returning a mutable collection as `IEnumerable` would not protect it: a caller could cast it back to the original collection type.

The contract requires explicit vertices. `SetEdge` checks both endpoints and weight rules before changing either direction. A new logical edge increases EdgeCount once; replacing its weight changes both reciprocal entries without changing EdgeCount. `TryGetWeight` returns false for an absent endpoint or edge, while degree/neighbor queries throw for an unknown vertex so it cannot masquerade as an isolate.

headings.title: Removal, Invariants, and Testing
body:
```{index} Removal, Invariants, and Testing
```

## Removal, Invariants, and Testing

```{index} edge removal; vertex removal; degree sum; graph validation
```

Removing an undirected edge deletes both reciprocal entries and reduces EdgeCount once. Removing a vertex deletes every reverse reference before removing its own dictionary. Its degree tells you how many logical edges disappear. Other vertices stay present even if they become isolated.

Trace removing Hall from the six-room example. Hall's neighbors are Lobby, Lab, and Office. Remove Hall from each of those neighbor maps, subtract three from EdgeCount, and delete Hall. Five vertices and one edge remain; Lobby and Lab are now isolates, Office–Storage remains, and Remote is unchanged. Removing Hall again returns false.

The representation invariant requires every neighbor label to name an existing vertex, no self-loops, nonnegative weights, equal reverse weights, and degree sum `2 * EdgeCount`. `IsValid` checks those rules in expected Θ(V + E) time. It still cannot prove that the data matches the intended floor plan, so compare edge membership and weights with an independent model too.

With neighbor hashes, `RemoveEdge` takes expected O(1) time. `RemoveVertex(u)` takes expected O(deg(u)) time because it removes a reference at each neighbor. The code does not mutate u's neighbor map while enumerating it; it changes the distinct maps belonging to those neighbors. Self-loops are rejected, so a reverse map cannot be the same map being enumerated.

`Degree` reads a stored dictionary count in expected O(1). `Neighbors` copies deg(u) entries, so it takes Θ(deg(u)) time and space. `Vertices` copies V labels. Defensive copying has a cost, but keeps callers from bypassing update rules.

## Turn Queue Events into a Traversal Loop
A facilities graph answers which rooms can be reached and how many doorways a shortest route uses. Every edge in this lesson contributes one hop. The queue is not a list of completed rooms; it holds discovered rooms whose neighbors still need examination. This is the queue policy from Chapter 15 applied to the graph model from the preceding sections.

Use directed edges A→B, A→C, B→D and C→D, plus an isolated E. Neighbor order is written explicitly. Begin with A discovered, distance zero and no predecessor. The small program exposes the traversal core; the full graph class and validation examples remain below.
Here membership in `distance` also means discovered, so a separate visited set would duplicate that fact. All endpoints are declared in this teaching graph. Production validation of unknown labels is retained in the complete implementation.

| Statement group | Meaning in the trace | Why the order matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dequeue current | Choose the oldest waiting room | Complete this layer before later layers |
| Test distance membership | Skip a previously discovered neighbor | C must not enqueue D a second time |
| Store distance and predecessor | Record the first discovery | A known room has one chosen route witness |
| Enqueue neighbor | Schedule its remaining work | Mark discovery before another parent can find it |

After A, the queue is B,C. After B, it is C,D; D already has distance two and predecessor B. When C examines D, the membership test succeeds and no new queue entry is added. A cycle back to A is harmless for the same reason: A was marked before processing began.

A predecessor map points backwards. For D, following D←B←A gives a reverse route. Reverse those labels to display A→B→D. A missing destination has no such chain; do not create a one-room route and call it reachable. The source itself is a valid one-room route with zero edges.

headings.title: Discover a Vertex Once, Then Process Its Neighbors
body:
```{index} Discover a Vertex Once, Then Process Its Neighbors
```

## Discover a Vertex Once, Then Process Its Neighbors

A delivery graph has edges A-B, A-C, B-D and C-D. Starting at A, how many roads are needed to reach each stop? Breadth-first search answers a minimum-hop question in an unweighted graph. It keeps a queue of discovered vertices whose outgoing neighbors still need examination. Discovery and processing are different events: a vertex can already be known while it is still waiting in the queue.

Mark a vertex discovered when it is enqueued. If you wait until dequeue, both B and C can enqueue D before D is processed. That duplicates work and makes predecessor choices harder to reason about. A visited/discovered set is therefore part of the algorithm's state, not merely an optional speed optimization.

| Processing event | Queue afterward | Newly discovered distances |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initialize A | A | A: 0 |
| Examine A | B, C | B: 1, C: 1 |
| Examine B | C, D | D: 2 |
| Examine C | D | None; D is already known |
| Examine D | Empty | None |

The table assumes that A lists B before C. A different neighbor order can choose another equally short predecessor route, but it does not change the minimum hop distance. Tests that insist on one exact path without specifying neighbor order can reject correct results. State the tie policy separately from the distance claim.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Recover a Path from Earlier Layers
body: ```{index} Recover a Path from Earlier Layers ``` ## Recover a Path from Earlier Layers When discovering a new vertex v from u, record predecessor[v] = u and distance[v] = distance[u] + 1. Following those predecessor links backward reconstructs a route to the source. Reverse the route to display it from source to destination. The source is a one-vertex route to itself; an unreachable known vertex has no source route. Do not fabricate a destination-only path when no predecessor chain exists. Why is the distance minimal? The queue processes vertices in nondecreasing discovered distance. All one-hop vertices are discovered from the source before processing can expose a two-hop successor, and the same reasoning repeats layer by layer. The first discovery therefore uses a shortest hop count. This reasoning relies on equal edge contribution, not on geometric closeness or vertex spelling. With arbitrary weights, fewer edges can be more expensive; Chapter 24 treats that different objective. For adjacency lists, visiting reachable vertices and their incident/outgoing entries costs work proportional to those entries plus vertex bookkeeping. A traversal of one component does not visit all disconnected components by magic. If the task is a full undirected component report, start a new traversal from each still-undiscovered vertex, including isolates. Guided exercise: add an isolated E and a cycle D-A to the graph. Predict which vertices are discovered from A, whether any is enqueued twice, and the result for a path to E. Then choose C before B in A's neighbor list. Explain which outputs may change and which correctness obligations remain fixed. ```{dropdown} Verification checkpoint E is unreachable from A; its route must remain absent. The cycle does not rediscover A because A was marked at initialization. Either A-B-D or A-C-D can be a shortest route to D under the chosen neighbor order; both use two edges. ``` ```{index} Graph Traversal: Reachability, Paths, and Components ``` A facilities team needs to know which rooms can be reached, how many unweighted links a route needs, and which rooms form disconnected groups. A representation stores connections; traversal systematically discovers what those connections imply. Start with declared vertices so isolated rooms remain visible. Every example includes the complete model. The implementation uses ordinary classes, loops, a queue, and a visited set.

headings.title: Watch the Suspended Neighbor Loop
body:
```{index} Watch the Suspended Neighbor Loop
```

## Watch the Suspended Neighbor Loop
Depth-first search is ordinary recursive control flow applied to a graph. A call must remember which neighbor it is considering while a child explores its branch. This connects the suspended calls in Chapter 17 to Chapter 20's cycles and shared destinations. A discovered set avoids repeated discovery; it does not erase the caller's unfinished neighbor loop.

Use the undirected diamond A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, and isolated E. In each array below, the listed neighbor order determines the trace. Watch enter and exit events separately. A vertex is entered once; returning from a child resumes an already active parent rather than entering that parent again.
C is first entered from D, not from A. A's neighbor loop has not finished, but C is already discovered by the time A resumes and considers it. C's DFS depth is three although A has a direct edge to C. A first DFS route therefore need not minimize hops.

| Event | Active frames from oldest to newest | What waits in the caller? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enter A | A | A will consider C after B returns |
| Enter B | A,B | B will finish after D returns |
| Enter D | A,B,D | D will finish after C returns |
| Enter C | A,B,D,C | C finds no undiscovered neighbor |
| Exit C | A,B,D | D resumes its neighbor loop |
| Exit D | A,B | B resumes |
| Exit B | A | A sees that C is already discovered |
| Exit A | Empty | Source traversal is complete |

Do not use the number of discovered vertices as the current stack depth. Four vertices have been discovered after C exits, but only three calls remain active at that point. Likewise, a visited neighbor alone is not enough to classify a directed cycle: completed and active destinations have different meanings.

## Extend Reachability into a Component Report
For an undirected graph, a component is the maximal group reachable from any of its members. Keep the discovered set across searches, then start another search from each undiscovered vertex. Starting a new traversal from a vertex that is already discovered would split or duplicate a component.

Guided task: after searching from A, which source starts another component? What is the answer for an empty graph? Then predict the report after adding isolated F. The following standalone example makes the labels visible without the full graph class.
E starts component two. An empty graph starts none; adding isolated F produces three. Component numbers depend on the declared start order, but membership equivalence does not: A and D must share a component and E must remain separate. Before independent practice, explain why these symmetric edges support undirected components while an arbitrary directed reachability report does not compute strongly connected components. The full implementations below retain their stronger input validation and source/path exercises.

headings.title: Finish One Branch Before Returning to Its Alternatives
body:
```{index} Finish One Branch Before Returning to Its Alternatives
```

## Finish One Branch Before Returning to Its Alternatives

Depth-first search follows an unvisited neighbor, completes the exploration reachable through that choice, and then returns to the caller's remaining neighbors. The control pattern connects to tree traversal, but a graph can have shared destinations and cycles. A discovered set prevents following those connections forever.

Use A with neighbors B and C, B connected to D, and C also connected to D. With B considered first, a recursive DFS can enter A, B, D and then C if the adjacency order supplies that route. When the call from D has completed, execution resumes in the suspended neighbor loop of its caller. A plain stack of vertices can provide a valid depth-first exploration policy, but reproducing exact recursive entry/exit timing requires storing enough progress to know which neighbor a suspended frame should consider next.

| Event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Enter a new vertex | Mark discovered; begin its neighbor sequence |
| Encounter an already discovered vertex | Avoid a second discovery; interpret the edge under the graph model |
| Return from a child | Resume the parent's remaining neighbors |
| Exit a vertex | Its chosen neighbor sequence is complete |

Do not infer a directed cycle merely from seeing an edge to any previously visited vertex. That destination might already have completed. Directed-cycle reasoning distinguishes an active unfinished path from completed exploration. In an undirected graph, the edge back to the parent also needs special treatment. A single Boolean visited flag solves repeated discovery; additional state or parent information may be needed for the specific cycle question.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Connectivity Depends on Direction
body:

## Connectivity Depends on Direction

For a symmetric undirected adjacency model, repeated traversals from undiscovered vertices partition the graph into connected components. Every vertex belongs to exactly one such component, and an isolated vertex forms a component by itself. Directed reachability is not symmetric: A may reach B even when B cannot reach A. Repeating ordinary forward searches in arbitrary order does not automatically compute strongly connected components.

Verification can check that each discovered vertex enters/exits once, parent-child call intervals are nested under the recursive model, and every reported reachable vertex has a path from the source. It should not assume that DFS yields minimum-hop paths. BFS has that guarantee under its unweighted model; DFS's first route may be longer.

Guided comparison: draw a graph where A connects directly to D but also begins a long chain that eventually reaches D. Process the chain neighbor first. Predict a DFS route and a BFS route. Then reverse one edge in the chain and identify which reachability claims must be reconsidered. Explain the observed difference using the frontier policy and edge directions rather than the generic phrase graph search.

## Derive a Count Before Naming a Growth Class

A report compares each invoice with every later invoice. There are n invoices, but not n squared distinct ordered loop-body executions in this particular program. The first invoice has n-1 later partners, the next has n-2, and the final invoice has none. Adding these counts gives n(n-1)/2. This exact count is quadratic even though it is not exactly n squared.

For n = 4, list pairs by index: (0,1), (0,2), (0,3), (1,2), (1,3), (2,3). Six comparisons are needed. This small instance checks whether a proposed formula counts self-pairs or counts each pair twice. It does not itself prove the formula for every n; the decreasing row lengths explain the general sum.

| n | Later-pair count | Rectangular all-pairs count n*n |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 6 | 16 |
| 8 | 28 | 64 |

The chosen basic operation matters. Counting loop-body visits, string comparisons, element copies or allocated objects can produce different exact counts. State the model before comparing algorithms. Fixed-width arithmetic is often modeled as constant work here; a proof about very large arbitrary-precision integers must account for growing operand size.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: A Bound Is a Statement with a Domain
body:
```{index} A Bound Is a Statement with a Domain
```

## A Bound Is a Statement with a Domain

Big-O describes an eventual upper bound up to a constant factor. A tight Θ claim also needs a matching lower bound under the stated model. Saying a function is O(n squared) can be true without identifying its tight growth; a linear function also has a quadratic upper bound for sufficiently large n. Use the distinction when a table asks for a tight class rather than any correct upper bound.

For n(n-1)/2 and n at least two, a constant fraction of n squared bounds the count below and one half of n squared bounds it above. Those inequalities connect the exact formula to the tight quadratic class. They are more informative than deleting terms by habit without saying what the approximation means.

Input-dependent cases need their own quantifiers. A first-match scan can stop after one comparison for a leading match and can examine n elements for a missing target. Worst case chooses a maximizing input at each size; expected case requires a probability model. Amortized analysis bounds a sequence of operations and does not require that the sequence be random.

Guided derivation: a loop doubles a counter from one while it remains below n. Write its tested values for n = 8 and n = 9, then state which operation you are counting. Explain why a one-step count difference at a boundary does not contradict logarithmic growth. Finally, distinguish total allocated bytes over a run from peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage.
A finance team can scan every expense once or compare every pair. Before timing either program, define the input and count the work. Analysis describes a cost model; measurement checks how that model behaves on a particular system.

## Bounds and Tight Growth

```{index} Bounds and Tight Growth
```

For nonnegative costs, `T(n) ∈ O(f(n))` means there are constants `c > 0` and `n₀` such that `T(n) ≤ c f(n)` for all `n ≥ n₀`. Ω supplies a lower bound; Θ supplies both bounds. These symbols describe a chosen cost function, not automatically a worst-case cost.

For `n ≥ 1`, `3n² ≤ 3n² + 5n + 20 ≤ 28n²`, so the cost is Θ(n²). It is also O(n³), an upper bound that loses useful precision. Saying O(n²) alone does not establish that the cost is quadratic: a linear cost also satisfies that upper bound. Logarithm bases differ by constant factors.

## Best, Worst, Expected, and Amortized Costs

```{index} Best, Worst, Expected, and Amortized Costs
```

A search can stop early. Best and worst cases vary over inputs of the same size; an expected cost needs a probability model. An amortized cost averages over a sequence of operations and does not require random inputs.

On nonempty arrays, this search has best-case Θ(1) and worst-case Θ(n) comparisons. If a successful target is equally likely at every index, its expected count is `(n+1)/2`, hence Θ(n). A geometric-growth array append has amortized Θ(1) cost even though one resizing append costs Θ(n). Expected hashing requires assumptions about key distribution and table policy; it is a different claim.

# Correctness and Invariants
```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
```{index} Make the Claim Strong Enough to Guide the Program
```

headings.title: Make the Claim Strong Enough to Guide the Program
body:
```{index} Make the Claim Strong Enough to Guide the Program
```

## Make the Claim Strong Enough to Guide the Program

A maximum routine is supposed to return the greatest value in a nonempty integer array. The phrase finds a maximum is too vague to determine empty behavior, duplicate handling or whether input may change. State the domain, output relation and mutation policy first. A proof cannot repair an unspecified contract after implementation choices have already been made.

Consider a left-to-right scan. After initializing best from the first element, let i denote the next unprocessed position. The invariant is that best is the maximum of positions zero through i-1. This relation mentions both the accumulated result and the processed boundary. Saying best is the maximum is not a useful invariant unless it explains maximum of which data at that point.

| Proof obligation | Reason for the scan |
| --- | --- |
| Initialization | The first element is the maximum of the one-element prefix |
| Maintenance | Comparing the next element extends the correct prefix by one |
| Exit | The processed prefix is the complete nonempty array |
| Termination | The number of unprocessed positions strictly decreases |

Initialization must match the domain. Setting best to zero fails on an all-negative nonempty input because zero may not occur in the array and is greater than every legitimate result. A positive-only test set would not expose this defect. The invariant makes the issue visible before a long list of tests is attempted.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Partial Correctness and Termination Are Separate Questions
```

headings.title: Partial Correctness and Termination Are Separate Questions
body:
```{index} Partial Correctness and Termination Are Separate Questions
```

## Partial Correctness and Termination Are Separate Questions

An invariant helps establish what is true if execution reaches the exit. A decreasing nonnegative measure, such as remaining positions, explains why the loop eventually reaches that exit. These are different obligations. A loop can preserve a useful relation forever while failing to advance, so preservation alone does not establish total correctness.

Early returns need a local justification. In first-match search, returning at position i is correct only if that element matches and no earlier position matched. The scan's processed-prefix relation supplies the second fact. A return from the middle of an algorithm does not automatically invalidate proof reasoning, but it needs an argument at that exit.

Tests and counterexamples complement these arguments. Empty input checks the domain policy; one element checks initialization; all-negative values challenge a careless initial value; repeated maxima check that equality is handled consistently. A passing finite set supports confidence without proving the invariant for all accepted inputs. A single valid-domain counterexample, however, disproves a universal correctness claim.

Guided proof repair: assume best starts at zero for input -8, -3, -5. Identify exactly which initialization claim is false. Replace the initialization and trace the maintenance steps. Then state what the routine should do on empty input under two possible contracts: reject it explicitly or return a success signal with no maximum. Do not silently treat zero as the maximum of no values.
A fast expense report is useful only if its totals and selected records satisfy the business rules. Specify the result first, then connect every loop step to that specification.

headings.title: Specifications and Failure Policies
body:
```{index} Specifications and Failure Policies
```

## Specifications and Failure Policies

```{index} Specifications and Failure Policies
```

For a maximum, require a non-null, nonempty array. Promise that the result is an input value and is at least every input value. Merely promising a large value is insufficient: returning int.MaxValue would satisfy that weaker promise. Define rejected inputs and whether failure changes state.

Runtime guards enforce this contract. Other algorithms may document a precondition rather than check it each time. Binary search requires sorted input; checking that condition costs Θ(n) and changes the cost of an individual search.

headings.title: An Invariant with an Exact Boundary
body:
```{index} An Invariant with an Exact Boundary
```

## An Invariant with an Exact Boundary

```{index} An Invariant with an Exact Boundary
```

At the head of the maximum loop, `1 ≤ i ≤ n` and `best` is the maximum of the processed prefix `[0, i)`. Half-open notation includes index zero and excludes index `i`; it avoids uncertainty about whether the next value has already been processed.

Initialization: at `i=1`, the prefix contains only `values[0]`. Maintenance: comparing the next value extends the prefix by one while preserving its maximum. At normal loop exit `i=n`, the prefix is the entire input, so the invariant gives both parts of the postcondition.

headings.title: Termination and Total Correctness
body:
```{index} Termination and Total Correctness
```

## Termination and Total Correctness

```{index} Termination and Total Correctness
```

An invariant explains the result if execution finishes: partial correctness. Total correctness also requires termination. A variant is a nonnegative integer measure that strictly decreases on each continuing iteration. For the maximum loop, `n−i` decreases by one.

An unchanged `remaining` could preserve a safety invariant while looping forever. The decreasing measure rules out that behavior. The third step of an invariant argument uses the exit condition to derive the result; it does not by itself prove that the exit will eventually occur.

headings.title: Early Return and First-Match Search
body:
```{index} Early Return and First-Match Search
```

## Early Return and First-Match Search

```{index} Early Return and First-Match Search
```

Specify first-match search: return the smallest matching index, or −1 when no match exists. Before testing index `i`, every index in `[0,i)` fails to match. Normal loop exit and early return require separate arguments.

An early return identifies a matching value and the invariant excludes earlier matches. At normal exit, the invariant excludes every index. Empty input returns −1 without an array access. The variant `n−i` proves the continuing loop terminates.

headings.title: Boundary Tests and a Counterexample
body:
```{index} Boundary Tests and a Counterexample
```

## Boundary Tests and a Counterexample

```{index} Boundary Tests and a Counterexample
```

Tests complement proofs by challenging contracts and implementation details. A common maximum bug initializes best to zero; the bug stays hidden on positive data. Test singleton, negative, duplicate, extreme, empty, and rejected inputs.

The reference comparison checks actual code on these inputs. The invariant covers every input satisfying the contract. Arithmetic behavior is part of the specification too: use a sufficiently wide type or a checked operation when a mathematical sum may overflow the chosen C# type.

body:


```{index} Analysis practice
```
Count nonnegative adjustments. State the processed-prefix invariant and variant; include zero as nonnegative.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^2102_correctness-1]: A specification must identify the allowed inputs, promised result, and failure behavior; a proof is only as useful as that specification.
[^2102_correctness-2]: Testing a finite sample generally cannot prove a statement over all possible input sizes. Boundary tests and counterexamples remain valuable implementation checks.

# Recurrences and Recursive Cost
```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
```{index} Account for the Children and the Work Around Them
```

headings.title: Account for the Children and the Work Around Them
body:
```{index} Account for the Children and the Work Around Them
```

## Account for the Children and the Work Around Them

A recurrence models the work of a recursive algorithm. It is not the algorithm's return-value equation unless the counted work happens to satisfy the same relation. A recursive sum may return a monetary total while its call count follows a completely different equation. Name the quantity being modeled and include the base cost.

For a one-step reduction, suppose C(0)=1 and C(n)=1+C(n-1). Unfolding gives C(n)=1+1+C(n-2), then n non-base contributions plus the base contribution. Thus C(n)=n+1 under this counting convention. Omitting the base call changes exact counts but not linear growth; state the convention so measured results and formulas can agree.

A halving recursion has a different depth. If each call makes one child of size floor(n/2), the active chain has logarithmic length, but a call that performs linear local work still contributes that work at every level. Do not confuse a halving input with automatically logarithmic total time.

| Recursive design | Work at each level | Number of levels | Resulting pattern |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One child smaller by one, constant local work | Constant | Linear | Linear total |
| One half-size child, constant local work | Constant | Logarithmic | Logarithmic total |
| Two half-size children, linear combine | About n across a level | Logarithmic | n log n total |

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Track Rounding and Live Storage
```

headings.title: Track Rounding and Live Storage
body:
```{index} Track Rounding and Live Storage
```

## Track Rounding and Live Storage

For odd n, two subproblems cannot both have size n/2 as an integer. A range split may have floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2) items. Together they must still cover the whole input without overlap or omission. Bounds can simplify rounding when justified, but an implementation must handle exact endpoints.

In a balanced two-child recursion, a level can contain many calls even though only one root-to-leaf path is active at a time in depth-first execution. Total calls, maximum active frames and allocated buffers are separate measurements. Merge sort's reusable buffer and recursive frames contribute different terms to auxiliary space. Cumulative writes also differ from simultaneous storage.

Overlapping subproblems change the count again. A naive Fibonacci recursion revisits the same numeric arguments through multiple branches. Memoization can collapse repeated computation into distinct solved states, but the first recursive path still needs stack space. Chapter 25 develops that transformation; a recurrence analysis should identify the repeated work rather than claiming that every branching recursion has the same cost.

Guided exercise: list the subproblem sizes for a balanced split of five items, continuing to singletons. Check that each level's item coverage is correct, count calls under an explicit base convention, and distinguish the deepest chain from the entire tree of calls. Then compare this tree with one that creates only a single half-size child per call.
A recurrence models work by input size. Keep the returned value, total calls, and maximum simultaneously active frames separate. These examples preview recursive analysis; Chapter 22 develops recursive programming.

headings.title: Base Cases and Linear Recurrences
body:
```{index} Base Cases and Linear Recurrences
```

## Base Cases and Linear Recurrences

```{index} Base Cases and Linear Recurrences
```
Let C(n) count calls, including the base call. For a nonnegative countdown, C(0)=1 and C(n)=C(n−1)+1. Expanding gives C(n)=n+1. The returned value below is n, which is a different quantity.

Time and stack space are Θ(n+1); for growing positive n, write Θ(n). Each call has constant local storage. Negative input would never reach zero in this model, so nonnegative input is a required precondition. Production recursive code needs a practical depth limit; .NET does not promise unlimited recursion or tail-call elimination.

headings.title: Halving with Integer Inputs
body:
```{index} Halving with Integer Inputs
```

## Halving with Integer Inputs

```{index} Halving with Integer Inputs
```
C(n)=1 for n≤1 and C(n)=C(floor(n/2))+1 otherwise. For n≥1 this gives floor(log₂ n)+1 calls. The number of reductions is one less than the number of calls.
For powers of two, the chain is n, n/2, …, 1. For n=9 the integer chain is 9,4,2,1. Depth and time are Θ(log n) for large n; zero and one remain constant-cost base cases.

headings.title: Two Branches and Work per Level
body:
```{index} Two Branches and Work per Level
```

## Two Branches and Work per Level

```{index} Two Branches and Work per Level
```

For a model with n=2^k leaves, define W(1)=1 and W(n)=2W(n/2)+n. At every internal level, the total combine work is n. There are log₂ n internal levels, plus n leaf units, so W(n)=n log₂ n+n. This models a merge-style algorithm without implementing sorting here.

For n=8, level work is 8+8+8+8=32, total calls are 15, and peak active frames are 4. Sibling calls occur sequentially, so they increase total calls without doubling stack depth. This counter program itself visits Θ(n) nodes; its returned work models an algorithm that actually performs n combine operations at each internal node.

headings.title: Rounding and Auxiliary Storage
body:
```{index} Rounding and Auxiliary Storage
```

## Rounding and Auxiliary Storage

```{index} Rounding and Auxiliary Storage
```
For arbitrary positive sizes, split into floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2), preserving all items. Using floor(n/2) twice loses an item for odd n. For n>1, both parts must be smaller than n.

The general model remains Θ(n log n) work. Its stack depth is Θ(log n), with constant storage per frame. A real merge sort usually needs Θ(n) auxiliary merge storage as well. Stack depth alone is not total auxiliary space. State how buffers are allocated and reused before claiming a memory bound.

headings.title: Branching and Repeated Subproblems
body:
```{index} Branching and Repeated Subproblems
```

## Branching and Repeated Subproblems

```{index} Branching and Repeated Subproblems
```
The naive Fibonacci call count obeys C(0)=C(1)=1 and C(n)=C(n−1)+C(n−2)+1. Repeated subproblems create exponential work. A recursion tree can be wide even when its depth is linear.

For n=6 there are 25 calls but only 6 active frames at the peak. The time is O(2^n), a useful upper bound; the tighter exponential growth is Θ(φ^n), where φ≈1.618. Stack space is Θ(n). Memoization reduces repeated work by retaining results; its implementation belongs in Chapter 25. Derive a recurrence from calls and nonrecursive work, include its base case, and distinguish the model from the code that calculates an estimate.

body:


```{index} Analysis practice
```
For n=8, print the number of leaves and total calls in a balanced two-branch recursion with constant work per node. Contrast this with a linear combine-cost model.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^2103_recurrences-1]: Recursion depth here counts active calls including the base call. Some texts count edges between calls instead; specify the convention.
[^2103_recurrences-2]: The power-of-two assumption simplifies exact level sums. Balanced integer splits retain the same asymptotic bound for other positive sizes.

body:
# Recursive Contracts and Divide-and-Conquer
```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
```{index} Let a Helper Promise Exactly One Smaller Problem
```

headings.title: Let a Helper Promise Exactly One Smaller Problem
body: ```{index} Let a Helper Promise Exactly One Smaller Problem ``` ## Let a Helper Promise Exactly One Smaller Problem A public method can accept a complete report while a private recursive helper accepts a suffix or range. The helper contract must name that smaller problem precisely. For a suffix starting at index i, the result might be the total of entries i through the end. The public caller starts with i zero; other starting indexes are an implementation detail rather than a burden placed on every client. The base case is an empty suffix, not a special final value guessed from one example. Its sum is zero. For a nonempty suffix, combine the first available entry with the helper's result on the remaining suffix. The progress measure n-i decreases by one, which connects the contract to termination. The caller still needs an arithmetic-range policy: termination does not prove that a fixed-width sum cannot overflow. For divide-and-conquer, represent a range as [lo, hi). Its length is hi-lo, and empty means lo equals hi. Splitting at lo+(hi-lo)/2 gives two adjacent half-open ranges. On five items, the lengths are two and three; neither item duplication nor equal lengths are required. What matters is complete, nonoverlapping coverage and strictly smaller children when recursion continues. | Design question | What to state before recursing | | --- | --- | | What does the helper return? | A result for this suffix/range | | When is the answer direct? | Empty/singleton or another explicit base | | What becomes smaller? | Remaining length or another well-founded measure | | How are child results combined? | An operation justified by the parent contract | Guided contrast: finding a maximum needs results from both halves, while a binary-search comparison chooses only one remaining half. Both use interval splitting, but they do not have the same call tree or work recurrence. Predict child calls for one size-five input under each algorithm before comparing their costs. For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading] ```{index} Recursive Problem Solving ``` Basic recursive cases, base answers, and call/return tracing are taught in {doc}`Chapter 17 <../17_trees/1701_tree_structure>`. Review that section before this optional extension. Here you develop helper contracts, progress arguments, resource limits, and divide-and-conquer design.

headings.title: Progress Measures
body:
```{index} Progress Measures
```

## Progress Measures

```{index} Progress Measures
```
A progress measure proves that recursion is moving in the right direction. The measure does not have to be a single number, but it must get closer to a base case.

The wrapper hides the helper index so clients cannot supply a negative or out-of-range start. Scan(index) promises whether the target occurs in the suffix [index,n). An empty suffix returns false; a matching first item returns true; otherwise the answer comes from the smaller suffix. The measure n−index decreases on every recursive call. Empty input needs no array access. Worst-case time and stack are Θ(n); a first-item match needs only one helper frame.

headings.title: Recursion and Iteration
body:
```{index} Recursion and Iteration
```

## Recursion and Iteration

```{index} Recursion and Iteration
```
Many recursive methods can be written with loops. Use recursion when the problem naturally breaks into smaller problems of the same shape, or when recursion makes the structure easier to see.

Both sums visit every item, taking Θ(n) time under the integer cost model. The recursive version retains Θ(n) active frames; an iterative sum retains Θ(1) auxiliary state. Recursion changes expression of control flow, not the amount of data that must be processed. Prefer the loop for long flat reports; recursion is particularly useful for balanced splits and nested structures.

headings.title: Recursive Risks
body:
```{index} Recursive Risks
```

## Recursive Risks

```{index} Recursive Risks
```

A recursive method with a missing base case or no progress can call itself forever until the program runs out of stack space. In C#, recursive calls are not something to use casually for huge linear loops.

Check input domain, direct base answer, and a well-founded progress measure before running recursive code. Do not intentionally trigger stack exhaustion in the browser. Tail-call elimination is not guaranteed for these C# methods. A finite domain and arithmetic range are separate from the proof of termination; validate both when designing the interface.

headings.title: Exercise
body: ```{index} Exercise ``` ## Exercise ```{index} Exercise ``` Recursively count positive expense adjustments in a suffix. Zero is not positive. State the helper postcondition and progress measure; test empty input. ```{index} Divide-and-Conquer Design ``` Divide-and-conquer algorithms solve a problem in three phases: divide the input into smaller parts, solve the smaller parts, and combine their results. Recursion is a natural implementation technique because each subproblem has the same shape as the original problem.

headings.title: The Pattern
body:
```{index} The Pattern
```

## The Pattern

```{index} The Pattern
```

A divide-and-conquer method usually follows this shape:

1. If the problem is small enough, solve it directly.
2. Divide the input into smaller pieces.
3. Recursively solve the pieces.
4. Combine the partial answers.

The helper promise is the maximum of the nonempty half-open range [start,end). The wrapper rejects empty input before recursion. For length>1, both child ranges are nonempty, smaller, disjoint, and together cover the parent, including odd lengths. Inductively correct child maxima combine to the parent maximum. The size measure end−start decreases. T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+T(ceil(n/2))+Θ(1), hence Θ(n) work and Θ(log n) stack. A loop also takes Θ(n) work with less stack: splitting alone does not make maximum selection faster.

headings.title: Halving Strategies
body:
```{index} Halving Strategies
```

## Halving Strategies


```{index} Halving Strategies
```
Some algorithms solve only one half after dividing. Binary search is the classic example: compare with the middle value, then search the half where the target could still be.
Precondition: input is sorted in ascending order and is not modified during the search. The result is any matching index, or −1 when absent; duplicates do not promise a first match. The candidate interval is [start,end). Sortedness justifies discarding the impossible side. Excluding middle from the right interval prevents repeating a one-item range. Each surviving range is smaller; an empty range stops recursion. Only one child is explored, giving T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+Θ(1) as a size model, Θ(log n) worst-case time/stack, and Θ(1) best-case time. Checking sortedness on every call would add linear work.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```
[^2201_recursion-1]: Tail-call optimization is not something introductory C# programmers should rely on. Prefer clear loops for simple linear repetition when stack depth could become large.
[^2201_recursion-2]: A recursive method can have more than one base case. The important point is that every path of recursive calls eventually reaches one of them.
