body:
# Stable Merge Sort and Verification
```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
```{index} Prove the Combining Step Before Hiding It in Recursion
```

headings.title: Prove the Combining Step Before Hiding It in Recursion
body:
```{index} Prove the Combining Step Before Hiding It in Recursion
```

## Prove the Combining Step Before Hiding It in Recursion

Assume two input runs are already sorted under the same policy. To merge them, compare their first unread elements and choose the smaller. No later element in either run can be smaller than that run's first unread element, so the chosen value is safe as the next output. Recursion supplies sorted runs; it does not remove the need to justify this combining rule.

Merge [2, 5] with [1, 5, 7]. Choose 1 from the right, then 2 from the left. At the tie between the two 5 values, choosing the left one first preserves relative order when these runs came from adjacent parts of the original input. After one run is exhausted, copy the remaining suffix of the other; it is already sorted.

| Output so far | Left unread | Right unread |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [] | 2, 5 | 1, 5, 7 |
| [1] | 2, 5 | 5, 7 |
| [1, 2] | 5 | 5, 7 |
| [1, 2, 5-left] | Empty | 5-right, 7 |

The invariant combines ordering and preservation: output contains exactly the consumed input occurrences in sorted order, and its final element is no greater than the remaining candidates. Keeping only the ordering claim would not rule out accidentally duplicating one occurrence and losing another.

Range/buffer implementations add an indexing obligation. Source and destination ranges must refer to the intended segments; copying into the wrong offset can produce correct tiny whole-array results and fail on an interior range. Trace a merge whose lo is not zero, and include odd lengths. A reusable buffer can reduce allocation without changing the merge contract.

Guided verification: label equal invoice amounts with original IDs. Check that sorted order holds, every original ID occurs exactly once, and equal-key IDs retain their arrival order. Then compare a nonmutating sort that returns a fresh outer array with an in-place sort. Both may order values correctly, but only one satisfies a contract that preserves the caller's original array order.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Combining Sorted Parts
body:
```{index} Combining Sorted Parts
```

## Combining Sorted Parts

```{index} Combining Sorted Parts
```
Merge sort depends on a combine step called **merge**. Given two sorted arrays, merge walks through both arrays and builds one sorted result.

Merge requires two inputs sorted under the same comparison, and returns a fresh sorted array containing every input occurrence. At the main loop head, k=i+j and result[0,k) is the stable sorted merge of the consumed prefixes. The next smallest unconsumed item must be at one of the two fronts. Choosing the left front on equality preserves original order. Once one side is exhausted, copy the other remainder without further comparisons. For total N>0, merging takes Θ(N) time/output space and at most N−1 key comparisons; empty sides can need zero comparisons but still require copying.

headings.title: Merge Sort
body:
```{index} Merge Sort
```

## Merge Sort

```{index} Merge Sort
```
Merge sort divides the array into halves until each piece has zero or one item, then merges sorted pieces back together.

The copy-returning contract leaves the input unchanged and returns a fresh array even for zero or one item. Slices allocate new arrays, making this version easy to read but allocation-heavy. T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+T(ceil(n/2))+Θ(n), so time is Θ(n log n) for n≥2. Stack depth is Θ(log n). The next section replaces slices with index ranges and a reusable buffer; it also verifies stability and preservation. Comparisons are only one part of sorting cost: copying still happens when a side is exhausted.

headings.title: Design Checklist
body:
```{index} Design Checklist
```

## Design Checklist

```{index} Design Checklist
```

When designing a divide-and-conquer algorithm, ask:

1. What is the smallest case I can solve directly?
2. How do I divide the input?
3. Do I solve one subproblem or multiple subproblems?
4. How do I combine the answers?
5. What recurrence describes the cost?

headings.title: Exercise
body: ```{index} Exercise ``` ## Exercise ```{index} Exercise ``` Merge two sorted invoice batches, including duplicates and an empty side. Verify the exact expected sequence, not just increasing order. ```{index} Merge Sort Lab ``` A finance team sorts invoices by amount while retaining the arrival order of equal amounts. Build correctness checks before comparing counts. Every code cell includes its own setup and implementation. Download {download}`the complete stable merge-sort source and reference checks <../../demos/22_recursion_divide_conquer/StableSort.cs>` for a console project.

headings.title: Trace Merge Fronts
body:
```{index} Trace Merge Fronts
```

## Trace Merge Fronts

```{index} Trace Merge Fronts
```
Track consumed indexes i and j and output index k. Equal keys take the left item first. Predict which side runs out, then trace both the comparison loop and the tail copies.

The invariant k=i+j and sorted consumed-prefix merge explains why no value disappears. The measure (left.Length−i)+(right.Length−j) decreases after every copy. Stability is relative to a comparison key; equal integer values cannot display record order, so use labeled invoices next.

headings.title: Sort Ranges with One Buffer
body:
```{index} Sort Ranges with One Buffer
```

## Sort Ranges with One Buffer

```{index} Sort Ranges with One Buffer
```

The public method clones the input once and allocates one reusable buffer. SortRange(start,end) sorts a half-open range. Sibling calls finish sequentially, then merge their sorted ranges into the matching buffer range and copy back. Counts reset at each Sort call.

Assume each recursive call correctly sorts its smaller range and preserves its items. The merge invariant establishes the same promise for the parent. Empty/singleton ranges return directly. Odd lengths are fully covered. The copied output and buffer use Θ(n) storage, and the stack adds Θ(log n); total auxiliary space is Θ(n). Across all levels there are Θ(n log n) writes, but cumulative writes are not peak memory. The original slice version also allocates across levels; separate total allocation volume from peak live storage.

headings.title: Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices
body:
```{index} Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices
```

## Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices

```{index} Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices
```

A stable sort preserves arrival order among equal amounts. Compare only the amount, and track identity separately. A consistent comparison must define an ordering; subtracting integer keys can overflow, so use CompareTo.

Changing the merge comparison from ≤0 to <0 would let equal right items overtake equal left items. Stability matters when reports preserve earlier arrival order or apply successive sorts. It is a property of the algorithm and comparison policy, not merely of sorted numeric output.

headings.title: Check Order, Preservation, and Copying
body:
```{index} Check Order, Preservation, and Copying
```

## Check Order, Preservation, and Copying

```{index} Check Order, Preservation, and Copying
```

Sortedness alone is insufficient: returning an empty array is sorted but loses every invoice. Compare against an independent sorted reference, check input preservation and array identity, and include empty, singleton, odd, duplicate, reverse, negative, and extreme cases.

headings.title: Compare Measured Operations
body:
```{index} Compare Measured Operations
```

## Compare Measured Operations

```{index} Compare Measured Operations
```

Count actual key comparisons and element writes. The asymptotic expression n log₂ n is a growth model, not an exact comparison count. Different orders can exhaust one merge side earlier. Buffer copy-back contributes writes even after comparisons stop.

For powers of two, this implementation performs exactly 2n log₂ n counted writes: one buffer write and one copy-back write per item per internal level. Clone and buffer allocation are setup and are excluded from that counter, but included in the algorithm’s overall cost. Recursion has 2n−1 calls for nonempty input. Time remains Θ(n log n); these are deterministic operation counts, not timings.

headings.title: Trace the Boundary Rather than Stopping at Equality
body:
```{index} Trace the Boundary Rather than Stopping at Equality
```

## Trace the Boundary Rather than Stopping at Equality
Chapter 16's any-match binary search can establish that a target exists. A report requiring every duplicate needs two boundaries. With sorted values 2,4,4,4,7 and target four, lower bound is the first value at least four; upper bound is the first value greater than four. Their half-open interval includes all three fours.

Maintain a candidate boundary interval [low,high], represented by the loop's half-open search range [low,high). High begins at Length; a result equal to Length is legal even though it is not a valid element index. Each comparison at mid removes a region whose relation to the target is already known.

| Search | low | high | mid/value | Update |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| Lower | 0 | 5 | 2 / 4 | high=2; an earlier equal may exist |
| Lower | 0 | 2 | 1 / 4 | high=1 |
| Lower | 0 | 1 | 0 / 2 | low=1; 2 is strictly below target |
| Upper | 0 | 5 | 2 / 4 | low=3; equality belongs before upper bound |
| Upper | 3 | 5 | 4 / 7 | high=4 |
| Upper | 3 | 4 | 3 / 4 | low=4 |

Both loops stop when low equals high. Equality moves high in the lower search, but moves low past mid in the upper search. The next cell makes that single policy difference explicit; using the same equality action for both endpoints would lose the duplicate range.
For five and nine, the empty intervals represent no matches. Do not read values[first] until first is in range and the result contract requires that access. Merely finding a valid insertion boundary does not establish equality.

Guided task: trace both searches for an empty array and then for 4,4,4 with target four. Explain why an all-equal input is a strong test of the comparison at equality. Then attach invoice IDs to the equal amounts and enumerate every ID in [first,after), preserving the distinction between sorted positions and original arrival positions.

```{dropdown} Check the boundary cases
Both endpoints of an empty array are zero without any element read. For three fours, lower is zero and upper is three, so every position belongs to the match interval. Stopping at the first equal midpoint would not establish either required boundary.
```

The focused loop counts neither timing nor comparer calls. The retained implementations below add explicit policies, instrumentation and assignment variations; compare them under the same contract before making workload recommendations.

headings.title: Duplicates Turn One Position into an Interval
body:
```{index} Duplicates Turn One Position into an Interval
```

## Duplicates Turn One Position into an Interval

A sorted array [2, 4, 4, 4, 7] contains three occurrences of four. An any-match search can return position one, two or three. An invoice report that needs every matching amount needs the whole interval, not a fortunate midpoint result.

Define lower bound as the first position whose value is at least the target, and upper bound as the first position whose value is greater than it. For target four, those positions are one and four, so the matching half-open interval is [1,4), with length three. For missing target five, both bounds are four; the empty interval represents no matches. A bound can equal Length, which is a boundary position rather than a valid element index.

| Target | Lower bound | Upper bound | Matching count |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | 4 | 3 |
| 5 | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| 9 | 5 | 5 | 0 |

The two algorithms differ at equality. Lower-bound search must keep the possibility of an earlier equal value; upper-bound search must move beyond all equal values. Copying one comparison into both versions can silently return a single endpoint twice. Trace an all-equal array and targets just below/above it to expose that mistake.

Ordering and equality policies must match the report's meaning. If invoices are sorted by amount, equal amounts are not necessarily the same invoice identity. If a search uses a different string comparer from sorting, the eliminated-region argument may fail. The returned interval identifies positions in this ordered representation, not original arrival positions unless that information is stored separately.

Guided task: manually find both bounds for target four in the example, then replace the three fours with labeled invoices. List the report IDs that should be returned and explain why a single any-match result is insufficient. Finally, account for preparing the sorted snapshot when comparing a batch of these queries with repeated scans.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
First-match linear search, iterative binary search, missing-target traces, and library return values are taught in {doc}`Chapter 16 <../16_searching_sorting/1601_searching>`. This optional extension studies equality policies, duplicate boundaries, and repeated-query workloads.

## Equality and Ordering Policies

```{index} Equality and Ordering Policies
```

Choose a supplier-name policy explicitly. Ordinal equality is case-sensitive; ordinal case-insensitive equality can treat names with different case as one key. Use an ordering compatible with that equivalence when sorting for binary search. String comparisons need not be constant-time in character length.

Comparison policy is part of the contract, not an incidental culture setting. For records, search the intended key; equality of whole records may be a different business rule. Binary searches below count calls to a three-way comparer, not each primitive relational operation inside that comparer.

headings.title: Lower and Upper Bounds for Duplicates
body:
```{index} Lower and Upper Bounds for Duplicates
```

## Lower and Upper Bounds for Duplicates

```{index} Lower and Upper Bounds for Duplicates
```

A lower bound is the first position with value ≥ target; an upper bound is the first position with value > target. Both can equal n. Lower-bound invariants: every index below low is < target, and every index at or above high is ≥ target. At low=high, that boundary is established. Upper bound replaces those relations with ≤ and >. Equality must keep searching rather than return early.

Equal records occupy [lower,upper), so upper−lower counts occurrences and lower identifies the first sorted-order match. Two boundary searches cost Θ(log n) worst-case probes; enumerating k matching records adds Θ(k) output work. The original arrival position cannot be recovered from a sorted amount-only array: retain record IDs or original indexes.

headings.title: Compare the Invariant That Each Sort Maintains
body:
```{index} Compare the Invariant That Each Sort Maintains
```

## Compare the Invariant That Each Sort Maintains

Selection sort, insertion sort and bubble sort can all order the same small invoice array, but they establish progress differently. Selection chooses the minimum from the unprocessed suffix and fixes one output position. Insertion preserves a sorted processed prefix while placing its next item. Bubble passes adjacent values so that one extreme settles at the remaining boundary. Trace that progress claim rather than memorizing three loops as unrelated syntax.

| Algorithm | Established region after progress | What a trace should show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Selection | Prefix contains the smallest required values | Minimum search and placement |
| Insertion | Processed prefix is ordered | Saved item, shifts and insertion |
| Bubble | Boundary extreme is settled | Adjacent comparisons and last relevant exchange |

Operation counts depend on which operation is measured. Swapping two elements is not the same event as shifting one value, and comparing loop bounds is not an element-comparer call. A comparison plot that counts swaps for one algorithm and assignments for another does not compare the same unit.

Stability is visible only when equal keys belong to distinguishable records. Strict-shift insertion can preserve tie order, while an ordinary nonadjacent selection swap can move an equal-key record past another. Check labeled IDs as well as sorted amounts. Sorting 2, 2 alone cannot show which occurrence changed position.

Guided prediction: use three labeled records with totals 2-A, 2-B, 1-C. Trace a conventional selection swap into the first position and inspect the final relative order of A and B. Then trace strict-shift insertion. Explain why both arrays can satisfy numeric ordering while only one preserves the original tie order.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
Sorting produces an ordered permutation of the input. The algorithms here mutate an array in place. Their counted key comparisons exclude loop-bound checks; swaps and insertion shifts are reported separately. All methods use the same explicit comparer.

headings.title: Swap and Preservation
body:
```{index} Swap and Preservation
```

## Swap and Preservation

```{index} Swap and Preservation
```

A swap exchanges two positions without losing a value. A temporary variable or tuple assignment preserves both originals; assigning values[a]=values[b] and then values[b]=values[a] would duplicate one value. Swapping a position with itself is harmless but adds unnecessary work.

The elementary sorts use Θ(1) auxiliary state beyond the input. A comparison policy must be consistent; compare integer keys with CompareTo rather than subtracting them, which can overflow. An in-place routine changes the supplied array, so clone it when preserving arrival order matters.

headings.title: Selection Sort and Its Prefix Invariant
body:
```{index} Selection Sort and Its Prefix Invariant
```

## Selection Sort and Its Prefix Invariant

```{index} Selection Sort and Its Prefix Invariant
```

At the start of pass s, [0,s) contains the smallest s input occurrences in sorted order. Scan [s,n), retain the smallest index, then swap it into s. The inner-loop invariant tracks the smallest value in the scanned suffix prefix.

The next chosen minimum extends the sorted prefix and leaves its elements no larger than the remaining suffix. Swaps preserve occurrences. There are exactly (n−1)+(n−2)+…+1=n(n−1)/2 key comparisons and at most n−1 actual swaps. Best and worst time are Θ(n²) for growing n, including sorted input. The shown implementation skips self-swaps. A long counter prevents count overflow on moderate large n.

headings.title: Insertion Sort, Shifts, and Nearly Sorted Data
body:
```{index} Insertion Sort, Shifts, and Nearly Sorted Data
```

## Insertion Sort, Shifts, and Nearly Sorted Data

```{index} Insertion Sort, Shifts, and Nearly Sorted Data
```

Before pass i, [0,i) is sorted. Save the current item, shift strictly greater predecessors right, and insert the saved item in the gap. During shifting the saved value is outside the array; include it when reasoning about occurrence preservation.

Equal keys are not shifted, preserving their arrival order. The sorted best case takes n−1 key comparisons and zero shifts; reverse-distinct input takes n(n−1)/2 comparisons and shifts. More precisely, shifts equal the number of inversions: pairs i<j whose earlier key is greater. With I inversions, this insertion implementation takes Θ(n+I) work for n≥1, which explains nearly sorted behavior rather than merely calling it fast.

headings.title: Bubble Sort and a Settled Suffix
body:
```{index} Bubble Sort and a Settled Suffix
```

## Bubble Sort and a Settled Suffix

```{index} Bubble Sort and a Settled Suffix
```

Each left-to-right pass moves the largest remaining item to the current end. The suffix beyond end is already sorted and in final positions; shorten the next pass. If a pass makes no swaps, the remaining prefix has no adjacent inversions and is sorted.

Strictly out-of-order swaps make this bubble variant stable. The no-swap exit gives Θ(n) best-case time on sorted inputs; the shrinking-end reverse case has n(n−1)/2 comparisons and swaps, hence Θ(n²). Empty/singleton arrays need no passes. These claims apply to this variant, not to a fixed-pass or full-width bubble implementation.

headings.title: Stability Is Visible on Records
body:
```{index} Stability Is Visible on Records
```

## Stability Is Visible on Records

```{index} Stability Is Visible on Records
```

Selection sort’s long-distance swap can reverse equal keys even though the minimum scan uses a strict comparison. Insertion and bubble preserve ties in their shown forms. Observe IDs as well as amounts.

Selecting C and swapping it with A gives C,B,A: the two 200-value invoices reverse. Stable output is C,A,B. Stability describes equal comparison keys, not equality of complete records. Do not infer stable behavior from one lucky run of an algorithm without that guarantee.
Library sorting, mutation, and stable report ordering are taught in {doc}`Chapter 14 <../16_searching_sorting/1601_searching>`. Use those contracts when comparing these optional implementations.

Select by contract and workload: insertion can suit tiny or nearly sorted teaching inputs, but quadratic sorts scale poorly in the worst case. Chapter 22’s stable merge sort has Θ(n log n) time and Θ(n) auxiliary storage. The library algorithms are the usual starting point for application code; custom comparisons still require a consistent order. Mutable records are not deep-cloned by making an array copy.

headings.title: Make Competing Implementations Answer the Same Question
body:
```{index} Make Competing Implementations Answer the Same Question
```

## Make Competing Implementations Answer the Same Question

An any-match binary search and a scan returning every matching invoice do not perform equivalent tasks. The former may stop after one occurrence; the latter must produce an entire result group. Before measuring, write a shared result contract and compare answers against independent expected results. Performance evidence about the wrong answer is irrelevant to the requested report.

Use four input shapes for sorting: already ordered, reverse ordered, all equal, and mixed with repeated keys. Keep the same original input for each algorithm by making independent outer copies before the runs. Running one algorithm after another on the same mutated array can give the second an easier already sorted problem. That is a workload change, not evidence that it is intrinsically faster.

| Measurement choice | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Element comparisons | Measures ordering queries under a shared comparer |
| Moves or writes | Exposes shifts and copying separately from comparisons |
| Preparation | Sorting/copying may precede the first search |
| Result production | Returning all duplicates can dominate one lookup |
| Validation | Must be equivalent, but should not be silently charged to only one candidate |

A recommendation should name the workload: data size, initial order, updates, query count, required result and storage policy. For an end-of-day immutable report, preparation can be reused across many searches. For frequently changing arrival data, maintenance or snapshot rebuilding belongs in the comparison. A single timing number without these assumptions cannot establish a general cutoff.

Guided recommendation: one customer asks for a single missing ID in an unsorted ten-item list; another asks for a hundred amount-range reports over an unchanged large snapshot. Explain why the same algorithm choice need not fit both. State what additional measurements would change your decision and keep correctness checks separate from the requirement-based argument.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
Use operation counts to support a purchasing report recommendation. Verify equivalent results before comparing costs. Clone input for each in-place sort and state whether counters include preparation or queries.

headings.title: Each Gap Pass Solves an Interleaved Insertion Problem
body: ```{index} Each Gap Pass Solves an Interleaved Insertion Problem ``` ## Each Gap Pass Solves an Interleaved Insertion Problem Shell sort connects to insertion sort by ordering positions separated by a chosen gap. With gap three, positions zero, three, six form one subsequence; positions one, four, seven form another. A pass applies insertion-like work within each subsequence. It does not claim the whole array is already sorted after that pass. As gaps shrink, long-distance disorder can be reduced before the final gap-one insertion pass. That final pass is necessary for ordinary total ordering; being ordered at gap three alone does not compare adjacent positions from different subsequences. A gap schedule must eventually reach one under the implementation's contract. Different schedules change which distances are addressed and how much work is performed. The retained powers-of-two, 3h+1 and 2h+1 variants are distinct experiments, not interchangeable labels for one verified complexity theorem. Measure the same input shapes and count the same operations before drawing a conclusion about a family. A successful sort on one array establishes neither a universal cost bound nor a universal best gap schedule. Guided trace: label positions zero through seven and draw the three gap-three subsequences. Then draw the single gap-one sequence. Explain why a swap or shift across a large gap may reduce later local work while still changing the relative order of equal-key records. Shell sort should not be assumed stable simply because its inner pass resembles a stable insertion implementation. For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading] ```{index} Shell Sort and Quicksort ``` This supporting lesson restores the advanced algorithms from the earlier CS1 reference in the current advanced sorting chapter. Read insertion sort and recursion first. It supplements the existing searching, elementary-sort, and workload lessons. These explanations and tasks retain the earlier CS1 teaching material.[^2304_advanced_sorts-restored]

headings.title: Shell Sort
body:
```{index} Shell Sort
```

## Shell Sort

```{index} Shell Sort
```

Shell sort applies insertion sorting to subsequences whose elements are separated by a gap. For gap four, the sequences start at positions zero, one, two, and three, visiting every fourth element. A distant exchange can remove several inversions, moving an out-of-place value toward its destination more quickly than adjacent exchanges alone.

A single gap does not necessarily sort the whole array. Repeat with decreasing gaps, ending at one; the final pass is ordinary insertion sort over the entire array. After a gap-four pass, each gap-four subsequence is sorted, but neighboring values can still be out of order. Trace this distinction before the final pass.

The earlier lesson compared gaps 8, 4, 2, 1 with a sequence based on `h = 3*h + 1`, giving 1, 4, 13, 40, 121, and so on. Generate useful gaps for the actual array length and apply them in reverse order. The maximum gap and recurrence both affect performance; do not infer a universal complexity bound from one timing experiment. The simple halving/power-of-two family can still require quadratic work in the worst case.


## Work the Two-Scan Partition Before Recursing
The conceptual smaller/equal/larger picture describes a goal, but the retained implementation uses two inward scans. It does not return a single final pivot position. Use the exact scan rule to determine the next recursive intervals; otherwise a correct-looking diagram can lead to incorrect code.

Start with 5,2,5,1,8 over inclusive indexes zero through four. The middle **position** is two, so the saved pivot value is five. The left scan stops at a value at least five; the right scan stops at a value at most five. If the scans have not crossed, swap those values and advance both scans, even when the values are equal.

| Step | left | right | Action and array |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Initial scans | 0 | 3 | Right skips 8; stop at 5 and 1 |
| Swap, then advance | 1 | 2 | 1,2,5,5,8 |
| Next scans | 2 | 2 | Left skips 2; both stop at the middle 5 |
| Self-swap, then advance | 3 | 1 | Array unchanged; scans cross |
| Recur | [0,1] | [3,4] | These are inclusive subranges, not pivot positions |

Partitioning has established separation, not a completely sorted recursive region in general. Here the displayed values happen already to be sorted after the partition. That coincidence does not eliminate the recursive work required by the general algorithm.
The fixed pivot value is copied before any swaps; it is not reread through a position that may now contain another value. Advancing both indexes after a swap guarantees progress when both stopped on equal values. The small method assumes a valid requested subrange; empty and singleton ranges return immediately. The retained comparison example includes Shell sort as well and remains available below.

Guided task: trace an all-equal three-element range. Fill left/right before and after each swap, then write the recursive intervals. As a separate variation, put sentinel values outside an interior requested range and predict which elements must remain unchanged.

```{dropdown} Check progress and the subrange contract
For three equal values, swap positions zero and two, then the middle with itself; left becomes two and right zero. Neither recursive interval has more than one element. For subrange sorting, the values outside the requested low/high endpoints are not part of any swap or recursive range and must remain unchanged. Verify that independently, rather than checking only global sortedness.
```

For independent work, preserve every original value and its multiplicity, not merely nondecreasing output. Equal-key records may exchange places, so this QuickSort is not a stable reporting sort. Pivot/input assumptions determine expected performance; the middle index does not guarantee a median value or balanced subproblems.

headings.title: Partition Establishes a Boundary, Not a Fully Sorted Array
body:
```{index} Partition Establishes a Boundary, Not a Fully Sorted Array
```

## Partition Establishes a Boundary, Not a Fully Sorted Array

Quicksort separates data according to a pivot policy and recursively orders the resulting regions. The partition contract must say where smaller, equal and larger values may appear and which indexes are returned. Different valid partition algorithms return different kinds of boundaries. Applying one algorithm's recursive endpoints to another partition result can skip items or recurse forever.

For values 6, 2, 5, 1, 4 with pivot value four, a conceptual partition separates values below four (2 and 1), equal to four, and above four (6 and 5). Their internal order need not yet be sorted. Recursion handles the smaller regions. This conceptual three-way picture explains the goal; the preserved implementation's actual partition form determines its exact index updates.

| Stage | What is established | What remains to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before partition | Pivot/comparison policy is known | Classify values |
| After partition | Values lie in allowed regions | Order each nontrivial recursive region |
| After recursive returns | Regions are ordered | Combine their boundary facts |

A progress argument must cover equal values as well as unequal ones. If a partition never advances on equality, an all-equal input can stall. If a recursive call receives the original full interval again, finding a plausible pivot did not guarantee termination. Trace empty, singleton, duplicate-heavy, already ordered and reverse-ordered cases.

Choosing pivots changes work distributions. Repeated highly unbalanced splits can yield quadratic work and linear recursive depth. A claim of expected good behavior needs assumptions about pivot selection or input distribution. It is not justified by one random-looking demonstration. An in-place partition can also reorder equal-key records, so ordinary quicksort is not automatically a stable report sort.

Guided exercise: take the exact partition rule in the example and annotate its scanned/unknown regions after each update. Record the returned boundary and write the two next recursive intervals before executing them. Check that together they cover all values requiring further work and that each nontrivial recursive interval is smaller. Then compare output occurrence counts with the original array; correct ordering alone does not prove nothing was lost.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Quicksort
body:
```{index} Quicksort
```

## Quicksort

```{index} Quicksort
```

Quicksort, also called partition sort, chooses a pivot and rearranges one subrange around it. The left scan skips values smaller than the pivot; the right scan skips larger values. When the scans stop before crossing, exchange the two values and advance both positions. Advancing after a swap is essential when values equal the pivot.

The partition loop maintains these statements: everything before the left scan is at most the pivot, and everything after the right scan is at least the pivot. The unclassified interval shrinks. After the scans cross, recursively sort the remaining left and right subranges. They are not individually sorted by partitioning, but no value in the left group belongs after a value in the right group.

The same method solves smaller ranges. Empty and one-element ranges are base cases. Quicksort averages `O(n log n)` comparisons under suitable pivot/input assumptions, but repeated unbalanced partitions can require `O(n^2)` work and deep recursion. Choosing the middle **position** does not guarantee choosing the median **value**. This implementation is not stable and uses recursive stack space.

headings.title: Identify the Objective That Makes the Exchange Work
body: ```{index} Identify the Objective That Makes the Exchange Work ``` ## Identify the Objective That Makes the Exchange Work Meeting scheduling can ask for the largest number of compatible meetings or for the highest total meeting value. Those are different optimization problems. Earliest finishing time supports the first objective under the half-open interval model; it does not automatically maximize a sum of business values. Suppose meetings are A=[0,2), B=[2,4), and C=[0,4). Choosing A then B yields two meetings, whereas choosing C yields one. Touching endpoints are compatible because the first interval excludes its finishing point. If the business instead requires a cleanup gap, feasibility changes and must be reflected in both selection and tests. The exchange proof begins with an optimal count schedule and compares its first meeting with the earliest-finishing eligible one. Replacing that first meeting by one that finishes no later leaves at least as much room for the remaining meetings. The count is preserved, so some optimum begins with the greedy choice. Repeat the argument for the remaining compatible problem. The proof depends on the objective and feasibility relation, not on the persuasive phrase make the best local choice. | Changed requirement | What must be reconsidered? | | --- | --- | | Maximize number of meetings | The count exchange argument applies under the stated interval assumptions | | Maximize meeting value | An early low-value meeting may block a more valuable one | | Require cleanup time | Compatibility must include the gap | | Allow zero-duration entries | Define their eligibility and ordering explicitly | Guided counterexample: give C value 100 and A and B value one each. The count-optimal schedule has value two, while C alone has value 100. Explain why this disproves reuse of the count rule for the value objective without contradicting its original correctness proof. Chapter 25 develops optimization states when a local exchange rule is not sufficient. For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading] ```{index} Greedy Choice and Correctness ``` A greedy algorithm chooses locally and commits. Specify the objective, feasible choices, tie policy, and reason a choice can belong to an optimum. Feasibility alone is insufficient.

headings.title: Exchange the First Choice
body:

## Exchange the First Choice

```{index} Exchange the First Choice
```

Let g be the globally earliest-finishing available meeting. Take an optimal schedule with first meeting o. Since end(g)≤end(o), replace o with g. Every later meeting starts at or after end(o), hence also at or after end(g); feasibility and count are unchanged. Thus some optimal schedule begins with g. Apply the same argument to the remaining compatible meetings.

The positive-duration assumption ensures g cannot also be a later meeting in the original schedule. After the exchange, the residual problem has the same shape. Induction on the number of available meetings establishes optimal count, rather than merely saying that g leaves room. The loop invariant can be strengthened: the accepted prefix can be extended to an optimal solution for the original instance.

headings.title: Keep Connectivity State Separate from the Cable Budget
body:
```{index} Keep Connectivity State Separate from the Cable Budget
```

## Keep Connectivity State Separate from the Cable Budget
A minimum spanning forest connects every pair of vertices that can be connected by the input, without paying for unnecessary cycles. This is different from a shortest route from one office. Kruskal processes edges by nondecreasing cost, but “choose cheap edges” is incomplete: an edge is accepted only if its endpoints are in different current components.

Union-find records those components. Each vertex starts as its own parent. `Find(v)` follows parent links to a root; equal roots mean already connected. `Union(a,b)` links the roots of two different components. Parent links here are bookkeeping, not the chosen cable edges. A parent link can point to an office with which there is no direct cable.

The small implementation below omits path compression so each parent change is easy to trace. Union by size attaches the smaller root's tree under the larger root. Sizes are meaningful at roots. The complete retained implementation adds path halving and graph validation after this walkthrough.
The edge input is already sorted in this teaching cell; a general Kruskal implementation must sort arbitrary input first. A connects to B at cost one, then B connects to C at cost two. The cost-five edge connects vertices with the same root and is rejected. Isolated D remains a separate component rather than receiving a fictional cable.

| Edge | Roots before decision | Decision | Component sets afterward | Budget |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| A-B, 1 | A and B | Accept | {A,B}, {C}, {D} | 1 |
| B-C, 2 | A and C | Accept | {A,B,C}, {D} | 3 |
| A-C, 5 | A and A | Reject cycle | {A,B,C}, {D} | 3 |

After the second row, parent[C] is A even though the accepted edge was B-C. Find returns a component representative, not a route. To print the chosen network, retain accepted graph edges separately. Path compression changes parent links to speed future finds without changing connectivity or the cable budget.

Acyclicity establishes feasibility but not minimum cost. For a current component, consider the cut separating it from the rest of its input-connected component. A cheapest available crossing edge is safe. If an optimum omits that edge, add it to the optimum: the resulting cycle contains another crossing edge. Replacing that edge by the chosen edge does not raise cost. Thus the accepted choices can remain part of an optimum. Apply this reasoning within each input component when the graph is disconnected.

headings.title: Connect Every Site Without Paying for a Cycle
body: ```{index} Connect Every Site Without Paying for a Cycle ``` ## Connect Every Site Without Paying for a Cycle A facilities team wants cable connecting all sites at minimum total cable cost. This objective concerns the sum of selected edge costs, not the travel distance from headquarters. Start with three undirected links: A-B costs 2, B-C costs 2, and A-C costs 3. Selecting the two cost-2 links connects all three sites for four. Adding A-C would introduce a cycle and increase cost without connecting a new component. Kruskal processes edges in nondecreasing weight. It accepts an edge when its endpoints are currently in different components. A disjoint-set structure records those components. Union does not mean join two vertex labels alphabetically; it combines the connectivity groups induced by already accepted edges. | Candidate | Before | Decision | After | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A-B, 2 | A / B / C | Accept | AB / C | | B-C, 2 | AB / C | Accept | ABC | | A-C, 3 | ABC | Reject cycle | ABC | Acyclicity proves that selected edges form a forest, but not that it has minimum possible cost. The safe-choice argument uses a cut separating a current component from the rest. A cheapest crossing edge can replace an appropriate crossing edge in an optimal solution without making that solution more expensive. That exchange connects the local greedy choice to a global optimum. It differs from simply observing that the next edge is inexpensive. Disconnected input has no spanning tree of all declared vertices. The meaningful extension is a minimum spanning forest, including isolated vertices in the component count. Negative edge weights do not break Kruskal's ordering/exchange reasoning, although the graph and edge contract must remain explicit. Equal weights can allow several correct forests; verify validity and optimum cost instead of requiring one exact edge list. Guided case: add isolated D. Does the algorithm need an invented high-cost edge to connect D? No, if the contract promises a forest it reports another component. Now change A-C to cost one. Trace the accepted edges again and derive the new total before running the preserved implementation. Check edge count V minus component count, connectivity, and cost as different obligations. For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading] ```{index} Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths ``` Facilities planning asks two different questions: which cables connect all offices at minimum total cost, and which routes minimize travel from HQ? Both use weights, but their objectives and graph models differ.


## Improve Tentative Routes Before Declaring Them Final

Routing asks the least cost from one source to each reachable destination. A tentative distance represents the best discovered route so far. Relaxing arc u-to-v compares the existing tentative value for v with distance[u] plus the arc cost. Replace it only when the new route is strictly better, and record u as predecessor.

Use directed arcs A-to-B cost 10, A-to-C cost 1, and C-to-B cost 1. Starting at A, B is first discovered at cost ten. Processing C improves B to cost two. A priority-queue entry for the old ten-cost B may still exist, so the implementation must distinguish current best distance from stale queued proposals.

| Freshly processed vertex | Best A | Best B | Best C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A at 0 | 0 | 10 | 1 |
| C at 1 | 0 | 2 | 1 |
| B at 2 | 0 | 2 | 1 |

With nonnegative arc weights, a fresh minimum tentative distance can be settled: an undiscovered cheaper route would need to pass through a frontier prefix no more expensive than that route, contradicting selection of the minimum. A negative later edge breaks this argument. Do not generalize from one negative-edge example that happens to return the right result.

When using duplicate queue entries, compare a removed entry's priority with the authoritative best distance. Skip stale entries rather than rescanning their neighbors as if the old route were current. Strict improvement avoids producing repeated equal-distance updates around zero-weight cycles. Tie ordering may choose different equally short predecessor paths without changing shortest distances.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

A known unreachable destination has no such path, while the source has a one-vertex zero-cost path to itself. ## Dijkstra with Nonnegative Directed Arcs

```{index} Dijkstra with Nonnegative Directed Arcs
```

Dijkstra minimizes path cost from one known source. Directed arcs here specify allowed travel direction; supply both directions when modeling two-way roads. Validate every arc, including unreachable ones, before running: weights must be nonnegative, endpoints known, and loops excluded by this teaching interface. Zero weights are valid. Nullable long distances represent infinity without confusing a valid int.MaxValue path with absence.

Relaxation replaces a tentative distance only on strict improvement. Each finite tentative distance corresponds to a discovered source route. A fresh minimum-priority pop has the final shortest distance: any hypothetical shorter route would first leave the already settled set with a prefix no longer than that route; nonnegative remaining weights cannot make a later prefix cheaper. Zero weights preserve the argument. Negative edges invalidate this reasoning, even if a particular example happens to produce correct output.

## Stale Queue Entries and Qualified Costs

```{index} Stale Queue Entries and Qualified Costs
```

Improving a distance enqueues a new entry; the old entry remains in the library queue. Compare its stored priority with the current best distance and skip stale entries. Strict improvement also avoids endless equal-distance updates around zero-weight cycles.

B first enters the queue at ten, then improves to two. Its old ten-priority entry is skipped. Each reachable adjacency list is scanned on its fresh pop; at most E successful relaxations enqueue entries. This lazy-duplicate implementation can hold O(E) queue entries and has O(V+E log(E+1)) time for nontrivial graphs, plus O(V+E) storage. An indexed decrease-key implementation has different queue/storage bounds. Equal priorities need not have stable library ordering; distances are correct and the chosen shortest predecessor route may vary on ties.

```{index} Reconstruct Only Reachable Routes
```

A predecessor records the previous vertex on a strict improving route. Follow predecessors backward and reverse with a stack. Return an empty path for a known unreachable vertex, a singleton for the source, and reject an unknown target. Distance/predecessor maps are read-only views; do not fabricate a one-vertex route for an unreachable destination.

Every returned route must begin at the source, end at its target, use directed arcs, and sum to the reported distance. Route reconstruction costs O(path length). Long accumulation avoids int overflow; checked arithmetic rejects overflow rather than silently wrapping. With int weights and finite simple paths in a practical array-sized graph, long provides ample range; its policy is still explicit.
```{index} Shortest Paths and String Matching ```

Algorithm assumptions determine what an answer means. BFS minimizes hops, Dijkstra minimizes nonnegative total weights, and a string matcher needs a precise equality and occurrence policy. Reusing justified information can eliminate repeated work without changing the contract.

Write down the objective, units, direction, required connectivity, and weight assumptions. Scheduling maximizes compatible count; MST minimizes network total; Dijkstra minimizes route cost from a source. Preserve the feasibility and optimality arguments separately.

A facilities decision can need all three models, but their numeric costs are not interchangeable. Cable cost can be currency, road cost travel time, and meeting objective a count. More realistic constraints may require a different algorithm entirely.

headings.title: Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule
body:
```{index} Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule
```

## Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule
A repeated subproblem is a question with the same complete state, not just a similarly named function call. With F(0)=0, F(1)=1 and F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2), the integer n fully identifies the question. Fix that definition before sharing results. Changing the base values creates a different sequence and invalidates an old cache.

For F(4), the naive call tree asks for F(3) and F(2). F(3) asks for F(2) and F(1), so F(2) is expanded twice. Termination is already guaranteed by decreasing n; the problem is repeated work.

```text
F(4)
  F(3)
    F(2)
      F(1)
      F(0)
    F(1)
  F(2)
    F(1)
    F(0)
```

There are nine invocations including base cases. Only four calls are simultaneously active on the deepest path. A cache can remove repeated expansion without turning the recursion into constant-depth execution.
The cell intentionally calls only a fixed valid argument. The complete APIs below retain domain and resource limits. Base cases are returned directly rather than stored; therefore computed counts non-base cache misses, not every call. Cache F(2) only after both dependencies return, otherwise another call could read an incomplete result.

| Event during F(4) | Completed cache afterward | Significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finish F(2) within F(3) | 2→1 | First non-base state completed |
| Finish F(3) | 2→1, 3→2 | Its dependencies were available |
| Request F(2) from F(4) | Unchanged | Cache hit avoids another expansion |
| Finish F(4) | 2→1, 3→2, 4→3 | Requested result is now complete |

For n≥2, there are n-1 distinct non-base states. Each is expanded once and makes two recursive calls, so total invocations are the initial call plus twice the number of expansions: 2n-1. For n=4 this is seven. Exact counts depend on this implementation's decision not to cache base cases; the linear growth claim does not depend on adopting this exact convention.

headings.title: Fill the Same States Without Recursive Calls
body:
```{index} Fill the Same States Without Recursive Calls
```

## Fill the Same States Without Recursive Calls
Tabulation stores the same mathematical answers but selects an order explicitly. For increasing i, both i-1 and i-2 already exist. Initialization supplies F(0) and F(1); it is not an incidental convenience. The small cell below makes every completed table entry visible.
Guided task: append the row for i=5, naming the two source entries and the result. Then describe why filling from n down to two would read entries that are still only default zero. Change n to zero and check why the guard on initialization of entry one is necessary.

```{dropdown} Check the dependency order
F(5)=F(4)+F(3)=3+2=5. Descending fill reaches F(5) before its non-base predecessors have been computed, so default zeros are not valid answers. When n is zero, the array contains only entry zero; writing entry one would be outside it.
```

For transfer, keep the recurrence but choose F(0)=2 and F(1)=1. Derive the first six values before adapting both strategies, and explain why the old cache must not be reused. The chapter homework uses another recurrence; first identify its states, base cases, dependency order and requested output. Rolling storage is appropriate when only the final value is needed, while a full table supports inspection of all earlier entries.

headings.title: Save Answers to Repeated Questions, Not Arbitrary Intermediate State
body:
```{index} Save Answers to Repeated Questions, Not Arbitrary Intermediate State
```

## Save Answers to Repeated Questions, Not Arbitrary Intermediate State

Fibonacci gives a small example where termination alone does not prevent repeated work. Computing F(5) asks for F(4) and F(3); computing F(4) asks for F(3) again. A cache can retain the completed answer for a numeric argument and reuse it when that same subproblem returns. The key is sufficient because the recurrence and base cases are fixed for this computation.

Memoization starts from the requested state and recursively solves missing dependencies. Tabulation chooses an order in which needed dependencies have already been solved. For Fibonacci, increasing argument order works because F(i) depends on smaller arguments. These are two execution strategies for a stated dependency structure, not two unrelated tricks for making code faster.

| i | F(i) | Dependencies already available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | Base case |
| 1 | 1 | Base case |
| 2 | 1 | F(1), F(0) |
| 3 | 2 | F(2), F(1) |
| 4 | 3 | F(3), F(2) |
| 5 | 5 | F(4), F(3) |

The table invariant is that every earlier stored entry has its correct specified value before the next entry is computed. Storing a result before all dependencies have been completed can cache a partial value as if it were final. Reusing one global cache across requests with different policies can likewise mix different problems under the same key.

Rolling storage keeps only the two predecessor values when only the final Fibonacci result is required. It cannot simultaneously promise to return all earlier table entries without retaining or recomputing them. This is a tradeoff between requested output and retained state. Memoization also does not eliminate recursive stack depth simply because repeated arithmetic has been removed.

Guided exercise: derive F(6) from the table, then sketch which repeated calls a naive recursion would make. Label cache misses and cache hits separately from active call frames. Finally, change the base values and explain why a cache produced under the previous definition cannot be reused without identifying which definition its keys belong to.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Memoization and Tabulation


## Memoization and Tabulation

A state identifies one smaller problem. A transition relates it to other states. Define the state, base cases, legal inputs, dependency order, and returned result before choosing a cache or table. Counting problems such as Fibonacci need a decomposition; minimum-coin optimization additionally needs optimal substructure.

headings.title: Repeated Work Is Visible
body:
```{index} Repeated Work Is Visible
```

## Repeated Work Is Visible

```{index} Repeated Work Is Visible
```

F(0)=0, F(1)=1, and F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) for n≥2. The argument strictly decreases, but the recursion tree repeats arguments. Count every invocation, including base cases; computed counts only non-base expansions. Compare the same n, not unrelated examples.

The naive call recurrence is C(0)=C(1)=1 and C(n)=1+C(n−1)+C(n−2); C(n)=2F(n+1)−1. Calls are exponential in n while active stack depth is Θ(n). This teaching implementation caps naive n at 25 to keep browser runs short; all Fibonacci APIs otherwise accept 0..92, the range that fits signed long. Invalid n is rejected before recursion.

headings.title: Memoization Stores Complete States
body:
```{index} Memoization Stores Complete States
```

## Memoization Stores Complete States

```{index} Memoization Stores Complete States
```

The cache key n fully identifies F(n) because the recurrence and base cases are fixed. Every cached value is a completed correct result. Compute a missing state recursively, then store it. Local cache ownership avoids mixing unrelated requests or caller-supplied incorrect entries.

For n≥2 there are n−1 distinct non-base states, 2n−1 calls including cache hits, and max(0,n−3) hits. Base results are not cached here. Expected constant-time dictionary lookup gives Θ(n) time, Θ(n) cache storage, and Θ(n) stack space. These are distinct costs. A fresh invocation starts a fresh cache; memoization does not make the recursive stack disappear. Induction proves correctness: bases are correct, recursive dependencies are smaller, and their sum is F(n).

headings.title: Tabulation Follows Dependency Order
body:
```{index} Tabulation Follows Dependency Order
```

## Tabulation Follows Dependency Order

```{index} Tabulation Follows Dependency Order
```

The invariant before iteration i is that entries 0..i−1 equal their specified Fibonacci values. Writing table[i] from i−1 and i−2 preserves it. Initialize entry one only when it exists; zero must work.

A full table costs Θ(n) time and Θ(n) storage without recursion. Rolling state keeps only the two needed predecessors, giving Θ(n) time and Θ(1) auxiliary storage when only the final value is requested. It cannot provide every historical table entry. Checked addition protects arithmetic; validating 0..92 also avoids computing an unnecessary F(93) on the final rolling update.


headings.title: Derive Every Entry of a Small Purchasing Plan
body:
```{index} Derive Every Entry of a Small Purchasing Plan
```

## Derive Every Entry of a Small Purchasing Plan
A purchaser can use unlimited packs containing one, three or four items and needs exactly six items. Largest-first gives 4+1+1, but 3+3 uses fewer packs. Dynamic programming improves the choice by comparing every legal final pack, not by repeatedly taking the largest.

Let best[a] be the minimum number of packs totaling a. Best[0]=0 represents the valid empty purchase. For each positive a, consider a final pack c with c≤a. Only reachable best[a-c] entries can supply candidates; their count plus one is a possible answer. Store both the lowest count and the chosen last pack. Null means unreachable, not zero packs.

| Amount a | Reachable candidates using last pack 1, 3, 4 | best[a] | Chosen last pack |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | Base case | 0 | None |
| 1 | best[0]+1=1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | best[1]+1=2 | 2 | 1 |
| 3 | best[2]+1=3; best[0]+1=1 | 1 | 3 |
| 4 | best[3]+1=2; best[1]+1=2; best[0]+1=1 | 1 | 4 |
| 5 | best[4]+1=2; best[2]+1=3; best[1]+1=2 | 2 | 1 |
| 6 | best[5]+1=3; best[3]+1=2; best[2]+1=3 | 2 | 3 |

The tie at amount five preserves last pack one when denominations are visited in ascending order and updates require a strict improvement. This is a deterministic witness policy; it does not change the optimum count. The following focused code uses a fixed valid input to expose the table updates. The retained full API performs validation and resource-bound checks.
Read the recurrence in the code: amount-pack selects the smaller state; previous+1 accounts for the final pack; the comparison retains the best candidate. A positive pack makes the dependency strictly smaller, so increasing amounts are a valid evaluation order. Zero or negative denominations would invalidate this reasoning and are rejected by the full API.

Reconstruction follows decisions backwards, not all table entries in descending order. For six, last[6]=3, so append three and continue with remaining three. Last[3]=3 reaches remaining zero. The two chosen packs sum to six and their count equals best[6]. A valid plan proves feasibility; the recurrence's comparison of all final choices establishes optimality.

headings.title: Guide an Unreachable Entry and Check Its Witness
body:
```{index} Guide an Unreachable Entry and Check Its Witness
```

## Guide an Unreachable Entry and Check Its Witness
Remove denomination one and ask for five using only three and four. Fill best[0] through best[5] before running a program. Do not initialize all counts to zero: that would make impossible remainders appear reachable.

```{dropdown} Check the smaller table
The counts are 0, null, null, 1, 1, null. Five is unreachable because neither remainder two nor remainder one is reachable. No reconstruction should start from five. Target zero is different: its count is zero and its valid plan is empty.
```

Now compare two records each worth three with unlimited denomination three. A target of nine is reachable with unlimited packs, but not from two one-use records. Amount alone is sufficient only when the available choices are unchanged after each use. The next backtracking lesson includes the position/inventory information needed for one-use choices.

Before the independent purchasing assignments, validate a candidate witness yourself: every pack is allowed, all values are positive, their total is the target, and their count matches the reported optimum. Then use a small independent reference to check the optimum. A program that prints two without a matching feasible witness has not completed the result contract.

headings.title: Define the State from the Choices That Remain
body:
```{index} Define the State from the Choices That Remain
```

## Define the State from the Choices That Remain

A purchasing team can buy unlimited packs of sizes one, three and four and wants exactly six units using the fewest packs. Greedily taking four first leaves two one-unit packs, for three packs total. Two packs of three use only two packs. The counterexample shows that a locally largest pack is not a generally safe choice for this objective.

Let B(a) be the minimum number of packs for amount a. The base is B(0)=0. To solve a positive amount, consider every permitted last pack c and a reachable predecessor amount a-c. A candidate solution has one more pack than B(a-c). Choose the minimum candidate. This considers the last step of every feasible optimum, rather than guessing which first pack looks largest.

| Amount | Best count for sizes 1,3,4 | One predecessor choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | Empty solution |
| 1 | 1 | 0 plus 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 plus 1 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 plus 3 |
| 4 | 1 | 0 plus 4 |
| 5 | 2 | 1 plus 4, or another optimal tie |
| 6 | 2 | 3 plus 3 |

Optimal substructure supplies the justification: removing the last pack from an optimal solution leaves an optimal solution to the predecessor amount. If a better predecessor existed, appending the same last pack would improve the supposed optimum. Positive pack sizes make predecessor amounts smaller, giving a valid tabulation order and terminating reconstruction.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

body:
```{index} Preserve Enough Information to Explain the Answer
```

## Preserve Enough Information to Explain the Answer

An optimum count is not the same output as an actual purchasing plan. Store a predecessor choice when an amount is improved, then walk backward to zero to reconstruct a witness. Validate that the witness sums to the requested amount and has the reported number of packs. If no predecessor is feasible, represent unreachable distinctly from the valid zero-pack solution at amount zero.

The state depends on inventory assumptions. If each invoice or pack position can be used only once, amount alone does not identify the remaining options. Chapter 25's backtracking lesson uses both a position and remaining target. Reusing an amount-only unlimited-pack recurrence for limited inventory can return an impossible plan.

Guided variation: remove size one and request five from sizes three and four. Explain why zero is not a valid optimum count for this request and why reconstruction must not loop forever through an invented predecessor. Then request zero and distinguish that valid empty solution from the unreachable positive amount. The preserved verification cases check both objective value and witness.

headings.title: Minimum Coins: Model Before Implementation
body:
```{index} Minimum Coins: Model Before Implementation
```

## Minimum Coins: Model Before Implementation

```{index} Minimum Coins: Model Before Implementation
```

A purchasing system uses unlimited packs of sizes 1,3,4. Minimize the number of packs totaling target six. Let B(a) be the minimum count for a; B(0)=0, and B(a)=min(1+B(a−c)) over positive denominations c≤a whose remainder is reachable. If no such predecessor exists, a is unreachable. Removing the last coin from any optimal plan leaves an optimal remainder plan: a better remainder would improve the original plan.

Positive denominations ensure a−c<a, so amounts in increasing order satisfy dependencies and reconstruction strictly decreases remaining amount. Nullable count distinguishes unreachable from a valid zero-coin plan. Duplicate denominations are normalized; ascending denominations and strict improvement make equal-count ties deterministic. Empty denominations can make only zero. Reject zero/negative coins: a zero coin breaks progress and a negative coin changes the state graph. The table invariant is that all smaller amounts have correct optima or correct unreachable markers; considering every possible last coin establishes the next entry.

headings.title: State Size, Numeric Size, and the Requested Result
body:
```{index} State Size, Numeric Size, and the Requested Result
```

## State Size, Numeric Size, and the Requested Result

```{index} State Size, Numeric Size, and the Requested Result
```

With target T and D input denominations, sorting/normalization costs O(D log(D+1)); filling the table costs O(Td) for d distinct denominations, and table storage is O(T). Reconstructing K chosen coins adds O(K) output space and time. This implementation caps T at one million as an explicit allocation policy. These costs depend on the numeric target, not just the number of digits encoding it: the method is pseudo-polynomial.

Memoization can avoid some states reachable from the requested state; tabulation can avoid recursion and simplify dependency order. Neither is universally better. An amount-only coin state is sufficient for unlimited coins. If each pack is available once, remaining inventory matters: amount alone loses essential information. Chapter 25’s subset search uses (position, remaining), which preserves which items are still available. Rolling storage also trades away reconstruction information unless another recovery method is supplied.

headings.title: Undo Exactly the Choice Owned by the Current Call
body:
```{index} Undo Exactly the Choice Owned by the Current Call
```

## Undo Exactly the Choice Owned by the Current Call

Backtracking explores alternatives while preserving enough state to return to a previous decision point. For one-use invoice reconciliation, each position can be included or excluded. A helper at position i with remaining target r represents a particular smaller problem: can some subset of positions i onward total r? Both i and r matter because they describe which choices remain.

For amounts 2, 3 and 5 with target five, one witness is 2 plus 3 and another is 5 alone. Choosing the first invoice changes the remaining target from five to three and advances the position. Excluding it leaves target five but still advances the position. If both branches kept the same position, the program could reuse an invoice whose contract permits only one use.

| Branch from position 0 | Next position | Remaining target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Include amount 2 | 1 | 3 |
| Exclude amount 2 | 1 | 5 |

When building a selected-position list, add the position for the include branch, explore, and remove that same choice when returning to explore an alternative. A saved result must be a snapshot if later mutations would otherwise change it. Assigning a result variable to the mutable working list only creates another reference to the changing list.

Signed amounts require care with pruning. The common shortcut remaining target below zero means impossible is unsafe when later negative adjustments can reduce a sum. Bounds based on the sums of remaining negative and positive amounts provide a justified possible range. Prune only when the requested remaining value lies outside that range. Pruning changes how much is explored; it must not discard a feasible solution.

Caching failed states can avoid revisiting the same impossible suffix/target pair. The cache key must identify the complete state under the fixed input and policy. A call budget is a separate implementation limit: exhausting it means the search did not finish, not that infeasibility has been proved. Preserve this distinction when reporting results to a user.

Guided trace: add a -2 adjustment after a temporarily excessive positive choice. Construct a target for which pruning on a negative remainder would lose a valid witness. Then compare a proven failed state with a stopped-by-budget state. Explain why only the former may safely be reused as evidence of impossibility.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

headings.title: Backtracking and Search Spaces
body:
```{index} Backtracking and Search Spaces
```

## Backtracking and Search Spaces

Backtracking is depth-first search through decisions. An invariant describes the partial choice; a base case records a complete result; undo restores shared state before a sibling branch. Pruning must exclude only impossible branches. Returning a witness allows the caller to check the decision.

headings.title: Choose, Explore, Undo, and Snapshot
body:
```{index} Choose, Explore, Undo, and Snapshot
```

## Choose, Explore, Undo, and Snapshot

```{index} Choose, Explore, Undo, and Snapshot
```

At position i, chosen holds exactly the included positions from 0..i−1. Include i, recurse to i+1, undo, then exclude i. At i=n, snapshot chosen. Positions distinguish equal-valued business records; choosing position zero twice is not allowed.

The include/exclude branches are disjoint and exhaustive, and each step reduces unprocessed positions, proving termination and completeness. Copying at a leaf prevents later undo from erasing saved results. There are 2^n leaves and 2^(n+1)−1 recursive calls. Total copied position entries are n·2^(n−1) for n≥1: enumeration takes Θ(n2^n) time and retained output space, even though the active stack and chosen list use only O(n). The teaching API limits n to 16 to bound retained output. Empty input has one subset, the empty subset.

headings.title: One-Use Subset Sum Needs a Two-Part State
body:
```{index} One-Use Subset Sum Needs a Two-Part State
```

## One-Use Subset Sum Needs a Two-Part State

```{index} One-Use Subset Sum Needs a Two-Part State
```

For signed invoice adjustments, ask whether some distinct positions sum to target. State (i,r) means: using only positions i..n−1, can we make remaining r? Include gives (i+1,r−value[i]); exclude gives (i+1,r). A zero remainder accepts the current subset, including the empty subset for target zero.

Each call advances i, so no position is reused and recursion terminates. The shared chosen list contains selected earlier positions; remaining equals target minus their sum. The implementation snapshots a successful witness and restores the list even on early success or a search-budget exception. A null witness means proven infeasibility; an empty witness is a feasible zero target. Use long sums and remaining amounts so two int values do not overflow.

headings.title: Prove Bounds Before Pruning
body:
```{index} Prove Bounds Before Pruning
```

## Prove Bounds Before Pruning

```{index} Prove Bounds Before Pruning
```

The rule remaining<0 is safe for nonnegative values because future additions cannot decrease the chosen sum. It fails for signed values: 8 followed by −3 makes five after temporarily overshooting. For a signed suffix define L(i) as the sum of its negative values and U(i) as the sum of its positive values. Every suffix subset sum lies in [L(i),U(i)]. Prune only if r lies outside those bounds. Being inside the interval does not guarantee feasibility.

Compute suffix bounds once in O(n) time/storage. The code checks success before suffix exhaustion, preserves both branches when necessary, and accepts zeros. The initial total bound check also runs in the unpruned comparison to avoid subtracting from an extreme impossible long target. Branch order affects measured calls when the search stops at its first witness; pruning has no universal speedup guarantee.

headings.title: Memoize Failed States Without Losing Choices
body:
```{index} Memoize Failed States Without Losing Choices
```

## Memoize Failed States Without Losing Choices

```{index} Memoize Failed States Without Losing Choices
```

Two different prefixes can leave the same (i,r). Their future feasibility is identical because the remaining positions and target are identical. Cache a state only after both branches fail. Do not cache only r: the same remaining amount with different inventories is a different question. Keeping only failed states avoids needing to store a prefix-dependent witness.

For nonnegative values and target T, reachable non-pruned remainder states lie in 0..T, so there are O(n(T+1)) possible states. Signed inputs instead depend on the attainable sum range, which can be large. Expected constant-time hash lookup gives work proportional to visited states/transitions plus pruning and terminal calls. Without effective caching or pruning, worst-case branching is O(2^n), with O(n) active stack/path space. This teaching implementation accepts up to 128 positions and a default million-call budget. Exhausting it throws with feasibility unknown; it must never return false as though the instance were solved.

body:
```{index} Permutations Use Every Position Exactly Once
```

## Permutations Use Every Position Exactly Once

```{index} Permutations Use Every Position Exactly Once
```

At each depth choose an unused position. Maintain used[i] exactly when i appears in order, and undo both structures. Labels can repeat while positions remain distinct. This is useful when two jobs share a display name but have different IDs.

There are n! position permutations; copying each length-n order requires Θ(n·n!) time and retained output space. Active state is O(n). The API caps n at eight for materialized results. Generating unique value permutations is a different contract and would need deliberate duplicate suppression. A streamed generator can reduce retained storage, but cannot eliminate the cost of producing all requested outputs.
