# Direct String Matching and Result Contracts
```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
```{index} Define What Counts as a Match Before Choosing an Algorithm
```

headings.title: Separate a Candidate Start from Its Matched Length
body:
```{index} Separate a Candidate Start from Its Matched Length
```

## Separate a Candidate Start from Its Matched Length
A direct matcher asks the same small question at each legal start: do all pattern code units agree here? There are two positions to track. Start chooses a candidate in the text; offset chooses a position inside the pattern. A mismatch rejects the current candidate only. The next start may still match, including an occurrence overlapping the previous match.

For text ABABA and pattern ABA:

| Candidate start | Character comparisons | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | A=A, B=B, A=A | Report 0 |
| 1 | B differs from A | Reject only this start |
| 2 | A=A, B=B, A=A | Report 2 |

The final legal nonempty start is text.Length-pattern.Length. A longer pattern has no legal start. The empty-pattern policy is separate: this book reports every boundary, including the one after the final text code unit. The focused example below assumes non-null strings; the retained full API also rejects null inputs explicitly.
Offset equals pattern.Length only when the whole pattern has matched. On a mismatch it stops earlier, so the candidate is not reported. Increasing start by one preserves overlaps. For the empty pattern, the inner loop runs zero times, offset already equals zero, and starts zero through text.Length are reported under the stated boundary policy.

Guided task: trace AA in AAAA and fill the starts without running code. Then change the outer update to advance by pattern.Length after a match. Which required starts disappear, and why is the modification incorrect for this contract?

```{dropdown} Check the overlap policy
The required starts are zero, one and two. Skipping two positions after a match loses start one. A non-overlapping API could choose that policy, but it would be solving a different problem. Tests must compare equivalent contracts.
```

For independent comparison with KMP, check empty text, empty pattern, longer patterns, repeated symbols, absent patterns and case differences before counting work. These examples compare ordinal UTF-16 code units. They do not normalize text or implement a culture-aware search. The retained hop-versus-cost discussion below is an objective-contract comparison linked to the graph chapters, not a prerequisite for the string algorithm.

headings.title: Define What Counts as a Match Before Choosing an Algorithm
body:
```{index} Define What Counts as a Match Before Choosing an Algorithm
```

## Define What Counts as a Match Before Choosing an Algorithm

A message filter searches text for a literal pattern. Decide whether matching is case-sensitive, whether all overlapping starts are required, and how an empty pattern is treated. These choices determine the correct result before any comparison-count claim can be made. The core examples compare ordinal UTF-16 code units; a returned position is an offset in that representation, not necessarily a user-perceived character count.

For text ABABA and pattern ABA, the starts are zero and two. Moving the candidate start by the pattern length after the first match would miss the overlapping occurrence at two. A direct matcher instead considers every candidate start whose remaining text is long enough, comparing pattern elements until a mismatch or a complete match.

| Candidate start | Comparison outcome | Report it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | ABA matches ABA | Yes |
| 1 | B differs from A immediately | No |
| 2 | ABA matches ABA | Yes |

The direct algorithm's simplicity makes it a useful independent reference for more elaborate matching. Its contract must still handle an empty pattern. Under the all-boundaries convention used here, an empty pattern matches before the first code unit, between adjacent code units, and after the final code unit. Thus text of length n has n+1 empty-pattern starts. Another API can choose another contract, but comparisons must use the same one.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Use Mismatches as Evidence
```

headings.title: Use Mismatches as Evidence
body:
```{index} Use Mismatches as Evidence
```

## Use Mismatches as Evidence

A mismatch at one candidate start establishes only that this candidate fails. It does not prove that the text contains no later occurrence. The outer loop advances the start; the inner loop advances the pattern position. Confusing those two positions can skip starts or compare the wrong slices.

With text length n and pattern length m, a direct comparison model can perform up to proportional to n*m work for nonempty patterns within the text. A long shared prefix followed by a mismatch can repeat work at many starts. The next lesson develops how prefix information can avoid some repetition. For short patterns or a small number of queries, a clear direct approach or a suitable library operation can still be a reasonable engineering choice; a more sophisticated algorithm is not required merely because it exists.

Guided check: find all starts of AA in AAAA, then an absent pattern longer than the text, then the empty pattern. Derive expected outputs manually. Use those cases when checking the preserved implementations so that a fast candidate cannot quietly change overlap or boundary semantics. Keep weighted-graph hop/cost reminders as links to Chapters 20 and 24; they are separate result-contract examples, not prerequisites for reading a string matcher.

headings.title: Direct Matching with an Explicit Contract
body:
```{index} Direct Matching with an Explicit Contract
```

## Direct Matching with an Explicit Contract


```{index} Direct Matching with an Explicit Contract
```
Search exact ordinal UTF-16 code units, returning every start position, including overlapping matches. A missing nonempty pattern returns an empty array. An empty pattern matches each boundary 0..text.Length; null arguments are rejected. Derived first-match clients return the first position or −1. Counts include every executed code-unit equality test, including mismatches.
The loop tests each legal start once. At offset j, the first j code units match; a mismatch rules out that start, while j=m proves an occurrence. For n text units and m>0 pattern units, worst-case comparison work is O((n−m+1)m) when m≤n, commonly written O(nm); m>n gives zero tests. Returned r positions cost O(r) storage. Empty patterns require O(n) output despite zero equality tests.
The distinction between minimum hops and minimum cost is developed with its full graph counterexample in {doc}`Shortest Paths and Dijkstra <../24_greedy_graph_optimization/2404_shortest_paths>`. String matching likewise begins by choosing an explicit result contract.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
```{index} Reuse a Prefix Only When It Is Also the Needed Suffix
```

headings.title: Build the Fallback Table Before Scanning Text
body:
```{index} Build the Fallback Table Before Scanning Text
```

## Build the Fallback Table Before Scanning Text
KMP avoids restarting a search from scratch after every mismatch. It retains a fact already proved: a suffix of the consumed text matches a prefix of the pattern. This connects direct matching's result contract to a different reuse rule. The goal remains all overlapping ordinal matches; changing the algorithm must not change that answer.

For each pattern position i, prefix[i] records the longest **proper** prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also its suffix. Proper excludes the entire segment. The number is a length, not an index of the next text character. For ABABACA, complete the table from left to right:

| i | Current segment | Border retained | prefix[i] |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| 0 | A | Empty | 0 |
| 1 | AB | Empty | 0 |
| 2 | ABA | A | 1 |
| 3 | ABAB | AB | 2 |
| 4 | ABABA | ABA | 3 |
| 5 | ABABAC | Empty | 0 |
| 6 | ABABACA | A | 1 |

At i=5 the candidate length is three, so the next expected character is pattern[3], B. C mismatches. Follow prefix[2] to candidate length one; pattern[1] is B, so C still mismatches. Follow prefix[0] to zero; pattern[0] is A, also a mismatch. Store zero. This is why a fallback can happen several times at one position without moving that position backwards.

The core schematic update is `q = prefix[q - 1]` when q>0 and the next character fails. q is the number already matched; q-1 is the last position of that matched prefix. Using prefix[q] instead confuses the current known prefix with a longer segment that was never established.
For AAAA, each new character extends the preceding border by one, but the final border has length three, not four. An empty pattern produces an empty table because the loop does not execute. The scanner handles that pattern before attempting to index it.

headings.title: Keep a Proven Suffix After Reporting a Match
body:
```{index} Keep a Proven Suffix After Reporting a Match
```

## Keep a Proven Suffix After Reporting a Match
Use pattern ABAB and text ABABAB. Its prefix table is 0,0,1,2. The scan keeps i as the consumed text position and q as the matched-prefix length.

| Consumed text position | Character | q before comparison | q after a match | Report/fallback |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 0 | A | 0 | 1 | None |
| 1 | B | 1 | 2 | None |
| 2 | A | 2 | 3 | None |
| 3 | B | 3 | 4 | Start 0; retain q=2 |
| 4 | A | 2 | 3 | None |
| 5 | B | 3 | 4 | Start 2; retain q=2 |

After the first match, AB at the end of the matched text is already a valid beginning of another occurrence. Keeping q=2 preserves the overlap at start two. Resetting q to zero would lose that occurrence. The focused scanner below repeats its own setup so it can run independently of the prefix-table cell.
This focused version assumes non-null arguments and demonstrates the invariant, not comparison instrumentation. The full retained API below validates arguments and counts comparisons under its declared convention. Do not copy exact comparison counts from a differently instrumented loop.

Guided task: fill the q values for AAAA in AAAAA and circle the fallback immediately after each full match. Then process ABABAC while searching for ABABAB: follow the repeated border failures at C without changing the consumed text prefix. Finally compare every reported start with the direct matcher before discussing speed.

```{dropdown} Check the overlap and work arguments
The first four A characters reach q=4, report start zero, and fall back to three. The fifth A reaches four again and reports start one. For ABABAC against ABABAB, the final C fails against B at q=5, then B at q=3, then B at q=1, then A at zero. No full match is reported. Across the whole scan, q can increase only with consumed characters; fallback decreases q. Total decreases cannot exceed total increases, which bounds fallback work linearly as well as the forward scan.
```

For independent transfer, preserve the direct matcher's empty, overlapping and ordinal policies, reuse a prepared pattern across several texts, and include preparation plus reported-result storage in the workload account. The examples below retain the complete API, counted comparisons and larger boundary matrix.

headings.title: Reuse a Prefix Only When It Is Also the Needed Suffix
body:
```{index} Reuse a Prefix Only When It Is Also the Needed Suffix
```

## Reuse a Prefix Only When It Is Also the Needed Suffix

KMP remembers how much of a pattern has already matched. After a mismatch, some of that matched text may also be a valid beginning of the next candidate match. The prefix table identifies such borders: proper prefixes that are also suffixes. Proper excludes the complete string itself, otherwise fallback would make no progress.

For pattern ABAB, the longest proper border of the whole pattern is AB, length two. For its prefixes A, AB, ABA and ABAB, the corresponding border lengths are 0, 0, 1 and 2. These are properties of the pattern; preparation can be reused when searching different texts under the same matching policy.

| Pattern prefix | Longest proper border | Length |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Empty | 0 |
| AB | Empty | 0 |
| ABA | A | 1 |
| ABAB | AB | 2 |

Suppose the matcher has recognized ABA of pattern ABAB and the next text code unit is C rather than the expected B. The matched prefix ABA has border A, of length one. It need not pretend that all recognized text is unrelated to the pattern. Falling back to a valid border keeps a suffix that already matches a prefix. If the new comparison also fails, repeat fallback through shorter borders. The text position can stay at the current unconsumed code unit while the matched-prefix length decreases.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
```{index} Separate Two Progress Arguments
```

headings.title: Separate Two Progress Arguments
body:
```{index} Separate Two Progress Arguments
```

## Separate Two Progress Arguments

During scanning, either the text position advances or the matched-prefix length decreases through valid fallback links. A decrease cannot happen indefinitely without intervening increases. This accounting explains a linear number of scan comparisons under the algorithm's model; the proof is not simply that the outer loop mentions each text position once. The inner fallback work must be accounted for too.

Preparation costs work proportional to the pattern length. Scanning costs proportional to text length, with output storage proportional to the number of reported matches. When the same pattern is searched in many texts, an owned prepared table can avoid repeating preparation. If the table is exposed for arbitrary mutation, callers can break the matcher invariant; ownership/copying rules from the object chapters remain relevant.

After a full match, fallback must preserve the possibility of overlapping results. Resetting the matched length blindly to zero can lose occurrences such as ABA at starts zero and two in ABABA. Empty patterns need their explicit boundary contract before normal prefix-table indexing, because there is no pattern position zero to compare.

Guided exercise: build the prefix lengths for AAAA and explain why the final border has length three, not four. Trace the all-match scan on AAAAA. Compare the start positions with the direct matcher, then compare complete preparation-plus-scan work for one text and for several texts. Equivalent answers come before performance claims.

headings.title: Proper Prefixes Survive a Mismatch
body:
```{index} Proper Prefixes Survive a Mismatch
```

## Proper Prefixes Survive a Mismatch

```{index} Proper Prefixes Survive a Mismatch
```

prefix[i] is the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also its suffix. Proper excludes the whole segment. For ababaca, the table is 0,0,1,2,3,0,1. If q units matched and the next comparison fails, only borders of the matched prefix can remain possible: set q=prefix[q−1] and try again.

Prefix construction maintains a valid border length for the already processed prefix. On mismatch, following the previous border chain finds the next possible border rather than resetting blindly or skipping a valid candidate. Successful comparisons increase q by at most one; fallback decreases it. Across all positions the total fallback work is linear in m. The owned table is prepared once and can be reused across multiple texts.

headings.title: KMP Keeps the Text Moving Forward
body:
```{index} KMP Keeps the Text Moving Forward
```

## KMP Keeps the Text Moving Forward

```{index} KMP Keeps the Text Moving Forward
```

Before each comparison, q code units of the pattern equal the suffix of text already consumed. After a mismatch, fallback preserves that invariant without moving the text index backward. After a complete match, fall back to the pattern’s longest border so overlapping occurrences remain discoverable.

Both preprocessing and scan use one counted equality test per candidate attempt, avoiding a hidden duplicate comparison in a while condition followed by an if. Preprocessing is O(m), each scan O(n), and the table O(m) space plus O(r) result storage. Total fallback decreases are bounded by total increases in matched length, which gives the linear bound despite the nested loop. Preparing for each request loses the benefit of repeated-pattern reuse.

headings.title: Measure a Complete Workload and Define Text Units
body:
```{index} Measure a Complete Workload and Define Text Units
```

## Measure a Complete Workload and Define Text Units

```{index} Measure a Complete Workload and Define Text Units
```

On repetitive text, direct scanning can repeatedly compare long matching prefixes. Include preparation in the KMP total, and reuse the same prepared pattern when comparing several texts. Operation counts are evidence, not timings.

UTF-16 offsets count code units, not user-perceived characters; a supplementary emoji takes two units. Exact ordinal matching performs no case folding, culture rules, or Unicode normalization. Canonically equivalent spellings can therefore differ. For ordinary application code, use .NET search APIs with an explicit comparison policy.[^2602_shortest_paths_strings-1] Do not claim this educational implementation outperforms the library without a controlled benchmark.

headings.title: A Limit on One Program Is Not a Lower Bound on Every Algorithm
body:
```{index} A Limit on One Program Is Not a Lower Bound on Every Algorithm
```

## A Limit on One Program Is Not a Lower Bound on Every Algorithm

A subset enumerator can examine 2^n choices. Doubling input from n to 2n changes that model to 2^(2n), the square of the previous count, rather than merely doubling the work. Write the model and its units before attaching elapsed-time estimates. A counter that computes the number 2^n with arithmetic has not itself enumerated every subset.

Now consider a set-cover task: select teams whose capabilities cover every requirement. A greedy rule can quickly produce complete coverage, yet another selection may use fewer teams. Checking feasibility means verifying every requirement is covered. Checking optimality means ruling out every better feasible selection under the model. These are separate obligations.

| Reported outcome | Evidence needed |
| --- | --- |
| Feasible cover | The selected teams cover all required capabilities |
| Optimal cover | Feasibility plus an argument/reference excluding better choices |
| Infeasible instance | Exhaustive or otherwise justified evidence that none exists |
| Search limit reached | A statement that the chosen procedure stopped before resolution |

An exact reference on tiny instances can validate a greedy counterexample. It cannot establish that exhaustive search will remain affordable on large inputs. Conversely, one slow exhaustive implementation does not prove that every possible algorithm needs that much time. Distinguish algorithm bounds, instance measurements, proven problem lower bounds and unproved general beliefs.

A practical recommendation can be honest without solving every theoretical question. State the input limits, objective, quality evidence and failure policy. If a budget-limited search stops, report unknown rather than impossible. If a heuristic is selected, state which guarantees are established and which are not; a successful example is not an approximation-ratio proof.

Guided comparison: a greedy cover uses three teams and an exhaustive tiny-instance reference finds a valid two-team cover. Explain what has been disproved and what has not. The example disproves optimality of that greedy rule on every input. It does not disprove the rule's usefulness under a stated time/quality tradeoff or prove a particular complexity classification.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]
Finish the course by linking contracts, correctness, cost, and requirements. A large search space motivates better algorithms and narrower requirements, but does not itself prove that every exact algorithm must enumerate that space. Download complete implementations and checks: [AdvancedChecks.cs](../../demos/26_advanced_graphs_strings_limits/AdvancedChecks.cs).

headings.title: Growth Models Are Not Benchmarks
body:
```{index} Growth Models Are Not Benchmarks
```

## Growth Models Are Not Benchmarks

```{index} Growth Models Are Not Benchmarks
```

Use exact integer arithmetic to compare candidate work functions. A subset search may have 2^n candidate sets; positional orderings have n! candidates. Models describe possible work, not measured runtime. A budget comparison needs declared units.

Constants, hardware, data distribution, preprocessing, memory, and required output affect actual feasibility. Pruning can help without changing an exponential worst case. Dynamic programming may replace a choice tree with a state graph, yet its numeric-state range can still be large. Enumerating a large family is not a lower-bound proof for a decision or optimization problem.

headings.title: Exact Search and a Concrete Heuristic
body:
```{index} Exact Search and a Concrete Heuristic
```

## Exact Search and a Concrete Heuristic

```{index} Exact Search and a Concrete Heuristic
```

A manager selects the fewest teams covering six required skills. Team masks are A={0,1,2,3}, B={0,1,4}, C={2,3,5}. Greedily selecting the team covering the most still-uncovered skills picks A, then B and C: three teams. The feasible pair B,C covers all six with two.

The exact method enumerates all team subsets up to the teaching limit of 20 teams; it skips candidates whose counts cannot improve the current best. This is safe pruning because adding a candidate of at least the current best count cannot improve a minimum-count objective. The greedy method deterministically breaks equal gains by first position. For this example, no one team covers all requirements, so the feasible two-team witness is optimal independently of the enumeration output.

headings.title: Guarantees, Heuristics, and Unknown Answers
body:
```{index} Guarantees, Heuristics, and Unknown Answers
```

## Guarantees, Heuristics, and Unknown Answers

```{index} Guarantees, Heuristics, and Unknown Answers
```

An exact algorithm must return an optimum or a proven no-solution answer when it completes. A heuristic may return a useful feasible result without an optimality claim. An approximation guarantee is a proved bound relating the returned objective to the optimum under stated assumptions; good performance on samples is not such a proof.

The cover heuristic here is used as a verified greedy counterexample; this chapter does not claim or derive a general approximation ratio for it. A zero-gain stop means remaining requirements are uncovered by every available team. Budget exhaustion in a general search instead means unknown unless a separate proof establishes infeasibility. Report coverage separately from team count: a smaller incomplete selection is not a better feasible solution. Changing requirements, permitting partial coverage, or limiting input sizes changes the problem contract.

headings.title: Validate Results Before Comparing Speed
body:
```{index} Validate Results Before Comparing Speed
```

## Validate Results Before Comparing Speed

```{index} Validate Results Before Comparing Speed
```

For each strategy verify that returned positions are distinct and legal, that their union equals claimed coverage, and that full coverage is achieved before comparing counts. Test zero requirements, empty teams, and impossible requirements.

For t teams, exhaustive enumeration costs O(t·2^t) time and O(t) auxiliary/output state in this implementation; greedy takes O(t·r) scans for r≤requirements selected teams, using fixed-width masks for at most 20 requirements. These are different algorithms with different quality contracts. Bit operations are constant time only under the fixed-width model used here.

headings.title: A Reviewable Final Comparison
body:


## A Reviewable Final Comparison

```{index} A Reviewable Final Comparison
```

Use a problem from your semester project or this chapter’s service network. Specify objective, input model, legal inputs, tie policies, output, and resource budget. Compare at least two strategies on identical cases. Include independently checked witnesses, exact operation-count definitions, qualified time/space costs, and a recommendation tied to the requirements.

Suitable comparisons include BFS versus DFS for reachability (BFS adds minimum-hop information), direct versus prepared-pattern matching under the same ordinal/overlap policy, or exact versus greedy team coverage with feasibility and quality reported separately. Keep any durable VS Code/GitHub capstone submission in the existing project/appendix track; this content section supplies the comparison method, not a new required assignment. Include empty, disconnected, repeated-prefix, and infeasible cases as appropriate. A defensible conclusion states where both algorithms agree, what extra guarantee one offers, and where the budget or data model changes the recommendation.

## The Microsoft Language and .NET Ecosystem

Before installing tools, it helps to know where C# sits. **.NET** is Microsoft's free, open-source platform for building many kinds of applications. It runs programs written in several languages, and it provides **app stacks**: libraries and templates for a particular kind of application. The tools you install in this section serve the whole platform, not only this course.

| Language | Role today | In this course |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C#** | Microsoft's most widely used .NET language; most of .NET itself is written in it | The language you learn |
| **F#** | Functional-first language, used for data-heavy and analytical code | Not covered |
| **Visual Basic** | Maintained for stability and C# interoperability, not receiving new features | Not covered |
| **C++/CLI** | Legacy bridge between C++ and .NET; Windows-only and maintained for compatibility | Not covered |

Because all .NET languages compile to the same runtime, a company can mix them: a C# order system can call a F# pricing library. Learning C# therefore also prepares you to read the others.

| App stack | Builds | Runs on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Console apps** | Command-line tools and batch jobs | Windows, macOS, Linux |
| **ASP.NET Core** (with **Blazor**) | Web sites, web APIs, and business back ends | Windows, macOS, Linux |
| **.NET MAUI** | Mobile and desktop apps from one code base | Android, iOS, macOS, Windows (no official Linux support) |
| **WPF, Windows Forms, WinUI** | Windows desktop business applications | Windows only |

You will start with console apps because they teach C# without a user interface. Later chapters and the project can build on web or desktop stacks; see the platform notes in the Group Project appendix.

This book uses **VS Code** with C# Dev Kit, which runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Facts here follow Microsoft's [.NET languages strategy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/languages) and [introduction to .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/introduction).

**Checkpoint:** A company wants a Windows-only desktop tool for its accounting staff and a web portal for customers. Which app stacks from the table fit each need?

## Install and Check the .NET SDK

**.NET** provides the runtime and libraries used by C# applications. The **software development kit (SDK)** includes the compiler and development commands needed to build and run them. The runtime executes compiled applications; installing only the runtime is not enough to develop them.

Install the **.NET 10 SDK** for your operating system and processor from [Microsoft's .NET 10 download page](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/download/dotnet/10.0). Select the SDK, rather than a runtime-only download. Microsoft provides [installation instructions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/install/) for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

After installation, open a new terminal and enter:

```console
dotnet --version
```

The version should begin with `10.`. Patch and SDK feature versions can differ; you do not need a particular patch number for these introductory examples. If another installed SDK is selected, inspect `dotnet --list-sdks` and confirm .NET 10 is present. If the command is not found, reopen the terminal and check the installation before proceeding.

**Checkpoint:** Explain the difference between the SDK used to develop a program and the runtime used to execute it.

## Prepare Your Terminal and Workspace

Read {doc}`Command Line Basics <command_line_basics>` for paths, prompts, and navigation. Open Windows Terminal with PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS, or a terminal with Bash on Linux. The terminal is the window; the shell interprets the operating-system commands you enter there.

Go to your home directory:

```console
cd ~
```

List its contents with `Get-ChildItem` in PowerShell or `ls` in Bash/Zsh. If you do not already have a `workspace` folder, create it:

```console
mkdir workspace
```

Enter it:

```console
cd workspace
```

Confirm the current location with `Get-Location` in PowerShell or `pwd` in Bash/Zsh. This is where you will create `HelloWorld` in Chapter 1.3. Do not run `mkdir workspace` again if that folder already exists.

**Checkpoint:** Identify your current folder and its parent. You should be at the operating-system shell prompt, ready to enter commands such as `dotnet --version`.


## Set Up VS Code for C#

After installing and verifying the .NET 10 SDK in the previous section, install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and open it. Read {doc}`Editing Tools <editing_tools>` for Explorer, saved files, extensions, and the integrated terminal.

Next, install Microsoft's **C# Dev Kit** (`ms-dotnettools.csdevkit`). It adds project management and testing support. **C# is a VS Code extension** that provides code completion and diagnostics. After installing C# Dev Kit, check that its **C#** and **.NET Install Tool** extensions are installed too; if either still shows **Install**, install it manually. See Microsoft's [C# setup guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/csharp/get-started).

Check the Extensions view to confirm that C# Dev Kit and its two dependencies are installed:

| Extension | Install separately? | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C# Dev Kit** by Microsoft | **Yes** | C# project management, testing, and development tools. |
| **C#** by Microsoft | If not installed automatically, install it manually | C# code completion and diagnostics. |
| **.NET Install Tool** by Microsoft | If not installed automatically, install it manually | Supplies .NET components needed by the editor extensions. |

The **.NET 10 SDK** is a separate download, not a VS Code extension. It provides the tools that build and run your C# projects. During setup, VS Code may also ask to install .NET components needed by its extensions; allow the installation and wait for it to finish. The extension-managed runtime supports the editor's tools, while the SDK builds and runs your applications. Seeing a different runtime version in an extension message does not mean your project has changed its target framework. Microsoft's [C# Dev Kit FAQ](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/csharp/cs-dev-kit-faq) explains these dependencies.

Use **File > Open Folder** to open your `workspace` folder. Use **Terminal > New Terminal** and run `dotnet --version` there to confirm VS Code can access the SDK too. Save a short `notes.txt` file in the folder and locate it in Explorer. You will create the actual C# project in Chapter 1.3.

When that project exists, open the **HelloWorld project folder**, containing both `Program.cs` and `HelloWorld.csproj`, rather than opening `Program.cs` alone. Allow the C# tools to load the project. If a warning says the active document is outside the workspace, check the open folder and reopen the file from Explorer. After moving files, close old tabs that point to their previous locations.

**Checkpoint:** Confirm C# Dev Kit, C#, and .NET Install Tool appear as installed in Extensions, your saved file appears in Explorer, and the integrated terminal reports a .NET 10 SDK. If C# Dev Kit is installed but C# still shows **Install**, install it before continuing. In Chapter 1.3, check that typing `Console.` in the loaded project's source offers member completions.

For version control and collaboration, see {doc}`Appendix C: Git and GitHub <../github>`.

## Try C# Interactively with CSharpRepl

Read {doc}`Interactive Language Environments (REPLs) <interactive_language_environments>` to distinguish a language prompt from an operating-system shell. A C# REPL helps you check expressions quickly; your saved console applications will use `Program.cs` and `dotnet run`.

Install [CSharpRepl](https://github.com/waf/CSharpRepl) from the operating-system shell:

```console
dotnet tool install -g csharprepl
```

If it is already installed, you can update it with `dotnet tool update -g csharprepl`. Start it:

```console
csharprepl
```

At its `>` prompt, enter an expression. The following transcript includes the prompt and displayed result; type only `2 + 3`:

```text
> 2 + 3
5
```

Try multiplication too:

```text
> 4 * 10
40
```

The REPL displays expression results automatically. In a console application, you will use `Console.WriteLine(...)` to display them. REPL entries can retain state during a session, so do not assume a snippet works independently unless you have supplied everything it needs.

Enter `exit` to return to the operating-system shell. If `csharprepl` is not found after installation, open a new terminal and follow its [installation troubleshooting](https://github.com/waf/CSharpRepl/wiki/Installation) for the global tool directory.

**Checkpoint:** Evaluate an expression, identify the C# prompt, and return to the shell. You are now ready to create and run your first console application in {ref}`program-structure`.


# Git and GitHub

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```
Use this appendix when you need to track or share saved project files. **Git** records versions locally. **GitHub** hosts Git repositories and supports collaboration. A **repository** holds the files and their history. Saving a file, committing it, and uploading the commit are separate actions.

headings.title: Why Use Version Control
body:
```{index} version control; why use version control; local and remote repositories
```

## Why Use Version Control
Version control gives you a record of your work that you can inspect, undo, and share. It helps individuals as much as teams: you can see what changed and when, return to a working version, and keep a copy off your own computer. It also replaces carrying files on USB drives or sending e-mail attachments, because you and your instructor can look at the same repository.

The basic idea is to keep a main copy of a project on GitHub (the **remote**) and a working copy on each computer you use (the **local** repository). Several steps stand between editing a file and changing the main copy, and each one is deliberate:

- **Track:** a new file is untracked until you `git add` it.
- **Commit:** changes to tracked files reach your local history only when you `git commit`.
- **Push:** committed changes reach GitHub only when you `git push`.
- **Ignore:** `.gitignore` lists files Git should leave out, such as `bin/` and `obj/`.
- **Pull:** changes made elsewhere reach your computer only when you `git pull`.

Keeping these steps separate protects the main copy from half-finished work. Other version control systems, such as Subversion and Mercurial, follow the same ideas with different commands. This book uses Git because GitHub hosts Git repositories and your course submissions use it.

headings.title: Prepare a Practice Repository
body:
```{index} Git installation; repository; git init
```

## Prepare a Practice Repository

Install Git using the [Git installation instructions](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-Installing-Git), then open a new terminal and run `git --version`. For GitHub work, use your own account and follow your course's repository and access instructions.

In a new folder separate from existing repositories, create `README.md` in your editor with a project title and one sentence describing its purpose. From that folder, initialize Git and configure the identity recorded on your commits:

```console
git init -b main
git config user.name "Your Name"
git config user.email "your-address@example.com"
git status
```

Replace the example identity with your own choices. Repository-local configuration applies here rather than changing all your projects. You can use a GitHub-provided private email address according to your account settings.

headings.title: Inspect, Stage, and Commit
body:
```{index} git status; git diff; staging; commit
```

## Inspect, Stage, and Commit

**Staging** selects changes for the next commit. A **commit** records the selected changes in local history. Start with one small, understandable change:

```console
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Describe the project purpose"
git status
git log --oneline
```

Review the staged diff before committing. A clean status after the commit means there are no uncommitted changes Git currently reports; it does not prove the work was uploaded.

Now edit and save the README. `git diff` shows unstaged changes to tracked files; `git diff --staged` shows the selected changes. New untracked files appear in `git status` and do not appear in the ordinary diff until tracked. Stage the intended files and commit again. A useful message describes the change, such as `Document how to run the report`, rather than `update`.

headings.title: Keep Generated Files Out of History
body:
```{index} gitignore; generated files
```

### Keep Generated Files Out of History

A `.gitignore` file lists paths Git should normally leave untracked. For a .NET project, include:

```text
bin/
obj/
```

Commit source, project configuration, and `.gitignore`; build output can be regenerated. Ignore rules do not remove files that are already tracked. Review `git status` before staging to see what the repository actually contains.

headings.title: Publish an Existing Local Repository to GitHub
body:
```{index} remote; origin; git push
```

## Publish an Existing Local Repository to GitHub

On GitHub, create a repository using the visibility and access required by your course. For this workflow, leave its initial README, license, and ignore options empty because your local repository already has history. Copy its repository URL. Authenticate using GitHub's supported HTTPS credential or SSH setup.

Replace `OWNER` and `REPOSITORY` below with the copied URL for your repository:

```console
git remote add origin https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git
git remote -v
git push -u origin main
```

A **remote** is a named connection to another repository; `origin` is a conventional name. Verify the URL before pushing. If `origin` already exists, inspect it before deciding whether its URL needs to change. The `-u` option records the branch's upstream connection for later pushes. Open GitHub and confirm that the expected commit and files are present.[^1]

headings.title: Start from an Existing Course Repository
body:
```{index} git clone; repository clone
```

### Start from an Existing Course Repository

If your instructor gives you an existing repository, clone it instead of creating a separate unrelated history:

```console
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git
cd REPOSITORY
git status
```

Replace the URL and folder name with the actual ones. Cloning copies the repository and configures `origin`. Do not repeat `git init` or `git remote add origin` inside that clone.

headings.title: Everyday Git Workflow
body:
```{index} Git workflow; version control habits
```

## Everyday Git Workflow
Use small commits to make your progress understandable and recoverable. Each commit should describe one logical change. Keep unrelated changes separate and inspect the diff before committing. A useful message names what changed, such as `Validate malformed CSV rows before parsing scores`, rather than `update`.

For a repository with an upstream branch already configured, begin a work session with a clean working tree:

```console
git status
git pull --ff-only
```

After editing, saving, and checking your program, review and record your changes. Replace `Program.cs` below with the specific files you intend to include:

```console
git diff
git add Program.cs
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Validate order input before calculating totals"
git push
```

This is the recurring cycle for individual work. For team work, use the branch and pull-request workflow below. If `git pull --ff-only` cannot update your branch, inspect the reported situation before continuing; do not discard your work to force an update.

headings.title: Work on More Than One Computer
body:
```{index} two computers; working between lab and home
```

### Work on More Than One Computer
GitHub also lets you move between a lab computer and your own. The remote copy is the meeting point, so each session follows the same cycle:

1. **Start:** run `git pull --ff-only` to bring down changes you pushed from another computer.
2. **Work:** create or change files, then run and check your program.
3. **Record:** run `git add` for the files you intend to include, then `git commit -m "message"`.
4. **Finish:** run `git push` before you leave, so the work is on GitHub.

If you forget the last step, your work stays on the first computer. Push at the end of every session. Pulling and committing are separate operations so that you decide when to combine other people's changes with yours. This matters little when you work alone and a great deal in a team; for a team repository, add collaborators in the repository's **Settings** on GitHub as your instructor directs.

headings.title: Collaborate Through a Branch and Pull Request
body:
```{index} branch; pull request; GitHub workflow
```

## Collaborate Through a Branch and Pull Request

A **branch** names a line of development. A **pull request** proposes combining changes and gives reviewers a place to inspect and discuss them. For an updated clone on `main` with no uncommitted work:

```console
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git switch -c report-heading
```

Edit the README or project, check the result, and commit the intended changes:

```console
git status
git diff
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Clarify the report heading"
git push -u origin report-heading
```

On GitHub, open a pull request from `report-heading` to the intended base branch. Review the diff, describe the change and its checks, and follow the course's review process before merging. GitHub's [Hello World tutorial](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/hello-world) provides a browser-based practice workflow.[^2]

If a pull or merge reports divergent history or conflicts, inspect the situation before proceeding. A conflict marks competing changes that require a deliberate final version. Resolve the content, remove the markers, and check the resulting program. History rewriting is beyond this introductory workflow.

headings.title: Resolve a Merge Conflict
body:
```{index} merge conflicts; conflict markers
```

### Resolve a Merge Conflict
A merge conflict asks you to decide how competing edits should be combined. Inspect the files reported by Git and read both versions around the conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`). Edit each affected area into the intended final content, then remove the markers.

Save the files, run the relevant program or tests, and review the diff. Stage the resolved files and follow Git's instructions to complete the merge or commit. Do not leave conflict markers in source code, and do not choose a version merely to make the warning disappear.

headings.title: Check Your Submission
body:
```{index} GitHub submission; commit verification
```

## Check Your Submission

Before submitting, confirm the intended files are committed and pushed, then inspect the repository on GitHub. Submit the repository, branch, or commit link specified by your instructor. Private repositories also require the instructor to have access. A saved editor file, a local commit, or a successful build alone is not evidence of a completed GitHub submission.

**Practice check:** Change the README and observe its status before staging, after staging, and after committing. Explain which action makes the new version visible on GitHub.

headings.title: Configuration and cleanup
body:
### Configuration and cleanup

```{index} Git; configuration and cleanup
```
| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `.gitignore` | File of patterns for untracked paths. |
| `git config --global user.name "Name"` | Set your default commit author name. |
| `git config --global user.email "email"` | Set your default commit author email. |
| `git config --list` | List effective configuration values. |
| `git clean -nd` | Preview untracked files/folders to remove. |
| `git clean -fd` **!** | Delete untracked files and folders. |
| `git gc` | Perform repository housekeeping. |
`git restore <file>` restores the working file from the index and discards unstaged edits. `git restore --staged <file>` instead resets that index entry to `HEAD` while preserving the working file. `git commit -am` does not include new untracked files. Plain `git stash` omits untracked files; add `-u` when you intend to save them too. Stash application can produce conflicts.

`git pull` fetches and then integrates according to its options and configuration; it may fast-forward, merge, rebase, or refuse the integration. Use the policy taught in your course. `git reset --hard` resets tracked files and can also delete untracked files that obstruct writing tracked paths. `git clean -fd` deletes untracked files/directories but normally respects ignore rules. Neither command is a substitute for a backup. `HEAD~1` requires an existing parent commit. `.gitignore` does not automatically untrack files already committed.
```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^1]: GitHub documents remote names and URLs in [Managing remote repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/git-basics/managing-remote-repositories).
[^2]: The [Hello World tutorial](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/hello-world) introduces repositories, branches, commits, and pull requests.

Command descriptions were independently checked and corrected using the official [Git command reference](https://git-scm.com/docs), especially [git-restore](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-restore), [git-pull](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-pull), [git-reset](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reset), and [git-clean](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-clean).

headings.title: Professional Practice
body:
```{index} professional practice
```

(professional-practice)=

# Professional Practice

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

This project reference expands Chapter 1.2 with licensing, attribution, AI assistance, accessible output, and professional communication. Its code examples assume methods and decisions from the early chapters.

Professional programmers are responsible for more than whether code runs. They must respect other people's work, be honest about where code came from, and build software that everyone can use. This section covers those responsibilities as they apply to coursework now and to jobs later.

headings.title: Who Owns Code
body:
```{index} intellectual property; software license
```

## Who Owns Code

Code is a creative work, so copyright protects it automatically: you may not copy someone else's code just because you can see it. A **license** is the owner's permission to use the code under stated terms. Two common open-source examples:

- The **MIT License** is *permissive*: anyone may use, copy, modify, and sell the code, as long as they keep the copyright and license notice.[^mit]
- The **GNU General Public License (GPL)** is *copyleft*: if you distribute a modified version, you must release it under the GPL as well.[^gpl]

Code written for an employer usually belongs to the employer. Code with no license at all is not free to reuse. A header comment is the conventional place to record ownership, license, and sources:

headings.title: Using AI Assistants Responsibly
body:
```{index} AI assistants; academic integrity
```

## Using AI Assistants Responsibly

AI assistants can generate code quickly, but they do not take responsibility for it. You do. Four habits keep their use honest and safe:

1. **Follow the policy.** In this course, use AI only when the assignment authorizes it. At work, follow your employer's rules.
2. **Understand and test what you keep.** If you cannot explain a line or show a test for it, it is not yet your work.
3. **Say where code came from.** Record AI assistance and borrowed code in comments or in your submission, as in the header above.
4. **Do not paste private data into AI tools.** Customer records, passwords, and confidential code may leave your organization's control once they are sent to an outside service.

headings.title: Designing for Everyone
body:
```{index} accessibility; internationalization
```

## Designing for Everyone

Software that only works for some people quietly excludes the rest. **Accessibility** means designing software that people with disabilities can use, for example with a screen reader or without a mouse. The *Web Content Accessibility Guidelines* (WCAG 2.2, a W3C Recommendation first published in October 2023) organize accessibility around four principles: content must be *perceivable*, *operable*, *understandable*, and *robust*.[^wcag]

Even a console program can follow these principles. Do not let color carry meaning by itself; say it in words:

Customers also read numbers and dates differently. The same price and due date look different in the United States, Germany, and Japan. .NET's `CultureInfo` formats values the way each audience expects:
A date written `11/3/2026` means November 3 to an American reader and 11 March to a German one. Formatting for the reader's culture prevents a costly misunderstanding.

headings.title: Communication and Sustainability
body:
```{index} professional communication; sustainability
```

## Communication and Sustainability

Two more responsibilities round out professional practice:

- **Communicate honestly.** Write error messages that tell users what happened and what to do next, and report project status accurately, including bad news such as a missed deadline or a defect you introduced.
- **Use resources wisely.** Computation consumes energy and hardware. An inefficient algorithm running on thousands of servers wastes both. Part VI of this book shows how to measure and reduce an algorithm's cost.

headings.title: Summary
body:
```{index} professional practice; summary
```

## Summary

Respect licenses and give credit for code you did not write, including code from AI assistants. Keep confidential data out of outside tools. Design so that everyone can use your software: words instead of color alone, and formats that match each reader's culture. Communicate honestly about what your software does and does not do.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^mit]: Open Source Initiative. *The MIT License*. <https://opensource.org/license/mit>

[^gpl]: Free Software Foundation. *What is Copyleft?* <https://www.gnu.org/licenses/copyleft.en.html>

[^wcag]: W3C (2023, updated 2024). *Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2*. <https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/>

# Project

After OOP (Chapters 10-12), instructors may select the {doc}`database business application capstone <databases/index>` as a persistence milestone. A separate {doc}`AI application extension <project/ai_extension>` adds one narrowly scoped suggestion feature with an offline demonstration. Neither is required for the core individual or group project.

Using AI during development is a different question. Follow the course policy, understand every submitted part, and record accepted suggestions and verification evidence. Paid AI access is not a requirement for the book's core exercises or review activities.
The course includes two projects that use what you have learned to build a complete program.

| Project | Work | When | Page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Individual project** | Alone | Midterm | {doc}`Individual Project <project/individual_project>` |
| **Group project** | Team of 3-4 | Final | {doc}`Group Project <project/group_project>` |

The individual project proves you can build a program on your own. The group project adds teamwork, shared design, and a larger program. Your instructor sets the dates for each project and its checkpoints.

headings.title: Platform Compatibility
body:
## Platform Compatibility

The course project is intended to give you a path to build a desktop application. Project instructions will identify the framework, supported operating systems, and required tools before you begin. Not every framework supports every desktop operating system.

For example, .NET MAUI supports Windows and macOS desktop targets, but Microsoft does not officially support Linux desktop apps with MAUI ([supported platforms](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/maui/supported-platforms?view=net-maui-10.0)). If you use Linux as your primary computer, do not assume a MAUI project will build or run locally. Contact your instructor before committing to an app idea so you can arrange an approved alternative or access to a supported environment. This limitation does not affect the book's regular C# exercises and console projects.

headings.title: Individual Project
body:
(individual-project)=

# Individual Project

The individual project is the midterm project. You build it alone, in VS Code, and submit it through GitHub. It shows that you can design, write, test, and explain a complete C# program without a team. The group project that follows builds on these skills.

headings.title: Objectives
body:
## Objectives

- Choose a small, realistic business or management problem and describe it clearly
- Design a program from input, processing, and output (the IPO model)
- Use variables, selection, loops, methods, and collections to implement it
- Test the program with ordinary and edge-case inputs
- Document how to build and run the program
- Use Git to save your work in steps

headings.title: Choosing a Topic
body:
## Choosing a Topic

Pick a problem a small organization might actually have. Examples:

- An inventory tracker for a campus store
- A shift scheduler for a restaurant
- An expense report summarizer for a project budget
- A grade or attendance calculator for a training program

Submit a short proposal first (the problem, who uses the program, and the inputs and outputs) so your instructor can catch topics that are too large or too small. A console application is the expected form. A desktop or graphical app is optional; see the platform notes in {doc}`Project <../project>`.

headings.title: Requirements
body:
## Requirements

Your program must:

1. Run with `dotnet run` on your computer without errors
2. Read input from the user or from a file and validate it
3. Use at least one method that takes parameters and returns a value
4. Use a loop and a decision (`if` or `switch`)
5. Store related data in a collection such as a `List<T>` or an array
6. Print clear, formatted results
7. Handle at least two kinds of bad input without crashing

Use only the C# features covered so far in the course.

headings.title: What to Turn In
body:
## What to Turn In

- A GitHub repository containing your project folder and a `README.md` that states the problem, how to run the program, and a sample run
- At least five commits with meaningful messages that show how the program grew
- A short written reflection: what you built, one design decision you would change, and one bug you fixed and how
- A short demo of the program in class, if your instructor asks for one

Submit the repository link through the course assignment system. Your instructor sets the due dates for the proposal, a progress check, and the final submission.

headings.title: How It Is Graded
body:
## How It Is Graded

| Area | What your instructor looks for |
| --- | --- |
| Correctness | The program runs and produces right results |
| Design | Clear methods, meaningful names, and sensible use of collections |
| Testing | Ordinary and edge-case inputs tried, and bad input handled |
| Documentation | A README someone else can follow |
| Process | Regular, well-described commits |

headings.title: Group Project

(group-project)=

# Group Project

The group project is the final project. You will work in a team of 3-4 people for the rest of the semester, applying what you learned in the individual midterm project to a larger program. See {doc}`Project <../project>` for how the two projects fit together and for platform notes.

headings.title: Objectives
body:
## Objectives

- Being creative, imagining and describing a program, and working it
  through to completion

- Working in a team:

  - Communicating to each other
  - Dividing responsibilities
  - Helping each other
  - Finding consensus
  - Dealing with conflict
  - Providing process feedback
  - Integrating parts created by several people

- Developing new classes to fit your needs

- Using the .Net API library

- Designing a program for refinement

- Testing

- Evolving a program

- Creating documentation for user and implementers

- Programming in the large -- not a small predefined problem

- Make something that is fun

See the project {file}`csproject_stub`, already discussed in class.

**What to turn in:**

- Periodic reports
- intermediate implementation
- a final presentation
- a final implementation
  including user and programmer documentation and process documentation

headings.title: Overview
body:
## Overview

You will be assigned to groups of 3-4 people to work on a project that
will extend until the end of the semester, with only a little other work
introduced in class, and of course your last exam. This leaves a month
of course time (in a regular semester)
for the project (classes, labs, dedicated homework time),
ending with presentations in final exam period. Your group will be
designing and implementing a project of your choosing. You could
choose to make a text based game, starting from our game skeleton or not,
or something completely different, started from scratch.
The project should have some clear focus or aim,
For instance a game should be able to be won.

Start by brainstorming and listing ideas -- do not criticize ideas at
this point. That is what is meant by brainstorming - having your internal critic
going inhibits creativity. After you have a large list from
brainstorming, it is time to think more practically and settle on one
basic situation, and think of a considerable list of features you would
like it to have. Order the features, considering importance, apparent ease of
development, and what depends on what else. Get something simple
working, and then add a few features at a time, testing the pieces added
and the whole project so far. Test, debug, and make sure the program
works completely before using your past experience to decide what to add
next. This may different than what you imagined before the work on your
first stage! Like the provided project, early stages do not need
to be full featured, but make sure that you are building up to a version
with an aim, and which includes interesting features. You should
end with a program that has enough instructions provided for the user, so
someone who knows *nothing* of your implementation process or intentions
can use the program successfully. Your implementation should also be
documented, imagining that a new team of programmers is about to take
over after your departure, looking to create yet another version.

headings.title: Your Team
body:
## Your Team

Your instructor will tell you about team makeup.

There are a number of roles
that must be filled by team members. Some will be shared between all
members, like coder, but for each role there should be a lead person who
makes sure all the contributions come together. Each person will have
more than one role. All members are expected to pull their own weight,
though not all in exactly the same roles. Everyone should make sustained
contributions, every week, documented in the weekly reports. Understand
that this project will be the major course commitment for the rest of
the semester. These roles vary from rather small to central.
Not all are important immediately.

headings.title: Roles
body:
## Roles

1. Leader: Makes sure the team is coordinated, encourage consensus on
   the overall plan, oversee that the agreements are carried through, be
   available as contact person for the team and the TA and your instructor.
2. Lead programmer: Keep track of different people's parts to make sure
   they fit together.
3. Coder/unit tester: *Everyone* must have a significant but not
   necessarily equal part in this job. Each person should have primary
   responsibility for one or more cohesive substantive units, and code
   and test and be particularly familiar with those parts. Do your best
   to make individual parts be cohesive and loosely coupled with other
   people's work, to save a lot of pain in the testing and debugging
   phase. When coding you are still encouraged to do pair programming,
   though what pair from the team is working together at different times
   may be fluid. The lead programmer might be involved in pairs more
   often than others, but be sure the other coders get to drive often.
4. Librarian/version coordinator: The default should be for you to have a
   box.com folder shared with your whole team and me and your TA, with all
   as editors. Your folder should have the name of your team.
   You should always have a folder that contains the latest working version
   of the project. You should also keep old versions, for instance copied into
   numbered version folders.
   Box does not handle successive versions automatically.
   You can choose
   to use the more capable professional combination of
   GitHub and {doc}`Git <../github>`.
   The latter will have a learning curve, and in that case this person
   should be the best informed on Git, and help
   the other team members.
5. Report coordinator: Gather the contributions for reports from team
   members and make sure the whole reports get to posted on schedule.
   Your instructor needs
   a clear idea of the contributions of each member each week. If a team
   member is not clear on this to the report writer,
   *the report writer needs to be insistent*.
6. Instruction coordinator: Make sure there are clear written documents
   and help within the program for the user, who you assume is not a
   C# programmer and knows nothing about your program at the start.
7. Documentation coordinator: Make sure the documentation
   is clear for method users/consumers.
   This includes the documentation for programmers
   before the headings of methods and classes.
   This is for any time someone wants to use (not rewrite) a class or
   method you wrote.
   Also have implementer documentation, for someone who will
   want to modify or debug your code and needs to understand the
   details of your internal implementations. The extent of this
   can be greatly minimized by good naming.
8. Quality manager: Take charge of integrated tests of the whole program
   (following coder's unit tests). Make sure deficiencies are addressed.

Conflict resolution: You will certainly have disagreements and possibly
conflicts. Try to resolve them within the team. When that is not
working, anyone can go to the instructor with a problem. Do not delay
coming to me if things are clearly not working with the team.

headings.title: The process
body:
## The process

Initial:

1. Agree on roles. These roles can change if necessary, but you are
   encouraged to stick with them for simplicity and consistency.
2. Agree on a team name and a short no-space abbreviation if necessary,
   and let me know it.
3. Brainstorm about the project. Distill the ideas into a direction and
   overall goals.

On individual versions (Two formal versions will be required):

1. Break out specific goals for the version. How are you heading for
   your overall goals? Are you biting off a significant and manageable
   amount? You are expected to check in with me on this part and 2 and 3
   before moving very far. This will be new for most of you.
2. Plan and organize the necessary parts and the interfaces between the
   parts.
3. Write the interface documentation for consumers of the code
   for the parts you plan to write.
   Agree on them. You need to do this eventually anyway. Agreement up
   front can save you an enormous amount of time! Do not let the gung-ho
   hackers take off before you agree on documented interfaces.
   We have seen it happen: If you do not put your foot down,
   you are stuck with a bad plan that will complicate things. Otherwise lots
   of code needs to be rethought and rewritten.
4. If more than one person is working on the same class, plan the names,
   meanings, and restrictions on the private instance variables -- all
   coders should be assuming the same things about the instance
   variables! Also agree on documentation for any private helping methods you
   share.
5. Code to match the agreed consumer interface and class implementation
   designs.
6. Check each other's code.
7. Do unit tests on your own work, and fix them and test again...
8. Do overall tests of everything together, and fix and test again...
9. Look back at what you did, how it went, what you could do better, and
   what to change in your process for the next version.

You are strongly encouraged to follow modern programming practice which
involves splitting each of these formal versions into much smaller steps
that can be completed and tested following a similar process. Order
pieces so you only need to code a little bit more before testing and
combining with pieces that already work. This is enormously helpful in
isolating bugs! This is really important. If you thought you spent a
long while fighting bugs in your small homework assignment, that is
nothing compared to the time you can spend with a large project,
particularly if you make a lot of haphazard changes all at once.

headings.title: Splitting Up The Coding
body:
## Splitting Up The Coding

Make good use of the
separation of public interface and detailed implementation.
If your project has loosely coupled class, the main part of the
public interface should be limited and easy to comprehend.

Ideally have one individual
(or pair) assigned a whole class. One useful feature for allowing
compiling is to first generate a stub file like we have given you for
homework, that includes the public interface documentation,
headings, and dummy return values
and compiles but does nothing.
*Post this under a box folder for the current version number.*
You will then provide your team members
with something that tells them what they can use and allows them to
compile their own part. Then later substitute more functional classes.

Your instructor and you will want to review your code. We do not want to have to
reread almost the same thing over and over: Use the editor copy command
with extreme caution. If you are considering making an exact copy,
clearly use a common method instead. If you copy and then make
substitutions in the same places, you are likely better off
with a method with the common parts and with parameters inserted where there
are differences. You can make a quick test with a
couple of copied portions, but then
*convert to using a method with parameters for the substitutions*.
Besides being a waste of effort to define seven methods each
defining a tool, with just a few strings differing from one method to
the next, we will require you to rewrite it, with one method with
parameters, and just seven different calls to the method with different
parameters. Save yourself trouble and do it that way the first time, or
at least after you code a second method and see how much it is like the
first one you coded....

If you are making many substitutions
of static textual data, put the data into a resource file in a variation
of the Fake Advise Lab.

You only want to commit working code into the shared current version folder.
Comment out incomplete additions that you want to show to everyone,
or comment out the call to a method that compiles but does not yet
function logically. An alternative is to have a separate folder for
in-process code to share for comment,
so you will not try to compile it with the current working version.

headings.title: Weekly reports
body:
## Weekly reports

Reports are due from the report writer each Tuesday.

1. Inside your team's box folder have a subfolder called WeeklyReports.
   A sample stub form to fill out on the computer is in
   [Weekly-Report.rtf](http://anh.cs.luc.edu/170/examples/Weekly-Report.rtf).
   Make the name of each weekly
   report document be the date it was due, like Mar26.rtf.
   It is easy
   to copy the table from this week to last week and edit it to show
   how much your plans matched reality.
   You should post a version for your team to look at first. Please distinguish
   drafts from the final version for me to look at. You might have a separate
   folder Drafts, and move the report into the WeeklyReport folder when
   it is final. Box easily allows moving files, but not renaming them.
2. Only one report should be generated each week, with the person in the role of
   report writer making sure a complete version is produced and placed in the
   WeeklyReport folder.
3. Under plans for the next week, include concrete tasks planned to be
   completed, and who will do them, with an informative
   explanation. The content and depth of the person's work should be clear.
   If you can state that clearly and be brief, great.
   The tasks do not only include coding: they can be any of the
   parts listed above, and for any particular part of the project, where
   that makes sense. *If individuals cannot state clearly what they are working on,*
   *then the team leader and lead coder have a significant issue in their leadership*
   *that needs to be addressed.*
4. In the review of the last week (after the first week) include the
   last week's plans and what actually happened, task by task,
   concretely, with enough detail to give an idea on the magnitude
   of the work. This can include the portion completed and/or changes in
   the plans and their reasons. "Still working on X" is not useful: Who
   was doing what? What methods, doing what, were completed? Which are
   in process? Which are being debugged? What part remains to be done,
   and who is it assigned to? The report writer is responsible to get a
   clear statement from each team member.

headings.title: Intermediate deliverables
body:
## Intermediate deliverables

These materials should be placed in a subfolder **Intermediate**
of your team project folder.
See the due date in the schedule.

- Copy the linked stub of
  [projectPlans.rtf](http://anh.cs.luc.edu/170/examples/projectPlans.rtf) document.
  Then complete it:

  - List the project roles again, and who ended up filling them. For
    coding, say who was the person primarily responsible for each
    part.
  - If you used old classes, like those from the skeleton project or a lab or
    somewhere else, say which ones are included *unchanged* or give a
    summary of changes.
  - If your documentation of methods is not generally done,
    say what classes got clear documentation (or individual methods if only
    some were done).
  - Where are you planning to go from here, and who you envision being
    primarily responsible for different parts?

- Include parts 2-4 listed below under Final Deliverables, but for an
  intermediate version that runs, and does *not* need to have the goal
  working yet. Have documentation of your methods, including summary description
  and description of parameters and return values.
  If for some reason you do not have all the documentation that you were encouraged
  to write *first*, at least be sure to have and point out significant examples of your
  clear documentation of purpose, parameters, and return values.
  This allows instructor feedback
  for completing the rest.

- The idea is to have everyone get an idea of what is expected, so we
  have no misunderstandings about the final version. We will give you
  feedback from this version to incorporate in the final version. We do
  not want to have to say anyone did anything "wrong" on the final
  version. We want to be able to concentrate on your creative
  accomplishments.

- Look through the list of deliverables again and make sure your collection is complete.

headings.title: Final Deliverables
body:
## Final Deliverables

**Group Submission**:

One submission of the group work is due one hour before the final presentations.

1. All files listed in parts 2-5.
   Also include a zip file, named with your team abbreviation,
   containing a Windows executable with (a separate copy of) any other
   image and data files needed. Test to make sure you can
   unzip and run the executable.
   The final submissions will be accessible to the whole class
   -- so we can all play them!

2. Source code. You can name the classes appropriately
   for the content of your game.

3. User instructions. These should be partly built into the program. The
   most extensive documentation may be in a document file separate from
   the program, if you like. (Plain text, MS Word, Rich text (rtf), or
   PDF, please.) The starting message built into the beginning of the
   game should mention the file name of such external documentation, if
   you have it.

4. Programmer documentation. Document the public interface for all
   methods in comments directly before the method heading.
   Add implementation comments
   embedded in the code where they add clarity (not just verbosity). You
   may have a separate overview document. Include "Overview" in the
   file name

5. Overall project and process review in a document named like the linked stub,
   [projectReview.rtf](http://anh.cs.luc.edu/170/examples/projectReview.rtf).

   - The first section should be Changes. So the instructor does not
     duplicate effort, please give an overview of the changes from the
     intermediate version. What classes are the same? What features
     were added? What classes are new? Which classes or methods were
     given major rewrites? What classes had only a few changes? (In
     this case try to list what to look for.)
   - List again the roles, and who filled them. For coding, say who was
     the person primarily responsible for each part.
   - What did you learn? What were the biggest challenges? What would
     you do differently the next time? What are you most proud of?
   - How could we administer this project better? What particularly
     worked about the structure we set up?

6. A 10-15 minute presentation of your work to the class in final exam
   period. What would you want to hear about other projects? (Say it
   about yours.) What was the overall idea? What was the overall
   organization? What did you learn that was beyond the regular class
   topics that others might find useful to know? What were your biggest
   challenges? Do not show off all your code just because it is there.
   Show specific bits that gave you trouble or otherwise are
   instructive, if you like.

Look through the list of deliverables again, before sending files,
and check with the whole team to make sure your collection is complete.

**Your Assessment of Individuals in the Group**:

This is due electronically 10 minutes after the final class presentation period,
from each team member, *independently*, turned in a manner specified by your
instructor, like other homework assignments.

Change the name of the linked stub file
[Indiv-Mem-Assessment.rtf](http://anh.cs.luc.edu/170/examples/Indiv-Mem-Assessment.rtf)
to your
teamAbbreviation-yourName.rtf.
You may want to tweak it after the
group presentation, but have it essentially done beforehand.

Writing this is NOT a part of your
collective group deliberations. It is individual in two senses: both
in being about individual team members and in being the view of *one*
individual, you. For this document only, everyone should be writing
separately, privately, and independently from individual experience.
If you lack data on some point, say so, rather than using what others are saying.

body:

Follow your course's AI policy. If permitted assistance contributes to the work, identify the tool/date, summarize the suggestion and your revision, and show the tests or traces you performed independently. Be prepared to explain and modify the code yourself. A polished generated result is not evidence of that understanding.

The core project can use collections and files. After OOP, instructors may select the {doc}`database capstone <../databases/index>` or the {doc}`AI application extension <ai_extension>`.
