headings.title: Databases and Bookstore Inventory
body:
(database_appendix)= # Databases and Bookstore Inventory Use this appendix as an **optional business application capstone after OOP (Chapters 10-12)**. It connects collections, files, classes, validation, and tests to persistent records in SQLite. An instructor may allocate about one to two weeks when assigning the track, or select it as a project milestone. It is not a prerequisite for completing CS1 or beginning the CS2 data-structures foundation. The connected example is a bookstore inventory application. Business examples earlier in the book can remain realistic with synthetic data, collections, and files; they do not all need databases. - **Relational data**: Tables and keys organize persistent business records. - **SQL**: Queries and change commands read and maintain those records. - **Parameterized command**: Values travel separately from SQL instructions. - **Inventory application**: Objects connect database rows to useful operations.

Learning Objectives

1. Model books and sales with primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints. 2. Write filtering, aggregation, join, and change commands. 3. Run a C# SQLite project and map query results into objects. 4. Implement and check inventory operations using parameters. 5. Explain why recording a sale and reducing stock should succeed together.

Appendix Flow

- {doc}`1. Relational Data and SQL ` - {doc}`2. C# and SQLite ` - {doc}`3. Bookstore Inventory Lab `

How to Use This Appendix

The first two sections cover tables, keys, constraints, basic queries and joins, parameterized changes, and a working C# application. Database administration, ORM frameworks, migrations, and advanced SQL tuning are outside this capstone's scope. The first two sections explain the concepts and a working application. The third is a connected lab completed in VS Code. The sales transaction is an extension. This appendix does not add a required week to either semester; instructors may use it as a project persistence milestone. Demonstrate that a validated change persists after closing and reopening the file database. Explain how the database enforces a rule that application code also checks. The sales extension illustrates two changes that must commit or roll back together.

Glossary

| Term | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Schema | The structure and constraints of database tables. | | Primary key | A value uniquely identifying a row. | | Foreign key | A reference to a related row. | | Transaction | A group of changes committed or rolled back together. | | Parameter | A separately supplied value used by a SQL command. |

headings.title: Relational Data and SQL
body:
# Relational Data and SQL

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

A text file is useful for a small export. A relational database becomes useful when records must be related, checked, queried, and updated over many program runs. Use a bookstore to connect the data model to familiar business questions: what is in stock, which books sell, and which records belong together?

The SQL below explains the model. Run queries against a disposable database using a SQLite tool, or adapt the command pattern in the next section. These fenced SQL examples are not browser Run C# cells.

headings.title: Relational Model
body:
## Relational Model

```{index} Relational Model
```
A database stores information so it can outlive one run of a program. A **relational database** organizes that information into tables with rows, columns, keys, and relationships.


```{index} table; database
```
```{index} row; database
```
```{index} column; database
```

headings.title: Tables, Rows, and Columns
body:
### Tables, Rows, and Columns

```{index} Tables, Rows, and Columns
```
A **table** represents one kind of thing: students, products, orders, books, tickets, or appointments. Each **row** is one item in that table. Each **column** stores one attribute of that item.

| StudentId | FirstName | LastName | Major |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 101 | Ana | Kim | IT |
| 102 | Miles | Chen | CS |
| 103 | Jordan | Smith | Data Analytics |

A good table usually has a clear noun as its name and one row per real-world item.


```{index} primary key
```
```{index} foreign key
```

headings.title: Primary Keys and Foreign Keys
body:
### Primary Keys and Foreign Keys

```{index} Primary Keys and Foreign Keys
```
A **primary key** uniquely identifies one row in a table. `StudentId` is better than `FirstName` because names can repeat.

A **foreign key** stores the primary key from another table. It lets tables refer to each other without copying the same information repeatedly.

| CourseId | CourseName |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | Intro to Programming |
| 20 | Database Systems |

| EnrollmentId | StudentId | CourseId |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 101 | 10 |
| 2 | 101 | 20 |
| 3 | 102 | 10 |

The `Enrollments` table connects students to courses. This avoids storing course names inside every student row.


```{index} relationship; database
```

headings.title: Relationships
body:
### Relationships

```{index} Relationships
```
Common relationships include:

- **One-to-many**: one customer can have many orders.
- **Many-to-many**: many students can take many courses, usually through a linking table such as `Enrollments`.
- **One-to-one**: one user has one profile, when the details are separated for security or organization.

When designing a database, first name the entities, then choose columns, then decide which keys connect the tables.


```{index} schema
```

headings.title: A Small Schema
body:
### A Small Schema

```{index} A Small Schema
```
A **schema** is the planned structure of a database. Here is a small bookstore schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE Books (
    BookId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    Title TEXT NOT NULL,
    Author TEXT NOT NULL,
    Price REAL NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE Sales (
    SaleId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    BookId INTEGER NOT NULL,
    Quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    SoldOn TEXT NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (BookId) REFERENCES Books(BookId)
);
```

`Books` stores facts about each book. `Sales` stores events that happened over time. The foreign key tells us which book each sale refers to.

headings.title: Practice
body:
### Practice

```{index} Practice
```
1. For a library system, list three tables you would create.
2. Choose a primary key for each table.
3. Identify one foreign key relationship between two tables.

headings.title: Queries
body:
## Queries

```{index} Queries
```
**SQL** is the language used to ask questions about relational data. The most common command is `SELECT`, which reads rows from one or more tables.


```{index} SELECT; SQL
```

headings.title: Selecting Columns
body:
### Selecting Columns

```{index} Selecting Columns
```
`SELECT` names the columns to return. `FROM` names the table.

```sql
SELECT Title, Author, Price
FROM Books;
```

Use `SELECT *` only for quick exploration. In application code, name the columns so your program depends on an explicit shape.


```{index} WHERE; SQL
```
```{index} ORDER BY; SQL
```

headings.title: Filtering and Sorting
body:
### Filtering and Sorting

```{index} Filtering and Sorting
```
`WHERE` keeps only rows that match a condition. `ORDER BY` controls the result order.

```sql
SELECT Title, Price
FROM Books
WHERE Price < 25.00
ORDER BY Price DESC;
```

The database does the filtering before your C# program receives the rows. That is usually faster and clearer than loading every row and filtering later.


```{index} aggregation; SQL
```
```{index} GROUP BY; SQL
```

headings.title: Aggregation
body:
### Aggregation

```{index} Aggregation
```
Aggregate functions summarize many rows into one result.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS BookCount,
       AVG(Price) AS AveragePrice
FROM Books;
```

`GROUP BY` summarizes rows within each group.

```sql
SELECT Author, COUNT(*) AS BooksWritten
FROM Books
GROUP BY Author
ORDER BY BooksWritten DESC;
```


```{index} JOIN; SQL
```

headings.title: Joining Tables
body:
### Joining Tables

```{index} Joining Tables
```
A `JOIN` combines rows from related tables. The `ON` clause says how the keys match.

```sql
SELECT Books.Title,
       Sales.Quantity,
       Sales.SoldOn
FROM Sales
JOIN Books ON Sales.BookId = Books.BookId
ORDER BY Sales.SoldOn;
```

This query reads sale rows and attaches the book title for each sale. Without the join, the sale row would only have a `BookId`.

headings.title: Practice
body:
### Practice

```{index} Practice
```
Using the `Books` and `Sales` tables, write SQL queries that:

1. list all books by one author;
2. show the three most expensive books;
3. count how many sales exist for each book; and
4. list sale dates with book titles and quantities.

headings.title: Changing Data Safely
body:
## Changing Data Safely

```{index} Changing Data Safely
```
Queries read data. Information systems also need commands that add, modify, and remove rows. These commands should be written carefully because they change persistent state.


```{index} INSERT; SQL
```

headings.title: Inserting Rows
body:
### Inserting Rows

```{index} Inserting Rows
```
`INSERT` adds a new row. Name the columns so the command stays readable if the table later gains another column.

```sql
INSERT INTO Books (Title, Author, Price)
VALUES ('Clean Code', 'Robert C. Martin', 39.99);
```

If the primary key is auto-generated, the database fills it in for you.


```{index} UPDATE; SQL
```

headings.title: Updating Rows
body:
### Updating Rows

```{index} Updating Rows
```
`UPDATE` changes existing rows. Almost every `UPDATE` should include a `WHERE` clause.

```sql
UPDATE Books
SET Price = 34.99
WHERE BookId = 1;
```

Without `WHERE`, the command changes every row in the table. That is rarely what you mean.


```{index} DELETE; SQL
```

headings.title: Deleting Rows
body:
### Deleting Rows

```{index} Deleting Rows
```
`DELETE` removes rows. It also needs a precise `WHERE` clause.

```sql
DELETE FROM Books
WHERE BookId = 1;
```

Many applications avoid hard deletion for important business records. They add a column such as `IsArchived` instead, so the history remains available.


```{index} parameterized command
```
```{index} SQL injection
```

headings.title: Parameterized Commands
body:
### Parameterized Commands

```{index} Parameterized Commands
```
Never build SQL by pasting user input into a string.

```csharp
// Unsafe: user text becomes part of the SQL program
string sql = "SELECT * FROM Books WHERE Title = '" + title + "'";
```

Use parameters instead. The SQL text and user data stay separate.

```csharp
string sql = "SELECT * FROM Books WHERE Title = @title";
command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@title", title);
```

Parameterized commands protect against SQL injection and also make values such as dates and numbers easier to pass correctly.

headings.title: Practice
body:

```{index} Practice
```
1. Write an `INSERT` command for a new book.
2. Write an `UPDATE` command that changes a book price by `BookId`.
3. Write a `DELETE` command that removes a sale by `SaleId`.
4. Rewrite this unsafe condition with a parameter: `WHERE Author = '" + author + "'`.

headings.title: Inventory Constraints and Money
body:
## Inventory Constraints and Money

```{index} Inventory Constraints and Money
```
The lab uses `Books(BookId, Title, PriceCents, Stock)` and `Sales(SaleId, BookId, Quantity)`. Prices are integer cents so a value such as 1999 represents 19.99 without binary floating-point rounding. Require nonnegative prices and stock, positive sale quantities, and a valid book for each sale.

```sql
CREATE TABLE Books (
    BookId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    Title TEXT NOT NULL,
    PriceCents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (PriceCents >= 0),
    Stock INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (Stock >= 0)
);
CREATE TABLE Sales (
    SaleId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    BookId INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Books(BookId),
    Quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (Quantity > 0)
);
```

The earlier `Books` and `Sales` schema illustrates relationships and dates; this smaller lab schema concentrates on stock. Use one schema consistently within a database. SQLite foreign-key checking is enabled explicitly when the application opens its connection.

Predict which constraint rejects each action: a negative stock count, a sale of zero books, and a sale for an unknown book. Then explain why valid individual rows still do not guarantee that a sale and its stock adjustment happen together.


```{rubric} Footnotes
```
[^1]: Use the supplied local teaching database, rather than a production database.

Download or clone the book repository and open `demos/_extras/bookstore_inventory/`. Its project file pins the SQLite provider version used by the reference implementation.

```sh
cd demos/_extras/bookstore_inventory
```

headings.title: Connections, Commands, and Disposal
Map Rows to Objects
body:
## Map Rows to Objects

```{index} Map Rows to Objects
```
`Book` groups an ID, title, price in cents, and stock. `Inventory.List` uses an explicit column order and reads each row into a new `Book`. `Find` returns either one book or `null`; missing data is an expected result, not automatically an exception.

Read `ReadBook` and match every reader position to its selected column. Predict what could go wrong if a query changed column order without updating the mapper. Keep each command's result shape explicit.

headings.title: Supply Parameters and Check Outcomes
body:
## Supply Parameters and Check Outcomes

```{index} Supply Parameters and Check Outcomes
```
`Add` passes the title, price, and stock as values. A title such as `Manager's SQL Guide` needs no manual quote replacement. `SetStock` uses an ID condition and reports whether exactly one row changed. Reject invalid quantities before sending the command, and keep database constraints as a second boundary.

In the source, compare `Find` with `SetStock`: both use an ID parameter, but one reads a row and the other checks the affected-row count. Explain the expected result for an unknown ID in each operation.

headings.title: Transactions for Related Changes
body:
## Transactions for Related Changes

```{index} Transactions for Related Changes
```
The optional `Sell` operation begins a transaction, reduces stock only if enough remains, inserts a sale, and commits. If the book is missing or stock is insufficient, it rolls back and returns `false`. If an unexpected error occurs before commit, disposal rolls back the uncommitted transaction.

Every command participating in the transaction sets its `Transaction` property. Updating stock and inserting the sale independently could leave only one change saved after a failure. Atomicity means these changes are committed together.

headings.title: Verify Before Extending
body:
## Verify Before Extending

```{index} Verify Before Extending
```

headings.title: Injection
body:
```{index} injection; SQL injection
```

## Injection
**Injection** happens when a program builds a command, such as a database query, by gluing user input into the command text. Input crafted by an attacker then becomes part of the command:

The second query treats supplied text as part of SQL syntax. This example builds strings only; it does not execute them. Use the parameterized commands taught in this appendix to pass values separately from command text. The input is then treated as data rather than SQL syntax.

`dotnet run -- --check` checks seed data, missing IDs, apostrophes in titles, updates, successful sales, overselling, and invalid inputs. Read the assertions before editing. Then run twice without `--check` and explain why the stored inventory persists while the check database starts fresh each time.

Keep real customer data and production credentials out of this exercise. For a semester project, document the schema, initialization, reset procedure, and tested failure cases alongside the program.


```{rubric} Footnotes
```
[^1]: Use the supplied local teaching database, rather than a production database.

headings.title: Graph Structures Lab
body: # Graph Structures Lab

```{contents}
:local:
:depth: 2
```

headings.title: Build and Inspect Route Data
body:
## Build and Inspect Route Data

```{index} weighted graph; route data; graph contract
```

Use the facilities team's six-room graph to verify the representation before adding search algorithms. Remote is an intentional isolate. Office–Storage has zero rounded minutes, an intentional boundary case. All other route costs are nonnegative, and each route is two-way.

Download {download}`the complete RouteGraph source and verification program <../../demos/20_graphs/RouteGraph.cs>` for a console project. Each example below includes its own setup and class so it can run independently.

headings.title: Updates and Boundary Checks
body:
## Updates and Boundary Checks

```{index} graph updates; isolated vertex; root-independent structure
```

Graphs have no distinguished root under this model. Any vertex may be removed without deleting the whole structure. Choose update expectations before running the following lifecycle.

| Update | Vertex count | Edge count | Reason |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Initial graph | 6 | 4 | Includes Remote and a zero-weight edge. |
| Replace Hall–Lab with five minutes | 6 | 4 | Same endpoints, updated weight. |
| Remove Hall–Office | 6 | 3 | Delete one logical edge in two directions. |
| Remove Hall | 5 | 1 | Remaining Hall–Lobby and Hall–Lab edges disappear. |
| Add Remote–Lobby | 5 | 2 | Previously isolated vertices become adjacent. |

The resulting graph remains disconnected: one component joins Remote/Lobby, one joins Office/Storage, and Lab is isolated. Update correctness is about preserving the stored relationships; a valid graph need not be connected.

headings.title: Export and Compare a Weighted Matrix
body:
## Export and Compare a Weighted Matrix

```{index} representation conversion; matrix equivalence
```

Export the same graph to a nullable matrix. Choose a label order and keep it with the matrix, because a cell's indexes have no meaning without that mapping. The converter's labels must be exactly the graph's distinct vertices; the example obtains them from a vertex snapshot.

Visit every stored adjacency entry and fill its cell. All other cells stay null. An isolate produces an empty row and column. The converter uses O(V²) time/space for array initialization plus O(V + E) work to enumerate the graph. The final representation still has matrix cost, even though the source is sparse.

Pair-by-pair comparison checks both presence and weight. Comparing only non-null weights could miss an unintended edge; treating zero as absence could miss the Office–Storage route. Matrix symmetry is necessary for this undirected model, but symmetry alone does not establish that all intended edges survived conversion.

headings.title: Validate a Supplied Walk
body:
## Validate a Supplied Walk

```{index} walk validation; weighted cost; direct edge
```

A walk checker receives a route chosen elsewhere. It does not discover a route or prove optimality. Validate each label and each consecutive edge, then sum the weights. A repeated vertex is legal for a walk, so a return trip contributes its edges again.

Use a long total to accumulate integer weights without overflowing an int on a long route. Return false for an empty route, an unknown vertex, or a missing direct edge. A known singleton route succeeds with cost zero. On failure, leave the output at zero rather than returning a partial trip cost.

The valid examples cost seven, eight, and zero minutes. The remaining examples are invalid. The first is a path; the second is a walk that revisits Lobby; the third demonstrates an isolated vertex. None of these results says that a route between two endpoints is shortest.

This wrapper snapshots V labels to check singleton existence, so setup takes O(V) time/space. Checking a supplied route of L labels then takes expected O(L) time under the hash assumptions. A graph API with direct vertex membership could avoid that snapshot; this implementation makes the tradeoff visible rather than hiding it.

headings.title: Exercise
body:
## Exercise

```{index} graph verification; exercise
```

headings.title: Summary
body:
## Summary

```{index} graph representation; verification
```

Graph storage must preserve its model rules across every update. Keep isolates, update both directions for undirected edges, distinguish zero from absence, and compare representations by both membership and weight. Validate a supplied walk before summing it; leave route discovery and optimization to the later algorithm chapters.

```{rubric} Footnotes
```

[^1]: Chapter 24 uses weighted graphs for greedy optimization; Chapter 26 develops traversal and reachability. This chapter supplies their representation foundation.

headings.title: Operator Definitions
Pictorial Playing Computer
body:
```{index} Pictorial Playing Computer
```

## Pictorial Playing Computer

Let us start pictorially playing computer on {file}`test_rational.cs`,
as a review of much of the previous sections. We explicitly show a local variable
`this` to identify the current object in an instance method or constructor.

The first line of `Main`,

    Rational f = new Rational(6, -10);

creates a new Rational, so it calls the constructor. At the very beginning of the
constructor, a prototype `Rational` is already created as the current object,
so immediately, there is a `this`.
The parameters 6, and -10 are passed, initializing the explicit local
variables `numerator` and `denominator`.
The figure illustrates the memory state at the beginning of the constructor call:

`{image} ../../figures/callConstructor.png :width: 124 pt`

Note the immediate value assigned to the numeric instance variables is zero: This is
as discussed in {ref}`default-fields`.
Of course we do not want to keep those default values:
The constructor finds the value of the local variable `numerator`, and needs to
assign the value 6 to a variable `num`. The compiler has looked
first for a local variable `num`, and found none.
Then it looked *second* for an instance variable in the object pointed to
by `this`. It found `num` there. Now it copies the 6 into that location.
Similarly for `denominator` and `denom`:

`{image} ../../figures/callConstructorCopied.png :width: 124 pt`

Then the constructor calls `Normalize`.
Since `Normalize` is also an instance method,
a reference to `this` is passed implicitly.
While illustrating the memory state for more than one active method,
we separate each one with a horizontal segment.

`{image} ../../figures/callNormalize.png :width: 124 pt`

Later `Normalize` calls `GCD`. Since `GCD` is static, note that the local
variables for `GCD` do *not* contain a reference to `this`.

`{image} ../../figures/callGCD.png :width: 124 pt`

At the end of `GCD` the `int` 2 is returned and initializes
`n` in the calling method `Normalize`.
Then `Normalize` modifies the instance variable pointed to by `this`,
and finishes.

`{image} ../../figures/finishNormalize.png :width: 124 pt`

That is the same object `this` in the constructor.
Just before the constructor completes we have:

`{image} ../../figures/finishConstructor.png :width: 124 pt`

Then in `Main` the constructor’s `this` is the reference to the new object
initializing `f`.

`{image} ../../figures/setF.png :width: 120 pt`

Consider the next line of `Main`:

    Console.WriteLine("6/(-10) simplifies to {0}", f);

We omit the internals of the WriteLine call, except to note that it must convert
the reference `f` to a string. As with any object,
it does this by calling the `ToString` method for `f`,
so the implicit `this` in the call to `ToString` refers to the same object as `f`:

`{image} ../../figures/callToString.png :width: 196.5 pt`

`ToString` returns “-3/5”, and it gets printed as part of the line generated
by `WriteLine`….

We skip the similar details through two more `WriteLine` statements and the
initialization of `h`:

    Rational h = new Rational(1,2);

The `WriteLine`
statement after that needs to evaluate `f.Add(h)`, generating a call to `Add`.
The next figure shows the two local variables in `Main`, `f` and `h`, each
pointing to a `Rational` object. The image shows the situation
in the call to `Add`, just before the end of the return statement,
when the new Rational is being constructed.

In the local variables for the method `Add`
see what the implicit `this` refers to, and what the
(local to `Add`) variable `f` refer to. As the figure shows,
this use of a local variable
`f` is independent of the `f` in `Main`:

`{image} ../../figures/callAdd.png :width: 132 pt`

Since the return statement in `Add` creates a new object,
the figure shows a call to the
constructor from inside `Add`. We do not go through the details of another
constructor call, but
`this` in the constructor points to the Rational shown and returned by
`Add`:

`{image} ../../figures/endAdd.png :width: 132 pt`

which gets sent to the `WriteLine` statement
and gets printed in `Main` as in the earlier code.

Make sure you see how the pictures reinforce these important ideas:

- Keeping track of the `this` with
  constructors and instance methods (but not static methods).
- The aliasing of `Rational` objects used as parameters explicitly or
  implicitly (`this`).

We have played computer before in procedural programming,
following individually explicitly named
variables. This has allowed us to follow loops clearly after the code is
written. The pictorial version with multiple object references and method calls
is also useful for checking on code that is written with many object
references.

When first *writing* code with object references that you are manipulating,
a picture of the setup
showing the references in your data is also helpful.
New object-oriented programmers often have a hard time referring to the
data they want to work with.
If you have a picture of the data relationships
you can point with a finger to a part that you want to use.
For example
in the call to `Add`, one piece of data you need for your arithmetic is
the `num` field in `f`. Then you must be carful to note
that *only local variables can be referenced directly*
(including the implicit `this`). If you want to refer to data that is not a local
variable, you must follow the reference path arrow that leads *from a local variable* to
an instance field that you want to reference.

`{image} ../../figures/pathToNum.png :width: 132 pt`

Then use the proper object-oriented notation to refer to the path.
In the example, it takes one step,
from local variable `f` to its field `num`, referred to as `f.num`.
Similarly the current object’s `num` is connected through `this`, but C# shorthand
allows `this.` to be omitted. And so on, for `f.denom` and `denom`.

Visually following such paths will be even more important later, when we construct
more complex types of objects, and you need to follow
a path through *several* references in sequence.

```{index} exercise; ForceMatch
```

So why the distinction? We have mentioned that new objects created in a class are
accessed indirectly via a reference, as with an array. As a general category,
they are called *reference objects*. We distinguished the types `int` and
`double` and `bool`, where the actual value of the data is stored in the space
for a variable of the type. They are *value types*. A struct is also a value
type. In practice this is efficient for small objects of a fixed size.
We made Rational a class because
you have already seen the class construct with
`static` entries, and classes are more generally useful.
In fact being a `struct` would be a good choice for Rational,
since it only contains two integers. Its size is no more than one `double`.

The behavior of a Rational is the same either way, because it is immutable. If we
allowed mutating methods, then a class version and a struct version would not behave
the same way, due to the fact the reference types can have aliases,
and value types cannot.

There are some more complicated situations where there are further distinctions between
classes and structs, but we shall not concern ourselves
with those fine advanced points in this book.

# Curriculum Alignment (IS2020 and CS2023)

The primary audience is students in College of Business information systems programs. The IS2020 mapping therefore comes first and explains the book’s contribution to that pathway. The CS2023 mapping follows as a reference for its broader computer science foundation and optional technical depth. Neither mapping establishes complete degree-program coverage.

headings.title: IS2020 Mapping
body:
(is2020-alignment)=

```{index} curriculum alignment; IS2020
```

## IS2020 Mapping

*IS2020: A Competency Model for Undergraduate Programs in Information Systems* provides curriculum guidance from the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and the Association for Information Systems (AIS), including for IS/MIS programs in colleges of business.[^is2020] Its competency areas describe degree-level expectations. The following mapping is the author's interpretation of this book's contribution, not a claim of complete program coverage or graduate competency attainment.

**Direct** means the book explicitly teaches relevant introductory knowledge and skills. **Partial** means it introduces selected topics. **Supporting** means activities can contribute when instructors assess them in context. **Outside scope** means another course must supply the area. These descriptions are local mapping labels, not IS2020 proficiency levels.

| IS2020 required competency area | Book evidence | Contribution and boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Foundations of Information Systems | Chapter 1: computing concepts, input-process-output, and development workflow; the database appendix: persistent data. | **Partial.** Introduces computing and information processing; organizational IS roles and enterprise processes need a broader IS foundations course. |
| Data / Information Management | Chapters 7-9: arrays, collections, files, and text; Database appendix: relational models, keys, SQL queries and changes, and a C# database workflow. | **Direct introductory contribution.** Supports representing and persisting application data; database administration and organization-wide data governance require further study. |
| IT Infrastructure | Chapter 1: compiler/runtime roles and edit/build/run; Appendix B: SDK, editor, terminal, and REPL setup. | **Partial.** Provides a development environment foundation; networking, cloud infrastructure, and production operations are outside this sequence. |
| Secure Computing | Chapter 6: validation and error handling; Chapter 1: introductory privacy; Chapter 9: masking, validation, and safe logging; the database appendix: parameterized SQL. | **Partial.** Teaches selected secure coding practices; infrastructure defense and organizational security management require other courses. |
| Systems Analysis & Design | Chapter 1: development workflow; Chapters 10-12: classes, encapsulation, interfaces, and object-oriented design; Group Project appendix: feature planning and refinement. | **Partial.** Supports small application design; stakeholder elicitation and formal analysis/modeling methods need dedicated instruction. |
| Application Development / Programming | Chapters 1-12: C# fundamentals, testing, collections, object-oriented programs, with optional database access in the appendix; Chapters 13-20: data structures and their algorithmic foundations; optional Chapters 21-26: deeper analysis and algorithm design. | **Direct introductory contribution.** This is the book's main role in an IS program. Web/mobile development and production deployment remain outside scope. |
| Ethics, Use & Implications for Society | Chapter 1.2: social impact, ethical analysis, introductory privacy, accessibility, attribution, and responsible AI use; Chapter 6: failure cases; Chapter 9: privacy practice; Appendix C: professional practice. | **Direct introductory contribution.** Cases support ethical reasoning; instructors should also assess it in project and organizational decisions. |
| IS Management & Strategy | Business examples supply application context throughout the book. | **Outside scope.** Business examples alone do not teach IS strategy, governance, sourcing, or investment decisions. |
| IS Project Management | Group Project appendix: roles, periodic reports, staged implementations, team coordination, and presentations. | **Supporting.** Provides practice opportunities; formal scope, schedule, budget, and risk management require additional instruction and assessment. |
| IS Practicum | Group Project appendix: integrated implementation, testing, documentation, demonstration, and individual reflection. | **Supporting.** Can contribute to a practicum when the instructor specifies organizational requirements and assesses integration. A programming project alone does not establish full practicum coverage. |

## IS2020 Course Use and Evidence

Chapters 1-12 provide the programming and information-systems foundation for the College of Business pathway. Instructors select Parts IV-V (Chapters 13-20) for the CS2 foundation. Basic Big-O, searching and library sorting, recursive calls, and graph traversal appear there without requiring Parts VI-VII (Chapters 21-26), which provide optional algorithmic depth.

The IS2020 elective area **Object-Oriented Paradigm** has relevant support in Chapters 10-12 and the interfaces and generics of Chapter 13. Other specializations, such as web programming, mobile programming, and user interface design, need additional material.

An instructor can use completed programs and tests for programming evidence, SQL and schema exercises for data-management evidence, Chapter 1.2 case analyses for ethics evidence, and project reports and demonstrations for integration evidence. The optional database appendix includes a connected inventory lab; assess its SQL and schema work separately when it is assigned.

This mapping records learning opportunities in the published sequence. A program-level review must separately establish the required knowledge, skill levels, dispositions, and assessment evidence across its courses.

## CS2023 Mapping

The book is mapped to *Computer Science Curricula 2023* (CS2023), the joint curriculum guidelines of ACM, IEEE Computer Society, and AAAI.[^cs2023] CS2023 organizes computer science into knowledge areas, each divided into knowledge units such as `SDF-Fundamentals`. Its introductory sequence is built mainly from Software Development Fundamentals (SDF) and Algorithmic Foundations (AL). Semester 1 of this book corresponds to the CS2023 *CS I* course and Semester 2 to *CS II*, plus part of a separate algorithms course.

| Ch. | Topic | Primary CS2023 units | Also touches |
|---|---|---|---|

Knowledge-area abbreviations: SDF (Software Development Fundamentals), AL (Algorithmic Foundations), FPL (Foundations of Programming Languages), SE (Software Engineering), DM (Data Management), SEC (Security), SEP (Society, Ethics, and the Profession), MSF (Mathematical and Statistical Foundations).

The mapping is a working draft. Chapter 1 introduces Society, Ethics, and the Profession (SEP), with further cases in Chapters 6 and 9 and Appendix C; coverage of functional and asynchronous programming is still being added. Formal languages and the mathematics units are left to theory and mathematics courses.
The integrated AI activities provide introductory AI literacy and programming-review evidence in Chapters 1, 3, 6, and 9. They do not constitute coverage of the full CS2023 Artificial Intelligence knowledge area or a machine-learning course. Database coverage depends on selecting the optional post-OOP capstone; it is not evidence that every CS1 adopter teaches SQL. The optional AI project extension is additional application practice, not a required outcome for the core route.

